- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmrbaoho4ysbv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Market regime \u2192 industry ETF leadership \u2192 strongest stocks inside the strongest industry ETF.\n\nVerdict\n\nYes, focusing on industry/sector ETFs breaking above/below moving averages is usually a cleaner signal than starting with individual stocks. Academic research found that a large part of individual stock momentum is explained by industry momentum: past winning industries tend to keep leading, and individual stock momentum becomes much less powerful after controlling for industry momentum.\n\nSo your idea is basically:\nFind the strongest \u201carmy\u201d first, then pick the strongest soldiers.\n\nThat is better than scanning thousands of stocks because industry ETFs filter out a lot of single-stock noise: earnings surprises, lawsuits, dilution, fraud, bad management, one-off news, etc.\n\nWhy the idea works\n\nWhen the market gets weak, institutions do not sell everything equally. They rotate. Money leaves weak groups and hides in stronger groups. If an ETF or stock refuses to break down while SPY/QQQ are dumping, that means buyers are absorbing supply.\n\nThe key signal is not just:\n\n\u201cThis stock is above the 50-day moving average.\u201d\n\nThe stronger signal is:\n\n\u201cThe market is weak, SPY is below short-term moving averages, but this industry ETF is still above its 50/100/200-day moving averages, its ETF/SPY ratio is rising, and its top stocks are holding up.\u201d\n\nThat is real relative strength.", "created": 1783467799924, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmqba6dkqrtvb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "To find very cheap stocks with huge upside potential, don\u2019t look only at a \u201clow price\u201d like $1, $3, or $5. A stock is cheap only if the business value is much higher than the market value.\n\nThe best metrics are these:\n\n1. Market cap vs opportunity\n\nThis is the first thing I check.\n\nA $3 stock with a $5 billion market cap may not be cheap.\nA $3 stock with a $100 million market cap could be cheap if the company has real assets, revenue, or a big catalyst.\n\nLook at:\n\nMarket cap\n= share price \u00d7 shares outstanding\n\nThen ask:\n\n\u201cCan this business realistically become worth 3x, 5x, or 10x more?\u201d\n\nExample:\n\nA company worth $200 million that could reasonably become worth $1 billion has 5x upside.\n\nA company already worth $10 billion needs to become $50 billion for the same 5x. Much harder.\n\n2. Enterprise value, not just market cap\n\nEnterprise value is often better than market cap because it includes debt and cash.\n\nEnterprise Value = Market Cap + Debt - Cash\n\nThis matters a lot with cheap stocks.\n\nExample:\n\nCompany A:\nMarket cap: $100M\nDebt: $400M\nCash: $20M\nEnterprise value: $480M\n\nThis is not as cheap as it looks.\n\nCompany B:\nMarket cap: $100M\nDebt: $0\nCash: $60M\nEnterprise value: $40M\n\nThis may be very cheap.\n\n3. Price-to-sales ratio\n\nFor small growth companies, P/S ratio is one of the most useful metrics.\n\nP/S = Market Cap \u00f7 Annual Revenue\n\nGeneral idea:\n\nP/S Ratio\tMeaning\nUnder 1\tPotentially cheap\n1\u20133\tReasonable depending on growth\n3\u201310\tNeeds strong growth\nOver 10\tUsually expensive unless elite growth\n\nBut you must compare it to the industry.\n\nA software company at 3x sales may be cheap.\nA low-margin retailer at 3x sales may be expensive.\n\nThe best setup is:\n\nLow P/S + fast revenue growth + improving margins\n\n4. Revenue growth\n\nHuge upside usually needs growth.\n\nLook for:\n\nRevenue growth year over year\n\n10\u201320%: decent\n20\u201350%: strong\n50%+: very strong\nDeclining revenue: dangerous unless turnaround\n\nBut growth alone is not enough. A company can grow revenue and still destroy shareholder value if losses are too big.\n\nBest combo:\n\nRevenue growing + losses shrinking\n\n5. Gross margin\n\nGross margin tells you if the business model has quality.\n\nGross Margin = Gross Profit \u00f7 Revenue\n\nHigh gross margins mean the company has room to become profitable.\n\nVe

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq9nunk0ivy5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This is actually a very sophisticated market concept, but the core idea is surprisingly simple.\n\nThink of it like a nightclub.\n\nBitcoin = the VIP section\nEthereum = the main dance floor\nAltcoins = the wild party in the back rooms\n\nMoney almost never goes directly from cash \u2192 random altcoins.\n\nInstead it usually flows:\n\nCash \u2192 Bitcoin \u2192 Ethereum \u2192 Altcoins\n\nThe author is saying that ETH/BTC is one of the earliest signals that the party is about to spread from Bitcoin into the rest of crypto.\n\nStep 1: What is ETH/BTC?\n\nETH/BTC is simply:\n\nBitcoin Price\nEthereum Price\n\t\u200b\n\n\nNot ETH/USD.\n\nNot BTC/USD.\n\nETH relative to Bitcoin.\n\nExample:\n\nBTC = $100,000\nETH = $2,000\n\nETH/BTC = 0.02\n\nLater:\n\nBTC = $110,000 (+10%)\nETH = $3,300 (+65%)\n\nETH/BTC = 0.03\n\nETH is outperforming Bitcoin.\n\nThe ratio is rising.\n\nThat's a huge clue.\n\nReal Life Example #1\n\nImagine 100 investors enter crypto.\n\nPhase 1:\n\nEverybody buys Bitcoin.\n\nBTC +50%\nETH +20%\nAlts flat\n\nNobody wants risk.\n\nThen investors get comfortable.\n\nThey say:\n\n\"Bitcoin already moved. What's next?\"\n\nNow they buy Ethereum.\n\nBTC +10%\nETH +40%\n\nETH/BTC explodes higher.\n\nThis is often the start of altseason.\n\nWhy ETH Leads\n\nEthereum is usually viewed as:\n\nSafer than most alts\nRiskier than Bitcoin\n\nSo it becomes the bridge.\n\nThink of it as:\n\nRisk Ladder\n\nCash\nTreasury Bills\nBitcoin\nEthereum\nSolana\nMid-cap alts\nMeme coins\n\nMoney climbs the ladder slowly.\n\nETH is the first rung above Bitcoin.\n\nWhat Does \"Bottoming and Ripping\" Mean?\n\nImagine ETH/BTC falling for 2 years.\n\nEveryone hates ETH.\n\nExample:\n\nETH/BTC\n\n0.08\n0.07\n0.06\n0.05\n0.04\n0.03\n\nThen suddenly:\n\n0.031\n0.034\n0.038\n0.045\n\nThat's the ratio bottoming and ripping.\n\nNot a little bounce.\n\nA powerful reversal.\n\nThe author believes those reversals often start major alt runs.\n\nHistorical Example\n\n2020\n\nBefore the huge altseason:\n\nETH/BTC stopped falling.\n\nThen ETH/BTC surged.\n\nAfter that:\n\nETH exploded\nSOL exploded\nADA exploded\nDOGE exploded\nDeFi exploded\n\nThe leadership rotated from BTC to ETH to everything else.\n\nWhat Is Leadership Rotation?\n\nLeadership means:\n\n\"What asset is attracting the most new money?\"\n\nSometimes:\n\nGold leads\n\nSometimes:\n\nTech stocks lead\n\nSometimes:\n\nBitcoin leads\n\nSometimes:\n\nEthereum leads\

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq8lde8rft4x", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES THE FED RAISING OR CUTTING INTEREST RATES AFFECT THE GLOBAL LIQUIDITY?\nThe Federal Reserve raising or cutting interest rates directly influences global liquidity\u2014the amount of money flowing through the world economy. Since the U.S. dollar is the dominant global currency, these moves ripple far beyond the U.S. Here\u2019s how it works, broken down simply:\n________________________________________\nFed Raising Interest Rates: Tightening the Spigot\nWhen the Fed hikes rates, it increases the cost of borrowing money in the U.S. This drains global liquidity in a few key ways:\n1.\tFewer Dollars Flowing: Higher rates mean U.S. banks and businesses lend less\u2014why borrow at 5% when it was 2%? Less lending shrinks the pool of dollars circulating, both domestically and globally, since U.S. credit often funds international trade and investment.\n2.\tStronger Dollar, Higher Costs: Rate hikes typically boost the DXY (dollar index) because investors flock to higher-yielding U.S. assets like Treasuries. A stronger dollar makes dollar-priced goods (oil, commodities) and dollar-denominated debt pricier for the rest of the world. Countries and companies with dollar debts need more local currency to pay up, squeezing their cash reserves and cutting liquidity.\n3.\tCapital Flows Back to the U.S.: Higher U.S. rates pull money out of riskier markets\u2014like emerging economies or global stocks\u2014as investors chase better returns in \u201csafe\u201d U.S. bonds. This outflow dries up liquidity in places like Brazil or India, where dollars were fueling growth.\n4.\tRisk-Off Mode: Expensive borrowing cools speculative bets. Investors dump stocks, crypto, and junk bonds for cash or Treasuries, reducing the money sloshing into riskier global assets. It\u2019s like the party\u2019s over\u2014everyone\u2019s hoarding instead of spending.\nReal Example: In 2022, the Fed raised rates from near 0% to 4.5% to fight inflation. The DXY jumped from 95 to 114, emerging market currencies tanked (e.g., India\u2019s rupee hit record lows), and global liquidity tightened\u2014Bitcoin crashed from $47,000 to $16,000, and stocks took a 20%+ hit.\n________________________________________\nFed Cutting Interest Rates: Opening the Floodgates\nWhen the Fed lowers rates, it makes borrowing cheaper, pumping liquidity into the global system. Here\u2019s how:\n1.\tMore Dollars Flowing: Lower rates spur U.S. banks and firms to borrow

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq8lde8rhffo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHICH HURT RISK ASSETS THE MOST FED HIKING RATES OR QT?\nWhen it comes to hurting risk assets\u2014like stocks, crypto, tech companies, or emerging markets\u2014both Fed rate hikes and quantitative tightening (QT) can deliver a beating, but QT tends to hit harder, especially in extreme doses. Here\u2019s why, broken down clearly:\n________________________________________\nFed Hiking Rates: The Slow Bleed\nRaising interest rates increases borrowing costs and tightens financial conditions. It\u2019s a steady punch to risk assets:\n1.\tHigher Borrowing Costs: Rate hikes make loans pricier for companies and investors. Growth stocks (like tech) and crypto projects, which often rely on cheap debt, get squeezed as funding dries up.\n2.\tStronger Dollar: Hikes boost the DXY (dollar index) as investors chase higher U.S. yields. A pricier dollar slams dollar-priced assets\u2014Bitcoin drops, emerging market stocks stumble\u2014since they\u2019re costlier for global buyers.\n3.\tRisk-Off Shift: Higher rates signal the Fed\u2019s slamming the brakes, spooking investors. They ditch speculative bets (Nasdaq, meme coins) for safer stuff like bonds, dragging risk asset prices down.\nDamage Level: Rate hikes hurt consistently but gradually. In 2022, the Fed\u2019s hikes from 0% to 4.5% tanked the S&P 500 by 20% and Bitcoin by 60%+. It\u2019s painful, but the pain builds over months as markets adjust.\nWhy It\u2019s Limited: If hikes are telegraphed (like 2022\u2019s cycle), markets brace for it. And if rates start low, early hikes don\u2019t sting as much\u20140% to 1% isn\u2019t a death blow.\n________________________________________\nQuantitative Tightening (QT): The Gut Punch\nQT is when the Fed shrinks its balance sheet, sucking cash out by selling bonds or letting them mature. It\u2019s a sharper blow to risk assets:\n1.\tLiquidity Vacuum: QT yanks dollars out of the system\u2014$50 billion a month in 2022, for example. Risk assets thrive on excess cash; when it vanishes, stocks, crypto, and junk bonds crater fast as banks and funds hoard what\u2019s left.\n2.\tYield Spike: QT drives up bond yields (fewer buyers = lower prices). Investors ditch riskier plays for Treasuries offering 4%+ returns, triggering outflows from equities and emerging markets. It\u2019s a stampede to safety.\n3.\tDollar Surge + Global Crunch: QT turbocharges the DXY\u2014fewer dollars = scarcity. This crushes commodity prices and slams countr

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq8lde8rs9c3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES THE FED QE OR QT AFFECTS GLOBAL LIQUIDITY?\nThe Federal Reserve\u2019s actions\u2014quantitative easing (QE) or quantitative tightening (QT)\u2014have a massive impact on global liquidity, which is basically the amount of money sloshing around in the world economy. Here\u2019s how each works and why it matters, explained simply:\nQuantitative Easing (QE): Flooding the System\nQE is when the Fed \u201cprints money\u201d (digitally) to buy assets like U.S. Treasuries or mortgage-backed securities from banks. This pumps cash into the financial system. Here\u2019s how it ripples globally:\n1.\tMore Dollars, More Liquidity: The Fed\u2019s purchases inject billions\u2014or trillions\u2014of dollars into U.S. banks. Those banks then lend, invest, or park that cash elsewhere, boosting the supply of dollars worldwide. Since the dollar\u2019s the global reserve currency, this floods international markets with liquidity.\n2.\tLower U.S. Yields, Global Hunt for Returns: QE pushes down U.S. interest rates (bond yields drop when prices rise). Investors\u2014pension funds, hedge funds, sovereign wealth funds\u2014chase higher returns elsewhere, pouring cash into foreign stocks, bonds, or emerging markets. This amplifies liquidity beyond U.S. borders.\n3.\tWeaker Dollar, Hotter Markets: QE often weakens the DXY (dollar index) because more dollars = less scarcity. A cheaper dollar makes commodities (oil, metals) and assets (stocks, crypto) more affordable globally, sparking risk-on buying and juicing liquidity further.\n4.\tCarry Trade Fuel: Low U.S. rates from QE make borrowing dollars cheap. Investors borrow in dollars, convert to higher-yielding currencies (like Brazilian real or Turkish lira), and invest there. This spreads liquidity but also risks blowups if the dollar reverses.\nReal Example: Post-2008, the Fed\u2019s QE rounds (2008-2014) pumped over $4 trillion into the system. Global liquidity soared\u2014emerging market stocks rallied, commodity prices spiked (oil hit $100+), and even Bitcoin got its early legs as cheap money flowed everywhere.\n________________________________________\nQuantitative Tightening (QT): Draining the System\nQT is the opposite\u2014 the Fed shrinks its balance sheet by selling bonds or letting them mature without reinvesting the proceeds. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq8lde8r4w2h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHY DOES DXY DUMPING PUMPS EQUITIES AND ALL ASSETS ESPECIALLY RISK ASSETS?\nWhen the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) \"dumps\"\u2014meaning the dollar weakens against major currencies like the euro, yen, or pound\u2014it tends to lift equities (stocks) and other assets, especially riskier ones like tech stocks, crypto, or emerging market investments. Here\u2019s why this happens, laid out simply:\n1. Cheaper for Foreign Investors\nA weaker dollar makes U.S. assets\u2014like stocks or real estate\u2014less expensive for investors holding stronger foreign currencies. Picture a Japanese investor with yen: if the dollar drops, their yen buys more dollars, so grabbing shares of Nvidia or Tesla becomes a bargain. This spurs buying, pushing equity prices up.\n2. Debt Relief for Borrowers\nLots of global debt (especially in emerging markets) is in dollars. When the DXY falls, those countries or companies need less of their local currency (now relatively stronger) to pay off dollar-denominated loans. This eases financial pressure, lowers default risks, and boosts confidence in riskier investments like stocks or high-yield bonds.\n3. Commodities Get a Boost\nA weaker dollar makes dollar-priced commodities\u2014like oil, gold, or copper\u2014cheaper for non-U.S. buyers. Demand rises, prices climb, and commodity-linked stocks (energy, mining, materials) rally. Since equities often ride broader economic vibes, this lifts the whole market, especially growth-oriented sectors.\n4. Risk-On Vibe Takes Over\nA dumping DXY often signals a \u201crisk-on\u201d mood. Investors ditch safe havens like the dollar or Treasuries and pile into riskier assets\u2014stocks, crypto, small-caps\u2014hunting for higher returns. This is especially true if the dollar\u2019s weakening because the Fed\u2019s cutting rates or pumping money, making cash cheap and plentiful again.\n5. U.S. Companies Cash In\nBig U.S. multinationals\u2014like Microsoft or Pepsi\u2014earn heaps overseas. A weaker dollar means those foreign profits (in euros, yen, etc.) convert to more USD, juicing their earnings. Stronger profits = higher stock prices, which lifts indexes like the Nasdaq or Dow and fuels the rally.\nWhy Risk Assets Shine Brightest\nRisk assets\u2014tech stocks, Bitcoin, meme coins\u2014thrive when money\u2019s loose and optimism\u2019s high. Dumping prices. This leads to capitulations and market bottoms.\nA swap with the Fed is a temporary agreement between the Federal Reserve and a foreign central bank to exchange currencies. This allows a foreign central bank to obtain U.S. dollars from the Fed in exchange for an equivalent amount of its own currency, based on the market exchange rate at the time of the transaction. The Fed uses swap lines to promote liquidity in global money markets and to minimize the risk that strains in foreign markets could spread to the U.S. market. Swap lines can also be used to support foreign economies during times of financial stress. To initiate a swap, a foreign central bank would contact the New York Fed and request to draw on its swap line. The two central banks would then agree on the amount of currency to be exchanged and the terms of the swap, including the interest rate to be charged. Once the swap is agreed upon, the foreign central bank would sell its own currency to the Fed in exchange for U.S. dollars. The foreign central bank would then lend the U.S. dollars to its domestic banks, which could then use the dollars to make loans to businesses and consumers.\nThe swap would be reversed at a predetermined date, usually within three months. At that time, the foreign central bank would return the U.S. dollars to the Fed in exchange for its own currency. Here is a simplified example of how a swap with the Fed might work: 1-The Bank of Canada (BoC) needs U.S. dollars to lend to its domestic banks.\n2-The BoC contacts the New York Fed and requests to draw on its swap line. 3-The two central banks agree to swap $1 billion of U.S. dollars for $1 billion of Canadian dollars.\n4-The BoC sells $1 billion of Canadian dollars to the Fed in exchange for U.S. dollars. 5-The BoC then lends the U.S. dollars to its domes

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq8fusm0tzou", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In a reverse repo, the Fed takes cash from banks (or other counterparties) in exchange for securities and agrees to return the cash (plus a small interest payment) later. This process removes cash from the financial system temporarily, reducing liquidity.\nThe Fed uses reverse repos to control excess liquidity. For example, if banks have too much cash (say, from stimulus programs or low borrowing demand), the Fed can use reverse repos to \u201csoak up\u201d some of that cash, preventing it from flooding the market and potentially causing inflation or destabilizing interest rates.\nThe \"Wednesday Level\" of reverse repos shows how much cash the Fed has pulled out of the system on that day. A higher face value of securities in reverse repos means more cash has been removed, tightening liquidity. A lower value means less cash is being removed, leaving more liquidity in the system.", "created": 1781118311621, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 53/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 94/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60nxsf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Signal: When the market relies on just a handful of giants, it\u2019s usually late in the cycle \u2014 think of it as the last push before weakness spreads everywhere.", "created": 1780966147545, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 95/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60klnt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why it matters: These \u201cmega-caps\u201d have huge index weights, so they can make the index look fine even if 80% of stocks are falling.", "created": 1780966147544, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 96/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60xa9w", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What it means: Sometimes the overall index (like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq) looks strong, but that\u2019s only because a few giant companies (Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, etc.) are carrying all the weight.", "created": 1780966147543, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 97/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60fy4q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why it matters: A healthy bull market has lots of stocks going up together. When only a few lead and the majority lag, it\u2019s often a sign that momentum is fading and risk is building.", "created": 1780966147541, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 98/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e608q31", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If the S&P 500 goes up but only a few stocks are actually hitting new highs, that means the rally is narrow and weak under the surface.", "created": 1780966147540, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 99/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60u5t8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What it means: Breadth = how many stocks are participating in a rally.", "created": 1780966147539, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 100/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e602eqm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Got it \u2014 let me break those down in plain language and connect the dots for you:", "created": 1780966147537, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 101/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60hh0f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "SINGS OF TOP: Equity Market Internals", "created": 1780966147530, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 102/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e603dag", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Crashes = liquidity + leverage unwinds.Almost every major global meltdown began with a liquidity shortage in the dollar system.", "created": 1780966147529, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 103/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60e8qg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "One signal alone \u2260 panic.But when multiple flash red (e.g., weak Treasury auctions + dollar shortage + VIX spike), the odds of a U.S. stock market dump rise sharply.", "created": 1780966147528, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 104/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60p68p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udd11 How Traders Use These Signals", "created": 1780966147527, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 105/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60r2od", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Rising credit default swaps on major banks = loss of confidence in financial stability.", "created": 1780966147526, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 106/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60dkwi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Europe\u2019s version \u2014 rising stress here often transmits to the U.S.", "created": 1780966147524, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 107/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60bohk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "ECB CISS (Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress)", "created": 1780966147523, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 108/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e6004zx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A composite of yield spreads, volatility, and funding stress \u2014 when it spikes, global markets often dump.", "created": 1780966147522, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 109/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60t758", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "OFR Financial Stress Index (FSI)", "created": 1780966147521, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 110/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60qwf2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Watch Turkish lira, Argentine peso, and Asian currencies. Weakness here often precedes broader turmoil.", "created": 1780966147519, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 111/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60t1k8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Oil, copper, and shipping rates often fall before recessions/crashes.", "created": 1780966147517, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 112/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60p7r2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A fast-rising dollar strains emerging markets and global trade.", "created": 1780966147515, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 113/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60dead", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Surging leverage (borrowed money in markets) precedes crashes \u2014 forced deleveraging accelerates dumps.", "created": 1780966147512, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 114/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60o2hu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Margin debt rising / then collapsing", "created": 1780966147511, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 115/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e6019wa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If only a handful of tech giants hold up indexes while everything else sells off, it\u2019s a late-cycle warning.", "created": 1780966147510, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 116/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e607d0o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Market rising but fewer stocks making new highs = unhealthy rally.", "created": 1780966147508, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 117/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60j1w8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When spreads blow out, it means investors expect defaults.", "created": 1780966147505, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 118/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e601z19", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Look at high-yield bond spreads (ICE BofA HY Index).", "created": 1780966147504, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 119/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60jmbz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A jump in VIX > 30 signals panic hedging.", "created": 1780966147501, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 120/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60r9y6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "VIX (Volatility Index) spikes", "created": 1780966147500, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 121/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e6054g0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But when the curve suddenly steepens after inversion, it often signals a credit crisis brewing.", "created": 1780966147498, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 122/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60e5pd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Inversions (short-term > long-term yields) are classic recession warnings.", "created": 1780966147497, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 123/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e60tizz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yield curve inversion / re-steepening", "created": 1780966147496, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 124/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z69uc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Lower demand in auctions means investors are backing away from Treasuries.", "created": 1780966147494, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 125/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zkxji", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bid-to-Cover ratio falling", "created": 1780966147493, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 126/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zdj8q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A weak Treasury auction with a big \u201ctail\u201d shows buyers demand higher yields \u2192 signals stress in U.S. government funding.", "created": 1780966147492, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 127/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z3vzt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Auction \u201ctails\u201d (high yield vs. expected yield spread)", "created": 1780966147491, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 128/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5znf56", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If cash drains from the Fed\u2019s RRP facility quickly, markets lose a cushion of liquidity.", "created": 1780966147489, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 129/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zm49q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Reverse Repo (RRP) balance plunges", "created": 1780966147488, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 130/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zqqir", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When dollar funding outside the U.S. (in Europe, Japan) becomes expensive, it signals global dollar shortage.", "created": 1780966147487, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 131/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zu8iv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cross-currency basis widening", "created": 1780966147486, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 132/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z3shd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Example: Sept 2019 repo spike foreshadowed later liquidity fragility.", "created": 1780966147485, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 133/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zb83z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If overnight funding costs (repo rates, SOFR) suddenly jump, it signals a shortage of cash/liquidity.", "created": 1780966147484, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 134/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zmewc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "SOFR spikes / Repo market stress", "created": 1780966147483, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 135/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zuddi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udc49 That\u2019s why whenever CNBC says \u201cDow is plunging,\u201d traders in Tokyo, London, Frankfurt, and S\u00e3o Paulo are already preparing for chaos.", "created": 1780966147479, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 136/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z2ku8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Psychological contagion amplifies.Panic in the U.S. is read as \u201cglobal crisis,\u201d so selling becomes worldwide.", "created": 1780966147478, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 137/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z18vx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Liquidity crunch spreads globally.Dollar shortages and forced selling make other markets collapse.", "created": 1780966147477, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 138/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z4vm2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "U.S. leads \u2192 the world follows.Whenever Wall Street sells off, the rest of the world mirrors it.", "created": 1780966147476, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 139/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zzfht", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udd11 Pattern Across All Crashes", "created": 1780966147475, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 140/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zsz10", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The U.S. dollar surged to a 20-year high, exporting financial stress globally.", "created": 1780966147474, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 141/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zmvow", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Emerging markets (like Turkey, Argentina, Pakistan) suffered currency collapses.", "created": 1780966147473, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 142/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z94sl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Europe fell into an energy + inflation crisis.", "created": 1780966147472, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 143/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z73fq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cause: Rising yields crushed valuations of tech and growth stocks.", "created": 1780966147471, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 144/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zy7w2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What happened in the U.S.:Inflation hit 40-year highs; the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates aggressively. Nasdaq fell ~33% in 2022.", "created": 1780966147470, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 145/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zrtz1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Governments and central banks launched trillions in stimulus to stabilize the system.", "created": 1780966147468, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 146/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zix58", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Oil prices went negative for the first time ever in April 2020.", "created": 1780966147467, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 147/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zui72", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Emerging markets were devastated by capital flight and collapsing commodity demand.", "created": 1780966147466, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 148/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z5ce2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "European stocks dropped over 30%.", "created": 1780966147465, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 149/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zen3z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cause: Sudden halt in global economy, uncertainty, panic.", "created": 1780966147464, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 150/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z215i", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What happened in the U.S.:In March 2020, as COVID spread, the S&P 500 plunged 34% in just 33 days \u2014 the fastest bear market in history.", "created": 1780966147463, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 151/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z989n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This was the worst synchronized global crash since the Great Depression.", "created": 1780966147461, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 152/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z1718", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global trade froze, commodity prices collapsed, emerging markets\u2019 currencies crashed.", "created": 1780966147460, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 153/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zpc3f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Asian stock markets plunged (Nikkei down 42% in 2008).", "created": 1780966147459, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 154/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zlzqy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "European banks (like UBS, Deutsche Bank, Barclays) faced collapse.", "created": 1780966147458, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 155/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zkclt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cause: Subprime mortgage crisis \u2192 housing bubble burst \u2192 toxic financial derivatives \u2192 banking crisis.", "created": 1780966147457, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 156/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zvfzy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What happened in the U.S.:The collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 triggered panic selling across Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell ~57% from peak to trough.", "created": 1780966147456, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 157/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zszqv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global investors pulled money from risky assets, crushing emerging markets too.", "created": 1780966147454, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 158/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z1u8m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Telecom stocks in Europe (like Deutsche Telekom) lost trillions in value.", "created": 1780966147453, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 159/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ztfyt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Tech-heavy markets in Europe and Asia crashed in sympathy.", "created": 1780966147452, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 160/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zlld9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cause: Overhyped internet companies with no profits, fueled by speculation.", "created": 1780966147451, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 161/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zso5l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What happened in the U.S.:Tech stocks, especially Nasdaq, collapsed after the internet bubble burst. Nasdaq fell almost 80% from its peak.", "created": 1780966147450, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 162/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zbsgx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The crash was so synchronized that it proved how interconnected global markets had become.", "created": 1780966147448, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 163/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z53r0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Markets from Hong Kong to Australia went into panic.", "created": 1780966147447, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 164/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zfpxf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "London\u2019s FTSE 100 lost 26% in two days.", "created": 1780966147446, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 165/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z3dnb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cause: Program trading (early computer-driven sell orders), rising interest rates, and overvaluation.", "created": 1780966147444, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 166/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zi3f3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What happened in the U.S.:On October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average crashed 22% in a single day \u2014 the biggest one-day percentage drop in history.", "created": 1780966147443, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 167/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5z8xsn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Algorithms and high-frequency trading accelerate this contagion across time zones (Asia markets open after U.S. close, then Europe, then back to U.S.).", "created": 1780966147438, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 168/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zll7f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Traders worldwide copy U.S. selling, creating a herd effect.", "created": 1780966147437, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 169/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zbelu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A big dump in the U.S. is seen as a sign of global recession, financial crisis, or systemic risk.", "created": 1780966147436, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 170/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zog62", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This feedback loop worsens the global market turmoil.", "created": 1780966147434, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 171/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5zacic", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This strengthens the dollar, hurting other countries\u2019 currencies and making their debt burdens heavier (especially emerging markets with dollar-denominated debt).", "created": 1780966147433, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 172/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yc6hu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In sell-offs, global investors rush to U.S. dollars for safety (the world\u2019s reserve currency).", "created": 1780966147431, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 173/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yki21", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Liquidity dries up everywhere, amplifying volatility.", "created": 1780966147429, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 174/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y39n3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Selling is not limited to U.S. stocks\u2014it spreads to bonds, commodities, crypto, and foreign equities.", "created": 1780966147428, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 175/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yhv3z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A \u201cdump\u201d often triggers margin calls (when leveraged investors must sell assets to cover losses).", "created": 1780966147427, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 176/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yexa8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This creates a chain reaction across Europe, Asia, and emerging markets.", "created": 1780966147425, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 177/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yiqzg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When prices collapse, these investors withdraw capital, leading to forced selling in other regions to cover margin calls or rebalance portfolios.", "created": 1780966147424, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 178/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yi10g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "International investors (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, hedge funds) hold huge stakes in U.S. equities.", "created": 1780966147423, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 179/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yd5b9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A sharp U.S. sell-off signals global investors that risk is rising everywhere, triggering worldwide panic selling.", "created": 1780966147421, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 180/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yam0n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Big U.S. indexes like the S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq are seen as benchmarks for global risk appetite.", "created": 1780966147420, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 181/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yicft", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The U.S. stock market (NYSE + NASDAQ) is the largest in the world, accounting for ~40% of global equity market value.", "created": 1780966147419, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 182/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yo6l2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In markets, a \u201cdump\u201d usually means a sudden, large, and rapid sell-off of stocks. When it happens in the U.S. stock market, it often sends shockwaves through all other global stock markets. Here\u2019s why:", "created": 1780966147417, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 183/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ymypa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "what is dump in us stock market causes chaos in all global stock markets?", "created": 1780966147416, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 184/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y241s", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "MEAN REVERSION STRATEGY DON\u2019T WORK IN PANIC AND CHAOS AND CRISIS BCS MARKETS JUST KEEP FALLING NONSTOP WITH NO RECOVERY. ESSENTIALLY BREAKING THE TRADITIONAL MEAN REVERSION STRATEGY.", "created": 1780966147415, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 185/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yfkuv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE EASIST WAY TO APPLY THE MEAN REVERSION STARTEGY IS BY USING THE BOLLINGER BAND AND WAITING FOR THE STOCK TO GET BACK TO THE MEAN AFTER HITTING THE BAND.", "created": 1780966147414, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 186/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yt7re", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES FINANCIAL CRISIS GET BIGGER AND CONTAGIOUS? AS THE US STOCK MARKET CRASH, PANIC SPREADS LIKE WILDFIRE. THE GLOBAL ECONOMY BUCKLES UNDER THE WEIGHT OF FEAR. JAPAN, TAIWAN AND SOUTH KOREA AND ALL EXPORTING COUNTRIES WHOSE ECONOMY RELIES ON EXPORTS. BUT AS AMERICAN AND WESTEN DEMAND CRUMBLES, JAPAN\u2019S AND ALL EXPORTING COUNTRIES CORPS ARE IN FREEFALL AS EARNINGS GET DECIMATED, FORWARD EARNINGS COLLAPSE. FACTORIES CUT PRODUCTION AND START LAYING OFF WORKERS. WORKERS JUST LOSING THEIR JOB STOP SPENDING AND START SAVING FOR A RAING DAY.", "created": 1780966147413, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 187/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ymov0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "CHEAP CREDIT AND RECKLESS SPECULATION ALWAYS FUEL AN ILLUSION OF ENDLESS GROWTH AND A FORVER STOCK PRICE INCREASE. BUT EVENTUALLY THE TRUTH AND THE REAL STATE OF THE ECONOMY BECOMES IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE.", "created": 1780966147412, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 188/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y3mit", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN PANICS AND CRISIS THE MARKET DOESN\u2019T CARE BUT IT WILL SOON.", "created": 1780966147411, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 189/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ynf7i", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN CRISIS AND PANICS THE BEST STRATEGY IS TO BUY IN FEAR AND WAIT FOR RATIONALITY TO RETURN.", "created": 1780966147410, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 190/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yrb0p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE MEAN REVERSION STRATEGY IS WHAT SEPERATES PROFESSIONAL TRADERS FROM NEWBIES. NEWBIES DON\u2019T UTILIZE THE MEAN REVERSION STRATEGY AND ITS BASED ON THE CONCEPT WHERE IF THE PRICE DEVIATES TOO FAR AWAY FROM ITS AVERAGE PRICE WHICH IS THE MOVING AVERAGE THEN IT WILL AT SOME POINT REVERT BACK ITS MEAN OT TO IT AVERAGE PRICE OR MA OVER A TIME PERIOD.", "created": 1780966147409, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 191/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y5ah8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "MOVING AVERAGES: they measure the average performance of a stock over a set number of days, so they generally serve as a trend indicator or trend tracker. For ex: if a stock price is above a MA so hence that it\u2019s in an up trend. If the stock price is below the moving average that suggests that the stock is in a down trend. BUT ITS NOT ONLY THE MOVING AVERAGES THAT SUCCESSFUL TRADERS LOOK AT. THEY FOCUS ON INDENTIFYING AND CAPITALIZING ON SIGNIFICANT PRICE DEVIATIONS FROM THE MA. IT\u2019S ABOUT HOW MUCH PRICES MOVE AWAY FROM THE MA. THEY SPECIFICALLY USE A SPECIFIC % THRESHOLD TO DETERMINE AN ENTRY OR EXIT PRICE. FOR THEIR TRADE. THEY USUALLY FOCUS ON 20 DAY MA, 25MA OR 50 DAY MA.", "created": 1780966147408, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 192/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ye1kc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "SUCCESSFUL INVESTORS HAVE A VERY SIMPLE, YET VERY VERY POWERFUL RULE: ONLY BUY STOCKS THAT ARE GOING UP. SPECIFICALLY, ONLY BUY STOCKS THAT ARE SHOWING STRENGTH AND HAVE A CLEAR UPWARD DIRECTION. AT THE CORE OF THIS STRATEGY IS: MOVING AVERAGES AND MEAN REVERSION.", "created": 1780966147407, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 193/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ylg8d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "TREND FOLLOW STRATEGY WITHIN SECTORS: YOU CHECK THE STOCK MKT ACROSS THE SECTORS. FOR EX: IN THE AVIATION SECTOR, ONCE MAJOR AVIATION STOCKS GAIN MOMENTUM AND START RALLYING, YOU LOOK FOR ANY OTHER AVIATION STOCK THAT STILL LAGGING BEHIND AND HASN\u2019T RALLIED YET. ANY STOCK THAT HASN\u2019T JOINED THE INITIAL BULL RALLY YET.", "created": 1780966147406, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 194/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yulou", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN FINANCIAL CRISIS LOWPRICES STOCKS GET WIPED EVEN MORE OVERNIGHT. THIS ISNT NORMAL SELLING, IT\u2019S OUTRIGHT PANIC.", "created": 1780966147405, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 195/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yyds4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN NORMAL TIMES WHEN STOCKS DROP TOO FAR AND TOO FAST, THEY ALMOST ALWAYS BOUNCE BACK. (THIS DOESN\u2019T WORK IN FINANCIAL CRISIS)", "created": 1780966147404, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 196/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ytkxe", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN A BIG CRASH, THERE IS ALWAYS MOMENTS OF IRRATIONAL PANIC.", "created": 1780966147403, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 197/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yqlld", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "STOCKS DON\u2019T FALL IN A STRAIGHT LINE.", "created": 1780966147402, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 198/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y2kex", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE QUESTION YOU SHOULD ALWAYS ASK YOURSELF: IF EVERYONE IS SELLING THEN WHO IS BUYING?", "created": 1780966147401, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 199/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ynsuw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udc49 The best investors treat risk assets like fire: powerful and useful if controlled, but devastating if mishandled.", "created": 1780966147400, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 200/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yr7bt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Expect the unexpected\u2014tail risks are more common than most models suggest.", "created": 1780966147399, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 201/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yhy27", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Study past bear markets (2000, 2008, 2020, 2022 tightening cycle) to understand how risk assets behave.", "created": 1780966147398, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 202/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ytoxv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Remember Buffett\u2019s rule: \u201cDon\u2019t lose money.\u201d Rule 2: \u201cDon\u2019t forget rule 1.\u201d", "created": 1780966147396, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 203/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y1fyc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Never risk permanent loss of capital on a single trade or asset.", "created": 1780966147395, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 204/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ycvdp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Patience and discipline are edge multipliers.", "created": 1780966147393, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 205/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yvn26", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Avoid overtrading\u2014activity \u2260 performance.", "created": 1780966147392, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 206/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yltdz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Avoid crowded trades where upside is limited but downside is catastrophic.", "created": 1780966147390, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 207/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yuq12", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Examples: distressed assets at liquidation value, deep out-of-the-money options with limited risk, or equities with cash balances covering most of market cap.", "created": 1780966147389, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 208/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ybcef", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Track macro indicators: yield curve, credit spreads, volatility index (VIX), and funding markets (SOFR, repo, RRP balances).", "created": 1780966147387, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 209/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ysto0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bear markets and crises often follow tightening liquidity (rising rates, shrinking balance sheets).", "created": 1780966147386, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 210/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yj0ig", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk assets perform best when liquidity is abundant (falling rates, expanding credit).", "created": 1780966147385, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 211/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y9k1k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Taking small losses early is far cheaper than holding through a collapse.", "created": 1780966147383, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 212/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y1fxh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Don\u2019t fall in love with a position\u2014the market doesn\u2019t care about your cost basis.", "created": 1780966147382, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 213/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5yfn5e", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Use leverage sparingly, if at all\u2014especially in volatile or opaque markets.", "created": 1780966147380, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 214/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ycxeh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Margin debt or options can wipe you out faster than fundamentals can save you.", "created": 1780966147379, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 215/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y1l1u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Avoid overexposure to illiquid assets if you might need cash within 12\u201324 months.", "created": 1780966147377, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 216/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5ylmlr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Keep a cash buffer (5\u201320%) for unexpected opportunities or emergencies.", "created": 1780966147376, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 217/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5y1jtz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Diversification won\u2019t eliminate risk, but it reduces the chance of catastrophic loss.", "created": 1780966147374, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 218/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xsvcp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Here are some of the most important investment principles and advice when dealing with risk assets (stocks, high-yield bonds, crypto, emerging markets, etc.):", "created": 1780966147370, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 219/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xinx0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bottom line: 4-week and 8-week bill auctions are the first place a liquidity crunch will show up. Watch for high tails, collapsing bid-to-cover, and surging dealer allotments there \u2014 those precede repo spikes and broader market stress by days to weeks. If you want, I can give you a table of historical bill auction stress events that occurred before major financial crises so you can use them as benchmarks for current monitoring. That would let you spot a 2008-style or 2020-style liquidity freeze early.", "created": 1780966147369, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 220/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xk6cn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What to look for in these auctions If any of these appear in short-bill auctions, it\u2019s a big red flag: High Tail \u2014 Actual high yield is way above the expected/when-issued yield. Low Bid-to-Cover \u2014 Drops below ~2.5 for bills or ~2.0 for notes/bonds. Weak Indirect Bidding \u2014 Foreign central banks pulling back. Primary Dealer Take-Down Spike \u2014 Dealers forced to absorb unwanted supply. Huge Spread Between High and Low Yield \u2014 Indicates volatile or nervous bidding.", "created": 1780966147368, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 221/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x6jjh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Auction types to monitor in order of earliest signal PriorityMaturity / TypeWhy it\u2019s early warningHistorical examples#14-week T-billPurest liquidity gauge; smallest duration riskSept 2019 repo crisis, March 2020 COVID shock#28-week T-billSame as 4-week but slightly less sensitiveLate 2007 pre-crisis stress#313-week T-billStill liquidity-heavy; can show funding rollover stressAug 2007 BNP freeze#42-year noteFirst coupon auction to show investor rate fearsSummer 2007\u20132008 before Lehman#530-year bondLate-cycle stress indicator; signals deep credit risk aversion2011 U.S. downgrade, debt ceiling episodes", "created": 1780966147367, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 222/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xoyud", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why short-term bill auctions are the earliest canary Bills = pure liquidity instruments 4-week and 8-week bills are the closest thing to \u201ccash\u201d in the financial system. Large banks, money-market funds, and collateralized lending markets use them heavily for repo and short-term funding. Liquidity stress shows up here first If dealers or money markets start demanding much higher yields to buy these, it\u2019s often because: They need cash urgently and are less willing to tie it up in bills. There\u2019s collateral hoarding in repo markets (similar to 2008 and September 2019 repo spike). Crisis progression often follows: Bill auction stress \u2192 Repo rate spikes \u2192 Broader bond market stress \u2192 Stock sell-off.", "created": 1780966147366, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 223/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xf1dl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If you\u2019re looking for the earliest warning of a liquidity crunch or impending financial crisis from U.S. Treasury auction results, you\u2019d want to watch the shortest-maturity auctions \u2014 particularly 4-week and 8-week T-bill auctions \u2014 before anything else. Here\u2019s why:", "created": 1780966147365, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 224/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xef9g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "From all the treasury auction which one would show liquidity crunch and financial crisis first?", "created": 1780966147364, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 225/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xeyht", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Buffett\u2019s 1999 message was precisely that secular bull or bear markets are shaped by the discount rate (i.e., interest rates) and corporate profitability, rather than growth in GDP alone. It\u2019s fair to say he elevated interest rates as the central lever\u2014although GDP and earnings trends still play a foundational role.", "created": 1780966147363, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 226/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xpvwo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "He noted that profits rebounded to 6%, helping fuel the bull market", "created": 1780966147362, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 227/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x9ax2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Profitability share of GDP matters", "created": 1780966147361, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 228/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x5fn7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "GDP supports earnings/profits and remains foundational\u2014just not the switching mechanism", "created": 1780966147360, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 229/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xu0k2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "He emphasized interest rates and valuations over GDP in explaining long-term market trends", "created": 1780966147358, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 230/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xi7fj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Buffet said secular markets are driven by interest rates\u2014not GDP", "created": 1780966147357, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 231/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x2520", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But not literally \u201call.\u201d GDP growth still matters\u2014because earnings and dividends ultimately depend on economic output. Buffett included profitability trends in the analysis, and GDP figures help frame those. However, in the context of switching between long bull and bear markets, interest rates and discounting are the primary drivers.", "created": 1780966147356, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 232/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xgc57", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Buffett\u2019s core point: Secular market regimes (bull or bear) are driven more by interest-rate trends and profitability than by raw GDP growth. GDP growth alone, no matter how robust, doesn\u2019t guarantee rising valuations if the discount rate (i.e., interest rates) remains high.", "created": 1780966147355, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 233/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xaxiv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So: \u201cIt\u2019s all interest rates and not GDP\u201d\u2014is that accurate?", "created": 1780966147353, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 234/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x5d69", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Buffett also argued that unless you assume either faster GDP growth, significantly higher corporate profits as a percentage of GDP, or further dramatic declines in interest rates\u2014none of which he believed were sustainable\u2014you shouldn\u2019t expect double\u2011digit, let alone 22%, annual returns.", "created": 1780966147352, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 235/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xqexf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "He stressed that interest rates exert a gravitational pull on valuations: higher rates demand higher returns, pushing prices down; conversely, falling rates boost present valuations.", "created": 1780966147351, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 236/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xgbf9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Buffett stated: \u201cAs is so typical, investors projected out into the future what they were seeing. \u2026 They were projecting high interest rates, they were projecting low profits, and they were therefore valuing the Dow at a level that was the same as 17 years earlier, even though GDP had nearly quintupled.\u201d", "created": 1780966147350, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 237/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x6e69", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1981\u20131998 (secular bull): With declining interest rates and recovering corporate profitability (profits as a share of GDP rising to around 6%), the market soared", "created": 1780966147349, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 238/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x1oku", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1964\u20131981 (secular bear): GDP and corporate profits rose dramatically, yet the Dow stagnated for 17 years.", "created": 1780966147348, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 239/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xyfos", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What Buffett Actually Said in 1999: In the article, Buffett contrasts two distinct 17\u2011year periods:", "created": 1780966147347, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 240/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x64l2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Warren Buffett article in November 1999 (for Fortune magazine) titled \u201cMr. Buffett on the Stock Market.\u201d In this article, he explicitly explained that long-term secular bull and bear markets are primarily driven by interest-rate dynamics\u2014not GDP growth. Let\u2019s take a closer look:", "created": 1780966147346, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 241/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x0141", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udccc In short: Buffett\u2019s statement is directionally true\u2014secular bull/bear markets are primarily a story of interest rates and discounting, not GDP growth. GDP growth tells you about the size of the pie, but interest rates tell you how much investors are willing to pay today for tomorrow\u2019s slice.", "created": 1780966147344, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 242/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x9u1s", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Structural factors like demographics, globalization, and technological change shape both earnings growth and the interest-rate environment.", "created": 1780966147343, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 243/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xwefw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Is it completely true? Not entirely. Interest rates are the dominant driver of long, secular market regimes, but: Earnings and productivity growth still matter over the long run. Low rates can\u2019t create lasting bull markets if earnings collapse. Inflation expectations are closely tied to rates, so you can\u2019t isolate them.", "created": 1780966147342, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 244/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xmdq0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2009\u20132021: Despite sluggish GDP, near-zero rates and QE fueled an enormous bull market.", "created": 1780966147341, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 245/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x0m32", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1982\u20131999: GDP growth was actually slower on average than in the 1950s\u201360s, but falling inflation and collapsing interest rates drove one of the greatest bull markets ever.", "created": 1780966147340, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 246/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x9zew", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Evidence: 1966\u20131982: U.S. GDP grew strongly, but stock returns were flat in nominal terms and negative after inflation. Why? Interest rates and inflation soared, depressing valuations.", "created": 1780966147339, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 247/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xeojn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Secular bull/bear cycles: Buffett highlighted how the 1982\u20131999 bull market coincided with falling interest rates (Volcker peak \u2192 Greenspan cuts), while the secular bear of the 1966\u20131982 period coincided with rising/stubbornly high rates and inflation.", "created": 1780966147338, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 248/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x9ck3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "GDP doesn\u2019t guarantee equity returns: An economy can grow quickly (higher GDP), but if interest rates are high, equity valuations may stagnate or decline. Conversely, modest GDP growth with ultra-low rates can produce huge bull markets (e.g., U.S. equities 2009\u20132021).", "created": 1780966147337, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 249/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5x0nz6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest rates determine valuations: Stock prices are the present value of future cash flows. When rates are low, the discount rate applied to earnings is lower, so valuations expand (P/E ratios rise). When rates are high, the discount rate is higher, so valuations compress (P/E ratios fall).", "created": 1780966147336, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 250/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xk53l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "You\u2019re right that Warren Buffett has emphasized interest rates many times, especially in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In his 1999 Fortune article (\u201cMr. Buffett on the Stock Market\u201d), he essentially argued that long-term secular bull and bear markets in equities are overwhelmingly driven by interest rates and the discount rate investors apply to future earnings\u2014not by GDP growth.", "created": 1780966147334, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 251/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x9e5xeezh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Warren buffet wrote an article in 1999 that said: \" you want to understand secular big long bull versus bear markets. IT'S ALL INTEREST RATES AND NOT GDP\".", "created": 1780966147333, "pinned": false, "source": "to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x99p5vodv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "RISKS AND COMPLEXITY: With their growing market share, shadow banks can amplify systemic risks, especially as their reliance on short-term funding exposes them to liquidity crises.", "created": 1780966141561, "pinned": false, "source": "THE US DOLLAR - BRENT JOHNSON.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 274/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x99p5xeeh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHY DO THEY MATTER? Shadow banks are deeply integrated into the financial ecosystem: Key Players in Credit Flow: They redistribute cash and collateral, enabling credit to reach borrowers that traditional banks might overlook. Intermediaries in Markets: They connect banks and borrowers, often providing liquidity through the wholesale markets.", "created": 1780966141560, "pinned": false, "source": "THE US DOLLAR - BRENT JOHNSON.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 275/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x99p51g95", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHAT ARE SHADOW BANKS? Shadow banks are financial entities that operate outside traditional banking regulations. They don\u2019t accept deposits like conventional banks but instead rely on wholesale markets to fund their operations. This includes money market funds, private equity firms, and entities involved in asset-backed securities. Since the 2008 financial crisis, shadow banks have taken on an even larger role as regulated banks retreated. Their flexibility allows them to navigate complex markets and offer specialized financial services. However, their lack of regulation can make them opaque and prone to risks.", "created": 1780966141559, "pinned": false, "source": "THE US DOLLAR - BRENT JOHNSON.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 296/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x99p5jfu9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW COME THE DOLLAR HIGHLIGHTS THE WEAKEST COUNTRIES IN THE EURODOLLAR SYSTEM? When countries borrow in dollars or issue bonds in dollars, they will eventually needs to print their currency to buy the dollar to pay back the bond if they don\u2019t have adequate dollars in reserve or they don\u2019t have enough dollars coming in to pay back the loan they obtained in dollar. So, if a country economy slows down which means they will be exporting less which means they will be getting less Dollars, that put a lot of pressure on them especially if the dollar was to surge which will cause their currency to fall versus the dollar. It\u2019s harder for them to get the dollars to service the debt. So, the higher the dollar goes the more the country is going to struggle and the more of their currency they have to print to buy the dollar to pay back the bond. For ex: if the yuan is at 7.5 vs the dollar when china issued the bond or borrowed the dollar loan in the Eurodollar market, and then it goes to 8.5 vs the dollar when its time to pay back the dollar loan, now they have lost %10 so the amount they borrowed just went up %10.", "created": 1780966141538, "pinned": false, "source": "THE US DOLLAR - BRENT JOHNSON.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 298/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x99p50uoc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES THE EURODOLLAR SYSTEM WORKS? China issues a bond in US Dollars to Bondholders in Australia. Since the US dollar is the world\u2019s \u201creserve currency\u201d, both parties agree to settle the transaction in dollars. When it\u2019s time for china to make a payment, they must have US dollars available to pay the debt. This demand for dollars can increase the dollar\u2019s value globally, as china either sources dollars from the United states or acquires them through international markets. So china needs to print it\u2019s currency to buy the dollar to pay back the bond. So if China economy slows down which means they will be exporting less which means they will be getting less Dollars, that put a lot of pressure on china especially if the dollar was to surge which will cause their currency to fall versus the dollar. It\u2019s harder for them to get the dollars to service the debt So the higher the dollar goes the more china has to print of its currency to buy the dollar to pay back the bond. For ex: if the yuan is at 7.5 vs the dollar when china issued the bond or borrowed the dollar loan in the Eurodollar market, and then it goes to 8.5 vs the dollar when its time to pay back the dollar loan, now they have lost %10 so the amount they borrowed just went up %10.", "created": 1780966141536, "pinned": false, "source": "THE US DOLLAR - BRENT JOHNSON.docx"}

But forecasting Fed policy is the easiest thing in the world bcs they tell you what they are going to do but the hard part is what's gonna happen as a result of that.\r\n\r\nThe Fed can control the very short end of the yield curve but they can't control the 5 year notes, 10 year notes, let alone the 30 year bonds.\r\n\r\nThe yield to maturity on 10 year Treasury notes is the benchmark security. If you are making investment decisions: The 10 year note is the right benchmark for the large long term investments bcs its an alternative place to invest money.\r\n\r\nAs the yield to maturity on the 10 year note go up that strengthens the dollar while the 10 year yield going down weakens the dollar.\r\n\r\nSigns of Collateral shortage: major dealers are bidding at auction for Treasury bills. The answer is the Fed bills cannot be \r\nre-hypothecated. THEY CANNOT BE USED AS COLLATERAL, BUT THE AUCTION BILLS CAN. So what that  tells you is there's collateral shortage. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1qrv3s32", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Rising bond market volatility typically reduces global liquidity by increasing trading costs, reducing market depth, and amplifying the transmission of shocks across markets. - `18:08:22` --- note 979/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 981/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1qrvji0v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Easier capital flows, stable global liquidity", "created": 1780965792363, "pinned": false, "source": "global  liquidity notes.docx"}
