- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qxdha", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This had 2 consequences: on the one hand, it increased the overcapacity of the export sector, further reducing the profitability and even the viability of the investments made. On the other hand, given the massive influx of capital, of cash, that continued to arrive, the loss of export momentum meant that the current account balance, that is, the difference between income and payments to the rest of the world, would register considerably large deficit levels. The fact was that accumulation of current account deficit\u2019s was being financed by foreign debt. To put it in perspective: in 1996 the foreign debt of these countries exceeded 165% of their gross domestic Product. Faced with such a scenario, only one turning point was needed, a minor interruption to turn the whole system upside down. And that\u2019s just what happened on 2 july 1997. in 1993, taking advantage of the enormous influx of capital that was flooding Southeast Asia, the Thai gov decided to create an entire international financial center in Bangkok with the intention of competing with Singapore and Hong Kong. To achieve this, the Thai gov eased regulations on the capital markets, introduced tax incentives and promoted the creation of a whole financial industry. Soon Bangkok was specializing in foreign exchange lending operations. That is borrowing capital nominated in major international currencies such as the dollar, and channeling it into all types of investment projects in local currency. This way Bangkok became one of the great gateways to the economies of southeast Asia. But what happened is that it\u2019s experience as a financial center was very limited and it\u2019s regulations were just ineffective. But do we remember what else was happening? the enormous influx of capital into Southwest Asia meant that large amounts of resources were invested in projects that would never be profitable. Resources that came from loans that there was little hope of paying back. And that is precisely what led to a growing deterioration in the credit portfolios of Thai financial institutions or in other words: A whole lot more Default. Loans in an erratic situation, that is, that began to have problems being repaid or paying interest, reached levels of between 15 and 24%. However none of this figures appeared in the banks annual accounts. lax of financial rules and lack of experience and supervision meant that loans in irregular situations were re
- `18:08:22` --- note 2436/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qis5u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Asian Crisis : south korea, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines: 2nd july 1997 - june 30 1998: in the early 1990s united states went through a mild economic crisis that ended with the 1991 Recession. This caused the US Federal Reserve to lower interest rates to well below the rates that existed in southwest asian countries. And this together with the high rates of economic growth that these countries had been registering, is what caused international capital to begin flooding into Souwest Asia. This new capital flood was added to the very high savings reserves that these economies already had. In other words, we are talking about a series of events that suddenly provided money for everything. A lot of capital was being invested in projects with little to no profitibality : just pure Speculation and so a bubble was created. When the united states started to recover ,and as the Federal reserve in United States began to raise interest rates, the attractiveness of these markets began to decline.The rise of interest rate in the united states led to an appreciation of the dollar and therefore of the currencies of those countries where were pegged to the US currency by a fixed exchange rate. That in it\u2019self was one of the great attractions those countries had for foreign investors. However, this appreciation of the currencies with respect to other currencies such as the Yen or the German Mark, caused these asian countries to lose competitiveness. To make things worse, in 1994 China had carried out a devaluation of the yuan of more than 30%. As a result, export growth began to slow down for south east asia in 1996.", "created": 1780965775849, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 2463/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qrqu4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cost push inflation negates itself (the cure for high oil prices is higher oil prices: higher prices destroy demand all on their own and hurt the economy causing inflation to come down on its own).", "created": 1780965775757, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q23q9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cost push inflation negates itself-whereas demand pull inflation feeds on itself.", "created": 1780965775756, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2465/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qrmq9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cost push inflation from the supply side is self-negating: The cure for high oil prices is high oil prices bcs when they get too high, people stop driving and they shut down various activities. By the way if you are unemployed, you are not buying any gasoline bcs you are not going anywhere. That's how cost push inflation tips into a recession and then prices com down.", "created": 1780965775749, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2466/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q5siy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Supply chain breakdown cause a lot of inflation. Inflation has two major sources: One is supply side which is called cost push inflation, that's energy price shocks, fertilizer shortages, strategic metal shortages, components suppliers who can't deliver parts to factories in Germany and they are shutting down. The other source of inflation is from the demand side, and that's called demand pull inflation basically psychological. Consumers pull demand forward. They're like her i was thinking about buying a refrigerator I better buy it today bcs the price is going up in six months. In the 70s the US had both, it started with cost push with the Arab oil embargo, but it ended up demand pull.", "created": 1780965775748, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

(watch Retail Money Market Funds (WRMFNS) to monitor if Money Market funds are hording cash or lending: Retail Money Market funds going up means they are haording cash, Retail Money Market funds going down means they are lending).", "created": 1780965775680, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2476/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qtzlr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Most Repo Market activity moves between four large banks: JP Morgan, Bank of America, Citi and Welss Fargo, a chart from BIS shows how the repo market is depending more and more on these four institutions basically if these banks even slightly reduce their lending the market would suffer massively.", "created": 1780965775679, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2477/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q3epz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "On September 16,17 2019 when rate spiked, the Karens were not willing to trade cash for securities at the usual rate, so the marks who need cash kept offering more and more and more until the FED arrived with help. When the Fed announced it\u2019s surprise repo operations, people wanted to know why the did Karens stop lending? Experts pointed to two financial deadlines that sapped cash out of the system on the same night causing a crunch: September 16th was the cutoff for banks to submit their quarterly tax payments so a lot of money that they might usually lend in the repo market was being sucked out of their accounts and deposited into the Treasury. Spetember 16th was also the day that $78 Billion of Treasury debt was scheduled to settle which just means another chunk of cash was being turned into securities that day too.", "created": 1780965775678, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2478/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qfa21", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In the repo market, karens and Marks all over the financial system lend back and forth for short periods, often overnight, and they do this at an enormous scale, usually, more than $1 trillion runs through it every day.", "created": 1780965775677, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2479/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q24gd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How the Repo market operates? The Repo market operates like an overnight pawn shop. Imagine 2 people Karen and Mark: Karen has $1000 and she would like to earn some fast interest on her money. Mark has a stack of treasury notes but no cash so he strikes a deal with karen, one treasury note for $100 but there is a catch. Mark has to agree to but that treasury note back tomorrow for $101. The difference between the price of the note on day one and day two that\u2019s the repo rate. If everything works properly Mark gets the cash he needs right when he needs it and karen makes some fast money. The Repo market functions in the same way you just have to replace the Karens with money market funds and other asset managers who are looking to make a little money without a lot of risk and replace the Marks with hedge funds, wall street traders, and banks who have a lot of assets but need cash on hand to fund their day to day trading.", "created": 1780965775676, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2480/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q92fp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo Market provides the cash the financial firms need to run their daily operations, it provides a lot of the grease that keeps the financial market wheels spinning. When the Repo Market chokes and cash stops flowing trouble can reverberate through the economy That\u2019s what happened in September 16,17 2019. And in response the Fed had to step in to help providing tens of billions of dollars to borrowers to keep the system running.", "created": 1780965775675, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2481/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qnhth", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo Rate: The cost of borrowing money overnight, it tracks how much banks and others pay for overnight loans using repurchase agreements. Repo Rate is funding source for treasuries, Repo Rate spiking signals liquidity plumbing issues. A sudden Sharp increase signals low liquidity (like 17 September 2019): it implies banks don\u2019t have cash to lend to each other requiring ongoing Fed Liquidity injections to bring the rate down.", "created": 1780965775673, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2482/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qrwun", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Monitoring these liabilities is important for central banks and policymakers, as they can affect the stability and functioning of the euro currency, international financial markets, and the overall economic conditions in the Eurozone and beyond. It is part of the broader analysis of international financial flows and their implications for monetary and economic policy.", "created": 1780965775672, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2483/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qxdfk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency Risk Management: Non-euro area entities that have significant liabilities in euros may engage in currency risk management strategies, such as hedging through derivatives, to protect themselves from adverse exchange rate movements.", "created": 1780965775671, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2484/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4q2er3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Impact on Eurozone Financial Markets: Large-scale issuances of euro-denominated bonds by non-euro area entities can impact the Eurozone's financial markets, influencing interest rates and the demand for euros in international transactions.", "created": 1780965775670, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2485/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qgyxm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Economic and Financial Stability: High levels of euro-denominated liabilities for non-euro area entities may indicate the importance of the euro in international finance. It can also reflect the exposure of these entities to fluctuations in the euro's value, which can impact their financial stability.", "created": 1780965775669, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2486/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qcvix", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Exchange Rate Risk: These liabilities are subject to exchange rate risk. If the euro strengthens relative to other currencies, it can increase the burden of debt repayment for entities holding euro-denominated liabilities. Conversely, a weaker euro can ease the repayment burden.", "created": 1780965775668, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2487/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qfcqh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The level of liabilities to non-euro area residents denominated in euros can have several implications:", "created": 1780965775667, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2488/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 2489/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qcmrw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Trade Payables: Companies outside the Eurozone may owe money to Eurozone businesses for goods and services traded in euros. These trade payables are liabilities denominated in euros.", "created": 1780965775665, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2490/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4qoyc2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bank Loans and Deposit\u2019s: Non-euro area banks or businesses may borrow money or hold deposits in euros. - `18:08:22` --- note 2491/12122  ---

(hedge funds would have emerging markets junk bonds \"bcs they invest in risky assets to stay in business\" and they can\u2019t use those junk bonds as collateral in the repo market \"nobody would wanna take them\" so they have to borrow short term liquid us treasuries from a pension fund or insurance company so they can use it as a collateral to leverage up.", "created": 1780965775593, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 2511/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4pg2q5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Treasuries are the Biggest underlying asset of which the entire world economy is levered. The immense global monetary system runs on us dollars. There just isn\u2019t enough collateral to go around (short term liquid us treasuries), that\u2019s why we witness collateral shortage when there is a liquidity squeeze. A lot of the collateral is just reused in the system. A hedge fund borrowing us treasuries from to leverage buying emerging market junk bonds. (Bcs nobody is gonna accept emerging market junk bonds as collateral, hedge funds have to put their hands on short term us treasuries so they have to borrow it. In the system both good and bad collateral are used. \" good collateral liquid short term us treasuries, bad collateral other bonds such as Corp bonds, mbs and junk bonds\". Bcs of the borrowing and reusing of collateral, just a small re-evaluation of the bad collateral would make everybody scrambling to get good collateral \"at any price\" to pledge it. (That\u2019s bcs of the multiplier effect of leverage and of borrowing and reusing collateral \"bad collateral in this instance\" so even a small re-evaluation would have huge catastrophic effect on the market.) To enhance their returns. So there is a collateral multiplier how many times a short term us treaury is BORROWED to be REUSED as collateral to support multiples secured financial trades and in derivatives.", "created": 1780965775564, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4p9d1g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "JPY strengthening and Japan interest rate starting to increase is very dangerous for yen carry trade investors and global liquidity. Yen is soo important for Global liquidity: dollar and yen are the two biggest liquidity providers in the world. The 3 major currencies in the world are : dollar, euro and yen. The Yen matters so much for global liquidity bcs of the yen carry trade. Yen have had QE (yield curve control) for decades now which means interest rates in Japan are extremely low : what that means investors can borrow in yen at 0 interest rate (yield curve control is what made interest rate this low) or very close to 0 Interest rate and they take that borrowed money and they invest it in other parts of the world : they invest in Emerging Markets, in foreign bonds, buy infrastructure overseas. Carry trade loans are deployed around the world. And bcs of the cheap money in Japan even if they make a 1% profit they are in profit. Japan start to feel some inflationary pressures so the markets wants rates to be a little bit higher as the bank of Japan weaken the yield curve Band and let it go from 0.5% to 1% (That\u2019s a 100% move so even though it doesn\u2019t much in absolute terms in relative terms they just \"doubled the level of interest rate\") so if investors have borrowed a lot in yen and levered that up and went and bought assets overseas which yield them 1 or 2% and now ur borrowing costs have went from 0.5% to 1% (and if bank of Japan lost control the borrowing rate might go up to 1.5%) So all of the sudden investors over leveraged carry trade will get unwind at a time and price they don\u2019t like. So the point is: as rates rise in Japan and those carry trade get unwound all that borrowed Japanese capital that\u2019s invested overseas comes flooding back into Japan to pay off the Japan loans causing liquidity to leave the overseas markets and go back to Japan. The liquidity fleeing the overseas markets will put pressure on asset price in overseas markets causing them to Dump and as the overseas asset prices Dump all the leveraged bets and loans gets liquidated basically causing a vicious cascading effect loop of leveraged loans liquidations and a Blackhole swallowing and draining liquidity fast. (Just like what happened in 2008 And 2020 when all the leveraged trades got unwind and u see prices collapse day after day after day bcs investors will sell everything they own to try to prevent the

- `18:08:22` --- note 2574/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4pbw7f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In global dollar shortage countries have to print more of their local currencies to buy expensive dollar DXY to service their debt which cause them inflation problems. The dollar demand is still there still the same but dollar supply isn\u2019t which cause DXY to pump. Fed raising rates to pump DXY in an environment of rising commodity prices is very painful for Rest of the world especially non energy and commodity producing countries. Rising commodities and rising DXY is very painful for foreign countries bcs if commodity is up 10% and DXY is up 10% it makes commodities up 20% in their local currencies (bcs commodities are priced in dollars) which put recessionary pressure on them slowing capital circulation in Eurodollar markets causing credit crunch and DXY to go even higher. It\u2019s just a vicious cycle.", "created": 1780965775444, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2575/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4puaws", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Dollar shortage creates BIG Problems in Emerging Markets: since global trade is denominated in $ importers need $ to pay for imports so when there is a $ shortage their central bank might not be able to provide them with the entire $ amount they need but maybe 10% of it which results in less goods imported which shrinks supply which increase the price for that good resulting in higher inflation. Also when importers can\u2019t import the raw material needed to produce goods they will cut production start laying workers off bcs they don\u2019t have much work for them resulting in higher Unemployment. cutting production cut their revenue making it harder for them to pay their Dollar loans back to the bank and pay their suppliers invoices which make them and the suppliers default on their bank loans which hurts banks causing a credit contraction and eventually the entire system just seize up and comes to a complete stop (Bank fractional Reserve nature and derivatives where bank lend collateral to each other makes the problem A LOT worst and can turn the problem into a systematic Risk affecting all the bank \"That\u2019s why Eurodollar Banks are very afraid to lend during liquidity drains bcs they wanna preserve their Dollar capital) Also, when importers have their cargos at the ports and they are waiting for $ from their central banks to pay for it so that it gets releases the $ might go higher in the few months span that they are waiting for the $ which means their cost go up so they have to increase their sales price increasing in higher inflation, also importers start raising their prices when they see the $ go up bcs they know their cost just went up. $ Shortage is a Vicious death spiral for Emerging Markets especial Non-Energy and Non-oil producers. So as the Eurodollar heats up liquidity is going to fall forcing countries to provide liquidity by printing more of their local currency (which weakens their local currency against the dollar and increase inflation in their countries) .So foreign govs have to flood their market with new collateral and new yen in order to offset the rise in Eurodollar interest rates ( to keep interest rates down) this Mega printing will cause a hyperinflation in those countries .This vicious death spiral Almost Always end up with them going to IMF requesting new $ loans, resulting with IMF forcing them to restructure their Economy and Float their currency against the Dollar.
- `18:08:22` --- note 2576/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4p1kn2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It\u2019s impossible for a bank to survive a bank rank based on how banks operate on fractional reserves: banks extend credit 10 to 1. For every 1 dollar deposited 10 dollars in credit is created and extended So it\u2019s really commercial banks that creates money. Real QE is money printing, and it needs to be ultimately facilitated through commercial banks. When commercial bank lend and extend credit they expand the monetary base and when the don\u2019t lend they contract the monetary base so without endless credit growth in the Eurodollar the system comes to a halt and eventually collapses while in the united states when there is a systematic issue the FED can come in and intervene and inject liquidity into the system to plug the hole, grease the system and get it to run again. That\u2019s why when analyzing the central bank responses we have to make sure to understand the size of the liquidity hole they are trying to plug and if the newly implemented measure would be big enough to plug that liquidity hole ( FED Always have to plug in liquidity hole for both united states and Eurodollar system bcs there is no other entity who can issue dollars).", "created": 1780965775442, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2577/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4p9002", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Eurodollar: when commerce takes place outside of the United States and it\u2019s denominated in Dollars that\u2019s a Eurodollar transaction: a Eurodollar credit has been extended. Based on the design of the system The money has to be circulating at a rate fast enough to service all the debts and to make everybody whole on the transactions and the debts that are owed within the system. If that doesn\u2019t happen the FED (the only entity in the world who can issue dollars) has to come into the rescue and inject new collateral into the system to keep it running or else the system is gonna come to a complete Stop. The problem the Fed doesn\u2019t have jurisdiction outside of the border of the united states and No other entity can inject new dollars new collateral base money into the system and so it\u2019s very important that the Eurodollar system functions on it\u2019s own as far as the circulation. There is no reverse gear that\u2019s the problem based on the design of the system it must grow it\u2019s like a shark swimming through the water it must just keep swimming if the shark stop swimming he sinks and he dies he can\u2019t breathe same with the Eurodollar system or really the entire monetary system if currency is not circulating the system seizes up and it dies. Bcs there is no entity outside of the United States who can inject new money and new collateral into the system it ultimately comes back onto the fed but it\u2019s ultimately also why the Eurodollar market collapses before the United States market.", "created": 1780965775441, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2578/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ph4gd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Eurodollar Market is a secondary derivatives market of the US Dollar market, It\u2019s the Eurodollar Market that makes the US Dollar so powerful.", "created": 1780965775440, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4omhfa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In addition to the indicators listed above, economists also track a variety of other indicators, such as consumer sentiment, business investment, and housing prices. - `18:08:22` --- note 2601/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4osvtq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is important to note that no single indicator can provide a complete picture of global growth. By tracking a variety of indicators, economists can get a better understanding of the overall health of the global economy and identify potential risks and opportunities.", "created": 1780965775211, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2602/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oyhpu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Sustainability: The degree to which a country's economy is able to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Sustainability is important for long-term economic growth and prosperity.", "created": 1780965775210, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2603/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4omjgo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Innovation: The rate at which new technologies and products are developed and adopted. Innovation is essential for long-term economic growth.", "created": 1780965775209, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2604/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oua47", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Infrastructure: The quality of a country's roads, bridges, airports, and other public infrastructure. Good infrastructure is essential for businesses to operate efficiently and to get their goods and services to consumers.", "created": 1780965775208, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2605/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oigwx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Education: The level of education of a country's workforce. A well-educated workforce is essential for economic growth.", "created": 1780965775207, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2606/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4op0gw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Income inequality: The difference between the incomes of the rich and the poor. High income inequality can lead to social unrest and political instability, which can harm economic growth.", "created": 1780965775206, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2607/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oemhy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Debt levels: The total amount of debt that a country, business, or individual owes. High debt levels can make it difficult for countries, businesses, and individuals to borrow money and invest, which can slow economic growth.", "created": 1780965775205, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2608/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4osicf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global economic confidence: A measure of the confidence that businesses and consumers have in the global economy. High global economic confidence can lead to increased investment and spending, which can boost global growth.", "created": 1780965775204, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2609/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ort1s", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Commodity prices: The prices of raw materials such as oil, gas, and metals. Rising commodity prices can boost the economies of countries that produce and export these commodities, but they can also raise costs for businesses and consumers.", "created": 1780965775203, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2610/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o7r56", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Exchange rate: The value of a country's currency relative to other currencies. A strong currency can make it more expensive for a country's businesses to export goods and services, and it can make it cheaper for consumers to import goods and services.", "created": 1780965775202, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2611/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o1jw6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stock market: The value of all publicly traded stocks in a country. A rising stock market indicates that investors are confident in the economy.", "created": 1780965775201, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2612/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ot477", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest rates: The cost of borrowing money. Low interest rates make it easier for businesses to invest and for consumers to borrow money to buy homes and other goods and services.", "created": 1780965775200, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2613/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4om2wq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Budget deficit: The difference between a government's spending and it\u2019s revenue. A large budget deficit can be a sign of economic weakness, as it means that the government is spending more money than it is taking in.", "created": 1780965775199, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2614/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o7uqy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Trade balance: The difference between a country's exports and imports. A positive trade balance indicates that the country is exporting more goods and services than it is importing, which is good for the economy.", "created": 1780965775198, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2615/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o3r5h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Imports: The value of goods and services that a country buys from other countries. Rising imports indicate that the economy is growing and that consumers and businesses are demanding more goods and services.", "created": 1780965775197, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2616/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otg6a", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Exports: The value of goods and services that a country sells to other countries. Rising exports indicate that foreign demand for the country's goods and services is strong, which is good for the economy.", "created": 1780965775196, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2617/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oxp29", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Industrial production: A measure of the output of the manufacturing sector. Rising industrial production indicates that factories are producing more goods, which is good for the economy.", "created": 1780965775195, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2618/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4opzct", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Retail sales: A measure of consumer spending, which is the largest component of GDP growth. Rising retail sales indicate that consumers are confident and spending money, which is good for the economy.", "created": 1780965775194, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2619/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4osdar", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Purchasing managers index (PMI): A survey of purchasing managers at manufacturing and services companies that measures their confidence in the economy. A PMI reading above 50 indicates that most purchasing managers are optimistic about the economy.", "created": 1780965775193, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2620/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oh42z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Consumer price index (CPI): A measure of inflation, which is the rate at which prices for goods and services are rising. A low CPI indicates stable prices, which is good for consumers and businesses.", "created": 1780965775192, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2621/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owigx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Unemployment rate: The percentage of the labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. A low unemployment rate indicates a strong economy with plenty of jobs available.", "created": 1780965775191, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2622/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owths", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Gross domestic product (GDP): The total value of all goods and services produced in a country's economy in a given period of time. GDP growth is a key measure of economic growth.", "created": 1780965775190, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2623/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oxso9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The following are 20 of the most important indicators to gauge global growth:", "created": 1780965775189, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2624/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ozv57", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "These indicators provide insights into the economic well-being of a country or region, allowing for meaningful comparisons between different points in time.", "created": 1780965775188, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2625/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ozv97", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Services Sector Growth: The growth of the services sector can indicate economic trends1.", "created": 1780965775187, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2626/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oodj2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest Rates: Central bank interest rates can influence economic growth and inflation3.", "created": 1780965775186, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2627/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oisiw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Retail Sales: Changes in retail sales can indicate consumer confidence and economic health3.", "created": 1780965775185, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2628/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o95ne", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Production and Manufacturing Statistics: These can indicate economic activity and growth3.", "created": 1780965775184, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2629/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ojjsh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bond Yields: The yield on government bonds can indicate investor confidence3.", "created": 1780965775183, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2630/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ouxh0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "House Prices: Changes in house prices can indicate economic trends3.", "created": 1780965775182, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2631/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ojfjn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stock Market Performance: The performance of major stock market indices can be a leading indicator of economic health3.", "created": 1780965775181, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2632/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o4uo3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Balance of Payments: This monitors a country\u2019s international transactions1.", "created": 1780965775180, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2633/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o35eo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Public Finances: These measure levels and changes in government incomes and expenditures1.", "created": 1780965775179, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2634/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oj8fk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Money and Capital Markets: These measure levels and changes in money supply and capital markets1.", "created": 1780965775178, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2635/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ozh4l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Trade Indicators: These measure levels and changes in international trade2.", "created": 1780965775177, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2636/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4on2jr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Industrial Production Growth: This measures the growth in industrial production2.", "created": 1780965775176, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2637/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o5yod", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Inflation Rate: This measures the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services is rising2.", "created": 1780965775175, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 2639/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ovt3h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Average Annual Wages: This measures the average annual wages in major developed countries2.", "created": 1780965775173, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2640/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ohoio", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Employment Rate: This measures the percentage of the total population that is employed2.", "created": 1780965775172, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o6ows", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Unemployment Rate: This measures the percentage of the total labor force that is unemployed2.", "created": 1780965775171, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2642/12122  ---
