- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oxd50", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Monitoring global indicators is essential for understanding the state of the world and making informed decisions. Here are 20 important global indicators to watch:", "created": 1780965775145, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2648/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4okawi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is important to note that no single indicator is perfect. It is important to look at a variety of indicators to get a complete picture of the economy.", "created": 1780965775144, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2649/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4okrgx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "By tracking these indicators, economists and investors can get a better understanding of the state of the global economy and identify potential risks and opportunities.", "created": 1780965775143, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2650/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oetet", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global financial markets: Global financial markets are where financial assets, such as stocks, bonds, and currencies, are traded. It is important to watch these markets because they can have a significant impact on the global economy.", "created": 1780965775142, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2651/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o70gy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global economic growth: Global economic growth is a measure of the growth of the global economy. It is important to watch this indicator because it affects all economies around the world.", "created": 1780965775141, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2652/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otzwi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Commodities markets: Commodities markets are where commodities, such as oil, gas, and metals, are traded. Commodities prices can have a significant impact on inflation and economic growth.", "created": 1780965775140, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2653/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o38bc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency markets: Currency markets are where currencies are traded against each other. Currency movements can have a significant impact on trade and investment flows.", "created": 1780965775139, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2654/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4or6ja", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bond market: The bond market is a market for bonds, which are government or Corporate debt securities. Bond yields are a measure of investor confidence in the economy and future inflation expectations.", "created": 1780965775138, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2655/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oseqv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stock market: The stock market is a measure of investor confidence in the economy. It is also a leading indicator of future economic activity.", "created": 1780965775137, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2656/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owreu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Government finances: Government finances can have a significant impact on the economy. It is important to watch indicators such as the budget deficit, debt levels, and interest payments.", "created": 1780965775136, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2657/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owdjh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Trade: Trade is a major driver of economic growth. It is important to watch indicators such as exports, imports, and the trade balance.", "created": 1780965775135, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2658/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4odx4l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Manufacturing activity: Manufacturing is a key sector of the economy. It is important to watch indicators such as industrial production, employment, and investment.", "created": 1780965775134, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2659/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o2yhp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Housing market: The housing market is a key driver of economic growth. It is important to watch indicators such as housing prices, sales, and starts.", "created": 1780965775133, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2660/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o4p6z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Industrial production: Industrial production is a measure of the output of the manufacturing sector. It is a key driver of economic growth and a leading indicator of future economic activity.", "created": 1780965775132, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2661/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o1gki", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Retail sales: Retail sales are a measure of consumer spending on goods and services. They are a key driver of economic growth.", "created": 1780965775131, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2662/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oc3hf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Purchasing manager's index (PMI): The PMI is a survey of purchasing managers in the manufacturing and services sectors. It is a measure of current economic conditions and a leading indicator of future economic activity.", "created": 1780965775130, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2663/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oam5d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Business confidence: Business confidence is a measure of how optimistic businesses are about the future of the economy. It is a leading indicator of investment and hiring, which are also major drivers of economic growth.", "created": 1780965775129, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2664/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o3n7b", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Consumer confidence: Consumer confidence is a measure of how optimistic consumers are about the future of the economy. It is a leading indicator of consumer spending, which is a major driver of economic growth.", "created": 1780965775128, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2665/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4olqbx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Exchange rates: Exchange rates are the prices of one currency in terms of another. They affect trade and investment flows.", "created": 1780965775127, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2666/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o3pg5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest rates: Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money. They are set by central banks and have a major impact on economic activity.", "created": 1780965775126, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2667/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otb5h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Unemployment rate: The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is not working but actively seeking employment. It is a measure of the health of the labor market.", "created": 1780965775125, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2668/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ofy17", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Inflation rate: The inflation rate is the increase in prices for goods and services over a period of time. It is a measure of how much purchasing power money loses over time.", "created": 1780965775124, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2669/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o1hru", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Gross domestic product (GDP): GDP is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country or region over a period of time. It is the most widely used measure of economic growth.", "created": 1780965775123, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2670/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4on987", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The following are 20 of the most important global economic indicators to watch:", "created": 1780965775122, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2671/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o37er", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "12- South Korea Exports: An insight into demand for one of Asia's key exporters especially technology.", "created": 1780965775121, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2672/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o7te7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "11- Japan Inflation: a measure of price pressures and tests of how long the world's most audacious monetary experiment continues.", "created": 1780965775120, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2673/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ouxeo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "10- China PPI: How much companies are charging at the factory gate in China provides a glimpse into global inflation trends.", "created": 1780965775119, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2674/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o5xxn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "9- China manufacturing PMI: China is the largest manufacturer of autos, smartphones and other goods the world over so this index provides a key insight into the heart of global production.", "created": 1780965775118, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2675/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owotg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "8- German IFO: The leading indicator of health in the euro area's lynchpin economy, it is based on a survey of about 7,000 executives in German manufacturing, services, retail, wholesale and construction companies. The aim is to gauge their assessment of how the economy stands and their outlook for it.", "created": 1780965775117, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2676/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4om57t", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "7- Euro Area Inflation: A gauge of inflation in the Euro area and the main measure watched by the European central bank.", "created": 1780965775116, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2677/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oj273", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "6- Chile Copper Exports: Chile's copper output. From autos to tv sets to high tech wiring everywhere needs copper and the Andean nation is the world's largest producer. if demand is strong, the world economy is likely to be too.", "created": 1780965775115, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2678/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ovszc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "5- Brazil GDP: a proxy of commodity exporters throughout the world.", "created": 1780965775114, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2679/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4obggk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4- US Personal consumption expenditures: The fed's preferred measure of inflation.", "created": 1780965775113, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2680/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oujpt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3- US Consumer spending: The US consumer is typically one of the pillars of the world economy and this shows how they are faring.", "created": 1780965775112, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2681/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oph2y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2- US Employment: A measure of how tight the labor market is running in the world's biggest economy.", "created": 1780965775111, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2682/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ocq3y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1- Global PMI: the health of manufacturing around the world, based on surveys of multiple purchasing managers on their activity. A number above 50 signals expansion.", "created": 1780965775110, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2683/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ogr2m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The 12 Global Economic indicators to watch:", "created": 1780965775109, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2684/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o4il1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Keep in mind that changes in interest rates in these countries can influence the attractiveness of Eurodollar investments and trading in the global financial markets.", "created": 1780965775108, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2685/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oq71n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar market is primarily influenced by the interest rates set by the Federal Reserve in the United States, as Eurodollars are U.S. dollars held in banks outside of the United States. Therefore, the most important country for Eurodollar interest rates is the United States. However, here are 10 countries whose interest rates can also have an impact on the Eurodollar market due to their economic significance and global financial interconnectedness: 1. United States (USD) 2. European Union (EUR) 3. United Kingdom (GBP) 4. Japan (JPY)", "created": 1780965775106, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2686/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o3qcx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar market is an important source of liquidity for the global financial system.", "created": 1780965775105, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2687/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oo40v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Swedish banks are major players in the Eurodollar market. Swedish banks are among the largest and most sophisticated lenders in the Eurodollar market. They account for a significant share of Eurodollar deposits and loans. Sweden is also important to the Eurodollar market because of its low interest rates. Swedish interest rates are among the lowest in the world. This makes Swedish banks attractive borrowers of Eurodollars. Sweden plays a vital role in the Eurodollar market by providing liquidity,", "created": 1780965775104, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2688/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oyzx7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is important to note that Eurodollar liquidity is affected by a variety of factors, including interest rates, economic conditions, and geopolitical events. The 3-month SOFR rate is just one of the most important interest rates that affects Eurodollar liquidity.", "created": 1780965775103, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2689/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oj8pt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Eurodollar futures prices: Eurodollar futures contracts are derivatives that track the expected value of the 3-month SOFR rate on a future date. Changes in Eurodollar futures prices can signal changes in market expectations for future SOFR rates and Eurodollar liquidity.", "created": 1780965775102, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2690/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4og8uj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Other SOFR rates: SOFR is calculated for a variety of currencies and maturities. Changes in other SOFR rates, such as the 6-month SOFR rate, can also affect Eurodollar liquidity.", "created": 1780965775101, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2691/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oq47r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Other interest rates that can affect Eurodollar liquidity include: Federal Reserve interest rates: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. Changes in Federal Reserve interest rates can have a significant impact on the global financial system, including the Eurodollar market. When Federal Reserve interest rates rise, it becomes more expensive for banks to borrow Eurodollars. This can lead to a decrease in demand for Eurodollars and a decline in Eurodollar liquidity. Conversely, when Federal Reserve interest rates fall, it becomes cheaper for banks to borrow Eurodollars. This can lead to an increase in demand for Eurodollars and a rise in Eurodollar liquidity.", "created": 1780965775100, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2692/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oia7l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When SOFR rises, it becomes more expensive for banks to borrow Eurodollars. This can lead to a decrease in demand for Eurodollars and a decline in Eurodollar liquidity. Conversely, when SOFR falls, it becomes cheaper for banks to borrow Eurodollars. This can lead to an increase in demand for Eurodollars and a rise in Eurodollar liquidity.", "created": 1780965775099, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2693/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4or964", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "most important interest rate that affect the Eurodollar liquidity: The most important interest rate that affects Eurodollar liquidity is the 3-month SOFR. SOFR is a benchmark for short-term interest rates at which banks can borrow funds. Eurodollar deposits are priced relative to SOFR, so changes in SOFR can have a significant impact on the demand for Eurodollars.", "created": 1780965775098, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2694/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4omjjc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Here is an example of a carry trade: 1- An investor borrows 100 million Japanese yen (JPY) at an interest rate of 0.1%. 2- The investor then invests the JPY in Australian dollars (AUD), which have an interest rate of 3.5%. 3- The investor earns a carry of 3.4% per year on the trade. 4- However, if the value of the JPY appreciates relative to the AUD, then the investor will lose money on the trade. For example, if the JPY appreciates by 10% against the AUD, then the investor will lose 10 million JPY.", "created": 1780965775097, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2695/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4onglq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is important to note that carry trades are risky. If the value of the funding currency (e.g., JPY or CHF) appreciates relative to the investment currency, then the investor will lose money. Additionally, carry trades can be leveraged, which can amplify both profits and losses.", "created": 1780965775096, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2696/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otwdq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Some of the most popular carry trade pairs include: AUD/JPY, NZD/JPY, SEK/JPY, NOK/JPY, AUD/CHF, NZD/CHF", "created": 1780965775095, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2697/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4obx0g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "These currencies are popular for carry trades because they have low interest rates relative to other major currencies. This means that investors can borrow money in these currencies at a low cost and then invest in higher-yielding currencies. The difference in interest rates is known as the \"carry,\" and it is the profit that investors hope to make from the carry trade.", "created": 1780965775094, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2698/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owpc2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The currencies most used in carry trade are: Japanese yen (JPY), Swiss franc (CHF), Swedish krona (SEK), Norwegian krone (NOK), Australian dollar (AUD), New Zealand dollar (NZD).", "created": 1780965775093, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2699/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oaxyr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is important to note that Chilean interest rates are just one factor that can affect global copper purchases. Other factors, such as global economic growth and the US dollar exchange rate, also play an important role.", "created": 1780965775092, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2700/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otgu9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A European copper trader may purchase Chilean copper futures contracts to hedge against price fluctuations. If Chilean interest rates are low, the cost of carrying inventory will be lower, making it more attractive to hold copper futures contracts. This can lead to increased demand for Chilean copper futures contracts.", "created": 1780965775091, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2701/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ovnly", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A Japanese electronics manufacturer may purchase Chilean copper cathodes to produce semiconductors. If Chilean interest rates are high, the peso will appreciate in value, making Chilean copper more expensive for the Japanese manufacturer. This can lead to decreased demand for Chilean copper cathodes.", "created": 1780965775090, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2702/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4or610", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A Chinese copper smelter may borrow money to purchase Chilean copper concentrate. If Chilean interest rates are low, the smelter will be able to borrow money at a lower cost, which will make it more profitable to produce refined copper. This can lead to increased demand for Chilean copper concentrate.", "created": 1780965775089, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2703/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oh4zg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Chile interest rate importance in financing global copper purchases: Chile is the world's largest producer of copper, accounting for about 28% of global production in 2022. Copper is a key industrial metal used in a wide range of products, from construction materials to electronics. As a result, Chile's interest rates play an important role in financing global copper purchases. When Chilean interest rates are low, it is cheaper for companies to borrow money to invest in copper production. This can lead to increased copper supply, which can help to keep copper prices down. Conversely, when Chilean interest rates are high, it is more expensive for companies to borrow money to invest in copper production. This can lead to decreased copper supply, which can help to push copper prices up. In addition, Chilean interest rates can also affect the value of the Chilean peso. When Chilean interest rates are high, the peso tends to appreciate in value. This can make it more expensive for foreign buyers to purchase Chilean copper. Conversely, when Chilean interest rates are low, the peso tends to depreciate in value. This can make it cheaper for foreign buyers to purchase Chilean copper. Overall, Chilean interest rates play an important role in financing global copper purchases by affecting both the supply of copper and the value of the Chilean peso. Here are some specific examples of how Chilean interest rates can affect global copper purchases:", "created": 1780965775088, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2704/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oe5ms", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "LIBOR creation: in late 60s Iran was out of money so the Eurodollar system invented LIBOR as a way for Iran to borrow in the Eurodollar market to finance large scale energy projects.", "created": 1780965775087, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2705/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4omfl6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "7-Swap lines are an important tool that the Fed uses to promote financial stability and to support the global economy.", "created": 1780965775085, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2706/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o038p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "6-Three months later, the BoC returns the U.S. dollars to the Fed in exchange for it\u2019s Canadian dollars.", "created": 1780965775084, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2707/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oaffn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-The BoC sells $1 billion of Canadian dollars to the Fed in exchange for U.S. dollars. 5-The BoC then lends the U.S. dollars to it\u2019s domestic banks.", "created": 1780965775083, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2708/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ofrp1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-The BoC contacts the New York Fed and requests to draw on it\u2019s swap line. 3-The two central banks agree to swap $1 billion of U.S. dollars for $1 billion of Canadian dollars.", "created": 1780965775082, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2709/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4obzcd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The swap would be reversed at a predetermined date, usually within three months. At that time, the foreign central bank would return the U.S. dollars to the Fed in exchange for it\u2019s own currency. Here is a simplified example of how a swap with the Fed might work: 1-The Bank of Canada (BoC) needs U.S. dollars to lend to it\u2019s domestic banks.", "created": 1780965775081, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2710/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otxo7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A swap with the Fed is a temporary agreement between the Federal Reserve and a foreign central bank to exchange currencies. This allows a foreign central bank to obtain U.S. dollars from the Fed in exchange for an equivalent amount of it\u2019s own currency, based on the market exchange rate at the time of the transaction. The Fed uses swap lines to promote liquidity in global money markets and to minimize the risk that strains in foreign markets could spread to the U.S. market. Swap lines can also be used to support foreign economies during times of financial stress. To initiate a swap, a foreign central bank would contact the New York Fed and request to draw on it\u2019s swap line. The two central banks would then agree on the amount of currency to be exchanged and the terms of the swap, including the interest rate to be charged. Once the swap is agreed upon, the foreign central bank would sell it\u2019s own currency to the Fed in exchange for U.S. dollars. The foreign central bank would then lend the U.S. dollars to it\u2019s domestic banks, which could then use the dollars to make loans to businesses and consumers.", "created": 1780965775080, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2711/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ognmt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Reserve balances are an important part of the US monetary system. They help to ensure that banks have enough money on hand to meet their obligations to customers and to the Federal Reserve.", "created": 1780965775079, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2712/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oa9uk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Federal Reserve uses reserve balances to implement monetary policy. For example, the Fed can buy and sell government securities to banks, which affects the amount of reserve balances in the banking system. When the Fed buys government securities from banks, it injects more reserve balances into the banking system. When the Fed sells government securities to banks, it drains reserve balances from the banking system. Here are some of the factors that can affect reserve balances: 1-Federal Reserve monetary policy actions: The Fed's monetary policy actions, such as open market operations and reserve requirement changes, can affect the amount of reserve balances in the banking system. 2-Bank lending: When banks lend money, they typically create new deposit\u2019s. These new deposit\u2019s require banks to hold more reserves. 3-Currency withdrawals: When customers withdraw cash from their bank accounts, the banks lose reserve balances. 4-Government spending: When the government spends money, it typically deposit\u2019s the money into banks' accounts. These new deposit\u2019s require banks to hold more reserves.", "created": 1780965775078, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2713/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4orm7k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Banks use reserve balances to settle payments with each other and with the Federal Reserve. Banks also use reserve balances to meet their reserve requirements.", "created": 1780965775077, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2714/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oyruj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Excess reserves: Any reserves that banks hold in excess of their required reserves.", "created": 1780965775076, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2715/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o54ae", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Reserve balances are the amount of money that depository institutions, such as banks, maintain in their accounts at their regional Federal Reserve Banks. Reserve balances are made up of two components: 1-Required reserves: The amount of reserves that banks are required to hold by the Federal Reserve. Required reserves are a percentage of banks' deposit liabilities.", "created": 1780965775075, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2716/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4obgrz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo transactions with the Fed are a safe and efficient way for banks and other financial institutions to borrow cash and for the Fed to manage the money supply.", "created": 1780965775074, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2717/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4owvr6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo transactions with the Fed are typically conducted through the New York Fed's Open Market Trading Desk. The Desk is responsible for implementing the monetary policy decisions of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).", "created": 1780965775073, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2718/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oce1q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "*Interest**: The interest rate in a repo transaction is called the repo rate. It represents the cost of borrowing for the financial institution. The difference between the sale price of the collateral and it\u2019s repurchase price at maturity is effectively the interest paid by the institution to the Fed.", "created": 1780965775072, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2719/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o23sp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed also conducts reverse repo transactions, in which it sells securities to counterparties with an agreement to repurchase them at a later date. Reverse repo transactions are used to drain money from the banking system and to raise short-term interest rates.", "created": 1780965775071, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2720/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o5bje", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A repurchase agreement (repo) transaction with the Fed works as follows: A counterparty, such as a bank or other financial institution in need of short-term funds approaches the Federal Reserve and sells a security to the Fed in exchange for cash. The counterparty agrees to repurchase the security from the Fed at a specified price and time in the future, typically overnight or for a few days. The Fed holds the security as collateral for the loan. Repo transactions are a common way for banks and other financial institutions to borrow cash from the Fed on a short-term basis. They are also used by the Fed to manage the supply of money in the banking system and to implement monetary policy. Here is an example of a repo transaction with the Fed: 1-A bank sells $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities to the Fed in exchange for $1 million in cash. 2-The bank agrees to repurchase the securities from the Fed at the same price the next day. 3-The Fed holds the securities as collateral for the loan. 4-The bank can use the cash from the repo transaction to lend to it\u2019s customers or to invest in other assets. The Fed can use the repo transaction to inject money into the banking system and to lower short-term interest rates.", "created": 1780965775070, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2721/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ofaga", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A Reverse Repo Spike means a DXY spike bcs Fed is sucking Dollars out of the market causing Dollar shortage.", "created": 1780965775068, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2722/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4otve9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "RRPs are a valuable tool for the New York Fed to manage the supply of reserve balances in the banking system and to implement monetary policy. RRPs also provide counterparties with a safe and secure investment opportunity.", "created": 1780965775067, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2723/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ow43t", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The counterparty earns a small interest payment on the transaction, which is currently set at the overnight interest on reserve balances (IORB) rate.", "created": 1780965775066, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2724/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o6giy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "RRPs are a safe and secure investment for counterparties because the New York Fed is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government. RRPs are also a very liquid investment, meaning that counterparties can easily sell their securities back to the New York Fed if they need to access their cash.", "created": 1780965775065, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2725/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oy26m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-The counterparty pays the New York Fed $1 million in reserve balances (The cash transferred by participants to the Fed effectively reduces the amount of reserves in the banking system, impacting the level of liquidity in the financial markets 'draining liquidity') .5-The New York Fed agrees to repurchase the Treasury securities from the counterparty for $1 million plus interest on the overnight reverse repo rate at a specific time in the future, typically the next day.6-At the end of the day, the counterparty has earned a small interest payment on its investment, and the New York Fed has temporarily injected reserves into the banking system.", "created": 1780965775064, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2726/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4olqq2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-The counterparty contacts the New York Fed and expresses interest in participating in an RRP. 3-The New York Fed sells the counterparty $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities.", "created": 1780965775063, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2727/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o2yli", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Here is a simplified example of how a reverse repo transaction with the Fed works: 1- A large money market fund (counterparty) wants to invest its excess cash overnight.", "created": 1780965775062, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2728/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4os92j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A reverse repurchase agreement (RRP) is a short-term transaction in which the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (New York Fed) sells securities to an eligible counterparty with an agreement to repurchase those same securities at a specified price at a specific time in the future. The counterparty earns a small interest payment on the transaction, which is currently set at the overnight interest on reserve balances (IORB) rate. RRPs are used by the New York Fed to manage the supply of reserve balances in the banking system and to implement monetary policy. When the New York Fed sells securities in an RRP, it injects reserves into the banking system. When the New York Fed repurchases the securities, it drains reserves from the banking system.", "created": 1780965775061, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2729/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oezrz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar system is the best reserve currency system that has been tried to date, it created an unparallel global prosperity humankind has never seen before.", "created": 1780965775060, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2730/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ol8s3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar system is a network of interbank relations that made possible the creation of additional supplies of dollars outside of the united states and beyond the control of the Federal Reserve.", "created": 1780965775057, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2731/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ovzsx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It wasn\u2019t the US gov that has throned the Dollar to become the world reserve currency instead it was the Eurodollar system bcs it effectively transmit and circulate money all throughout the global economy.", "created": 1780965775056, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2732/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o30ug", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why the Eurodollar runs on claims of US dollars instead of physical US dollars? \"Providing reserves and exchanges for the whole world is too much for one country and one currency to bear\" Robert solomon; a very influential FED monetary official.", "created": 1780965775055, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2733/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o6abr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Global Reserve currency: a vehicle or middle currency which intermediates between different places using different currencies so that everyone can easily, efficiently transact (trade & finance) with one another using a common medium. 1- it has to be widely available. 2-it has to be widely acceptable\". A global reserve currency has to be made available is as many places as possible and has to be made acceptable in those places.", "created": 1780965775054, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2734/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o7vbs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If you are a Swiss bank or any other bank in the world you can post your excess local currency as a collateral to borrow in US dollar and then you can relend those US dollars all through the rest of the world. The Eurodollar system is a global telecommunication system that elegantly match banks that have US dollar with those who actually need it whether or not they are in the same country or continent.", "created": 1780965775053, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2735/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4orhg7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Banks outside of the United States have been taking deposit\u2019s and making loans in currencies other than their local currency on a much larger scale than before, 'and in the process emerged an efficient interbank market in US dollar' and other foreign currency deposit\u2019s, helping to channel short term funds internationally from lenders to borrowers. While this mass of operations has come to be called the Eurodollar, other countries particularly Japan and Canada play a prominent part in it\" BIS", "created": 1780965775052, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2736/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oskw2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar system resembles more a global network of banks who transact with one another engaging in currency lending telecommunications : Banks transacting in a common medium (Us dollar) which they can swap in and out of their local currencies or other currencies, for ex: it could be a bank in Switzerland who have Swiss franc who then swap them into dollars and they intermediate through a US dealer in dollars who then swaps them into yen to lend to a company in Japan in order to finance its operation to bring its products into the global economy. The Eurodollar creates this seamless efficiency where money suddenly is able to move seamlessly and efficiently all over the world throughout a common medium that's available all over the place.", "created": 1780965775051, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2737/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ob5l4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"The emergence at that time of a fully integrated and active foreign exchange market enabled banks to take in deposit\u2019s denominated in foreign currencies,\"swap\" them into dollars and use the dollars for investment in the Eurodollar market.: FRBNY. So we have some European, Japanese and other ROW banks who have excess cash, they have cash that they would like to lend but don\u2019t necessarily have excess opportunities in their domestic markets within their local jurisdictions. If only they had a way to take advantage of a trade where they would lend money to someone on the other side of the world really needs excess currency in order to conduct trade, finance, investments whatever his needs might be. so we have this linkage of excess monetary funds, the ability to take one currency swap and swap it into another currency while the dollar stands between these two currencies, and mover money around the world in a highly efficient fashion. Eurodollar system move money all throughout the world to where the system judges the money needs to go. In a globalized economy there is a need for money to finance all of these globalizing economic processes from trade to investments. We have one bank in one country that have excess funds and we have a company in another country that needs financing, and we have the Eurodollar system in between the bank and the company for a seamless integration of various banking system, various currency denominations all flowing through one single central medium it\u2019s called the US dollar, it\u2019s denominated in US Dollar and we can call it the Euro dollar Network. So if you are a Swiss bank or any other bank in the world you can post your excess local currency as a collateral to borrow in US dollar and then you can relend those US dollars all through the rest of the world.", "created": 1780965775050, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2738/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ore8a", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"The dollar reigns supreme in FX swaps and forwards. its share is no less than 90% and 96% among dealers. Both exceed its share in denominating global trade (about half) or in holdings of official fx reserves (two thirds). In fact the dollar is the main currency in swaps/forwards against every currency\" BIS", "created": 1780965775049, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2739/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o1dy5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So in the Eurodollar system we have ALL these claims on US dollar deposit\u2019s when we don't really have any actual US dollars.", "created": 1780965775048, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2740/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o5qwr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Eurodollar banks who aren\u2019t holding any physical US dollar deposits in the vault engage and transact of all kinds of claims on US dollar deposits in the form of derivatives (FX SWAPS).", "created": 1780965775047, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2741/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o8evv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Eurodollar banks don\u2019t have a large vault in which they have these actual physical US dollar deposits, but they have a ledger claim on US dollar deposit in some bank, and then this bank relend that claim to another bank who then has that claim and likely that bank relends that claim someplace else. So these Eurodollar banks create these US Dollar claims and then transacting these claims all throughout the world.", "created": 1780965775046, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2742/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4o6mp2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Since many Eurodollar banks that obtain dollar deposits in the Eurodollar market redeposit these funds with other banks (they act as intermediaries), the overall claims on these interbank dollar deposits are multiples of these dollar deposit\u2019s\" FRBNY. Basically, if the actual dollar deposit in the deposit is $1M, the claims on that $1M is probably $10M (that\u2019s bcs of the bank fractional reserves lending). So we have a Eurodollar market where we have JUST claims on US dollars (not even the US dollar deposit\u2019s themselves just claims on them) at banks around the ROW and then these banks take these dollar deposit claims and relend them to other banks in the market so we are building chains of liabilities in US dollar denominations and that\u2019s why collateral just disappear from the Eurodollar global system within seconds at the smallest global Risk arising. The Eurodollar system runs on a fictious ledger money system (ghost money)", "created": 1780965775045, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

Now what are the factors that determine the inflation risk? It\u2019s the size of gov deficit\u2019s bcs the bigger the gov deficits are the more inflation that the gov is likely to create. so when you have large fiscal deficit\u2019s you would expect to have a higher premium on longer term bonds. If the yield on a 6 month treasury is 5.5% and 30 year treasury yield is 4.7% that\u2019s not how a yield curve works it\u2019s positively slopped. so just by looking at the average premium in 80s,90s and 2000s If the yield on a 6 month treasury is 5.5%, the 30 year treasury yield should be at least 7.5%.", "created": 1780965775044, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 2748/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4oyl0c", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why lower bond prices are actually a strength for the US Dollar? The reason that as bond prices has fallen while the US dollar has pretty much gone up in correlation with it is bcs everybody needs dollars to operate on the global stage. And if you already have to own a certain currency to operate on the global stage and now you also get paid A LOT MORE to hold that currency than you get paid to hold a competing currency that you don\u2019t even need to operate on the global stage it makes the decision even easier than it was before . So in other words when big global dollar receivers receive those dollars and they need to save them in order to buy oil or buy another import or to trade on the global stage they save them in the form of US treasury bonds now they may decide to hold those in short term t bills, US agency bonds, or long US treasury bonds, it all kind of depends on what exactly they are trying to accomplish and over what time period they want to hold those savings but that is the form in which they hold their savings. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n42va", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4- The exporter, upon receiving the LC, can proceed with the production and shipment of the goods or the provision of services, knowing that they will receive payment as long as they comply with the LC's terms. 5- The exporter's bank ensures that the documents presented by the exporter (such as shipping documents, invoices, and certificates) match the LC's requirements before releasing payment to the exporter. Import letters of credit provide security for both the importer and exporter in international transactions. For the importer, it ensures that they only make payment when they receive the necessary documents and are satisfied with the shipment. For the exporter, it guarantees payment once they fulfill the terms of the LC. This financial instrument helps facilitate international trade by reducing the risk associated with cross-border transactions.", "created": 1780965775012, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nbjky", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FX Swaps which are the most part of the Eurodollar shadow banking system are almost just like credit card debt , you can pay off $20 of credit card debt ($10 principal and $10 interest)with $10 all day no problem as long as you have velocity (the speed at which money circulates in the economy) so as long as things are good, global economy is good , Corps making money they can pay interest on that debt no problem all day long but if they don\u2019t have velocity (global economy is bad Corps revenue diminishing) they are done sauce, they are fucked. This explains part of why global monetary policy need to keep growing or else it will collapse in it\u2019self and how derivatives (fx swaps) are like a plague that cause contagion bcs if one company defaults that means the other company got burned which means it will default on other companies and defaults and chaos just spread like a wildfire.", "created": 1780965774923, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2786/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nsaul", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FX Forward is a contract that say two companies are gonna settle two currencies at this price in this future date that can be its own separate contract or that can be part of the FX swap, it\u2019s basically the conclusion of the FX SWap.", "created": 1780965774922, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2787/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nrqqs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What\u2019s FX SWaps? There are many many types of FX swaps a Bank can do FX swap with another bank or with a non bank entity . But we gonna focus on the kind that is used for global manufacturing, global growth and Eurodollar system .you got an entity in united states and you got an entity in Germany and the German entity does business in the united states so they need to borrow dollars, and the US entiry does business in Germany so they need to borrow Euros but if the German entity tried to borrow dollars in the united states they get charged a high interest rate and if American entity in Germany tried to borrow in euros they get charged a high interest rate as well. so what both companies do is that they go through an intermediary like a bank JP Morgan for ex. then the American company borrow in dollars in USA and the German company borrows in Euros in Germany where they can get the cheapest rate and then they SWAP , that\u2019s the FX SWAP. Then the German entity pays interest rates in euros and the American company pays the interest rate in dollars. And All of this is done off Balance sheet so it\u2019s all in the shadow banking system as if it almost didn\u2019t exist. To simplify FX Swaps : The American company who does business in Germany took a loan for the German company in it\u2019s local currency the dollar and would pay interest on that loan for her and the German company who does business in united states took out a loan for the American company in euros and pay interest in that loan. And they just swap those loan amounts at a future date, they did this to avoid paying a very high interest rate if they were to acquire a loan on a foreign country as a foreign entity.", "created": 1780965774921, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2788/12122  ---

They are the biggest part of the euro dollar system that is most likely to cause trouble in times of DXY strengthening and interest rate hikes: On a typical day there is about four trillion running through Euro Dollar shadow banking system, it doesn\u2019t show up on on banks balance sheet. Dealers are so incredibly important, they are the vital part of the Eurodollar system.", "created": 1780965774920, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n6n3x", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Short-term liquidity spread: 3-month AA financial commercial paper minus 3-month Treasury bills (T-bills). If this spread is positive, then illiquid assets are paying higher rates to compensate for the lack of liquidity and thus there is a liquidity premium. This metric spiking is a sign for Low Liquidity in short term. This metric spiking is a sign for Low Liquidity in short term.", "created": 1780965774918, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2791/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nx6ep", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3 Month Commercial paper-Fed Fund Rate: When the 3-month commercial paper rate is higher than the federal funds rate, it suggests that Corporations and financial institutions are paying a premium to access short-term funding compared to the interbank lending market. This could indicate tighter credit conditions, increased perceived risk in the Corporate sector, or a higher demand for short-term funding. Conversely, when the 3-month commercial paper rate is lower than the federal funds rate, it implies that Corporations and financial institutions can access short-term funding at a lower cost compared to interbank lending. This could indicate more favorable credit conditions, lower perceived risk in the Corporate sector, or a lower demand for short-term funding.", "created": 1780965774917, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2792/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4njiee", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The 3-month commercial paper rate represents the interest rate at which Corporations and financial institutions can borrow funds by issuing commercial papers with a 3-month maturity.", "created": 1780965774916, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2793/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ntvfd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions (banks) lend funds to each other overnight to meet reserve requirements. It is set by the Federal Reserve and serves as a benchmark for short-term interest rates in the economy.", "created": 1780965774915, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ndgfa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The difference between the 3-month commercial paper rate and the federal funds rate can provide insights into the liquidity and credit conditions in the financial markets.", "created": 1780965774914, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

A higher interest rates means bonds are actively sold.", "created": 1780965774862, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2821/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nzqzc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Coupon Total Return = Coupon interest payment + the bond price change.", "created": 1780965774860, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2822/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ntlaq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The problem with fed rate raising rates to fight inflation is that they don\u2019t know how much to raise rates , they tend to overdo it, they don\u2019t think a soft landing becoming a crash landing into a recession or smthg even worst, there are unintended consequences all over the place especially in a highly levered global financial system when u start monkeying around with markets bad stuff happen that the FED could have never foreseen so there is a lot of risk associated with it.", "created": 1780965774859, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2823/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nqdwt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Where as a recession only affects those who lost their jobs and their immediate family and friends that\u2019s maybe 5 to 10% of the population but inflation affects everybody that\u2019s why it matters.", "created": 1780965774856, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2824/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n0fb2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What is the difference between inflation and Recession and why FEd fights Inflation at all cost? Inflation is a loss of purchasing power, it\u2019s means you need more money to buy the same thing you bought previously wether that\u2019s last year or last month, it reduces people standards of living. Inflation affects 100% of the population, it affects Elon Mask, it affects TESLA but yes he has money to deal with it but it still affects him. It affects someone who is on public assistance, it affects EVERY single person.", "created": 1780965774855, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2825/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ne31y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When interest rates go up, asset prices go down bcs the cost of money goes up.", "created": 1780965774854, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2826/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nj4w3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest rates can be thought of as the \"cost of money\" - higher interest rates make borrowing the same amount of money more expensive.", "created": 1780965774853, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2827/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n2g41", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "BTFP is an expansion of loans: banks showing up at the FED discount window which is a lending facility and they say everybody wants their money back and i don\u2019t have cash but i have a billion dollar worth of securities and loans will you take them as collateral and give me a billion dollar loan? BTFP is just a temporary expansion of the balance sheet that will wind down when the banks pay back those loans, those loans are collateralized so if the banks don\u2019t pay FED sell collateral and wind down the balance sheet anyway.", "created": 1780965774850, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2828/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n5gjw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bank assets are loans and securities they own, bank liabilities: customer deposits.", "created": 1780965774848, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2829/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n14ak", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And A global Bond market sell off will cause a global Risk off, volatility in the very highly levered bond market will cause Chaos and Dump in the bond market which will push investors to deleverage and Risk off which will dump Bond aggregates and PUMP DXY.", "created": 1780965774847, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2830/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ne81u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But the probability of the FED driving chaos in the bond market to pump DXY is very very small bcs bond markets are globally interconnected so a chaos started in the foreign bond markets will eventually cause chaos in the American bond Market as well. But in theory that\u2019s how they can just throw the bond market into total chaos.", "created": 1780965774846, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2831/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nbfd5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A recession is a 2 negative quarters. There has never been 2 negative quarters that hasn\u2019t resulted into a recession.", "created": 1780965774844, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2832/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n31sz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What are the 3 trends that always led to a stable low inflation that allow the feds to have rates near 0 which led to a stable and booming economic markets? Cheap labor, cheap goods and cheap energy. And when any of those ends, inflation spike and fed have to hike rates to tame inflation which will contracts the economy.", "created": 1780965774842, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2833/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n3ost", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And what did we learn in 2008 you can be solvent and viable and 10 minutes later you are JUST DONE. so what did the bank of England do? they just announced QT a week prior, they reversed it and bought a whole bunch of bonds to Ram up the price way up so that when these firms mark their price they are not below capital requirements.", "created": 1780965774839, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2834/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nqpou", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bond investors were just getting killed bcs they were owning bonds on leverage. Things got sooo bad in the market that there was a real fear, At 2 pm london they got a tap on the shoulder from BlackRock that said we are not gonna price our liability duration instruments any more bcs we just can\u2019t (they are leveraging vehicles as well) and they just realized what\u2019s gonna happen at 4 oclock is a bunch of firms are gonna come out and say that they are under regulatory capital and like a lot of other financial firms we borrow every day in the overnight market in order to fund ourselves and when black rock announce that they are not gonna price their liability duration instruments any more, those financial firms are just not gonna get funding.", "created": 1780965774838, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2835/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nx1k2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Let\u2019s remember the bond market is owned by a bunch of levered players so when the bond market price is tanking, the gov yields are soaring 3,4, it even got to 5% on the 30 year.", "created": 1780965774837, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2836/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ncbti", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The British Gilt crisis, the biggest DUMP in the British bond market in 240 years: Once elected British PM proposed to cut taxes and reduce regulations to try to spur economic growth and to make ends meet UK would just borrow more money. But the issue the UK had 10% inflation and inflation was expected to hit 13 to 15% or even higher, in this high inflation environment UK prime minister decided that she is going to supercharge the economy with a ton of stimulus well hell inflation then is gonna go to 20%. The fear in the British market was that what she is proposing is actually going to work and it\u2019s going to create tons of stimulus and a ton of inflation. So the uk bond market and the British pound imploded on themselves bcs if they going to stimulate a 10% inflationary environment investors don\u2019t want anything to do with their currency or with their bond market so they gov yield went up and their currency fell.", "created": 1780965774836, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2837/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ngrxh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The problem with the bond market is that it can crowd up. when the fed wants to sell that extra slack of treasuries every month. well who\u2019s gonna buy it at the time when the bond market is crowded? well somebody will. but how? well the fed will just lower the price by keep raising the interest rate until they suck the money out of somebody else to get that extra slack funded (by finding a buyer for that extra slack). There are no bad bonds there are only bad prices. you can fund anything you want in the bond market, you might not like the interest rate that it has to be financed at but it can be done.", "created": 1780965774821, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2838/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n25fi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The magnificent seven stocks are about 75% of the gains in the S&P in 2023, if you take them out and you look at the other 492 companies in the S&P they are only up 3% in 2023, the Russell 2000 is up 4% in 2023, Micro Cap which is the bottom 1000 companies in the Russell 2000 they are still down on the 2023 year. All of this has been caused by interest rates bcs the magnificent 7 stocks are like central banks or govs they don\u2019t care what interest rates are but the retailers and the joan fabrics of the world interest rates matter to them.", "created": 1780965774814, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2839/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nez90", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "what\u2019s a long duration growth stock? it\u2019s a company whose cash flows are big way off in the future as opposed to cyclical stock whose cash flows are big right now. So when interest rates go up and you start discounting those future cash flows that hurt long duration growth stocks (most of them are tech stocks) that\u2019s why Nasdaq was down so much in 2022.", "created": 1780965774813, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2840/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n81gy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "China is the elephant in the room, they are the Factory of the world so they are so important for global economy you just can\u2019t ignore it. if they are doing great that has huge influence bcs that would be good for the overall global economy not just China, if they are struggling that has huge influence bcs that would be bad for the overall global economy not just China.", "created": 1780965774792, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2841/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 2842/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4neegh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Certain assets tend to be very explosive so when they go, they REALLY go for ex: crypto, commodities, penny stocks, tech stocks but currencies don\u2019t do that they trend in a band,", "created": 1780965774790, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2843/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n03fm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So if an investor live in a country that have negative interest rates but there is a country with very high interest rates wouldn\u2019t he have a desire to invest over there? So obviously the answer is YES. Interest rates are important bcs they represent the amount you can earn on your investment ultimately that\u2019s what incentive people to invest their money, it\u2019s to earn returns and the way you earn return on cash is through interest rate so interest rates drive currencies and they are the most important factor and who sets up interest rates? Central banks. That\u2019s why currencies go nuts when central banks change their interest rate policies. II- Also trade drives currency flow and demand. So what drives currencies? what drives them long term is prices and stickiness of prices and inherent prices of things, over the medium term ( 3 to 6 months) it\u2019s interest rates, and over the short term ( 2 weeks to 3 months) it\u2019s momentum and trend following so when price tend to move in one direction it really does move and that driven sort of like market hysteria. And over the short term you have mean reversion moves.", "created": 1780965774789, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2844/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4naere", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What influences the currencies market? Each market is very specific in terms of the factors that drives it and so when you come to currency markets it\u2019s ALL about interest rates. So the question is WHY? Well at least over the short term at least 3 to 6 months. Currency is Cash and what do you do with cash? you stick it in a bank and the bank will pay you interest rate.", "created": 1780965774788, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2845/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nkvs6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "a lot of technical indicators are nothing more than adding a whole bunch of numbers together and dividing them by something. A moving Average is nothing more than expression of of Momentum, so MA 20 is add the last 20 price numbers together and divide by 20. RSI: look at the positive returns then look at the negative returns to the average then divide one by the other.", "created": 1780965774787, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2846/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nk3lv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What\u2019s the difference between an indicator and a strategy? An indicator is a component of a trading strategy so it\u2019s an input that will cause a particular bias in the market but that bias is usually used in a binary way: buy or sell but it\u2019s more important than that it\u2019s about how much do you buy how much do you sell and ultimately when do you get out and how do you protect of i you look at a portfolio view you have indicators per asset that then have to be combined for instance it could be that in one indicator you have less confidence and then you look at another indicator and then you weigh them appropriately. So an indicator is about allowing you to create a bias about the future while a strategy about combining these strategies into a trading view.", "created": 1780965774785, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2847/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 2865/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n7kh5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "currency : a country has lots of flows to other countries. These cross-boundary flows are either in terms of capital investments or trade, which ultimately arre affected and have an effect upon currencies. So what we are saying is rather than just looking at one stream of communication between 2 countries inCorporate Everything, look at all the various streams and there are lots of different methods of doing that but one of the easiest one is the country trade balance (this doesn\u2019t apply to the US and funding countries whom currency demand come from capital investments flows ex: Switzerland, Singapore)", "created": 1780965774749, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2866/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nw2lh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency indices are the best way of fitting macroeconomic ideas or views about a country vs another country. It\u2019s Basically a relative game: we are comparing how we think this country would be doing vs this other country. So country A and B might both be in a bad economic cycle but if country A is kinda of a better shape (let\u2019s say it\u2019s economic downturn is less severe) than country B than the currency of country A is gonna appreciate vs Country B currency.", "created": 1780965774748, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
