- `18:08:22` --- note 2896/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4niu8c", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Volatility: While AUD/JPY can experience some price fluctuations, it has historically been less volatile compared to other carry trade pairs, making it a somewhat safer choice for traders. It's important to note that the popularity of specific currency pairs for carry trades can change over time due to shifts in interest rate differentials, economic conditions, and market sentiment. Traders should conduct thorough research and analysis before implementing any carry trade strategy and consider the current interest rate environment and economic factors that may affect their chosen currency pair. Additionally, risk management is crucial when engaging in carry trades, as exchange rate movements can lead to significant gains or losses.", "created": 1780965774712, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2897/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ndeir", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Aussie yen AUDJPY is a currency pair that sometimes exhibit\u2019s sort of risk assets price action largely due to its use as a carry trade. A carry trade is basically when you sell or borrow with or fund with a low yielding currency like the yen and you buy a relatively higher yielding currency like the Aussie Dollar. By doing so you are capturing the yield differentials between AUD rates and JPY rates and bcs yen rates are always like on the floor perpetually for many decades, yen has been used as the go to cheap funding currency. AUDJPY used to be the go-to carry trade currency pair, it still is to a certain extent but it really was bcs of the fact that Japan yields were on the floor and Aussie rates yielded several points higher. So what happens every trading day that investors have a positive carry trade (positive yield spread) they get their trading account credited, so what traders would do is to go long the AUD/JPY carry trade and use leverage and by using leverage it juices up your carry returns and then you use those proceeds to go long Risk assets or anything really. in mid 2000s Japan retail massively crowded into the Aussie yen carry trade and much of that found it\u2019s way into help fuel the subprime CDO Bubble in the US leading up to 2008 and then pre-Lehman brothers\u2019 collapse in like July 2008 the leverage long AUDJPY carry trade saw a face ripping vicious unwind in which AUDJPY basically got cut in half within 3 months. Aussie Dollar got destroyed, yen surged. since then, AUDJPY carry trade still be used on and off as a carry trade of choice to fund risk positions such as being long spx and so therefore AUDJPY and SPX would sometime correlate and correlate very tightly. The currency pair that has historically been one of the most popular choices for carry trade strategies is the \"AUD/JPY\" pair, which involves trading the Australian Dollar (AUD) against the Japanese Yen (JPY). Here's why AUDJPY pair is often favored for carry trades: 1-Interest Rate Differential: Australia has historically offered higher interest rates compared to Japan. Traders would borrow Japanese Yen (JPY) at low-interest rates and invest in Australian Dollars (AUD), which provided a higher yield due to Australia's higher interest rates. 2-Liquidity and Stability: Both the Australian Dollar (AUD) and Japanese Yen (JPY) are considered major currencies and are relatively stable compared to some other currencie
- `18:08:22` --- note 2898/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n40h0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar is frequently used as a funding currency in carry trades, especially when interest rates in the United States are low, as it provides access to a wide range of higher-yielding currencies. 4-Australian Dollar (AUD): The Australian dollar is a popular target currency for carry trades because of Australia's relatively high-interest rates compared to other developed economies. 5-New Zealand Dollar (NZD): Similar to the Australian dollar, the New Zealand dollar is often used in carry trades due to New Zealand's comparatively high-interest rates. 6-Euro (EUR): The euro can be involved in carry trades, especially when there is a significant interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, making it an attractive target for investors. 7-British Pound (GBP): The British pound can also be part of carry trade strategies, with traders borrowing in currencies like the Japanese yen or Swiss franc and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in GBP.", "created": 1780965774706, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2899/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nba8o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Swiss Franc (CHF): The Swiss franc has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Switzerland's traditionally low-interest rates. 3- Taiwan New Dollar (TWD): The Taiwan New Dollar has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Taiwan traditionally low-interest rates", "created": 1780965774705, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 2907/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n13u1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Central banks, policymakers, and economists often monitor the REER to understand the dynamics of a country's exchange rate and its potential impact on the economy. It helps them make informed decisions about monetary policy, trade policies, and other economic measures.", "created": 1780965774696, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2908/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4n9rig", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Real Broad Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is useful for assessing a country's competitiveness in international trade. If the REER appreciates, it may indicate that a country's goods and services have become more expensive relative to its trading partners, potentially leading to a decrease in exports and an increase in imports. Conversely, if the REER depreciates, it may indicate improved competitiveness in international markets.", "created": 1780965774695, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2909/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nkn4d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-Index Calculation: Combine all these factors to create an index that reflects the real, inflation-adjusted value of the home country's currency against a basket of foreign currencies.", "created": 1780965774694, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2910/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4nsmfy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Trade Weights: Apply trade weights to the currencies of the trading partners. The weights are typically based on the volume of trade between the home country and its trading partners. This means that currencies of countries with which the home country has a higher volume of trade will have a larger impact on the REER.", "created": 1780965774693, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2911/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mu69h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Inflation Adjustment: Adjust the nominal exchange rate for differences in inflation rates between the home country and its trading partners. This is usually done by dividing the nominal exchange rate by a measure of relative price levels or consumer price indices in the home country and its trading partners.", "created": 1780965774691, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2912/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m2l16", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1-Nominal Exchange Rate: Start with the nominal exchange rate, which is the current market exchange rate between a country's currency and a basket of foreign currencies.", "created": 1780965774690, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2913/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mqr01", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Real Broad Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is a measure used in economics and finance to assess the value of a country's currency in comparison to a basket of other currencies, adjusted for inflation. It is called \"real\" because it takes into account changes in the price levels or inflation rates in different countries. The \"broad\" aspect means that it considers a wide range of trade partners and currencies rather than just a few major trading partners. Here's how the calculation generally works:", "created": 1780965774689, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mv3v5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Banks create money out of thin air when it hands out a loan, when borrowers go and get a loan like a mortgage the bank open them a deposit account and deposit that mortgage or that loan money into that deposit account basically creating money out of thin air. So when deposit\u2019s flee banks at the rate they are doing now in 2023 bank walk it severely impacts their ability to generate or create new money and that severely impacts their ability to hand out loans and that\u2019s why only the magnificent 7 stocks are doing great in 2023 while the other 2993 companies are struggling, it\u2019s not only not banks not handing them loans and credit why they are struggling but their conduit for financial services. As bank not in the greatest profitability position, pain in 2993 companies will keep mounting. So bottom line as long as the bank walk continues the bank stocks will continue to struggle, and the further away you get from your ability to borrow from Corporate bond market and the more you are reliant on banks the more your company will be struggling and the more your stock will be struggling and that\u2019s not by coincidence. In essence the companies relying on banks for credit and financial services are having harder times compared to the magnificent 7 stocks who can be somewhat independent from banks. so while the bank walk always end up showing up in the economy and it\u2019s not gonna entirely gonna crash the system but nevertheless it\u2019s gonna be a dull drag on the economy and companies. Banks can always raise deposit rates to hold on to deposit\u2019s but that kills their profitability, they keep the banks deposit\u2019s low so that that money becomes very profitable for them and the bank walk just continue, they are in a very difficult position.", "created": 1780965774667, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mcwvp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The bank walk: Phone Technology has made it very easy to move money out of banks that are zero yielding or 1% yielding deposit account to 5% money market fund and treasury bills. in United states the Deposit rate is 0.5% while money market fund rate is 5.25% so there is a difference of 4.7% giving huge incentives for people to move their money from banks checking account to money market fund. So as bank customers leave we witness a problem of profitability for banks, banks borrowing from depositors and giving depositors 0.5% and as a bank you can go buy a tbill a 5.25% pocketing 4.7% . As people leave and banks have to raise their deposit rates or go borrow from money markets at 5% they cost of funding goes up , their net interest margin is squeezed and that\u2019s why the profitability of bank stocks came under pressure and that\u2019s why bank stocks have been performing poorly.", "created": 1780965774663, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m05hc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "You can\u2019t taper a Ponzi, Once you start pyramiding debt on top of debt you really can\u2019t taper it bcs it\u2019s a system that has to grow in order to not crash. And that's so often attributed to the United States bcs of its large budget deficit and the USA took a large debt that it can never pay back. That\u2019s 100% true you can\u2019t taper a Ponzi and that\u2019s why the US Economy and that\u2019s why the US monetary system design has to keep growing and why it will probably eventually lead to either the inflation of the currency or a crash of the system. But that also applies to the rest of the world in an even bigger magnitudes bcs they use the Eurodollar market, and the Eurodollar market is even more leveraged and an even bigger Ponzi scheme than the United States. And the money in that system is not owed to the United States, it\u2019s rest of the world countries owing money to each other so it\u2019s China owing money to Russia and turkey owing money to Egypt. So if in the Eurodollar they just stop using it and they just get rid of All their US dollar liabilities (debt) then they are also getting rid of all their Eurodollar assets and Eurodollar assets are a huge part of the assets of the Rest of the world countries.", "created": 1780965774659, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mk5mf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Britton woods was the architecture of the international monetary and financial system. Britton woods put the dollar at the center of the world's financial system and uses the IMF and the world bank to police like deficits and surpluses in order words to manage imbalances between economies and the US military to oversaw or backstop the entire system of world trade and capital flows. so what does Britton woods means in plain English: it means that the US is playing BANKER of the world. People criticize the USA for having a whopping current account deficit and they keep saying well of course this is about the lack of competitiveness of US industry that\u2019s just complete BULLSHIT. What it shows you is the SUPER competitiveness of USA finance that\u2019s what is really telling you bcs the balance of payments by definition must balance and if you have got a big surplus on your financial side, you by definition gonna have a deficit on your manufacturing or trade side and that\u2019s exactly what\u2019s happening on the USA balance of payments book. What the USA does is that it acts as the banker of the world and that\u2019s what the dollar system or the international financial system is, so if the Rest of the world wants to borrow dollars they borrow dollars and the US supplies them US bank supply and if they want to invest their surpluses in US financial markets they can and that works seamlessly as it has done for decades. So the question can Russia, China or any other country provide a rival World Bank in service? Absolutely no way, they are decades away from getting anywhere near that. Can they redenominate part of their trade in yuan or other currency? yeah sure they can but is that gonna be a big difference? No it\u2019s like basically measuring Park avenue in Kilometers not miles and trying to argue which one is longer, you are just changing the denomination of the unit. what really matters is acting as the banker of the world and that\u2019s what the US does and what\u2019s the dollar is all about.", "created": 1780965774651, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mq2ja", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Term premium is like a risk premium that is embedded in the bond that covers your interest rate risk over the life of the bond so in other words it\u2019s trying to adjust or cover compensate for potential volatility. Now you would normally expect that term premium on a 10-year bond would average about 50 basis points. what that means is that if you had perfect foresight of all the policy interest rates that the federal reserves were going to put in place over the next 10-years, the 10-year bond should yield you 50 bips more than that average of interest rates. Term Premium is Always mean Reverting meaning that it doesn\u2019t how high and how low they go they will always revert to 50 basis point over time. Huge buying pressure of treasuries due to collateral shortage depress the term premium significan\u2019tly causing it to go negative in extreme dire collateral shortage cases.", "created": 1780965774645, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

BOJ has done yield curve control for years in order to keep rates in Japan very low, so now with inflationary pressures coming up they have had to potentially start loosening the band within which they have allowed the JGB the Japanese Gov bond to trade. The problem with doing that is that if they start to raise the band within which the jgb can trade (by just not buying jgn Japan gov bond) that has the potential to strengthen the currency ( bcs they don\u2019t have to print money to buy jgb and also higher Japan yields would attract investors to the Japanese currency) so they can save the currency by letting the bond float a little bit more . The problem is that if interest rates rise in Japan, then jgb prices falls which will blow a bill hole in Japanese banks, pension funds and insurance companies balance sheets bcs they all have a negative yielding jgb so interest rate doesn\u2019t really to raise by much to cause Japan bond prices to fall to throw their finances and balance sheets into chaos. (look at what happened to American banks when interest rates rose and bcs they had long maturity bonds on their balance sheet it just sent them into chaos, Japanese financial entities are even in a worst situation bcs not only they have low yielding gov bonds on their portfolio but a negative yielding ones). So Japan central bank are in a very delicate place. which one do they save the national currency or the bond market, ultimately, they will save the bond market bcs that\u2019s how gov get funded and if the bond market blows up the whole economy blows up. The process by which they would try to save the bond market will kill the currency (JPY has lost 50% of it\u2019s value over the last 20 years). And what\u2019s the consequences of that? the consequences of keeping the bond market safe but letting the currency continue to fall ( bcs they have to print yen to buy bonds to keep bond yield low to save the bond market) is that as the yen falls it puts more pressure on the yuan and the reason why that\u2019s important that\u2019s bcs Japan and China are two rival competitors and China is already dealing with deflationary pressures from their real estate market so as the yen falls vs the yuan that puts even more deflationary pressure on China (bcs they have to lower their currency to
- `18:08:22` --- note 2953/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mym2q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The way that currency pegs work is that when these other countries have excess supply of dollars or when they get dollars. Their central banks take the dollars and buy up their local currency in the open market which keeps which keeps their currency roughly in line with the US dollar. it\u2019s a way to artificially keep their local currency strong. So as long as they have enough dollars to buy up their local currency it\u2019s No problem and as long as dollars continue to flow in it\u2019s no problem but when dollars start to dry up and even worst when dollars start to flow out then where do the dollars come from to keep those pegs? So in the scenario where the dollar rises a lot or there is a credit contraction or a Global Credit Event causing dollar liquidity to dry up, it becomes harder for those countries to maintain those pegs and countries will never give you a heads up or say that they are going to let the peg go but eventually as their dollar reserves start to dwindle they have to make a decision do we keep throwing good money after bad and spending it on a currency peg that\u2019s eventually going to break anyway or do we save our dollars so we can buy things like grain and oil and food and other much needed commodities. So if countries can no longer get dollars to maintain those currency pegs then they break and when currency pegs break typically they don\u2019t move 5 to 10%. Typically, they move 20, 30, 40%. This is the type of things u can bet on with a very small amount of money, if you are wrong u lose a little bit but if you are right, you make a killing.", "created": 1780965774638, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mxwvj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Globalization: Everyday businesses are more and more reliant on global supply chains to ensure that products are produced and provided in the best country possible. You want smthg manufactured cheaply produce it in China (that\u2019s why China is very important for global inflation and deflation of goods and products), you want smthg built it to the highest standards build it in Germany. Products are produced and provided in the best country possible bcs of comparative advantage (do what you do well) for ex: Germany has can produce cell phones very easily they have the infrastructure and technical expertise to do so but Germany has very expensive and limited labor, stringent environmental regulations, and it\u2019s not close to the component material suppliers for cell phones so German iphones would cost an astronomical amount ( about $4,000 vs the $750 they cost now made in China) that\u2019s bcs China is more suited to mass medium quality manufacturing. China has a much larger low skilled labor force, looser environmental regulations and it\u2019s the home of the factories that make the components that make the phones. That\u2019s why countries just stick to doing what they do best, so Germany just stick to producing cars (Germans have the knowledge to make the best quality cars) and China just stick to producing phones. This way we have a lot of cheap phones and a good amount of good quality cars. So, countries will just sell to the world the products they produce best and just buy from the world the products they don\u2019t produce. So in this case Germany will sell China cars and buy it\u2019s iphones. To do so in the global trade, countries use their currencies for trade but of course Chinese iphone manufacturers aren\u2019t interested in in being paid in German euros and German car manufacturers aren\u2019t interested in being paid in Chinese yuan so THEY TRADE THEIR CURRENCIES, this makes a secondary market bcs suddenly you are not only exchanging cars and phones but also euros and yuan. So the foreign exchange market has grown so large bcs global trade has grown to require it. The Bretton woods conference which established a gold standard for currencies took place in july 1944 in the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods Washington. A total of 44 countries met with attendees limited to the allies in World War 2, the conference established the international monetary fund and the world bank But

- `18:08:22` --- note 2963/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4myo2n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Consumer Spending: Lower interest rates can make it more appealing for consumers to use credit for purchases, leading to higher consumer spending and increased demand for goods and services. 4-Export Competitiveness: In some cases, lower interest rates can lead to a weaker currency, making exports more competitive on the global market and potentially boosting exports. It's important to note that while low interest rates can stimulate economic activity in the short term, they can also have side effects like encouraging excessive borrowing, inflating asset bubbles, and impacting savers who rely on interest income. Central banks need to carefully balance these factors when setting interest rates to achieve their economic goals.", "created": 1780965774627, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2964/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m84xr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Boost Investment: Lower borrowing costs can incentivize businesses to make capital investments and expand their operations. This can lead to job creation and increased economic output.", "created": 1780965774626, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2965/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mfqdi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stimulative measures, on the other hand, are often associated with low interest rates. When an economy is facing a slowdown or recession, central banks might lower interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending. This can:1- Encourage Borrowing and Spending: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing, making it more attractive for individuals and businesses to take out loans for various purposes, such as buying homes, making investments, or expanding businesses. This increased borrowing and spending can boost economic activity.", "created": 1780965774625, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2966/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mlzwl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-Foreign Investment: High interest rates can attract foreign investors seeking higher returns on their investments. This can lead to an appreciation of the domestic currency, which makes exports more expensive and imports cheaper. As a result, the trade balance may be affected negatively, potentially slowing down economic growth.", "created": 1780965774624, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2967/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4md3qu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Debt Servicing: High interest rates can make it more difficult for individuals and businesses to service their existing debts. This can lead to financial stress and potentially result in defaults or bankruptcies. Consequently, spending may decrease as people focus on repaying debts.", "created": 1780965774623, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2968/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mb1f9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Borrowing Costs: High interest rates mean that borrowing money becomes more expensive. This can discourage individuals and businesses from taking out loans for purchases such as homes, cars, and capital investments. The higher cost of borrowing reduces overall spending, which can slow down economic activity.", "created": 1780965774622, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2969/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m011a", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "High interest rates are generally not considered stimulative for an economy; rather, they are often used as a tool to control inflation and manage economic growth. In the context of monetary policy, interest rates can be used by central banks to influence the level of economic activity. Here's how it works: 1-Incentive to Save: High interest rates provide individuals and businesses with a greater incentive to save money in banks and other financial institutions. When interest rates are high, the returns on savings accounts and other fixed-income investments become more attractive. This can lead to reduced consumer spending and business investment, as people opt to save their money instead of spending it.", "created": 1780965774621, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 2970/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mmhov", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why do inflation take a very long to come down once it spikes very hard (past 5%)? CPI stays high for a while bcs of shelter index (housing and owner equivalent rents) which makes up 25% of CPI, so you need to wait for people to start signing new leases (leases are usually 12 months) and add 6 months for the Data processing for it to reflect the new correct figures. So, we are talking 18 months of Delay (12 months to resign a new lease and 6 month to process the new data. so even when food prices come down, gas prices come down, owner equivalent rent will keep the CPI figures high for another 18 months anyway regardless of what happens with the other CPI components (food, gas and others). Also, Owner Equivalent Rent is 25% of CPI while gasoline is 6% and food is 14%. So, unless equivalent rent comes down, CPI won\u2019t come down even if gasoline and food prices come down (bcs of how big of a percentage in CPI home equivalent rent is). so the shelter index is 4 times as high as energy (gasoline) so energy would have to have a four times as big a percent move to offset the shelter index move either to the upside or to the downside.", "created": 1780965774616, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mriod", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The central bank of Japan behind its doors many of the decisions that led to the great Japanese bubble were made. Which obviously put a strain on the Japanese export machine after all 40% of all Japanese exports went to us consumers. To try to deal with the situation and avoid the risk of crisis the gov and the central bank of Japan decided to do 2 things: 1-Boost domestic demand : consumption 2-implement a loose monetary policy to try to compensate for the effects of the plaza accord so in the following 2 years interest rates were reduced by 50% , also the gov increased public spending and Japanese banks encouraged by the country\u2019s own authorities began to lend enormous amount of money to families and companies so they can launch themselves into the real estate and capital markets. Between 1985 and 1989 Japan experienced a massive bubble: the average price of housing increased by more than 300% and nikkei index tripled its value to represent one third of the world\u2019s total market capitalization. Zytec: a financial engineering technique had a lot to do with Japan bubble. Taking advantage of the low interest rates the big Japanese conglomerates began to take out large loans to finance the purchase of shares and real estate smthg that allowed fatten their bottom lines why bcs at the time accounting standards allowed these companies to present capital gains as income so the more shares were revalued the greater the benefit\u2019s. In other words, the more money companies borrowed and the more shares they bought the higher share price rose which in turn increased the company's profit\u2019s and the cycle started over and with higher profit\u2019s they had more capacity to borrow and so on again and again. More than half of the companies listed on the tokyo stock exchange were involved in this system: in 1988 : 38% of toyota's profit, 65% of Nissan\u2019s profit\u2019s , and 63% of sony's profits were generated by this activity. By the end of the 1980s between 40 and 50% of the Corporate profits of all the Japanese companies were generated using this financial technique , a technique that

Pressure from the united states led finance ministers and central bank governors of the five most industrialized countries in the world ( united states, Japan, France, Germany , united kingdom) to make an agreement at a meeting held at the plaza hotel in new york to intervene in the foreign exchange market in order to devalue the dollar. - `18:08:22` --- note 3000/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m0uv6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yuan fixing typically refers to the daily reference rate set by the People's Bank of China (PBOC) for the Chinese yuan (CNY) against the U.S. dollar (USD). This rate helps guide the trading range within which the yuan is allowed to fluctuate in the foreign exchange market. The PBOC aims to manage the yuan's value to ensure stability and prevent extreme fluctuations. This practice is common among many countries with managed exchange rates.", "created": 1780965774589, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3001/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mvztl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "There are some big benefit\u2019s to having a low valued currency. For starters, if you currency is less valuable then importing stuff becomes more expensive. And this sounds bad but it\u2019s actually good for producing nations bcs it gives domestic made good an advantage as it makes domestic made goods cheaper to local citizens than foreign goods. For ex: if someone is tossing up between a Cadillac and a Mercedes, they might be pretty cost comparable. if the US dollar looses half or it\u2019s value though, then that Mercedes is going to be twice as expensive to purchase bcs it\u2019s going to take double the amount of American dollars to pay the German auto manufacturer in euros. which would make the American car buyer just stick with the Cadillac even if that means getting a lower quality car but hey it\u2019s half the price, and hey look American auto manufacturer lives to see another day. This currency manipulation or drop in the ex, would achieve the same goal as tariffs but it does not break any rules of any trade agreements that will normally stipulate that tariffs are banned. So devaluing the currency is big win for local industry.", "created": 1780965774588, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3002/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mu1c3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency manipulation achieve the same goal as tariffs but it does not break any rules of any trade agreements where usually tariffs are banned. Devaluing the currency is big win for local industry as it made domestic goods cheap and imported good expensive (by making local currency cheap and foreign currency expensive). Also it boost exports by making domestic products cheaper for foreigners overseas.", "created": 1780965774587, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3003/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mhb3p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Nations want to export lots of goods and services and import what they really need to. This relationship of imports vs exports is noted as a trade surplus if a nation exports more than the import or trade deficit if they import more than they export.", "created": 1780965774586, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3004/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mdiax", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Other, cheaper currencies become more advantageous to spend. In a way, currency itself can be viewed as a product, whose price is based on demand. As China has seen rapid and intense economic growth, they've attempted to stem the inevitable devaluation of their currency as their trade surplus grows. This is done through currency manipulation, which is when one country uses its local currency to buy huge amounts of foreign currency. That makes it possible to prevent its local currency from strengthening (weakening it), while also strengthening the foreign currencies as well, and keeping them from becoming too competitively cheap. So how does this work in action? According to Economic policy institute, China spent half a trillion dollars in 2013 alone purchasing foreign currencies with the goal to weaken the yuan and strengthening the purchased foreign currencies. This currency manipulation around the world cost the USA between 2.3 and 5.8 million jobs, as well as hundreds of billions in trade deficit. Like all trade relations, currency manipulation is an inherently self-serving and competitive move by many countries. In August 2015, they devalued their currency by nearly 2% against the US Dollar, forcing China's trade balance to favor exports over imports.", "created": 1780965774585, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3005/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4me3pu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency manipulation is the way countries attempt to avoid the negative market effects of having a strong currency. The value of a currency is essentially dependent on how much or how little it is used, which in turn is dependent on how strong a country's trade balance is. When China has a trade surplus, people in other countries basically have to buy Chinese currency in order to buy Chinese goods. With an increase in demand, the price or value of the currency goes up. However, as currencies get stronger, it becomes more expensive to purchase goods.", "created": 1780965774584, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3006/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mkm6b", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And lower interest rates can lead to higher inflation. This could all lead to lower, not higher, economic growth in the long run. To generate long term inclusive and sustainable growth, gov need to go beyond short-term spending and focus on strengthening their institutions, reinforce their infrastructure and consistently delivering basic services for their citizens like education, health. By doing do economic growth can support inclusion by creating jobs, lifting living standards and ensuring opportunities for all.", "created": 1780965774583, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3007/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mowgx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What can gov do to increase economic growth? A gov can do a variety of things to boost economic growth. For ex: it can increase spending or lower taxes. Central banks can also lower interest rates to make it cheaper to borrow or invest which can help boost spending in the short term. But also, higher gov spending and lower taxes could also create unsustainable debts.", "created": 1780965774582, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3008/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mv0wl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Real GDP: GDP adjusted for inflation: if the nominal GDP grows by 10% and inflation is around 5% then real GDP growth is 5%.", "created": 1780965774581, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3009/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mrl0q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "GDP or Nominal GDP: Add all market values of all the goods and services produced in the economy in a year. GDP is not a measure of accumulated wealth. An economy can be poor, but it can have high rates of GDP growth.", "created": 1780965774580, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3010/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4m2iwh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why does Economic growth matter? Economic growth is important bcs more production usually means more jobs, higher incomes and less poverty so a better living standard. How is economic growth measured? Growth is measured by changes in GDP.", "created": 1780965774579, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3011/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4meq9m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Economic growth is the total increase in the value of all goods and services a country produce (like: bread, cars, machinery, hotel stays, restaurant meals) each year compared to last. For ex: let\u2019s imagine an economy that only produces cars, in the first year they produced 1000 cars, while in the second year they produced 1050. The real GDP growth in the second year would then be 5% (the 50 extra cars). Growth can also be negative for ex: if an economy that only produce cars produce 1000 cars in the first year and 900 cars in the second year then we would have a negative growth a 10% decline.", "created": 1780965774578, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3012/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mdysw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Unlike Euro, Canadian dollar and other currencies, who are positively correlated to equities. The US Dollar tends to be negatively correlated with equity markets, especially during times of market stress. This means that it tends to rise as the world stock markets fall, and vice versa. This can be a good source of diversification for foreign investors investing in American stocks overseas, as the currency gains of the US dollar help minimize the losses in a falling local stock market.", "created": 1780965774577, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3013/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mfxb9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currencies in countries with strong fundamentals tend to revert to their means and are less volatile over long periods of time, unless the Country is in a crisis then the currency just keeps losing value over time.", "created": 1780965774576, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3014/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4meqom", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What's an Emerging Market? the term \" Emerging Markets\" was introduced in 1981 by a world bank employee, who was promoting an investment fund for developing countries. Historically, the term emerging market has been applied to low-income countries that are experiencing strong economic growth. While many factors affect stock market returns, a growing economy helps create a positive environment in which companies can thrive and increase profit\u2019s. So rapid economic growth should imply a high stock market return. But is this always the case? China and India, two countries that have been the fastest growing economies among the G20 for the last 10-years. During that decade, the stock market returns of India and China have been well below those of the United States, whose economic growth has been much more modest at just 2% compared at 6.7% growth in China and 5% growth in India. - `18:08:22` --- note 3021/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mx1od", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Capital flight refers to the rapid movement of large sums of money or assets out of a country, often driven by economic, political, or social uncertainties. Signs of capital flight may include: 1-Sudden Currency Depreciation: If a country's currency experiences a rapid decline in value against other currencies, it could indicate that investors are withdrawing their funds from the country, leading to increased demand for foreign currencies. 2- Deteriorating Balance of Payments: A country's balance of payments is a record of it\u2019s economic transactions with the rest of the world. If a country's balance of payments shows a significan\u2019t outflow of capital, it could suggest capital flight. 3- Decline in Foreign Reserves: Central banks hold foreign reserves to stabilize their currency and meet international obligations. A sudden decrease in foreign reserves may suggest that capital is leaving the country. 4- Increased Demand for Safe-Haven Assets: During periods of capital flight, there is often an increased demand for safe-haven assets like gold, U.S. Treasuries, or stable foreign currencies as investors seek to preserve their wealth. 5- Rising Interest Rates: If a country experiences a sudden and significan\u2019t rise in interest rates, it could be an attempt to attract capital back into the country by offering higher returns on investments. Also a sign of investors Dumping the country sovereign Bonds which is leading to a spike in yield which is reflected in the spike of interest rates 6- Bank Runs: In extreme cases, capital flight may result in bank runs, where depositors rush to withdraw their funds from banks due to fears about the stability of the banking system. 7- Economic Instability: Widespread economic uncertainty, recession, high inflation, or volatile markets can lead investors to move their capital to more stable and predictable environments. 8- Government Measures: If the government implements restrictive capital controls, such as limit\u2019s on the amount of money that can be taken out of the country or restrictions on foreign exchange transactions, it may be an indicator that capital flight is occurring or anticipated.", "created": 1780965774543, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3022/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mbuvd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Financial Repression ALWAYS leads to capital flight bcs of the carry trade. This will most likely benefit the US dollar and US assets as the capital flight would flow into the USA. And also, it will most likely benefit the countries with the lowest debt to GDP such as Hong Kong and Kuwait.", "created": 1780965774542, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mpzon", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Commercial paper is a type of debt security that Corporations use as an alternative to loans to raise capital. Commercial paper is a short-term, unsecured debt obligation typically issued by large banks and Corporations. The nature of commercial paper makes it most suitable for institutional investors and perhaps wealthy individuals to buy it directly. Smaller investors are most likely to have exposure to it through products such as money market funds. Commercial paper is issued by large institutions to raise money to cover short-term financial needs. It pays fixed interest rates and has maturities ranging from as few as one to as many as 270 days.", "created": 1780965774508, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mnzux", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The reason the Dollar is the world's reserve currency is bcs the dollar has embedded advantages :1- Above all the United States have the rule of law. 2- United States is the only country in the world with a bond market big enough to absorb global savings, the US treasury market is huge and very liquid with a big infrastructure ranging from primary dealers who bid at auctions, settlements, clearance, futures hedging, options hedging, depository trust Corporation.", "created": 1780965774391, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3072/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4mtq4i", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How is the price of a currency determined? The price of a currency is closely tied to supply and demand. When the demand increases for Bonds, goods, services and investments the price of the currency goes up. On the other hand, when the Fed print more dollars thereby increasing the dollar supply. The price of dollar cools off and go down. Speculators can also lead to a rise of the dollar. Economic and political conditions of the issuing country affect the price of the currency if the country is going through a political conflict or an economic crisis then the value of it\u2019s currency Dump. The value of a currency is also linked to the future prospects of it\u2019s issuing country, a country that is said to have a good future prospect if it has inflation and unemployment under control and have a sound economic policy. A good prospect may need to increase demand enhance higher value.", "created": 1780965774387, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l41im", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1-Japanese Yen (JPY): The Japanese yen has historically been a popular currency for carry trades due to Japan's long-standing low-interest rate policy. Traders often borrow yen at low rates and invest in higher-yielding currencies. 2-Swiss Franc (CHF): The Swiss franc has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Switzerland's traditionally low-interest rates. 3-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar is frequently used as a funding currency in carry trades, especially when interest rates in the United States are low, as it provides access to a wide range of higher-yielding currencies. 4-Australian Dollar (AUD): The Australian dollar is a popular target currency for carry trades because of Australia's relatively high-interest rates compared to other developed economies. 5-New Zealand Dollar (NZD): Similar to the Australian dollar, the New Zealand dollar is often used in carry trades due to New Zealand's comparatively high-interest rates. 6-Euro (EUR): The euro can be involved in carry trades, especially when there is a significan\u2019t interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, making it an attractive target for investors. 7-British Pound (GBP): The British pound can also be part of carry trade strategies, with traders borrowing in currencies like the Japanese yen or Swiss franc and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in GBP.", "created": 1780965774359, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3080/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l3c7g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FOREX is one of the most influential markets in the world. FOREX daily trading volume is more than the annual GDP of all but two of the largest nations on Earth China and the USA. - `18:08:22` --- note 3096/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lfwze", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How can EM keep their economy afloat without solely relying on monetary policy? Most EM rely on the monetary policy to do all the heavy lifting and monetary policy does have some spill overs. For ex: Japan use monetary expansion to stimulate the economy but that has led to currency depreciation and Japan whole point of doing it is to depreciate their currency to boost their exports, but Japan is a big global powerhouse and most EM just use monetary policy to get by and dig their way out of trouble which just cause inflation and currency depreciation in those countries. EM should have better policies: fiscal and structural policies, better labor and product markets, better financial markets so that they don\u2019t have to rely so much on monetary policy to keep their economies afloat which is the case in many EM economies. Maybe it would be better if in EM you have financial markets that when money comes in from abroad can be intermediated into long term investments maybe into infrastructure, into other productivity enhancing investments that creates much less turmoil in financial markets.", "created": 1780965774319, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 3125/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ljmrl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FX SWAP interest Rate and FX Swap roll overs: A foreign exchange swap, also known as an FX swap, is an agreement to simultaneously borrow one currency and lend another at an initial date, then exchanging the amounts at maturity. The swap rate is calculated as the difference between the interest rates on one currency and another. For example, if the USD interest rate is 3% and the EUR interest rate is 2%, then the USD/EUR swap rate will be 1%. The spread over LIBOR is defined as the difference between LIBOR and the swap rate.", "created": 1780965774251, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

So as people are trying to get their hands on collateral (US treasuries), the price of treasuries pump and because investors need dollar to buy US treasuries and because the price of treasuries just pumped that means global investors need more and more dollars to buy and, in a world, structurally short of dollars as is we see why this sudden bigger new demand for dollar would pump the dollar price.", "created": 1780965774239, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 3145/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lp0e1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar has become a comprehensive blackhole: we have securities dealers inside the US funding their credit activity which is floating Corp credit, Corp bonds or municipal bonds by borrowing outside the United States in the Eurodollar market instead of borrowing inside the US (that\u2019s bcs is it\u2019s much cheaper to borrow in the Eurodollar through FX swaps).", "created": 1780965774230, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3146/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 3147/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l0q7y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "As interest rates go up fixed income bond prices fall. well, what\u2019s the biggest source of collateral is? US treasuries. - `18:08:22` --- note 3148/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4liv8h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How do Fed contracts credit and dump asset prices to slow down economy and slow inflation by raising rates? Everything in the world is priced off the 10-year US treasury bcs it\u2019s the global Risk-free rate. So as the risk free rate rises (as the 10-year us treasury yield rises) it has a dramatic impact on a number of different asset classes, if you do a discounted cash flow analysis as 10-year yield rises now you are dividing by a bigger number, and when you divide by a bigger number you get a smaller evaluation so that has an impact on market prices and this why the FED hike rates that\u2019s why the FED wants higher rates bcs it\u2019s the way the bring down asset prices and slow the economy and as a result bring down inflation. So as interest rates go up you discount your cash flow at a bigger number, so you get a lower valuation. As interest rates go up fixed income bond prices fall. well, what\u2019s the biggest source of collateral is? US treasuries. So as US treasuries fall the collateral off which new loans can be made which is the entire system (the entire system runs off new loans being made), as the collateral value falls less new loans can be made which slows down credit and lending and as a result you get a slowing down in the economy.", "created": 1780965774227, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lks7l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why do financial crisis Always to happen in the fall around September? Corps must satisfy regulations: Corp Quarterly tax payments and liquidity coverage ratio at the end of each quarter (March, June, September, December) and since two for those Quarterly filing and payments fall in the period between September to December and since the last quarter of the year that\u2019s why Corps usually holds tight to their liquidity to meet the regulations and only would lend out their excess liquidity in good times. So Corps may have reserves available but are unable to lend them out as they need to hold on to them to satisfy the regulations particularly at the end of the quarter like in September or in December since that\u2019s when reporting take place and they will want their own balance sheet to look safer so banks be holding to their reserves for themselves. There are two financial deadlines that suck cash out of the system on the same night causing a crunch. September 16th was the cutoff date for banks to submit their quarterly tax payments, so a lot of money that they might usually lend in the repo market was being sucked out of their accounts and deposited into the treasury. For ex in the September 2019 crash: September 16 was the deadline for quarterly tax payment and September 16th was also the day $78 Billion of treasury debt was scheduled to settle which means just another crunch of cash was being turned into securities on that day too, you add to that the Liquidity Coverage Ratio that requires banks to keep a certain amount of reserves or cash on hold at the FED at all times which aims to improve the banking sector's ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress, bank argued that keeping bank reserves with fed on hold makes it harder for them to lend out cash on a dime when money gets tight. Fed has signaled they would rather provide the extra liquidity into the system than lower LCR (liquidity coverage ratio) and since then the FED has done just that. In October 2020 Fed announced they be buying $60 billion a month in short term treasury debt and continue to do so until at least June 2020 so they took in treasuries and gave out cash to the market which meant they provided money into the system to borrow even if the Repo players stop lending again, it aims to boost reserves allowing banks to stay liquid without violating the rule and in doing so it\u2019s keep the wheels of fina

- `18:08:22` --- note 3185/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lvozo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo Market provides the cash the financial firms need to run their daily operations, it provides a lot of the grease that keeps the financial market wheels spinning.", "created": 1780965774182, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3186/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lq8zk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Never forget, when the Fed raises rates, they raise rates on the whole world.", "created": 1780965774181, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3187/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ljb7w", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "To monitor global liquidity, We have to monitor: First and foremost Central bank balance sheets and second Money Supply for US, EURO area and Japan.", "created": 1780965774180, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3188/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l5vr3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE aims to boost reserves allowing banks to stay liquid without violating the liquidity coverage ratio rule and in doing so it\u2019s keep the wheels of financial system spinning.", "created": 1780965774179, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3189/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l9jek", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Philips curve: Relationship between unemployment and inflation: there is an inverse relationship between the two variables. In other words, when unemployment is high, inflation is low, and vice versa.", "created": 1780965774177, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3190/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4liqb6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The whole idea of tightening policy is to affect financial conditions. To the extent that Higher bond yields produce tighter financial conditions. That\u2019s exactly how monetary policy works. Basically, by the bond yields going up the bond market would be doing the FED job for them by tightening financial conditions.", "created": 1780965774176, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3191/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l5kku", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Interest rates is the only tool the fed have to bring inflation down.", "created": 1780965774175, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3192/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lbyj4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Expected changes in Fed policy affects financial conditions and persistent changes in financial conditions affects economic activity, hiring and inflation.", "created": 1780965774174, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3193/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l4955", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Term premium: the compensation for holding longer term securities.", "created": 1780965774173, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3194/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lolrx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How does financial conditions changes affect the economy? The standard channels are: DXY Exchange rate, asset prices, interest sensitive spendings.", "created": 1780965774171, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3195/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lfi0r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Institutions go to the Repo Market when they need to borrow cash for their day-to-day activities.", "created": 1780965774170, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3196/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lk27o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How did institutions end up with so much cash after covid QE (the money that piled into reverse repo after that)? To keep interest rate positives after all the covid QE printing, they removed the requirement of banks to need to have collateral on their balance. Basically, they said just keep the cash u don\u2019t need to buy the collateral to meet the requirement of a certain percentage of US treasuries in the banks\u2019 balance sheet to stay solvent and financially sound.", "created": 1780965774166, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3197/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l13iv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Persistent changes in financial conditions can have implications for the path of monetary policy.", "created": 1780965774159, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3198/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lfovl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Longer term bond yields play an important role in tightening financial conditions.", "created": 1780965774158, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3199/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lmuf5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Actual and EXPECTED changes in the stance of Monetary policy affects broader financial conditions which in turn affect economic activity, employment and inflation.", "created": 1780965774157, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3200/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lf9eb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Tight monetary policy put downward pressures on economic activity and inflation.", "created": 1780965774156, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3201/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lwrqt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed hiking rates strengthen the Dollar. Rising rates keep the dollar stronger.", "created": 1780965774154, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3202/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lacut", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the US gov budget deficit grow, global investors will still buy treasuries, but they have to be paid the right price to do so. Whenever we see a huge flood of new supply of treasuries, we see bond price go down and yields go up to make the new supply of treasuries attractive enough for global investors to buy them.", "created": 1780965774153, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3203/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lyt67", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Wars are inflationary so the Fed would most likely hold rates high during wars.", "created": 1780965774152, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3204/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lsucz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Financial collateral is incredibly important, there isn\u2019t a part of the monetary system, the financial markets or the real economy that collateral does not impact.", "created": 1780965774150, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3205/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lu4av", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Financial collateral is not just some quirk of the banking system, it is in many ways the lifeblood if not the essence of the Eurodollar system it\u2019self.", "created": 1780965774149, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3206/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ld2cx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Treasury yield curve, Eurodollar futures yield curve and German Bund yield curve ALL inverted are the best single indicator for a recession, it signals Manheim MEGA DUMP is coming, the last time we saw all of them inverted at once was in 2007 just ahead of the 2008 financial catastrophe. When these inversion start, they are about a year forward.", "created": 1780965774146, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3207/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l945w", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What does a liquidity crisis look like to mom and pop? It looks like can\u2019t get a loan, interest rates on credit card and mortgages go up.", "created": 1780965774145, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3208/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l5ah4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Inverted yield curve, big deal. The yield on a one-year bill is higher than a 10-year treasury note. Okay so if i lend u money for a year i might want a certain interest rate, but if im gonna lend you money for 10-years i would want a higher interest rate bcs there's more risk, inflation, credit risk, etc. So why is the yield on that 10-year note lower than the one-year bill, it makes no sense except unless you think smthg bad is gonna happen like a really bad recession then that yield on that 10-year note looks really good bcs you are gonna have huge capital gains when that yield actually collapses. The Fed can control the very short end of the yield curve but they can't control the 5 year notes, 10-year notes, let alone the 30 year bonds. So, an inverted yield curve is telling you smthg really bad is gonna happen otherwise those long-term bond yields wouldn\u2019t be lower.", "created": 1780965774144, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3209/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lifiq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "August 17th, 1998, Russia defaulted on their external debt and the ruble was grossly devalued, we came within hours of shutting every market in the world. It began with the Russian default and that started a global liquidity crisis that went around the world. Long term capital management had $1.4 Trillion of derivatives, and everyone goes: \"oh long term capital lost a lot of money in Russia\" but they didn\u2019t they lost about $100 Million in Russia but they lost close to $4 Billion on everything else bcs in a liquidity crisis people sell everything, it's not a question of \"Do you have Russian bonds?\" NO THEY SELL EVERYTHING. SPREAD WIDEN. NOT ENOUGH COLLATERAL. MARGIN CALLS. PEOPLE BLOWN OUT OF THEIR POSITIONS. THAT\u2019S WHAT A GLOBAL FINANCIAL CRISIS LOOKS LIKE", "created": 1780965774140, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3210/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lisfc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But that started in June 1997 when Thailand broke the peg to the dollar starting a run on the bank in Thailand, it spread to Malaysia, Indonesia, South Korea, and then it went to Russia long term capital.", "created": 1780965774139, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3211/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lrr48", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The last two super liquidity crises when the world almost completely collapsed were: 1998 (long term capital management, Russia) and 2008 (during Lehman Brothers). Sunday September 15th Lehman Brothers filed bankruptcy electronically on a Sunday night, but that crisis started in 2007, so it took a year for that crisis to go around. Same thing with long term capital it came to a head in September 1998 we were hours away from shutting every financial market in the world.", "created": 1780965774138, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3212/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lgowu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In 1990 we had a mild recession and there was no financial panic. 2020 was interesting, technically we can call it a recession but the economy drops 31% annualized after they shut down the economy, they say in 2 quarters (Q1,Q2) but if you break it down it was March and April which happen to fall in 2 Quarters and took both quarters negative but it was really 2 months down 31% annualized in 2 months and then up 35% by the 3rd Quarter so maybe that was technically a recession but that was not a financial panic: the stock market fell but the banks didn\u2019t fail: nobody was lined up to take the money out of citibank etc. So you can have recessions without panics and you can have panics without recessions. October 19th, 1987, Dow falls 22% in one day with no recession but sometimes they do go together. In 2008 they did we had both, we had a financial panic: Bearn Stearns, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Lehman, AIG all fell. Morgan Stanley was days away and then Goldman and Citi would have been right behind them. And the economy collapsed, and the stock market fell well over 50%, i think 60%. So, 2008 was an example of both.", "created": 1780965774136, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3213/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lcez7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A really important distinction between a recession, even a really bad one and a financial crisis bcs they are two different things, they can come together. For ex: in 1998 we had an acute financial crisis, 1994 the tequila crisis, then there was the bond market massacre. There have been these financial crises, but there was no recession in 1998 in fact the Nasdaq went to the moon in 1998. But the opposite is true you can have a recession without a financial panic.", "created": 1780965774135, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3214/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lm0gc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "DV01 concept: which is the dollar value of one basis point and what it means is if interest rates go up 25 basis points what\u2019s the change in the price of securities. In other words, what's the rates up prices down, rates down prices up that's just bond math but it's not uniform or linear at all levels of rates. So when you are at higher rates the DV01 is lower and at lower rates the DV01 is higher, which means the impact of every basis point increase in interest rates is greater at lower levels. So in other words raising rates from 0.5% to 2.5% is much more damaging to prices then going from 8% to 10%. Much higher interest rates, whole different world. But the impact of that on bond prices is less than going from 0.5% to 2.5%. And this plays out in derivatives world bcs that's another factor, along with scarcity of collateral, shortage of dollars, quadrillion dollars in notional de-leveraging balance sheets and a higher DV01, meaning these interest rate hikes do more damage per basis point to bond prices than if they were at a higher level and that\u2019s definitely a cause for concern.", "created": 1780965774134, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3215/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4l7r0j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Treasury yield curve is a short-term bet on a long-term rate. Yield curve should be upward sloping just bcs time value of money and uncertainty, etc. If i lend for a longer period of time or make a further forward bet, I should get a higher rate. Well, how come people betting on overnight rates a year or two years from now think that rates are going to be lower? And that shouldn't happen. The only explanation for that is we're going to get into recession, It's going to get a lot worse.", "created": 1780965774133, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3216/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lw2mo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Eurodollar futures curve is a long-term bet on a short-term rate bcs the Eurodollar future is it's like we are betting on what an overnight rate is going to be two years from now.", "created": 1780965774132, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3217/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lkfwn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A Dovish Monetary policy can be used to support bonds through QE (printing money and buying bonds to lower interest rates which will increase bond values). A Hawkish Monetary policy can also be used to support currencies by higher rates and QT. But Monetary policy can't save both bonds and the currency at the same time. Ultimately the govs has to choose ONE and they ALWAYS choose to sacrifice the currency in order to save the system (the bond market) that\u2019s bcs the bond market is tied to the equity markets and to the financial markets and to everything else.", "created": 1780965774129, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3218/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ljnad", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Govs often find themselves in a dilemma whether to save the system (the bond market) or to save the currency. They often choose to save the bond market bcs that\u2019s how the gov is funded and also the bond market impacts the equity market, impacts financial markets, impacts pensions, impacts banks.", "created": 1780965774128, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3219/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lun15", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When do Fed pivot and start cutting rates? The Fed is a reactionary agency not an anticipatory agency. Shit has to be hitting the fan for them to step in and save the market, that\u2019s why they cut rate and inject liquidity it\u2019s bcs they are trying to stop the mega dump carnage and they are throwing everything they can at it trying to stop that mega dump. Fed will pivot and cut rates if the market sells off or if there is some kind of a risk off event that forces them to come in and save the market then of course they will pivot but unless we are in a crisis, if we were to just go sideways in the S&P 500 for a year or even down 10%, 15% or even 20% in the S&P500 or the broad markets over the next 12 to 15 months and if unemployment ticked up slowly that wouldn\u2019t cause them to pivot but if we have one of the kneejerk elevator shaft drawdowns in the broad risk markets and we have a liquidity crisis then of course fed will be forced to step in to save the market but barring a major bloody dump in the market and unemployment just suddenly going up through the roof the fed won\u2019t step in.", "created": 1780965774127, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3220/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4ln2dg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed tighten monetary policy by hiking rates increasing Fed funds rate and decreasing securities holdings. And it loosens monetary policy by cutting rates and increasing security holdings.", "created": 1780965774126, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3221/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4luamj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But it happens over the course of a year or longer. What we see the bank saying is: I don\u2019t want Corp bonds as collateral, I don\u2019t want your mortgages as collateral, I don\u2019t even want ten-year Treasury notes as collateral.", "created": 1780965774107, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3222/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lajiu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How could there be a global dollar shortage after the Fed just printed $9 Trillion? What people don\u2019t understand is that behind the curtain, off balance sheet: There are $1 Quadrillion of derivatives.", "created": 1780965774103, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3223/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4lpood", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "40 weeks to 80 weeks since halving has been a proven as a consistent profit taking time frame. Bitcoin Top has ALWAYS occurred 40 weeks to 80 weeks (between 335 days and 487 days from halving). In every bitcoin cycle people predict much higher prices than bitcoin actually goes to, it seems like bitcoin Always seem to fell short from the price target that most people set. So traders and investors don\u2019t take profit\u2019s bcs they are waiting for a specific price that never shows up. There is a solution for this: Instead of focusing on price we should focus on time. 40 weeks to 80 weeks since halving has been a proven as a consistent profit taking time frame.", "created": 1780965774102, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3224/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 3225/12122  ---

Monitors google trend search terms such as: \"How to Buy Crypto\", \"Bitcoin\", \"doge\". A top is the google trend search term always marked the top.", "created": 1780965774096, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3226/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k02bg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stock prices are inversely valued based on interest rates. So, all else being equal, if interest rates go up, stock prices should come down. Same with bonds, if interest rates go up then bond prices come down, they're the opposite of rates.", "created": 1780965774086, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3227/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k279s", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "As the yield to maturity on the 10-year note go up that strengthens the dollar while the 10-year yield going down weakens the dollar.", "created": 1780965774083, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3228/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k24zb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The yield to maturity on 10-year Treasury notes is the benchmark security. If you are making investment decisions: The 10-year note is the right benchmark for the large long-term investments bcs it\u2019s an alternative place to invest money.", "created": 1780965774082, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3229/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k0g2m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed can control the very short end of the yield curve, but they can't control the 5-year notes, 10-year notes, let alone the 30 year bonds.", "created": 1780965774081, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3230/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k0luf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Forecasting the consequences of Fed policy is difficult. But forecasting Fed policy is the easiest thing in the world bcs they tell you what they are going to do but the hard part is what's gonna happen as a result of that.", "created": 1780965774080, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
