- `18:08:22` --- note 3234/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kpeto", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If reverse repo facility dry up there 0 money there, the gov would try to borrow from the treasury general account (the gov checking account) but that would signal a MASSIVE EMERGENCY and at that point the only way out will be the Federal Reserve. One option the Federal Reserve would have at that point is to restart Quantitative easing (QE is when the Federal Reserve buys assets just like treasuries which grows the Fed balance sheet, they buy them by digitally printing money and that new cash ends up in the hands of the US gov just like it happens anytime even a regular bank purchases a US treasury lending the money to the US gov. If QE isn\u2019t enough to make up for the lack of liquidity in the system, at that point they may need to engage in the Japan playbook and start yield curve control.", "created": 1780965774067, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3235/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k81wu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A sell off in US Treasuries is a massive disruption in what is supposed to be the most liquid and safest financial asset in the world. IF US TREASURY MARKET ISN\u2019T SAFE NOTHING IS SAFE AT THE POINT.", "created": 1780965774066, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3236/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kgtya", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bid to cover ratio: The difference between the numbers of dollars there are that the gov could borrow and the number of dollars is trying to borrow on that day.", "created": 1780965774064, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3237/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k190e", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Allotted at High % usually is about 32%. In September 11, 2008 it was 82.6%. the global financial crisis hit one week later. Another important metric for liquidity is the Bid to Cover Ratio, the higher the bid to cover ratio the more liquidity and vice versa. (September 15, 2008, financial crisis happened the same day of the issue date of the treasuries, we can find both metrics in the treasury auctions results). If we ever see a tail in the 4, 5, or 6bp range (0.4%, 0.5%, 0.6%, this would be considered disastrous in the bond world and mean things are breaking in US Treasuries.", "created": 1780965774063, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3238/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k9qk3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "One of the most important metric for liquidity that warns us about financial crisis and global liquidity crisis is: \"allotted at High %\", \"comparing high yield to interest rate\" and \"Bid to Cover Ratio\" in Treasury auctions.", "created": 1780965774061, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3239/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4khz88", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2- A High allotted at High % (September 11,2008 10-year auction allotted at high % was 82.6% and tail was 40 basis points 0.4%), (March 11, 2020, 10-year auction Allotted at high was 74.94% and tail was 40 beeps or 0.4%). So Both 2008 and 2020 black swans had a very high allotted at high % (double what it would be in Normal times 82% and 74% vs 32% in Normal times) and a tail that's 20 times higher what it would be in normal times (40 beeps 0.4% vs 1 or 2 beeps 0.01% or 0.02% in normal times). A high Allotted at high % also marked EVERY crypto TOP (November 8, 2017, 94.01% and 60.17% October 12,2021).", "created": 1780965774057, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3240/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k93m2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "0.4% might not sound like a Big Deal to you but in the Treasuries world that is considered ABSOLUTELY CATASTROPHIC.", "created": 1780965774056, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3241/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k7eja", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So if we ever see a tail in the 4, 5, or 6bp range (0.4%, 0.5%, 0.6%, this would be considered disastrous in the bond world and mean things are breaking up in US Treasuries.", "created": 1780965774055, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3242/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kaljs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What's considered NOT NORMAL in a treasury auction? 1- A Long tail: simply visualizing what the difference is between what the gov wanted to borrow their debt at and what they ended up having to pay for ex: if they wanted to borrow at 5% and ended up paying 5.02%, The tail or the difference is 2 basis points 0.02%. Usually, the tail or the difference doesn't dip below 1 basis points or 0.01% but every once is a while it dips below 2 basis points 0.02%.", "created": 1780965774054, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3243/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kncdg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When looking at treasury auctions TO ANALYZE LIQUIDITY and to look for warnings of black swan events or financial crisis it\u2019s very important to make sure we are looking at the 10-year treasury auction bcs it\u2019s the MOST important one.", "created": 1780965774052, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3244/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k3ty9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And at some point, you unwind it, but what you usually do is just roll it over. So a phone call to the Fed will get you All the treasury bills you want. So why doesn't that solve the problem? The answer is the Fed bills cannot be rehypothecated. They can't be used the way the dealers want. They can't send them to Deutsche bank. But if i buy the bills at auction I can. And so there's a liquidity preference for buying treasury bills at auction because I can pledge them to somebody else and that's what they do. But if i do the reverse repo, I got to hang on to them bcs the Fed won't let me rehypothecate them. And so that's why the yield to maturity at auction is lower than what the Fed will give you for basically for free. But it's another one of these weird, quirky little inversions but it tells you smthg , it tell you there's a Dollar shortage and that will get worse as we go into recession and credit losses pile up and banks get stressed and balance sheets get reduced and dealers say it's Treasury bills give me a four week bill, you know. That's going to drive the Dollar Higher against basically the Euro.", "created": 1780965774051, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3245/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k9623", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed will actually give you all the treasury bills you want. All you have to do is just do a reverse repo with the Fed. You deposit your cash with the Fed and they send you Treasury Bills, and it can be overnight, one week, whatever.", "created": 1780965774050, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3246/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kzdp5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The economy is turning down and Everyone is worried about this. Well, if you are Deutsche Bank or Barclays or HSBC or Unibanco or Bank Santander, you have a central bank that doesn't print dollars. ECB can print all the Euros it want but it doesn't print dollars. Where are you gonna get the dollars? Well, if you want to buy dollar denominated Treasury bills, you got to get dollars so you can pay for them. THAT'S WHAT WILL DRIVE THE DOLLAR HIGHER. So you are desperate, THEY HAVE TO GET DOLLARS TO PROP UP THEIR OWN BANKS, if you are the people's bank of China, you've got to prop up the Chinese banking system. If you are the Swiss National bank, you've got to prop up Credit Suisse, etc and if you a foreign central bank you gonna need dollars to prop up your own banks and banking system.", "created": 1780965774049, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3247/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kdcoz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So what supports that? How do you get a $1 Quadrillion position (thousand trillion)? Well, the answer is collateral, but not that much. It's kind of like 1% collateral under the 1 quadrillion. So, in a credit crunch, when going into a recession, what do banks say to each other and what do banks say to hedge fund clients in terms of the quality of collateral? They say i don\u2019t want your mortgages, I don't want your Corporates, i don\u2019t even want ten-year treasury notes, i don\u2019t want five year treasury notes, I WANT TREASURY BILLS, THAT IS THE BEST, THE LEAST VOLATILE, MOST LIQUID, MOST CREDITWORTHY INSTRUMENT IN THE WORLD. And in a world where balance sheets are contracting, credit fears are rising.", "created": 1780965774048, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3248/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k8ru5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Global Dollar shortage: If we are expecting a bad recession and if we have an inverted yield curve which is a reliable warning of recession. We should ask ourselves: What's behind the curtains? what are the real reasons that are making the yield curve inverted Sending a very bad signal? The answer is there's a mad scramble for dollars. There is a serious dollar shortage, and people roll their eyes like wait a second , you know China is dumping their treasuries, Brazil dumping treasuries so what do you mean there is a dollar shortage? Well there is a dollar shortage and we can see it but there is a reason for it. One Quadrillion is 1000 Trillion, that's approximately the notional value of all the derivatives, off balance sheet derivatives of all the banks and hedge funds in the world, it's about 1 Quadrillion. We're talking options, futures, swaps, swap options, FX forwards.", "created": 1780965774047, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3249/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kof6d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yield Curve inversion is a sign of Dollar Shortage. When yield curve uninvert that signals DXY is about to pump. (US05Y-US10Y) (US03Y-US10Y)", "created": 1780965774046, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3250/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kiqhy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "TREASURY BILLS ARE THE BEST, THE LEAST VOLATILE, MOST LIQUID, MOST CREDITWORTHY INSTRUMENT IN THE WORLD.", "created": 1780965774045, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3251/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kmzi3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The stability of the Monetary system doesn't depend on who sells what for dollars. They Money doesn't disappear it has to go back into the system, it's a closed circuit, that's how the Eurodollar system works. But it presupposes that you can always borrow in the Eurodollar market. In other words, that closed circuit analogy is correct, provided the big banks are willing to lend to each other. When big banks stop lending to each other causing the money supply in the Eurodollar to shrink that is a heart attack in the global financial system.", "created": 1780965774044, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3252/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kciky", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "where does the money come from that runs the economy? It comes from the commercial banks, it comes from M1 Money supply and M2 Money supply which are created by the commercial banks at will.", "created": 1780965774043, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3253/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kxudt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "and Eurodollars in particular is a mad scramble for dollar based, high quality, dollar-based collateral. And that's what's driving the dollar.", "created": 1780965774042, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3254/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kppgu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Give me at a stretch, I'll take a two year note with a haircut or what i really want are 30, 60, 90-day bills. I want treasury bills. And so, you got to go out and get the Treasury bills and they're dollar denominated, which means you need dollars. So, if you are Credit Suisse or Barclays or Hong Kong, Shanghai or Deutsche Bank, you don't live in a country that prints dollars, the US does but the European central bank doesn't. So, there is this enormous demand for dollars, not bcs they love the dollar but bcs they need to buy dollar denominated collateral of a very high quality in order to pledge as collateral to support the Quadrillion derivatives position as plus any other trading they're doing. And so that's the clue, that's the secret that unlocks the whole mystery, which is it doesn't matter what the debt to GDP ratio is, the deficit, labor participation rate. None of those matters, what's going on, Not in M0 but in M1", "created": 1780965774041, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3255/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k6grd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How can you have a dollar shortage with trillions of dollars in new printed money? Well, you have $1 Quadrillion ($1000 Trillion) of derivatives in the banking system. So that slice, whether it's the $7 trillion of M0, or the $24 Trillion of M1 that must support $1 Quadrillion of derivatives. Now it's not dollar for dollar but you had to put some collateral, and then you get into the collateral issues of, well what's a good collateral? The answer is and this is what the banks are saying to each other and that's what happened in 2008: the banks are looking at each other saying: i don't want your Corporates, I don't want your mortgages, I don't even want your 10-year notes.", "created": 1780965774040, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3256/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kpac7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "M0 Money supply is very important for liquidity and the financial markets but it\u2019s irrelevant to the Economy, it just doesn't matter when it comes to the Economy.", "created": 1780965774039, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3257/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k4hhl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Excess reserves: bank deposit\u2019s at the Fed.", "created": 1780965774037, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3258/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k34wu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed discount operation: Fed says to the banks send us your bonds and we will give you cash.", "created": 1780965774035, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3259/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kz8oy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Quantitave Tightening: Fed do QT by letting bonds mature and not reinvesting.", "created": 1780965774034, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3260/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k7b24", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed cutting rates at the same time they are expanding their balance sheet is the MEGA QE. Bcs every 1% rate cut has the same effect as the FED expanding their balance sheet by $ 1 Trillion so cutting rates at the same time of expanding the balance sheet is like expanding the balance sheet double the amount but we should always remember Monetary policy works with a lag.", "created": 1780965774033, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3261/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4korrz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Monetary policy works with a lag.", "created": 1780965774032, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3262/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4khmbd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Every 1% of Fed rate hikes is equal to Fed shrinking it\u2019s balance sheet by a $ 1 Trillion.", "created": 1780965774031, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3263/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kmrs0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In addition to raising rates don't forget QT. It's very hard to estimate the monetary impact of shrinking the balance sheet, but the best estimate is for every trillion dollars that Fed shrink it\u2019s balance sheet, it\u2019s probably equal to a one percentage point hike in the Fed funds rate. So the tightening has been more than just taking the Fed funds rate up. You also have to take into account QT.", "created": 1780965774030, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3264/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k0zfz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yield Curve control is saying Im gonna buy as many of them as needed to maintain a specific interest rate and a specific price. Both QE and yield curve control are GUARANTEED TO CAUSE INFLATION.", "created": 1780965774029, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3265/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kogvp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What's the difference between Quantitative easing and yield curve control? QE and yield curve control are qualitatively two different things: QE is saying Im going to buy a certain number of assets every month.", "created": 1780965774028, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3266/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kvk9p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Gov having to pay a tail of 0.4% higher than interest rate might not sound like a Big Deal to you but in the Treasuries world that is considered ABSOLUTELY CATASTROPHIC.", "created": 1780965774027, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3267/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4kznlz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Commercial banks\u2019 lending does matter and the Eurodollar do matter. That's how we run the system.", "created": 1780965774024, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3268/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x1e4k1uex", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE FEDERAL RESERVE HAS TWO MANDATES: 1- TO MAINTAIN STABLE PRICES (CONTROL INFLATION). 2- MAINTAIN MAXIMUM EMPLOYMENT.", "created": 1780965774023, "pinned": false, "source": "Financial Notes to print.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 3270/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0ot2n9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Is it necessary to use technical indicators when you trading? Absolutely Not, they are just a filter to filter out noise when applying macro trends. Technical indicators along chart patterns they are more to serve as tool to timing the market in the short term (over a day period or even a week), to time entries and exits but Macro is the king that rules.", "created": 1780965733286, "pinned": false, "source": "Final printing notes 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3271/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0o7dur", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Technical indicators: are nothing more than expressions of filters so a technical indicator is nothing more than a filter that tries to get rid of noise, some of them are lagging and some of them try to be forward looking by looking at turning points in the market. The question you have to ask yourself is not whats the magic behind this filter but how persistent is the behavior in the market that will allow you to apply the filter so what you tend to find is that certain types of indicators are very good when the market is quiet when we dont expect a lot of news announcements to come bcs the one thing that shocks the market is news that then creates policy shifts and anticipation about the future as as long as your are okay with applying these things during periods where you dont expect big shocks then yes technical indicators should work just fine.", "created": 1780965733285, "pinned": false, "source": "Final printing notes 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3272/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0os4o7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And While bonds were getting crushed during fed hikes stocks actually either stayed flat or went higher in all the previous fed rate hikes. For ex: between 1977 to 1981 fed hiked rates from 5.5% to 20% so fed fund rate had a growth rate of 290% , the logn term bonds dumped 35% while stocks went up 30%. between 2015 and 2018 fed hiked rates from 0.25% to 2.5% a rate growth of 900% long term bond dumped 15% while S&P went up 30%. Between 2022 and 2023 fed hiked from 0.25% to 5.50% a fed fund growth rate of 2000% long term bonds dumped by 35% while stocks intially dumped 25% they recovered and end up only down 5% by the end of 2023.", "created": 1780965733284, "pinned": false, "source": "Final printing notes 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3273/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0oco8o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "people say higher interest rates are bad for stocks, as soon as interest rates start going up you should sell stocks but the reality is the S&P500 went up during everyone of those hiking cycles. Now it didnt go up a lot and a lot of times it ALWAYS went up kinda of AT THE END bcs people were anticipating a FED pivot and rate cuts were coming soon. But at every single rate hike stocks only went PUMPED after a DUMP, so once the fed start hiking stocks DUMP and then they would recover toward the end of the hiking cycle as the market anticipate a fed pivot.", "created": 1780965733283, "pinned": false, "source": "Final printing notes 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 3274/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0mbcvn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How does Reverse Repo facility prevent liquidity issues? Reverse Repo prevents the federal gov from going out there and say hey we need to borrow money and then regardless of the rate they offer nobody has any dollars to lend to them. When Fed pause hiking rates which means they don\u2019t need the Reverse Repo as a floor underneath interest rate to move higher to keep them from falling. Usually when the money leaves Reverse Repo facility it goes to short term treasuries. As the US gov has to borrow more and more and more they would have to continue to pay higher and higher interest rates as they pay these higher interest rates, they become more attractive bcs that\u2019s a better return than what the FED is paying in the reverse repo facility. Jerome Powell once said that the treasury general account would be rebuilt using the reverse repo facility. Banks and Money Markets usually park their money RISK FREE either in Reverse Repo facility (that acts as a floor) or short-term treasury bills and they would usually go with which one in the two is paying a higher interest rate. - `18:08:22` --- note 3285/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0h0l80ki", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Once a significant volume of fails occurs, lenders of collateral sometimes also withhold collateral bcs they are concerned that existing fails diminish the likelihood of that collateral being returned to them. Such withholding can be self-fulfilling bcs withholding scarce collateral can increase the incidence of fails in and of itself. Finally, a seller may be unable to deliver a security bcs of a failure to receive the same security in settlement of an unrelated purchase. This can lead to a \"daisy chain\" of fails, where A's failure to deliver bonds to B causes B to fail on a sale of the same bonds to C, causing C to fail on a similar sale to D and so on. A daisy chain becomes a \"round robin\" if the last participant in the chain is it\u2019self failing to the first participant \". FRBNY fails Data", "created": 1780965733061, "pinned": false, "source": "Final printing notes 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 4325/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpplj50", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Deflationary pressure in a country refers to a sustained decrease in the general price level of goods and services within that country over time. This phenomenon typically occurs when the supply of goods and services outpaces the demand for them, leading to a decrease in prices. Deflation can have various causes, such as reduced consumer spending, decreased business investment, technological advancements that increase productivity and reduce production costs, or tight monetary policies by central banks. While a moderate level of deflation can sometimes be beneficial as it increases the purchasing power of consumers and encourages consumption, prolonged deflation can have detrimental effects on the economy. It may lead to lower corporate profits, reduced wages, increased debt burdens, and postponed consumption as consumers anticipate further price decreases. This, in turn, can lead to a downward spiral known as a deflationary spiral, where falling prices and demand create a self-reinforcing cycle of economic contraction. Central banks and governments often implement various monetary and fiscal policies to combat deflationary pressures and stabilize the economy, such as reducing interest rates, implementing quantitative easing measures, increasing government spending, or cutting taxes to stimulate demand and encourage inflation.", "created": 1780965727676, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 4372/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpprwbq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It's important to remember that economic indicators are not standalone measures. They are interconnected, and changes in one indicator can affect others. This is why economists and analysts look at multiple indicators to get a comprehensive understanding of the economy. By understanding these indicators, investors can make more informed choices and better navigate the complex world of finance and economics.", "created": 1780965727643, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4373/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2akwae", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u270d\ufe0f Auto-generate daily macro summaries, sentiment scores, and regime insights", "created": 1780965727643, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4374/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppi022", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3- Lagging indicator are data points that confirm or validate trends that have already happened. These indicators include metrics such as inflation rates, the change in labor costs, and gross domestic product or GDP. lagging indicators provide a retrospective view of the economy and are used to assess the impact of previous events or policies. GDP is probably the most widely known lagging indicators used by policy makers. It measures the total value of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. changes in GDP can indicate shifts in business activity, investment levels, and consumer spending. Another vital lagging indicator is the consumer price index CPI. CPI tracks changes in the average price level of a basket of goods and services commonly purchased by households. It provides insights into inflationary pressures and is crucial for policymakers in determining monetary policy. Fluctuations in CPI can impact purchasing power, interest rates, and central bank policies, all of which have implications for investment performance.", "created": 1780965727642, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4375/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2aa0zg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udd0d Power your macro narrative tracker and explainable divergence tools", "created": 1780965727642, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4376/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpptfhn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2- Coincident Indicators provide information about the current state of the economy. They reflect ongoing economic activity and can include date points like retail sales, industrial production, payroll emplyment and personal income. Coincident indicators are particularly useful at gauging the pulse of the economy in the present moment. For ex: payroll employment, which represents the total number of paid full time and part time workers in both public and private sectors. This indicator provides an understanding of the health of the job market and overall economic conditions. When more businesses are hiring, its signals to market participants that businesses are performing well and can also lead to expectations that people will spend more due to their higher incomes. Another coincident indicator is retail sales, because it points to consumer confidence and economic demand. Retail sales data tracks the total revenue generated by retail establishments, indicating consumer spending patterns. When sales are higher and people are spending more, companies in the retail sector of the stock market tend to perform better.", "created": 1780965727641, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4377/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2agyza", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83e\udde0 Enable Fed/ECB/BoJ/PBoC statement interpretation", "created": 1780965727641, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4378/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppb1ii", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "These indicators help economists predict the direction of the economy. One of the most well-known leading indicators is stock market indices such as the S&P 500 which measures the performance of the largest publicly traded companies in the US. Stock prices may anticipate economic turning points, both up and down, and can provide insights into market sentiment, investor confidence, and overall financial conditions. Another important leading indicator is building permits for new private housing. In most areas, building permits are issued before construction can begin. An increasing number of building permits signifies a strong demand for real estate and predicts an upturn in construction activity. When individuals are feeling financially secure, and have confidence in the economy, they are more likely to purchase homes, and building permits reflect increasing consumer confidence.", "created": 1780965727640, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4379/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2aqzqc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udd17 Connect GPT-4o for fast, real-time AI analysis", "created": 1780965727640, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4380/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpp5z5p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1- Leading indicators signal potential future changes in the economy. They can include data points like stock market performance, building permits and consumer confidence surveys.", "created": 1780965727639, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4381/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpph3jp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "There are 3 main types of economic indicators: leading indicators, coincident indicators, and lagging indicators.", "created": 1780965727638, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4382/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpp83y0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Economic Indicators are statistical data points that provide insight into how an economy is performing.", "created": 1780965727637, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4383/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppwbj4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What are Economic Indicators? Economic Indictors assess the health of a country's economy.", "created": 1780965727636, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4384/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2abu9f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Once I have that, I\u2019ll integrate AI summaries, sentiment scoring, divergence analysis, and central bank interpretation.", "created": 1780965727636, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4385/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppgiwr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "5-Multiplier Effect: The relationship between bank reserves and lending is amplified through a concept called the money multiplier effect. When banks make loans, the money supply increases. This newly created money can then be deposited in other banks, which in turn allows them to make additional loans based on their excess reserves. This process continues, effectively creating more money in the economy for every dollar of new reserves injected by the Fed.", "created": 1780965727635, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4386/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2a9d43", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "GPT-4o (faster, real-time, good balance for summaries + NLP)", "created": 1780965727635, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4387/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppqucr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-Monetary Policy: The Fed uses its control over the money supply and interest rates to implement monetary policy objectives. By adjusting the level of bank reserves, the Fed can influence the overall level of economic activity. For example, during times of economic slowdown, the Fed might increase bank reserves to encourage lending and stimulate economic growth.", "created": 1780965727634, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4388/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2agpmq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "GPT-4 (more accurate, slightly slower)", "created": 1780965727634, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4389/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpp981r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Interest Rates: The Federal Reserve influences the amount of bank reserves in the system through open market operations, which involve buying or selling government securities. When the Fed buys government securities, it injects money into the banking system and increases the level of bank reserves. This can lower the federal funds rate (the interest rate at which banks lend to each other overnight) and encourage banks to lend more, as they have more funds available to do so.", "created": 1780965727633, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4390/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2a1ds1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Let me know if you want to use:", "created": 1780965727633, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4391/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppe8c6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Lending Capacity: Banks make loans to individuals, businesses, and other entities using a portion of their excess reserves (reserves above the required amount). When banks have more reserves, they have a greater capacity to make loans. Conversely, if banks have fewer reserves, their ability to lend is constrained.", "created": 1780965727632, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4392/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppfcsq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1- Reserve Requirements: Banks are required to hold a certain percentage of their deposits as reserves. These reserves can be held either as physical currency in their vaults or as deposits at the Federal Reserve. These reserves serve as a cushion against potential withdrawals and are also a regulatory tool to ensure the stability of the banking system.", "created": 1780965727631, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4393/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cppqq6g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why bank reserves is a great barometer for liquidity? Bank reserves held with the Federal Reserve (the Fed) play a crucial role in influencing bank lending and, by extension, the broader economy. The relationship between bank reserves and lending is primarily through the mechanism of the money supply and the Federal Reserve's control over it. Here's how it works:", "created": 1780965727630, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpojxq1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Each EM has its own specific risks, but all EM have 3 main risks: 1- Exchange rate: Currency fluctuations in EM generally tend to be greater and they can have a significant inpact on returns. for ex: MSCI india index over the past 10 years has returned 11.42% per year in local currency ( Rupee), but only 6.71 % in US Dollars, as the Rupee has depreciated by more than 50% against the us dollar over that period. 2- Hyperinflation Risk : Ex: Argentina has had hyperinflation for 20 years, annual inflation in argentina has exceeded 20% in the last 10 years. Even though Argentina main stock index generated over 50% per year in Argentinian pesos, after the impact of depreciation, the return was like 7% per year in US Dollars or 10.3% in Canadian Dollars. Which is good, but at the cost of extreme volatility. 3- Geopolitical instability : The Russian stock market has completly collapsed since the Ukraine invasion. And yet Russia is part of BRICS which includes countries identified as major emerging economic powers.", "created": 1780965727535, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpoxgkl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How does Reverse Repo facility prevent liquidity issues? Reverse Repo prevents federal gov from going out there and say hey we need to borrow money and then regardless of the rate they offer nobody has any dollars to lend to them. So at least for the next amount of money held in the reverse repo facility the gov need to borrow that wont happen. The reverse Repo facility is there in order to provide that liquidity.", "created": 1780965727528, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4504/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpo2fg6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Reverse Repo facility is really like an overflow for the banking system for the extra dollars in the system so that they flow into short term treasuries and push interest rates negative without the reverse repo facility without that overflow of dollars those extra dollars in the system they would push interest rates negative. So the FED uses the Reverse Repo facility as a pan underneath an overflow valve to suck the extra dollars that the system couldn\u2019t handle without pushing interest rates negative.", "created": 1780965727527, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4505/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpou4sy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Reverse Repo facility is there to provide a floor underneath interest rates that means Fed funds rate is higher than it would be without the reverse repo facility. So as long as there is money in the Reverse Repo facility that means that the natural rate without that money in there would have been lower.", "created": 1780965727526, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4506/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpo1okt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When banks have liquidity problems they go to the feds as a last resort and obtain loans against collateral at a rate slightly above feds funds rate.", "created": 1780965727525, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4507/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpowrpv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The discount rate/discount window, which represents the rate commercial banks can use to borrow directly from the Fed and is typically only used in times of liquidity stress, acts as the ceiling to the FFR range.", "created": 1780965727524, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4508/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b29enln", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bonus: \ud83c\udfa8 Design Polish (Optional if you want it beautiful fast)", "created": 1780965727522, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4509/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpog7gw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Reverse Repo facility is the tool the Fed uses to put a floor underneath interest rates. They do this by simply paying an interest rate on any cash that comes in to the Reverse Repo facility (Fed pay Reverse Repo a 0.5% interest rate higher than bottom end of the target range of the Federal funds rate). Its a powerful tool since parking money with the FED would guarantee a Risk Free return in the entire market. Fed opens up the Reverse Repo facility and start paying some interest to capture all the extra dollars stemming from a QE or a dollar printing spree so that it doesnt flood the market and by the Fed paying interest rate on the Reverse Repo the banks wont have to buy thing like tbills and push interest rates negative bcs in 2020 and first half of 2021 interest rates were already so low on that short term gov debt that if banks would have used that influx of deposit and then bought collateral like tbills with it they could have absolutely pushed interest rates negative and so over the course of the next couple of years FED continued to pay higher and higher interest rate into the Reverse Repo facility so that banks and money markets would continue to put more and more cash in there and since they neede to start tightening they needed the Reverse Repo facility to put a floor underneath interest rates and by slowly raising the interest rate they paying on the Reverse Repo facility that floor underneath interest rates would be going higher and higher. When Fed pause hiking rates which means they dont need the Reverse Repo as a floor underneath interest rate to move higher to keep them from falling. Usually when the money leaves Reverse Repo facility it goes to short term treasuries. As the US gov has to borrow more and more and more they would have to continue to pay higher and higher interest rates as they pay these higher interest rates they become more attractive bcs thats a better return than what the FED is paying in the reverse repo facility. Jerome Powell once said that the treasury general account would be rebuilt using the reverse repo facility. Banks and Money Markets usually park their money RISK FREE either in Reverse Repo facility (that acts as a floor) or short term treasury bills and they would usually go with which one in the two is paying a higher interest rate. So if FED wanna keep money in the Reverse Repo facility they just have to continue to jack up the interest rate they pay
- `18:08:22` --- note 4510/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpolda0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The reverse repo facility is one of two tools that FED uses in the Repo market. The Fed has both the standing Repo facility and the reverse repo facility. In the Repo market FED will intervene either to keep rates low where they want them or to keep rates high where they want them. If Fed wants to keep rates lower than where they normally would be they use the standard Repo facility to put a lid on interest rates to prevent them from going higher but if Fed wants to keep rates higher than they would be normally they will use the reverse repo facility to put a floor underneath the interest rates to prevent them from going lower (starting March 2021 Fed started to use their Reverse Repo facility to keep a floor underneath interest rates) .", "created": 1780965727520, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpoyiqx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How does reverse repo award rate affect liquidity? It dictates if investors and institutions better off investing their money in the market (when reverse repo award rate is very low and doesnt yield them nothing) or be better off just parking their money with the fed and earning a nice yield risk free (when reverse repo award rate start going up)", "created": 1780965727519, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 4515/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpn9z95", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bank reserves are a great barometer of liquidity in the system. In a Reverse Repo transactions: The counterparty pays the Fed X million in reserve balances (The cash transferred by participants to the Fed coming out of the bank reserve balance with the FED effectively reduces the amount of reserves in the banking system, impacting the level of liquidity in the financial markets 'draining liquidity') So we have X million in Cash transfered from the banks reserves to the FED reserves which will knee cap its lending operation by 10 times that amount bcs of the fractional reserve lending requirement which will drain liquidity out of the system. In a Repo transaction: A bank sells $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities to the Fed in exchange for x million in cash. So the FED credit the Bank reserve balance with x Million in cash. So now the bank have X million more on its reserve balance which will increase its lending capacity by 10 times bcs of the fractional reserve requirement lending which will increase liquidity in the system. SWAPS : FED and a foreign central bank exchanging currencies. This allows a foreign central bank to obtain U.S. dollars from the Fed in exchange for an equivalent amount of its own currency, based on the market exchange rate at the time of the transaction. And that foreign central banks will chaneel those US dollars to its local banks. So SWaps increase US dollar holdings the Eurodollar banks therefore increasing liquidity in the Eurodollar system. When Fed sells securities in an RRP, it injects reserves into the banking system. When the New York Fed repurchases the securities, it drains reserves from the banking system. So by the FED controlling banks reserves either by REPO or Reverse REPO it can control liquidity in the system.", "created": 1780965727517, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4516/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpni9mz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The secondary use case has also been as a way to absorb liquidity out of markets and tighten financial conditions. This works because the cash deposited at the RRP facility is siloed away from the broad financial market and therefore makes for tighter liquidity conditions.", "created": 1780965727516, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 4518/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpn1p6f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It is typically used as a mechanism to set a floor on short term money market rates as it is the only rate that money market funds can earn directly from the Federal Reserve and therefore has the lowest credit risk out of all their allocation options.", "created": 1780965727515, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpn5k1r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Overnight Reverse Repo Rate (RRP) is the rate the Fed pays on reverse repo operation transactions where both commercial banks and money market funds swap cash for short term treasuries borrowed directly from the Federal Reserve at a certain rate.", "created": 1780965727514, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4521/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnyblq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This determines how much liquidity gets drained out of the market. when its very low Banks are forced to invest their capital to get a Return when this starts going up it dries liquidity off the market bcs banks get Risk Free Return just by parking their capital with the fed .", "created": 1780965727513, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4522/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnexwh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What would make the fed pivot is a problem in the funding market: treasury auctions, collateral agreements, reverse repo.", "created": 1780965727512, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4523/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 4524/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpny9aa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It's worth noting that the specific details and mechanics of reverse repo operations can vary across central banks and countries. The reverse repo rate set by a central bank is typically a tool to manage short-term interest rates and liquidity conditions in the economy, and it is separate from the policy interest rate (such as the federal funds rate in the United States) that is used to guide monetary policy.", "created": 1780965727511, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4525/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnzk97", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The reverse repo rate serves as a floor for short-term interest rates in the economy because it represents the rate at which financial institutions can invest excess funds in low-risk assets, typically government securities. By adjusting the reverse repo rate, central banks can influence short-term interest rates and the overall level of liquidity in the financial system.", "created": 1780965727510, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4526/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b29jjlh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Enables subscriptions for your platform (Free tier + transaction fees)", "created": 1780965727510, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4527/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpn6k1x", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Reverse repo transactions are used by central banks as a monetary policy tool to manage liquidity in the financial system. When the central bank raises the reverse repo rate, it incentivizes banks to lend money to the central bank instead of lending it to other institutions or individuals. This helps to reduce the amount of money available in the banking system, which can help control inflationary pressures.", "created": 1780965727509, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4528/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnnio2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The reverse repurchase agreement (reverse repo) rate is the interest rate at which the central bank borrows money from commercial banks and other financial institutions by selling securities, typically government bonds, with an agreement to buy them back at a later date. In other words, it is the interest rate paid by the central bank to absorb excess liquidity from the banking system.", "created": 1780965727508, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpna38u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Difference between SOFR and LIBOR (EURODOLLAR). SOFR is secured lending used overnight in the US, SOFR spot market is HUGE but its future market is TINY but it has been growing tremendously and projected to be as big or maybe overtake LIBOR futures market in 2023 . LIBOR is unsecured lending used OFFSHORE. LIBOR spot market is tiny but its futures market is huge. since SOFR is secured financing and LIBOR is unsecured LIBOR trades at a premium (rates are higher) than sofr bcs its Offshore unsecured lending. SOFR is used a ton in the spot market LIBOR is used a ton in the futures market. LIBOR was replaced by SOFR, LIBOR isn't used anymore.", "created": 1780965727502, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4536/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnqk8j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "(SOFR previously known as LIBOR; SOFR was chosen to be the successor to LIBOR for the global rate of lending for short term cash \"Overnight\")", "created": 1780965727501, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4537/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnzmn6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A sudden Sharp increase signals low liquidity (like 17 September 2019): it implies banks don't have cash to lend to each other requiring ongoing Fed Liquidity injections to bring the rate down.", "created": 1780965727500, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4538/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpnp198", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "SOFR: is a broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight (Limited to overnight transactions only) collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities in the repurchase agreement (repo) market. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpn5wsn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "There is a relation between a countrys bond market and its currency and the last thing any country wants to see is that the rate that they have to pay on their sovereign bonds to be spiking bcs often that's a sign of distress or people wanting to get paid more to hold a potentially defaulty bond but it is different when the US does it than when ROW does it thats bcs the USA is the global Reserve currency and as the system is designed now if you operate on the global stage you have to have dollars to do it. in 2023 the USA purposefully raising interest rates, they are purposefully tightening policy they want interest rates to go up and stay higher for longer (FED chairman jerome powell has been saying this all year in 2023) so the idea that the yield on us treasuries is going up a lot is a signal that the ROW is rejecting the dollar and rejecting and boycotting us treasuries is just not true. While in other countries when yield spike thats an indication that you dont want to hold that currency bcs there is counterpary risk (bond might default) but on the contrary in the USA and bcs there is so much demand for the US dollar and people have to use it for global trade and to borrow and pay off loans in the eurodollar system wether they want to or not . - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cplo4ic", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"The negative yen basis swap acts like LEVERAGE where even yields on the interim \"investment\" are negative. Any speculator or bank with spare dollars could lend them in a yen basis swap meaning an exchange into yen. Because you end up with yen you are forced into some really bad investment choices such as sightly negative Japanese 5 year gov bonds, but that is just part of the cost of keeping risk on your yen side low. Instead, the real money is made in the basis swap it\u2019self since it now trades so highly negative. The very fact of that basis swap spread means a huge premium on spare dollars, which is another way of saying there is a dollar shortage. BCS of the shortage and it\u2019s premium, you can swap into yen and invest in negative yielding JGBs in size and still make out handsomely\" Real Clear Markets, Everywhere you look there's a Dollar shortage.", "created": 1780965727247, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkmpy2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fx swaps for Japanese Banks: \"As a Japanese Bank, you've got yen (you are drowning in yen reserves) and if YOU DON\u2019T LIKE THE HIGH EFFECTIVE COSTS OF STRAIGHT US DOLLAR REPO YOU CAN GET THE US DOLLAR FUNDING YOU NEED VIA A CURRENCY SWAP. Here, the only part that's really different is that you've pledged the yen as one piece of the deal. The goal remains the same: to increase yield on safe instruments without incurring too much additional risk. For the most part, in this foreign context that means currency risk. You've got yen to swap for dollars, and now there the RISK that the dollar moves ADVERSLY against the yen which could DESTROY all your carefully laid plans. But the FX swap takes care of that bcs it is set so that the value of the yen you swap for dollars today is the same as when the derivatives expires in the future. No exchange Risk.\"", "created": 1780965727245, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4759/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2981uj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83e\udde0 2. Real-Time Macro Anomaly Scanner", "created": 1780965727245, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4760/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkid31", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Funding requirements means the aggregate of all amounts necessary to fund the Loans. \" If you don\u2019t like the effective high cost of straight US Dollar Repo you can get the US dollar funding you need via a currency swap.\" So basically global investor use FX swaps to be funded for short term collateralized Dollar loans bcs it\u2019s 96% cheaper than traditional Repo or unsecured loans. \"A typical day sees almost $4 Trillion in new FX swap contracts, most of which involve a payment of US Dollars. Unlike for Repo and other forms of debt, the full attendant payment obligations arising from FX swaps ARE NOT reported on a balance sheet\" BIS. \" These transactions are functionally equivalent to borrowing and lending in the cash market, Yet corresponding debt is not shown on the balance sheet and thus remains obscured\" BIS", "created": 1780965727244, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4761/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkk1rq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Now currency swaps is a little bit different, same general idea as an fx swap but currency swaps tend to be longer dated and they also in exchanging currencies at the start and the end , they can also exchange coupons of interest rates payments along the way but the principles are largely the same here. An fx swap is essentially a funding vehicle for whatever general purpose. Top five banks reported roughly a third of global outstanding positions in the FX system and the top 25 banks account for more than 80% of the fx system so it\u2019s the dealer banks and in particular the US banks that are really in the center of the FX swap Eurodollar shadow banking system. They are incredibly important to maintaining operations, smooth flow of US dollars and collateral throughout the global system. \" Our approach to multilateral netting shrinks funding requirements by over 96% on average\" CLS the biggest FX swaps Data source.", "created": 1780965727243, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4762/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b29v0fx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cJobs beat by 200k but USD fell \u2014 crowd fading Fed tightening\u201d", "created": 1780965727243, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4763/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkpzrj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "There is a difference between an FX swap and a currency swap. FX swaps tend to be shorter term in nature (less than one year) and they look like an exchange of currency : i give you some dollars you give me some yen and then at some point in the future i give you back the yen you give me back the dollars and everyone is happy and while that\u2019s true and that\u2019s technically true you have to look at a currency swap or an fx swap in this case as a COLLATERALIZED loan , Im giving you dollars that you likely need and you giving me yen not because i want yen but bcs yen is in fact the collateral, i could use the yen to choose different varieties of collateral (i can use it for carry trade or invest it in Japan short term gov bonds). That\u2019s the problem with fx swaps (which illustrate the weak breaking point of the entire shadow system) : it\u2019s collateral used for derivatives is pledge into more derivatives . For ex: investor A take some yen as a collateral for an fx swap. He then pledge that yen to do a carry trade so when that carry trade blows up then that didn\u2019t only liquidated the collateral for loan B but also the collateral for loan A bcs that how the investor acquired the yen collateral to start with. And that\u2019s why when things go bust everyone is desperately searching for collateral ( well bcs the collateral for the 1st loan or derivative has been used as a collateral for a second derivative or loan) and all the sudden BOOM liquidity poof just disappeared within MINUTES. So fx swap is a collateralized loan sorta of like a synthetic Repo, it\u2019s mainly to borrow dollar on the global stage on a collateralized basis.", "created": 1780965727242, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4764/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpk7atz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "US banks and Dealers are primary centerpiece of the entire FX swaps and Eurodollar shadow banking system even between Japanese banks and Euro banks where European banks are wanting to swap euros into yen they will actually swap euros into dollars and then swap dollars into yen intertubing through US banks likewise Japanese banks looking to swap yen into Euros will swap yen into dollars and then dollars into Euros intermediating through US banks. \"In EUR/USD FX swaps, US banks tend to borrow euros from Euro area banks and then channel the Euros to Japanese banks. In JPY/USD FX swaps, US banks borrow yen from Japanese banks and channel the yen to Euro area banks.\" BIS \"US banks stand out as pivotal FX swap intermediaries. In particular, Japanese banks that swap out of the yen and into Euros, and euro area banks swapping in the other direction. both transact via the US Dollar mainly with US banks rather than with each other.\" BIS. Dealer take a maturity transformation Risk especially with their Yen and Japanese counterparties. The Japanese yen counterparties want to borrow dollars long term meanwhile the US banks that are providing dollars through FX markets are borrowing dollars in short term arrangements from Money Market funds or other sources (So when Money market yields go up bcs of fed funds rates going up that means the rate on borrowing on FX swaps will get up since dealers have to make a mark up in top of their borrowing cost from Money markets which means it will shrink liquidity inf FX swap market (Eurodollar and Shadow banking system). So essentially the dealer banks are taking some Rollover Risk by borrowing short term and then relending those dollars long term especially to Japanese investors who will then relend those funds to China. \"Top rated Bank and Non bank borrowers based in the Euro area took advantage of the negative EUR/USD basis swap spread by issuing dollar bonds. Hedging the on-balance sheet dollar liability made these issues dollar suppliers in EUR/USD FX derivatives\" BIS. This is another example of what could go wrong and how a dollar surge and US rate hikes would blow up collateral in the Eurodollar system we have European banks issuing dollar bonds with Dollars they don\u2019t even have and can\u2019t even put their hands on them in time of turmoil.", "created": 1780965727241, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4765/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b29htxl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Compares real-time price action to historical macro reactions", "created": 1780965727241, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4766/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkf9gp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Dealers who are the entity that facilitate and conduct FX swaps are simply pocketing spreads for doing all the different Fx swap transactions: matching cash lending with cash borrowing, matching collateral that comes up available with collateral needs that arise along the way. \"First, dollar lending via FX derivatives has grown as this activity has become lucrative. The dollar basis, ie the premium earned (over money market rates) by lending dollars against other currencies via an FX derivative, has profited banks with ample dollar cash funding\" BIS", "created": 1780965727240, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkwlto", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global investor move to US treasuries not necessarily bcs they don\u2019t US gov bonds are safe but bcs it\u2019s the most liquid market in the world, so global investor might say: \" this is a good place to put my money when the storm blows yes i might lose some money but that\u2019s ok bcs the most of my principal is preserved\" so a flight a Us treasuries might be a flight to liquidity rather than a flights to safety. but for global central banks with 100s of billions of dollars there is just no escape bcs there is no other market that can absorb that large number of money. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkb3z8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Once a significant volume of fails occurs, lenders of collateral sometimes also withhold collateral bcs they are concverned that existing fails diminish the likelihood of that collateral being returned to them. Such withholding can be self-fulfilling bcs withholding scarce collateral can increase the incidence of fails in and of it\u2019self. Finally, a seller may be unable to deliver a security bcs of a failure to receive the same security in settlement of an unrelated purchase. This can lead to a \"daisy chain\" of fails, where A's failure to deliver bonds to B causes B to fail on a sale of the same bonds to C, causing C to fail on a similar sale to D and so on. A daisy chain becomes a \"round robin\" if the last participant in the chain is it\u2019self failing to the first participant \". FRBNY fails Data", "created": 1780965727178, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkn2kr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Doing all of these collateral transformation and securities lending transactions is what made the Eurodollar system so liquid and so effective and it\u2019s also what made it so incredibly DANGEROUS.", "created": 1780965727176, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpklbjp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Imagine as insurance company that wants to engage in a derivatives transaction. To do so, it is required to post collateral with a clearinghouse, and, bcs the clearinghouse has high standards, the collateral must be \"pristine\" that is, it has to be in the form of treasury securities. However, the insurance company doesn\u2019t have any unencumbered treasury securities available - all it has in unencumbered form are some junk bonds. Here is where the collateral swap comes in. The insurance company might approach a broker dealer and engage in what is effectively a two way repo transaction, whereby it gives the dealer it\u2019s junk bonds as collateral, borrows the treasury securities, and agrees to unwind the transaction at some point in the future. Now the insurance company can go ahead and pledge the borrowed treasury securities as collateral for it\u2019s derivatives trade. Of course, the dealer may not have the spare treasury securities on hand, and so, to obtain them, it may have to engage in the mirror image transaction with a third party that does say, a pension fund. Thus, the dealer would, in a second leg, use the junk bonds as collateral to borrow treasury securities from the pension fund.\" The motivation of the pension fund is to make a lil bit of spread in lending the securities. So as far as the Eurodollar market place is concerned we actually have a risky piece of collateral that is resued over and over and over and that collateral forms the basis of all these other transactions in the Eurodollar market place.", "created": 1780965727175, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpk76ja", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why is the Market is systematically short collateral and securities? Hedge funds by leveraging their returns they simply wants to borrow as many funds as they can as cheaply as they can. So if you are a hedge and u want to invest in junk bonds, the cheapest way to finance that trade to get the most leverage is to post the junk bonds as collateral in a short term financing arrangement, short term financing arrangement is what\u2019s gonna get you the lowest rate and you want to be collateralize bcs that\u2019s the least risk : Shortest term and least risk means the lowest rate and maximum amount of leverage, but you can\u2019t do that necessarily with a junk bund and you can\u2019t do that unless you are connected to the short term funding markets (Eurodollar system), so you contact a broker dealer bank and say i want to be involved in repo and they say that\u2019s fine i will be happy to arrange that for you but in order to get the best terms you have got to give me access to the security that you want to buy so you want to fund this transaction repo , i have got to use that security on your behalf in the repo market (the hedge fund has to give the broker dealer bank the ability to reuse the security on it\u2019s behalf in order to secure the cheapest best financing that it can find in the repo or secured financing markets. So the hedge fund is not actually lending the security to the broker dealer bank to act on it\u2019s behalf, instead what the hedge fund is doing is transferring the full title of that security to the broker dealer and in exchange the broker dealer is promising TO GIVE THAT SAME SECURITY BACK AS NECESSARY for when the hedge fun wants to sell it or a similar security doesn\u2019t have to be the same exact one as well as to pay all of the interest and coupon payments that accrue during the lifetime of this secured financing transaction, so what the hedge fund actually has is a promise from the broker dealer to give back same or similar security when it ask for it back and to pay the coupon payments during the life of this transaction in exchange of hedge fund giving up legal titles of the security bcs the broker dealer is going to reuse that security which means it needs to be able to relend that security in the Eurodollar market place. So we are doing all of this to obtain the highest form of leverage, the safest least risky forms of financing transactions all through the euro dollar

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpkzms8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The duration is a mathematical measure: in 1981 when the 30 year bond had a 14% coupon the duration was 6.5 that meant if the yield went from 13 to 14 you lost 6.5% of your money but you were getting a 14% coupon so basically you had to have a 250 basis points rise in rates and you still broke even but when you get to 2021, the duration bcs interest rates fell it\u2019s called positive convexity it\u2019s out to 22 years so every 100 basis point hike move will cause a 22% dump and then you wind up with a coupon around 2 so all you need is a 30 or 40 basis point move in interest rates to get completely wiped out and you are going to be at a loss for the entire year. that\u2019s why the losses in the bond market in 2022 were sooo huge, that\u2019s the inherent risk in bonds and if you go into negative interest rate then the equation just blows up and that\u2019s what we saw in Europe and Japan.", "created": 1780965727166, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

So, a US So we can look at the global FX swaps as almost a global US Carry trade done with US dollar in the aspect where if DXY was to pump or if US interest Rate was to go up that would blow up that position and that cause liquidity to evaporate and dry out from the entire Eurodollar system.", "created": 1780965727145, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpjulac", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Even though different FX Swaps and global derivatives carry the same Risk as a US Dollar carry trade bcs when DXY pump or interest rate go up that blows up that FX swaps position exactly as in the carry trade and that cause liquidity to evaporate and dry out from the entire Eurodollar system. This is how an FX swap transaction is done: A US Bank borrow dollars from money market fund let\u2019s say at 1% and lend it to a Japanese bank at 2% (the Japanese bank would give YEN collateral to the US bank to hold for the length for the loan not bcs the US bank needs it but just as a form of security, the US bank would take that yen and pledge it as a collateral for derivatives or at least invest it in Japanese gov bond to earn a yield while it\u2019s holding that yen for the term of the loan ) Since Japanese banks like to borrow in long term , what the US dealer banks would do is borrow in short term and lend in long term so they just borrow in short term and rollover into long term (let\u2019s say US dealer bank lend $10,000 to a Japanese bank for 3 years term: US banks would from money markets or other source for 1 years and then at the end of that 1 year they would either roll that loan over or pay off that loan and borrow another loan and the end of of year 2 again they would either roll over that loan or pay off that loan and borrow another loan that\u2019s how they make up the 3 year loan basically by obtaining 3 one year loans and just rolling them over). But by doing so they are carrying a longevity and currency Risk. Bcs if they borrow the first year at 1% and lent at 2% for 3 years, when it\u2019s time to rollover the loan or get a new loan at the beginning of year 2 if interest rate went up to 4% now the US dealer bank have a HUGE PROBLEM BCS THEY LENT AT 2% so now they are 2% under water for that loan so basically the interest rate going up blew up that FX Swap. Also currency risks pose a threat to FX swaps bcs if they borrow dollar and lend dollars and were given yen to hold as a collateral, as dollar go up and yen dumps now the amount of yen the hold for collateral is worth A LOT less than the value of the dollar they lent out, so if that trade was to blow up the amount they would be recouping is gonna be worth a lot less than what they lent out leaving them with Big losses , even if everything goes as planned and the trade doesn\u2019t blow up since the amount of yen the hold as collateral would
- `18:08:22` --- note 4877/12122  ---

(Dealer failure to deliver and Deliver Failure to receive are Huge red flags for trouble in the FX swaps Eurodollar shadow banking system).", "created": 1780965727143, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpj7srz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "But there can be 4-week bills, 8-week bills, 6 month bills. That\u2019s the best form of collateral. The most liquid, easily traded, low volatility, easy to repledge, is by far the BEST form of collateral. That's all the banks want right now. But if you are a foreign guy, you need dollars to buy the dollar-based collateral. If you want Treasury Bills that are denominated in dollars, you need dollars to buy the bills. That\u2019s why the US Dollar is so strong. People say wait a second the US has a multi-trillion-dollar annual budget deficit, a massive trade deficit, 132% debt to GDP ratio, $31 Trillion in debt and going into Recession so how can the Dollar be so strong? The answer is everything i just said has nothing to do with the demand for dollars in the international foreign exchange markets. What's driving the demand for dollars is the need to get dollars to buy dollar denominated collateral, specifically Treasury Bills to post as collateral to support the $1 Quadrillion of derivatives. And that\u2019s going to persist for until the system crashes.", "created": 1780965727141, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpie9r7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Nasdaq Investors biggest mistake is that nasdaq keep pumping in anticipation of fed rate cuts but the Fed wont cut rates until markets crash (which signal Desperate need for liquidity) and as long as markets are pumping fed wont cut rates. (markets pumping signal there is liquidity so there is no need to inject any liqudity from the FED) The fed would only cut rates if growth slows and if growth slows the Nasdaq which have pumped the most is also going to pull back the most in the downturn.", "created": 1780965727043, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpiq5c8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "For the FED to cut and go back to an easy monetary policy or even doing QE there is gotta be a lack of liquidity and markets are crashing Big time not just a small pull back.", "created": 1780965727042, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
