- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpiansn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FED first move after equities start crashing is typically not enough to inject enough liquidity and stabilize the market so more FED moves and actions are required and thats why markets keep crashing even after feds first rate cuts bcs they are just not enough. Thats why FED actions are gradual: they usually start with a small rate cut and if markets keep dumping, they do a big rate cut and if that doesnt stabilize markets they cut fed fund rate close to 0 and if that doesnt stibilize market they do QE and start buying Treasuries and other assets to inject liqudity directly into the market.", "created": 1780965727041, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4979/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpiyr61", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "For the fed to cut their must be smthg wrong with the economy and growth and there is a hole in the economy and liquidity that the FED is trying to fill. Unless the FED immediately go back to a stimulative effort that we know is big enough to fill the hole (cut rates to 0 and do QE) , the first move is typically not enough to fill the hole so more FED moves and actions are required Thats why when the first cut happens equities continue to sell off bcs oftentimes that firt cut move isnt enough to fix the damage and counteract the now deflationary forces as opposed to the inflationary forces. So If equities are moving higher there is no lack of liquidity therefore no need for the FED to cut rates and even do QE (FED would only do QE if the first move \"usually a small rate cut\" wasnt enough and A LOT of liquidity needs to be injected to stop market Dump and stabilize the markets)", "created": 1780965727040, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4980/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 4981/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpi2p7q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "If look at any FED hiking cycle and FED cutting cycle: FED typically hike hike hike then the economy and growth slows and rolls into recession and the FED start to cut rates. Typically its when they start to cut that equities start to sell off and the reason they are cutting is bcs equities are selling off and when that happens equities typically do not turn around and start rising immediately just bcs FED did one cut. FED often have to do more than one cut and make some other move to stop the equities DUMP.", "created": 1780965727039, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 4982/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpiyza8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bonds rally when fed funds rate peaked and rate cuts are anticipated, stocks rally on earnings and whats seen as good or bad for the economy, raging inflation is seen as really bad while increasing rates on an inflation environment is soon as good eventhough increasing ratea is usually bad for stocks on a normal environment. Crypto and gold only rally on an increased liquidity environement where fed cut rates and inject liquidity increasing its balance sheet. No crypto rally has occured until bond rally happened first. And thats bcs its the rate cuts that leads to a bond rally and a rate cuts injects liquidity into the system.", "created": 1780965727038, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpi3ab8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The immense global monetary system runs on us dollars. There just isnt enough collateral to go around (short term liquid us treasuries), thats why we witness collateral shortage when there is a liquidity squeeze. - `18:08:22` --- note 5015/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpifnx4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Swaps: Loans extended by the Fed to friendly countries to help with Dollar shortage in the EuroDollar Market (Dollar shortage causing Dollar to be too strong) (usually Swap lines are extended in 30 days tenor but during crises are extended in 7 days or even overnight tenor). Swaps are form of a loan that has to be paid back with interest. How does the Swap line mechanism work? The Friendly countries have an account at the FED so the US will deposit Dollars in those foreign countries account at the FED, at the same time those countries will deposit their own currency in an account for the FED at their Central Bank. And then the USA and the friendly country have to SWAP Back 30 days, 7 days or overnight with interest paid to the USA. So when the USA is printing money to give the Rest of the world, the Rest of the world is printing even more Money to give to the USA.", "created": 1780965727020, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5016/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpielf0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "AND THIS IS EXACTLY WHY IN TIMES OF FINANCIAL CRISIS AND COLLATERAL SHORTAGE LIQUIDITY POOF LITERALLY JUST DISAPPEARS WITHIN SECONDS FROM THE GLOBAL MARKETS, THATS BCS OF THE BANKS FRACTIONAL LENDING THERE JUST ISNT ENOUGH MONEY IN THE BANK VAULTS TO COVER ALL THE LOANS THAT HAVE BEEN EXTENDED OUT. THERE IS ONLY 10% IN HARD CASH OF THE MONEY IN THE BANK VAULTS FOR THE LOANS THAT HAVE BEEN EXTENDED OUT.", "created": 1780965727019, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5017/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpih2qv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Liquidity expands in a global growth environment: \" A customer Alpha deposit $10,000 into the Bank. The Bank would then set aside 10% : $1,000 in vault and then loans out the rest of his money $9,000. Then another person B comes in asking for a car loan of $9,000, the Bank loans out $9,000 from Customer Alpha original Deposit to borrower B. Borrower B would pay the car seller C the money. Then car seller C would deposit the money into the Bank (its treated as a new deposit) and the whole process would be repeated all over just like customer Alpha Deposit. So the Money keeps getting redeposited and reloaned until the initial Deposit of $10,000 becomes $100,000 So the Euro Dollar Bank just created $90,000 out of thin air just by loaning out the money. And then the reverse process cause Liquidity to Contrats in Global growth environment: When Cutomer B defaults on the $9,000 then Bank only have $900 in the vault and the rest was loaned out. So Every Default is 10 times more than the amount the bank has kept in the vault to cover it ( because they just keep 10% in vault and loan out the other 90% ). This force banks to tighten and not issue new credit because they new the money to cover for the Default. So in Expansion: $10,000 becomes $100,000 in new loans ( expanding money supply). And in contraction: $10,000 default cause a $100,000 contraction in money supply.", "created": 1780965727018, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

When oil Doubles in a year a Recession have always followed in few months lag.", "created": 1780965726876, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5128/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cph3rew", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Oil runs the world : when oil goes up 20 % and dollar goes up 20% (and bcs oil is priced in dollars in the global markets) then oil just went up 40% against Rest of world (ROW) currencies, which force ROW to print more money to be able to buy the same amount of oil (which results in weakening local currency and high inflation) Thats why non oil and non energy producing countries are the ones which local currencies weakens the most againt the Dollar in Global Dollar shortages.", "created": 1780965726875, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgqye9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "JPY is a funding currency bcs Japan is an elderly society that\u2019s sitting on a lot of cash. They need to find yield. So they go overseas to find yield since Japan yield is at - 0.1% . So when Japan central bank cap yields through yield control , Japanese investors go overseas and they buy sovereign treasuries especially us treasuries since it\u2019s viewed as the world safest asset which keep us treasury yields down ( bcs Japanese investors buying the bond push the bond yield down) which is kinda like an unofficial yield control on the united states sovereign yields curve which results in keeping united states rates down which uplift risk assets (bcs low rates results in high liquidity) also it results in sp 500 hitting new highs and for congress to run a deficit. Japanese investors also buy bonds in Europe and EM which keep global sovereign yields down (the Japanese buying global sovereign bonds which put down pressure on those yield is acting almost as an unofficial yield curve control for the US and the rest of the world)", "created": 1780965726789, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpghjhe", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "what carry traders REALLY want or rather what THE ENEMY of a levered carry trader is : Yield Volatility bcs if you are long Aussie yen carry trade and capturing that yield spread on leverage, things are great as long as that yield spread either stays static from when you open the trade or if it widens BUT if the Aussie to JGB yield spread were to COMPRESS either bcs JGB yields go up or Aussie yields pull down causing that yield differential to narrows then carry traders accounts gets debited by the broker and if they are on a lot of leverage their positions gets liquidated. Thats why the biggest enemy of a levered carry trader is YIELD VOLATILITY, carry traders dont want yields on either side to SWING AROUND, they just want them to STAY STILL and that way they can just maintain their yield spread especially if they are using leverage.", "created": 1780965726787, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5214/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b27tfxm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Spikes = breakdown in private lending", "created": 1780965726787, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5215/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgh4ha", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "These funding currencies are selected because they offer access to cheap borrowing, which allows traders to amplify their potential profits when investing in higher-yielding assets. However, it's important to note that carry trades also come with significant risk, as exchange rates can fluctuate, potentially eroding profits and even leading to losses if the currency exchange rates move unfavorably. Traders should carefully assess market conditions and risk factors before implementing carry trade strategies.", "created": 1780965726786, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5216/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b2787gx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udcc9 Repo and Reverse Repo facility usage", "created": 1780965726786, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5217/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgq95v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The most common carry trade funding currencies historically have been: 1-Japanese Yen (JPY): The Japanese yen has been a popular funding currency for carry trades due to Japan's long-standing low-interest rate policy.2-Swiss Franc (CHF): Switzerland is known for its traditionally low-interest rates, making the Swiss franc another frequently used funding currency in carry trade strategies.3-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar can also serve as a funding currency in carry trades, particularly when interest rates in the United States are low. Traders borrow dollars at a low rate and invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere.4- Euro (EUR): The euro may be used as a funding currency when there is a significant interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, allowing traders to borrow euros at a lower cost.", "created": 1780965726785, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5218/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 5219/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpg9p5d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "what are carry trade funding currencies? Carry trade funding currencies are the currencies that traders typically borrow or sell short as part of a carry trade strategy. These currencies are chosen because they have low-interest rates, making them suitable for borrowing funds at a lower cost. The proceeds from selling or borrowing these currencies are then used to invest in higher-yielding assets denominated in other currencies. The goal is to profit from the interest rate differential or \"carry\" between the funding currency and the target currency.", "created": 1780965726784, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5220/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b27zeh7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83e\uddef 4. Broader Systemic Stress / Crisis Warning Indicators", "created": 1780965726783, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5221/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgw1tk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar is frequently used as a funding currency in carry trades, especially when interest rates in the United States are low, as it provides access to a wide range of higher-yielding currencies. 4-Australian Dollar (AUD): The Australian dollar is a popular target currency for carry trades because of Australia's relatively high-interest rates compared to other developed economies. 5-New Zealand Dollar (NZD): Similar to the Australian dollar, the New Zealand dollar is often used in carry trades due to New Zealand's comparatively high-interest rates. 6-Euro (EUR): The euro can be involved in carry trades, especially when there is a significant interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, making it an attractive target for investors. 7-British Pound (GBP): The British pound can also be part of carry trade strategies, with traders borrowing in currencies like the Japanese yen or Swiss franc and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in GBP.", "created": 1780965726782, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpg4yvf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Liquidity in the financial Markets: In the Repo Market: money market funds and other asset managers who are looking to make a little money without a lot of risk are the lenders. Hedge funds, wall street traders, and banks who have a lot of assets but need cash on hand to fund their day to day trading are the borrowers.Thats why its important to focus on Money Market funds if they are just hoarding cash which means they arent lending , or their cash holding is decreasing which means they are doing more lending and flowing cash into the market instead of hoarding it, That's what determines how much cash is in the plumbing system. \"MMMFFAQ027S: Money Market Total Funds\"", "created": 1780965726743, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgedm2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "These signs often appear in conjunction with each other and can contribute to financial market turbulence and economic instability, necessitating responses from central banks and policymakers to alleviate liquidity pressures.", "created": 1780965726741, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5269/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgb727", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "10- Corporate Defaults: Increased corporate defaults, particularly among entities with significant dollar-denominated debt, can indicate difficulties in accessing dollar funding.", "created": 1780965726740, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5270/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgov5f", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "9- Market Volatility: Heightened volatility in foreign exchange markets, particularly involving emerging market currencies, can be a sign of stress related to dollar shortages.", "created": 1780965726739, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 5272/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpg8807", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "8- Rising Dollar Swap Rates: An increase in the cost of dollar swap lines or a widening of swap spreads may indicate strains in the offshore dollar funding markets.", "created": 1780965726738, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5273/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpg0rbm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "7- Increased Dollar Borrowing Costs: Borrowers outside the United States may experience higher borrowing costs in dollars due to tighter credit conditions or increased risk premiums.", "created": 1780965726737, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5274/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpg5tos", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "6- Central Bank Interventions: Central banks may intervene in currency markets to stabilize their currencies against the dollar, indicating pressures stemming from a shortage of dollars.", "created": 1780965726736, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5275/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgqyt5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A global dollar shortage can manifest through various signs across financial markets and economic indicators. Some common signs include: 1- Currency Depreciation: A weakening of currencies against the US dollar can indicate a shortage of dollars in global markets. Countries facing liquidity issues may see their currencies depreciate as demand for dollars rises. 2- Rising Interbank Rates: An increase in interbank lending rates, particularly in dollars, suggests that financial institutions are facing difficulties in accessing sufficient dollar liquidity. 3- Increased Demand for Dollar-denominated Assets: Heightened demand for US Treasury securities and other dollar-denominated assets by foreign investors seeking safety or liquidity can signal a shortage of dollars in global markets. 4- Emerging Market Stress: Emerging market economies may face difficulties in servicing their dollar-denominated debts, leading to financial instability and currency crises. 5- Reduced Cross-Border Lending: Banks may become more cautious about lending in dollars across borders, leading to a decrease in cross-border lending activity.", "created": 1780965726735, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5276/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpgmj3g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Financial crisis can have one or more quiet periods that last few months where everything seems fine again and things seems like they went back to Normal only for the financial crisis to come at full swing blowing up the whole market. And that's why we should never try to get in front of financial crisi and just kick back and let it play its full course which will take about 1 year or longer to fully cleanse the market.", "created": 1780965726734, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpftifv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Usually when the market is very concentrated : IT'S THE END OF THE MOVE. And the reason it's the end of the move it signal there isnt enough money to lift up the whole market, there is just enough money to lift up a handful of stocks and those handful of stocks go and the rest of the stocks just kinda sits there. And thats why walstreet need the fed to cut rates and end QT , get the money print going bcs there isnt enough money to keep everything going from ths stock market to the foreign stock markets to bitcoin to gold. The market need the fed to keep pumping up money. That's why the Fed is so important. The stock Market is 44 Trillion while the economy is 28 Trillion. So the stock Market is almost 2 times the size of the economy. The sheer Trillions of dollars that it would take to lift all the 3000 stocks in the Russell to use one example we just dont have it right now THATS WHY WE HAVE CONCENTRATION. THATS WHY INVESTORS ALL PILE IN INTO CONCENTRATIONS. The bottom 1000 companies in the Russell 2000 employ 12 million people those stocks arent doing anything they are down on the year. If you take the fabulous four : Amazon , Meta, Microsoft and invidia out of the Nasdaq 100 The other 96 stocks are down on the year as a group there isnt enough money to take those 96 stocks plus those fabulous four to go up and that's what usually happens. We saw this in late 60s, in 73 , in 2000, when we saw BIG CONCENTRATED periods in the market and a crash Always followed. Thats why there is this need for the fed to pump in money , to cut rates to stop QT , to help feed the beast. When we see the large concentration that doesnt mean the stock market is gonna peak in a week. It could peak in a year or two years or it could be peaking this week but concentration is typically the action you see toward the end of the game not in the beginning or in the middle of the game. When the Market gets too concentrated we gotta focus on the stocks making the concentration bcs the moment those tose stock lose momentum the entire market is gonna blow up", "created": 1780965726724, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 5334/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpfs60l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed uses the discount rate as a ceiling for the federal funds rate. The discount rate is the interest rate that the Fed charges banks for loans through the discount window. Banks are unlikely to borrow from the banks at a rate higher than they can borrow from the FED. As a result, the discount rate acts as a ceiling on the federal funds rate.", "created": 1780965726688, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5335/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0b27zmsh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\ud83d\udd0d Keyword/phrase detection: \u201cstrong labor market,\u201d \u201cinflation persistence,\u201d \u201cbalance sheet normalization,\u201d etc.", "created": 1780965726688, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5336/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpfgk1z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which banks lend reserve balances to each other overnight. The Fed does not directly set the federal funds rate, but it can influence it by setting the IORB. By raising or lowering the IORB and reverse repo award rate the Fed can effectively set a floor for the federal funds rate. The Fed uses the discount rate as a ceiling for the federal funds rate.", "created": 1780965726687, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpfg3qa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Italian gov bonds over the last half decade have become an important part of the overall Eurodollar system not just the Euro denominated secured lending system but the entire Eurodollar framework bcs italian gov bonds are the most plentiful source of gov bonds in Euro denominated collateral which means they crucially important for the operation of European banks and as we know the European banks are a huge part of the Eurodollar system, the Germans don\u2019t issue that many gov bonds. \"In Eur/USD fx swaps, US banks tend to borrow Euros from euro area banks, and then channel the euros to Japanese banks. In JPY/USD fx swaps, US banks borrow yen from Japanese banks and channel the yen to Euro area banks\" BIS. According to European Repo Market survey: \" Italian gov securities expanded from 21.3% of ATS trading in December 2005 to 42.6% in December 2021.\" In other words, Italian instruments were backing nearly half of all Automatic trading systems (ATS) in repo, therefore a decent proxy of what's going on Euro-wide. Over the same timeframe, German bonds had been 44.6% of ATS repo back in 05 but were just 13.8% by june last year. With so much of the secured Euro markets depending upon italian sovereigns, what happens when spreads on italian sovereigns blow out to 250 bps above their German counterparts (BTPbund)?\". So if there's an issue with the biggest form of collateral in Euro denominator terms that\u2019s gonna be an issue for European banks therefore a source of potential problems for the entire Eurodollar system. Italian bonds bcs they are so plentiful, there is just so many more of them and bcs of the way the Euro system actually is put together it\u2019s highly fragmented (existing in separate parts, pieces or factions) and highly segmented (divided into parts that are loosely connected to each other) where italian bonds during good times of relaxed monetary policy they get treated with the other core bonds such as the German buns or french oats but during periods of rising strain and monetary stress, this huge chunk of what used to be core gov bond collateral start to get transformed into and perceived in the same way as some of the other peripheral bonds and bcs the European debt system is highly segmented when Italian bonds start to be reevaluated in the same way as Portuguese or Greek bonds that causes enormous stress and strain bcs there just isn\u2019t enough other core bonds available to

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpf320m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When we mention global collateral oftentimes, we think that's treasuries and treasury bills and that\u2019s an important part and the biggest part of it but it also consists of Japanese gov bills and italian gov bonds too. All these pieces fit together in a Eurodollar fabric that's often intermediated by US dealers. So it's not necessarily about US treasuries sometimes we see collateral problems begin in the smaller parts of the Eurodollar system that can then spill over across the entire Eurodollar system (Japanese gov bills and italian bonds and they are smaller parts of the Eurodollar when compared to Us treasuries collateral). So we have to pay attention to more than just US treasuries for warnings about where stresses might be building up in the overall global system. So as we all know we have the US treasuries, the Japanese gov bonds (that\u2019s a big one) but we also have the italian gov bonds.", "created": 1780965726664, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpezpk9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In a recession : when a Corp income falls then their ability to service their debt also falls causing it\u2019s Corp bond to be downgraded by the bond ratings company (Moody\u2019s, s&p Fitch) The fundamental problem is that most of US Corp bonds half of them which are investment grade bonds are just one notch above the junk bond threshold so if they get downgraded all the investment grade funds ETF will be forced to sell them (bcs their ratings got lowered to a junk bond status while the investment grade bond funds are only for investment grade bonds \"highest quality of Corp bonds\") causing the company's credit spread to widens costing the Corp more to refinance it\u2019s debt or pay off it\u2019s debt later on . Bcs when it refinances a new debt it will be financed at the higher yield so it\u2019s debt servicing costs will be higher. so unless it's revenue increases, to offset the higher debt servicing costs, the probability of the Corp default on it\u2019s debt increases. This event would cause contagion. the market will panic, worrying about other companies getting downgraded so even companies which are sounds will see their credit spread increase so they could in turn be downgraded.", "created": 1780965726622, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpeuni9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Financial crisis and Bad things Always happen in the Fall. At the end of the quarter especially September and December big banks hold to their Liquidity to meet the: Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) regulations requirement when reporting to the feds take place and they want their own balance sheets to look safer. Big banks holding liquidity drains liquidity from the Market so in time of low liquidity that can make things worse and leads to a financial crisis. (September 16th and November 16th). the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is a regulatory requirement established by the Basel III framework for banking supervision. The LCR is designed to ensure that financial institutions have enough high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to cover their short-term liquidity needs during a period of financial stress. LCR dictates that Banks should have enough high-quality liquid assets to cover their expected cash outflows over a 30-day stress scenario. High-quality liquid assets typically include cash, central bank reserves, Treasuries and a certain Corporate security that are easily convertible to cash without significan\u2019t loss of value.", "created": 1780965726605, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 5467/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpepgax", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why would Japanese investors (the biggest holders of us treasuries) move to Japanese bonds even if they are just offering %0.60 on Japan 10-year bond instead of us bonds that are offering 5.75%? That\u2019s bcs when Japanese investors invest in USA bonds, they also have to take currency risk. if they own American bonds, they ultimately have to convert them back to Yen and by factoring in the currency risk then they risk losing money on a depreciating currency. with all the volatility and uncertainty in the yen. they would rather take %0.65 and not having to worry about the currency moving 3% or 4% or 5% against them potentially wiping all the profit\u2019s they made from the %5.75 USA bonds yields and even putting at a loss. So, if Japanese bond yields start rising even by a tiny %0.1 or so, we will see more and more Japanese investors moving to Japanese bonds bcs markets are anticipatory and they would anticipate higher and higher Japanese bond yields hikes to follow.", "created": 1780965726588, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpewowp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Both Singapore and Hong Kong have play significan\u2019t roles in the Eurodollar market due to their status as major global financial centers providing liquidity to Asian economies.", "created": 1780965726586, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5470/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpebz22", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Hong Kong and Singapore (Singapore 30) tell us about Global Risk bcs they are a financial hub specializing in foreign exchange lending operations. That is borrowing capital nominated in major international currencies such as the dollar and channeling it into all types of investment projects in local currency for the Emerging Markets in Asia. So a downturn in Hong Kong and Singapore signals global liquidity drying up. The well-established financial markets in Singapore and Hong Kong provide access to capital for companies in the region. They are home to numerous venture capital firms, investment banks, and other financial institutions that facilitate fundraising and capital allocation.", "created": 1780965726585, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5471/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cperkul", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why do countries keep foreign exchange reserves? 1-to fund imports 2-to service debt 3- stabilize and defend local currency: Only with the dollar reserves can the country sell dollars and buy local currency to defend it and stabilize it 4- Confidence of markets: markets want to see that u have enough international reserves to take care of any short term, medium term or long term obligations. 5- To serve as a Buffer for unforeseen circumstances for shocks that hasn\u2019t been accounted for.", "created": 1780965726579, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpel2vn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Each EM has it\u2019s own specific risks, but all EM have 3 main risks: 1- Exchange rate: Currency fluctuations in EM generally tend to be greater and they can have a significan\u2019t impact on returns. for ex: MSCI India index over the past 10-years has returned 11.42% per year in local currency (Rupee), but only 6.71 % in US Dollars, as the Rupee has depreciated by more than 50% against the us dollar over that period. 2- Hyperinflation Risk: Ex: Argentina has had hyperinflation for 20 years, annual inflation in Argentina has exceeded 20% in the last 10-years. Even though Argentina main stock index generated over 50% per year in Argentinian pesos, after the impact of depreciation, the return was like 7% per year in US Dollars or 10.3% in Canadian Dollars. Which is good, but at the cost of extreme volatility. 3- Geopolitical instability: The Russian stock market has completely collapsed since the Ukraine invasion. And yet Russia is part of BRICS which includes countries identified as major emerging economic powers.", "created": 1780965726568, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5486/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpeoi5j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When things go really bad, they tend to go bad for All economies, and even more so for the Emerging Markets, which tend to be hit much harder during a crisis.", "created": 1780965726567, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpd2c01", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Every time interest rates move 100 basis points 1% how much does bond price move? When coupons (bond yields) are very low or negative (Europe, Japan) the durations are extremely long meaning that the prices of long duration bonds are VERY VERY sensitive to little movements of interest rates especially when you don\u2019t even have a coupon to cushion you. This is what called modified duration in the bond market. Bond prices are very very sensitive to very small interest movements when the coupon (yield is very low or negative) bcs of the rate of growth in interest rate, for ex: if fed funds rate is 0.25% and fed hike rates to 0.5% yes it\u2019s only 0.25% hike on a nominal term but it\u2019s a 100% hike on growth term, the fed funds rate just DOUBLED regardless of how low it is in Nominal terms. 1% to 2% interest rate hike is A LOT more problematic than a 10% to 20% interest rate hike.", "created": 1780965726496, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdeaoa", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The bond market is 100 times bigger than the stock market. Something else people don\u2019t realize about the bond market: How much money do you need to manage a billion dollars in the bond market? None it\u2019s all leverage, you can leverage the bond market to infinity, you can call Goldman sachs and say hi Im jim bianco i would like to buy a billion dollars\u2019 worth of bonds. they would say: oh you jim Done. Do bond investors need more than a dollar? No not necessarily it\u2019s all leverage. In the Equity market you need at least half a billion dollar to buy a billion-dollar worth of stocks. so there is a lot of leverage in the bond market. How do Gov Bond investors leverage work? And why would anyone do it? The bond market is a highly levered market, If you are a sophisticated financial institutions you can trade treasuries and gov bonds on a 100% leverage. So they buy $100 Million worth of bonds and they have no money (they just pick up the phone and call a dealer and they will get those bonds without putting no collateral) once receiving the bonds institutions pledge those $100 Million of bonds in the Repo market and they get an overnight loan to pay off those gov bonds and they just keep rolling that loan every day. So the bond market has tremendous leverage in it and it has always had that and that\u2019s why the bond market has always been unstable over the years. if you buy $100M of bonds and finance the whole $100M and the price falls 10 points to $90M you are $10M underwater so you need to come up with $10M RIGHT NOW to pledge as a collateral so you keep your position from getting liquidated. So how do you come up with with? you have other bonds that you own outright that aren\u2019t being financed so you pledge those bonds as more collateral in order to keep your position from getting liquidated.", "created": 1780965726488, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

Treasuries ALWAYS are in high demand bcs other than being the center piece of global collateral, after 2008 financial crisis US regulators set up new regulations for banks, pension funds and insurance companies (Basel 3 and Solvency 2 laws) that require them to hold US treasuries in their balance sheets (banks own 5.46% , state and local gov 4.93%, private pension funds 2.33%, insurance companies 1.27% of total Us treasuries so the total is 14% of US treasuries Total supply just go to these institutions just to satisfy regulatory capital requirement. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdejpm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When US Dollar spikes, EM have to print money to service their debt and buy commodities and raw materials. Which makes EM Corps life hell bcs a devaluing EM currency will make commodities and raw materials very expensive and also it makes their products and services cheaper in USD terms which generates less revenue in Dollar terms for them. so they profit margin get squeezed, they get squeezed from both ends. ( A higher inputs cost in USD and a lower revenue in USD). The only to get out of this is by growing and increasing production to make up for the lost revenue)", "created": 1780965726471, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5575/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpd4xzq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk Free as it relates to treasuries NEVER was meant to insinuate any time between the time the bond was issued and the times of maturity. There is ALWAYS interest rate risk in bonds, the risk free connotation comes from the fact that you will get paid back in dollars at maturity. but the biggest piece of collateral in the entire global monetary system is US treasuries and if you can constrict the price of US treasuries then you can constrict the amount of money or credit that is extended off of those treasuries so FED don\u2019t mind when bond prices are down when they wanna constrict credit, they purposefully hike rates to crash us treasuries prices to lower collateral value (since us treasuries are the most used collateral globally) which will lower the amount of credit extended therefore lower money supply in the market which will lower inflation. (the same mechanisms works backward if they wanna increase inflation and credit (money supply) in the market they just lower fed rates to pump us treasuries price.", "created": 1780965726470, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5576/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdxc9c", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How do Central banks slow down the Economy to ease up inflationary pressure? One of the ways they slow the Economy is bcs its debt based if they contract the collateral off of which loans are made and used to justify the extension of credit then that contracts Credit extensions (the level of money that's in the market) then as that money supply contracts inflation will come down. So Basically, the FED use the collateral as a tool to either expand of shrink money supply.", "created": 1780965726469, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5577/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdhkwr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Large Mega cap Companies (Magnificent 7 stocks: Facebook + Apple + Tesla + Nividia + Microsoft + Amazon + Google) don\u2019t need banks, they are almost like central banks in and of themselves, they can borrow in capital markets, they have no problem getting financial services, they are entities on their own. These companies can go to the Corporate bond market and borrow at rates very close to what the US gov gets. But when you get to the mere mortal companies the other 2993 of the Russell3000 they need banks, they need financial services, they need money transfer facilities, they need loans, they need a lot of services from banks. This squeeze that we are seeing in banks might be holding back a lot of those other companies which why collectively they only pushed the index 3% Not much more profit than what you would have been in money market funds bcs money market funds are up 2.6% for the year. Unlike the mega companies who can borrow directly from the Corp bond market, When the Bottom 1000 or Bottom 1500 companies of the Russell 3000 needs money they have to borrow from the banks and in times when banks are raising their rates bcs of the bank walk those companies have to pay a higher cost for credit which squeezes their profits.", "created": 1780965726468, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 5619/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpd7zuc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Seasonality: if you go back 20 years, 30 years, usually the end of october is usually the weeks the low in the markets and from there we tend to see a rally going into the 1st of january.", "created": 1780965726423, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5620/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 5623/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 5625/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdibex", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Some of the strongest rallies occur in a downtrend in the bear market", "created": 1780965726417, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5626/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdw5vt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It's not about picking Tops or Bottoms, It's about knowing where we are in the cycle and then riding these trends.", "created": 1780965726416, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5627/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdqzrc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Sovereign debt default cycle: In summary: increased cost of borrowing \u2192 debt grows faster than expected \u2192 external demand for debt decreases \u2192 interest rates increase more \u2192 need for more debt \u2192 debt spiral \u2192 default.", "created": 1780965726414, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5628/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpd0ikt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So I would rather own equity in the company than be a bondholder bcs what inflation ends up doing id it ends up transferring wealth from creditors to debtors. So i would rather own the company than the bonds of the company, which are going to be eroding away in value bcs of inflation.", "created": 1780965726413, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5629/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpd60sr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In an inflationary environment, you want to own companies that have pricing power. You want to own companies that are selling products and services that people need and they will pay for. Products that they will continue to buy even if the price goes up. Whereas you don\u2019t wanna own the stock of the companies that are selling products that people only buy after they buy all the things they need, then if they have any money left over, they buy these other things that they want. People just give up, they don\u2019t have any money left over after you pay your rent, electricity, food, insurance, taxes, after your pay for all the necessities if there's nothing left over. Well, there's nothing left over. And if you can't go out and narrow it anymore, there's no credit floating around anymore bcs everything is tightening up. Well, a lot of these companies are going away. So you want to own companies that have pricing power, but also in an inflationary time period, you want to own companies bcs they own real assets, they have resources, they have plant equipment, they have things that have value and that will hold value even as paper claims are losing value.", "created": 1780965726412, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5630/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdhsfr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The treasury yield curve is a short-term bet on a long term rate. The Eurodollar futures curve is a long term bet on a short term rate. Bcs the Eurodollar future is like we are betting on what an overnight rate is gonna be two years from now. Once Eurodollar start inverting it takes it 2 years to reach the bottom. The Eurodollar curve shouldn\u2019t be inverted That should never happen. it does happen but it should not happen. yield curves should be upward sloping just bcs time value of money and uncertainty, etc if i lend you for a longer period of time of make a further forward bet, i should get a higher rate. well, how come people betting on overnight rates a year or two years from now think that rates are going to be lower? And that shouldn't happen. The only explanation for that is we're going to go into a recession. It's going to get a lot worse.", "created": 1780965726411, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5631/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpdwlh3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Simple Guide to Moving averages: 5 EMA: short term trend.` 10 EMA: strong Momentum.` 20 EMA: Dynamic Support & Resistance.` 50 EMA: Long term support & Resistance.` 100 EMA: First Hurdle between 50 & 200 EMA.` 200 EMA: LAST LINE OF DEFENSE.", "created": 1780965726410, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5632/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpduvvo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Signs of global liquidity crisis: Inverted Eurodollar futures curve, Inverted Treasury Yield Curve, Negative Swap Spreads, Treasury Bills auctions with the Yield to maturity below what the Fed will give you for a phone call, Fails to deliver and Fails to Receive spiking.", "created": 1780965726408, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5633/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcgnbo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In 1990, we had a recession but there was no financial panic. In 2008 we had both they kinda came in together.", "created": 1780965726405, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5634/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcu7o6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A global financial crisis (a global liquidity crisis) is different from recessions. Financial panics and recessions are two different things. They can come separately, in 1998 we had a financial panic but there was no recession.", "created": 1780965726404, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5635/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcxd5i", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed has a dual mandate: price stability and low unemployment. INFLATION IS JOB ONE.", "created": 1780965726403, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5636/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpclusq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Supply chain breakdown cause a lot of inflation. Inflation has two major sources: One is supply side which is called cost push inflation.", "created": 1780965726402, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5637/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpckhyx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What's good collateral and why dollar spikes in crisis? in tough times like in 2008 banks tell each other: i don\u2019t want your Corporates, i don\u2019t want your mortgages, i don\u2019t even want your 10-year notes. Give me at a stretch, i will give you I'll take a 2 year note with a haircut or what i really want are 30,60,90 day treasury bills. I just want very short-term treasury bills, so you gotta go out and get the treasury bills and they are dollar denominated, which means you need dollars. So if you are a credit Suisse or Barclays or Hong Kong , shanghai or Deutsche bank, you don\u2019t live in the US, the country that prints the dollar, the US does but the European bank doesn\u2019t.", "created": 1780965726389, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5638/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpclys4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why there is a global dollar shortage? How can we have a dollar shortage with the Fed printing trillions of dollars in new money? You have $1 Quadrillion of derivatives in the banking system as a whole, so that slice of $7 Trillion of M0 total money supply or $24 Trillion of M1 that has to support $1 Quadrillion of derivatives. And btw a Quadrillion is 1000 trillion.", "created": 1780965726388, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5639/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpc31zn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The first people to figure out recession are business owners, they see it. If inventories are sky high, and new orders are being slashed you are not moving anything by truck. If you are in the trucking business you see it in real time.", "created": 1780965726386, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5640/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcr9ju", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global recessions are RARE. We had financial crisis in 2008 even though Australia did power through it and we had one in 2020 during the pandemic lockdown, but they are unusual. Usually one country or a group of countries are in a little bit of trouble, but another group powers through and can even pull the recession country or group out of difficulty. BUT WHEN GLOBAL GDP DECLINES THAT'S RARE.", "created": 1780965726383, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5641/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcf9gu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When you talk about reserve currency, you have to understand what that means. It\u2019s not like the people's bank of China has a bunch of $100 Bills on pallet\u2019s stacked up in the basement. When people say \"reserve currency\", what they really mean IS THE CURRENCY OF THE BONDS THAT THEY INVEST IN. In other words, their dollar denominated assets in a form of treasury bonds or notes. That\u2019s what China actually have on their books not like dollars per se. So, if you want to hypothesize that the Chinese yuan is going to replace the US Dollar as the global reserve currency, where is the yuan bond market? It just doesn\u2019t exist. Very small scale, very illiquid, no primary dealers, No when issued trading, No auctions, No Repo, No settlement clearance, None of the PLUMBING AND THE MACHANICS of a mature bond market such as the United States. And above all they don\u2019t have the rule of law. So the absence of rule of law number one. Number two: The absence of the infrastructure, the plumbing. Are the two reasons why the yuan and the ruble will not replace the dollar as a reserve currency bcs they don\u2019t have the bond markets and they are not gonna have them any time soon.", "created": 1780965726382, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5642/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcz8zi", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "You want assets that are going to be immune from the global liquidity crisis. What are they? Land, real estate, gold, silver, fine art, natural resources, water, energy, oil. If you want to be in stocks, buy the stocks of companies that produce natural resources such as ExxonMobil, Chevron. in a global liquidity crisis regular stock gets hammered, banks are going to be in distress, money market funds are going to be in distress. That's what a liquidity crisis is.", "created": 1780965726381, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5643/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcg2t4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "We know exactly what the Feds are gonna do bcs they always tell us exactly what they are gonna do so all we have to do is listen to them and believe them.", "created": 1780965726378, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5644/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcyoa0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And when they do, they may pivot at that time. But when they do it won\u2019t be for a good reason, it will be for a very bad reasons meaning a bad recession and stocks have plunged. So when Fed cut rates don\u2019t cheer too loudly bcs it will be in a world where we have a severe recession, higher unemployment, and crashing stock prices are the norm.", "created": 1780965726377, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5645/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcza4z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When Fed pivot it's not for a good reasons, it will be for a very bad reasons. Meaning we are in a recessions and stocks have plunged. Usually when Fed start raising rates, they Always over tighten causing a very severe recession.", "created": 1780965726376, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5646/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcws12", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why Inflation and interest rate coming down too fast is bad for stocks? If inflation come down fast and interest rates come down fast that\u2019s bcs we are in a very severe recession. And so if that's the case stocks are gonna plunge 30,40,50%. So if you are rooting and forecasting lower rates, understand what that means, it means that we are in a every severe recession and therefore stocks are gonna plunge. So be careful what u wish for.", "created": 1780965726375, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5647/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcvlbd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Manufacturing capacity utilization and backlogs \"Manufacturers Unfilled Orders tell us how Manufacturing is doing RIGHT NOW and warn us of BLACK SWANS.", "created": 1780965726372, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5648/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcv97z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "United States ISM Non manufacturing prices have been a great tool to predict future inflation.", "created": 1780965726361, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5649/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpceuq7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The best economic forecaster is the inside of the stock market. The performance of cyclicals versus defensive stocks that always leads the real economy it doesnt lag it. It shows you when you are getting an upturn so if you see cyclical stocks beginning to pick up thats a really good sign. Also yield curve steepening thats a good sign, also looking at monetary hedges: precious metals , bitcoin when they pump thats a good sign. Also Tech stocks should lead bcs they are long duration investments.", "created": 1780965726355, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 5653/12122  ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 5654/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpcm9d5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Economic Boom weakens Dollar bcs there is so much Liquidity issued through new loans and Credit.", "created": 1780965726344, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5655/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpc01ql", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What determines Dollar strength or weakness is : Interest rate differential between the US and the Rest of the World (especially Europe and Japan), Economic Growth differential between the US and the Rest of the World ( Especially Europe and Japan), and it\u2019s safe Haven status especially in economic crisis and wars.", "created": 1780965726343, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5656/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpc8xrj", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Illiquidity is a vicious cycle: illiquidity leads to fire sale dumping prices big times which leads to even more illiquidity which leads to even more vicious fire sale which trigger a panic and chaos in the market where investors start selling ALL investments at any price just to exit the market. - `18:08:22` --- note 5657/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpbdco1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What is the carry trade? Some countries have higher interest rates than others and so it\u2019s natural to want to invest in those higher interest rate countries. For ex: in the 90s a favorite carry trade was buying dollars and selling yen so it meant borrowing in yen where the interest rate was close to 0 and then investing in dollars where you were getting 5%. Well that just sounds great. Well it\u2019s great as long as the currency is moving to ur advantage or holding still. Bcs there are two components to the carry trade: the interest rate differential but there is also the move in the currency so you want the currency to move in your favor as well so for instance let\u2019s look at the dollar/yen: if you buy dollar yen you are earning 5% a year then you are hoping that dollar will appreciate against the yen as well so you will be double dipping and you get a double whammy and that\u2019s really what the carry trade does. The carry trade says or postulates that the higher interest rate currency will actually attract investors which will make the currency move in your favor and you are going to double whammy on the market move as well as the interest rate which is much higher than the currency that you are selling effectively borrowing against. The carry trade works however the carry trade is a macro expression that the world is benign, when the world goes pear-shaped carry trades get unwound heavily and a nice example is 1998 as well as 2007. in 1998 people had to unwind dollar yen bcs they were incurring losses and getting liquidated on a lot of other positions primarily driven by the Russian default. In October 1998 Dollar yen more or less within a day managed to move from 120 to 104 or lower so there are 17 big figures in a day where sometimes price just gapped. This is like a 17% move on the currency in one day which is virtually unheard of and there was blood on the street on this and people lost Billions of dollars on this. So when you have these massive global shocks carry trades get affected and so in 2007 you had a very similar situation, there was already the flare up into the great financial crisis, the credit crunch that we saw and what happened in August of 2007 was again that the yen crosses bcs again yen was at the time a favorite funding currency meaning a currency with low interest rate that allows me to borrow in yen and invest in higher yielding currencies those yen crosses got he
- `18:08:22` --- note 5709/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpbfejy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE and QT are directly opposite to each other. During QE the Fed prints money and buys assets and they take assets out of the financial marketplace, and they insert cash. Quantitative tightening is the opposite, those assets the Fed bought are debt, debt gets paid off which means as those treasuries mature dollars are getting paid to the Federal Reserve and they are ceasing to be in circulation, they literally cease to exist. When the Federal reserve is engaging in QT, they don\u2019t even have to do this passively by just letting debt getting paid off they can be even more aggressive and actually sell debt back onto the marketplace but either way dollars are leaving circulation making liquidity scarcer. This is both true in absolute terms and in ratio terms: the relative amount of liquidity relative to the amount of assets or collateral in the system.", "created": 1780965726216, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5717/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22` --- note 5759/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpai9m3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the Federal gov borrows money, they do that by selling a bond, we call them treasuries.", "created": 1780965726161, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5760/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpaafor", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "During 2018 and 2019 when the Federal Reserve was engaging in Quantitative tightening obviously liquidity was becoming more and more scarce during that time THIS BLEW UP IN THE FACE OF FINANCIAL MARKETS in September of 2019 in September of 2019 everybody needed cash but nobody had cash it just wasn\u2019t available the repo market blew up overnight cash market became extremely expensive and then the FED had to intervene again, they did this by returning to QE; you can clearly see their balance sheet expanding again, reversing the QT from before injecting new cash into the system, buying assets out of the system.", "created": 1780965726160, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5761/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpax2jg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed balance sheet growing increases liquidity in the financial system and the Fed balance sheet shrinking will decrease liquidity in the financial system. That\u2019s because the mechanics of QE and QT are directly opposite to each other. During QE the Fed prints money and buys assets and they take assets out of the financial marketplace, and they insert cash. Quantitative tightening is the opposite, those assets the Fed bought are debt, debt gets paid off which means as those treasuries mature dollars are getting paid to the Federal Reserve and they are ceasing to be in circulation, they literally cease to exist. When the Federal reserve is engaging in QT, they don\u2019t even have to do this passively by just letting debt getting paid off they can be even more aggressive and actually sell debt back onto the marketplace but either way dollars are leaving circulation making liquidity scarcer. This is both true in absolute terms and in ratio terms: the relative amount of liquidity relative to the amount of assets or collateral in the system.", "created": 1780965726159, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5762/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa59z4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT is the opposite of QE; QT is the process by which the Federal Reserve balance sheet actually shrinks.", "created": 1780965726158, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5763/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpahkb8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE doesn\u2019t directly influence of control the actual money supply M2 in other words bank deposits like your dollars in your bank account instead it increases the base layer of money or in other words Bank reserves, those increased bank reserves then give banks the ability to lend money into existence which then increases M2. So, QE lays the foundation for the capability for more money in circulation. It does not directly cause it but for banks that base money those reserves are liquidity.", "created": 1780965726157, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5764/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpaovax", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Quantitative Easing QE: the process where the Federal Reserve prints money out of thin air and purchases assets from financial markets, mostly US Treasuries and they are purchasing these treasuries from Banks. As the Fed buys these treasuries from the open markets, the banks that sell the treasuries to the FED get this cash and then with that Cash they\u2019re able to do anything they want and usually they just turn around and buy more treasuries. This process increases the money supply, and it increases both the absolute level of liquidity in the system and the ratio of liquidity relative to the amount of collateral in the system because the Fed is injecting dollars into the system while withdrawing the treasuries or assets or collateral from the system so there\u2019s more reserves more liquidity more cash and less collateral less assets less treasuries.", "created": 1780965726156, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5765/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpaq45e", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "As the gov increases its borrowing or in other words the deficit gets worst these treasuries flood the system and when increased borrowing happens at the exact same time as the Federal Reserve is tightening you get liquidity issues fewer dollars in circulation while there\u2019s an increasing demand for these dollars. Both things happened in 2018 and 2019. (To spot this look at the Fed balance sheet and federal deficit and surplus). And when these things happen the market reacts extremely poorly take for instance the taper tantrum that happened at the end of 2018 where the stock market fell over 20% and the only thing that stopped this market collapse was the Federal Reserve promising to stop raising interest rates and the market started expecting future interest rates cuts and the time before that when we experienced liquidity issues was the great financial crisis in which the stock market fell 57% from top bottom and the secured overnight financing rate spiking always preceded those crisis warning us about low liquidity and cracks in the system. SOFR starting to spike is a sign that conditions are worsening and about to blow up and we are about to see consequences so be very careful.", "created": 1780965726155, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5766/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa9lr3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Every single time the FED was doing QT we had a Repo Market liquidity crisis.", "created": 1780965726154, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5767/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa7jmc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why are Repo Rate and SOFR so important? Because NOT A SINGLE financial institution in THE WORLD can exist without easy and cheap access to overnight cash and as the reserves in the financial system dwindle down the access to that liquidity becomes more expensive as liquidity gets scarcer by the day.", "created": 1780965726153, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpae7gg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "BTP BUND and Claims on euro area residents denominated in foreign currency are great barometers for Euro area and Eurodollar liquidity and they predict black swan and financial crisis ahead of time. A spike in euro area residents denominated in foreign currency is signal of Eurodollar liquidity shortage and always followed with FED intervening by injecting dollars in the Eurodollar system through swaps.", "created": 1780965726130, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5788/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa3uka", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why is Bank Reserves with the FED is a great barometer for liquidity? Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires banks to keep a certain amount of reserves or cash on hold at the FED at all times which aims to improve the banking sector's ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress, bank argued that keeping bank reserves with fed on hold makes it harder for them to lend out cash on a dime when money gets tight. So when liquidity is low especially close to the dates when reporting take place and when liquidity is tight , financial institutions will want their own balance sheet to look safer so banks be holding the little bit of their reserves for themselves however when FED is doing QE taking in treasuries and giving out cash to the market which means Fed is injecting cash into the system for everyone to borrow even if the Repo players stop lending again financial instituions dont really have to worry about cash bcs there is plenty of it in the system , QE aims to boost reserves allowing banks to stay liquid without violating the liquidity coverage ratio rule and in doing so its keep the wheels of financial system spinning. A higher bank reserves would allow bank to lend more and a lower bank reserves would force banks to lend less.", "created": 1780965726129, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5789/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpagobh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "By tracking these indicators and data series, investors and policymakers can gain a better understanding of the overall level of global liquidity. - `18:08:22` --- note 5790/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpak9w3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bloomberg and Reuters: These financial data providers publish a variety of data series on global liquidity, including asset prices, credit spreads, and market sentiment indices.", "created": 1780965726127, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5791/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpalkl9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Federal Reserve Bank of New York: The Fed publishes a number of data series on global liquidity, including the weekly money supply report and the quarterly flow of funds report.", "created": 1780965726126, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5792/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpakcfm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bank for International Settlements (BIS): The BIS publishes a number of indicators on global liquidity, including the global liquidity indicators (GLIs). The GLIs track a variety of factors, including cross-border loans, international debt securities, and foreign exchange reserves.", "created": 1780965726125, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5793/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa73r3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Here are some specific data sources that can be used to track global liquidity:", "created": 1780965726124, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5794/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpal0ty", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In addition to these quantitative indicators, it is also important to consider qualitative factors when tracking global liquidity. For example, it is important to monitor the sentiment of investors and market participants. If investors are becoming more bearish and risk-averse, this can lead to a decrease in liquidity.", "created": 1780965726123, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5795/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpabzza", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-Asset prices: Asset prices, such as stock and bond prices, can also be used to track liquidity. - `18:08:22` --- note 5796/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa1zf0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Credit markets: Credit markets are another important source of liquidity. - `18:08:22` --- note 5797/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpap8p8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Money supply: The money supply refers to the total amount of money in circulation in an economy. - `18:08:22` --- note 5839/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpapj52", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "ONCE carry trades start to lose big it\u2019s not just a blip and a reverse they start to accelerate the DUMP it\u2019s like a waterfall DUMP (that\u2019s bcs of the immense leverage in carry trade: most carry trades are levered to the tit\u2019s to maximize profit). so there are carry trade strategies that have this type of waterfall behavior and if you can actually anticipate or find when it\u2019s first going off a cliff you can just stop yourself and get out of the trade unwinding your positions and your Risk asset positions basically just shutting down the whole system bcs you are anticipating smthg really nasty to happen and that\u2019s what happened on the 25th of july 2007 already the Nikkei started to collapse, volatility in Japan started to go up, VIX was going up. So yes carry trades have that nasty component and that\u2019s a feature of these types of systems so you have systems that bleed you money but then knock it out of the ballpark so that\u2019s trend following or you have system that grind as turn slowly slowly slowly and All the sudden we see a Huge Waterfall Nasty DUMP. So when you are trading carry trade you Always have to be mindful to detect that big initial shock Dump bcs that\u2019s a very strong indicator you need to get out or else your entire portfolio is about to get wiped out. Carry trades have that signature of wanting to get off a cliff so when it\u2019s about to get off a cliff the best thing to do is just to get out. the carry trade is a theme of eating like a bird and shitting like an elephant.", "created": 1780965726067, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5840/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpaxbwb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "As long as the funding country (Japan or switzerland) pin down yields and keep manipulating to stay low at certain determined range (which will keep devaluing the currency) and as long as the funding currency is stable or depreciating. And As long as the country where the carry trade is invested hikes rates or keep them stable (just not suddenly cutting them creating volatility) and the currency of the country where the carry trade is invested is stable or appreciating then the carry trade is profitable and will be leverade and used to invest in Risk assets around the globe providing them with liquidity causing Global Risk assets to PUMP. A wind down and Dumping of the carry trade will drain liquidity injected into Global Risk Assets causing them to DUMP.", "created": 1780965726066, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5841/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpacutn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The biggest enemy of a levered carry trader is YIELD VOLATILITY, carry traders dont want yields on either side to SWING AROUND, they just want them to STAY STILL and that way they can just maintain their yield spread especially if they are using leverage. the narrow of the yield carry trade: either by the yield of the borrowing currency go up or by the yield on the invested currency going down would cause a levered carry trader to get liquidated thats why YIELD volatility cause carry trader to get liquidated which unwind their positions which DUMP RISK assets around the globe.", "created": 1780965726065, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5842/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa7t7m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Currency Volatility: ideally in a carry trade u want the currency that u borrowed from to go down and the currency that u invested in to go up. If the currency that u borrowed from goes up against that currency that u invested in that's gonna erase all the profits u made from the interest rate differential and thats gonna BLOW UP ur carry trade.", "created": 1780965726064, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5843/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpadudq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yield volatility: if the interest rate in the country u borrowing from shoots up which make ur borrowing very expensive and ur carry trade might not even be worth it or if the interest rate in the country u invested in goes down which again makes ur carry trade not worth it.", "created": 1780965726063, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 5844/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x0cpa9e9s", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What would make a carry trade blow up?
