- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zh7h7r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bank create money out of thin air when it hands out a loan, when borrowers go and get a loan like a mortgage the bank open them a deposit account and deposit that mortgage or that loan money into that deposit account bascially creating money out of thin air. Banks are in the business of creating money but they cant do it into infinity bcs Banks have loan to deposit ratio, capital ratios, and lots of regulations and FDIC , Federal Reserve and Office controller of currency metrics to adhere to in order to limit the amount of money that they can create. So when deposits flee banks at the rate they are doing now in 2023 bank walk it severly impacts their ability to generate or create new money and that severely impacts their ability to hand out loans and thats why only the magnificent 7 stocks are doing great in 2023 while the other 2993 companies are struggling, its not only not banks not handing them loans and credit why they are struggling but their conduit for financial services. As bank not in the greatest profitability position, pain in 2993 companies will keep mounting. So bottom line as long as the bank walk continues the bank stocks will continue to struggle, and the further away you get from your ability to borrow from corporate bond market and the more you are reliant on banks the more your company will be struggling and the more your stock will be struggling and thats not by coincidence. In essence the companies relying on banks for credit and financial services are having harder times compared to the maginificent 7 stocks who can be somewhat independent from banks. so while the bank walk always end up showing up in the economy and its not gonna entirely gonna crash the system but nevertheless its gonna be a dull drag on the economy and companies. Banks can always raise deposit rates to hold on to deposits but that kills their profitability , they keep the banks deposits low so that that money becomes very profitable for them and the bank walk just continue, they are in a very difficult position.", "created": 1780965710730, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhhzd6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHY DID THE MEGA 7 OUTPERFORMED THE REST OF THE MARKET (DID 2800% SINCE 2012 WHILE S&P 500 DID 280% IN THAT TIME PERIOD). Large Mega cap Companies (Magnificent 7 stocks: Facebook + Apple + Tesla + Nividia + Microsoft + Amazon + Google) dont need banks, they are almost like central banks in and of themselves, they can borrow in capital markets, they have no problem getting financial services, they are entities on their own. These companies can go to the corporate bond market and borrow at rates very close to what the US gov gets. But when you get to the mere mortal companies the other 2993 of the Russell 3000 they need banks, they need financial services, they need money transfer facilities, they need loans, they need a lot of services from banks. This squeeze that we are seeing in banks might be holding back a lot of those other companies which why collectively they only pushed the index 3% Not much more profit than what you would have been in money market funds bcs money market funds are up 2.6% for the year. Unlike the mega companies who can borrow directly from the corp bond market, When the Bottom 1000 or Bottom 1500 companies of the Russell 3000 needs money they have to borrow from the banks and in times when banks are raising their rates bcs of the bank walk those companies have to pay a higher cost for credit which squeezes their profits.", "created": 1780965710729, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}

THEY ARE USING ALMOST THE SAME STRATEGY AS THE CARB LENDING BRITISH INVESTORS WERE USING IN THE 1920S. Carb lending is what fueled 1927 to 1929 us stock Boom and Bust: carb lending was used to lend people money to buy stocks on margin with 20% interest rates. Also while bank of england rate was 4%, Financial speculatives in uk (which was the global hedgemon at the time) saw that they can make a lot more money in carb lending. So they would make 20% off the bat to lend money to people to buy stocks on margin, plus they had their money parked in the US stock market which was just booming AND they also had the Dollar sterling rate in the favor (sterling was weakening vs the dollar). BTITISH FINANCIERS WERE LIKE: \"I DONT WANNA INVEST IN GERMANY, IM GONNA LEND PEOPLE TO INVEST INVEST IN THE US STOCK MARKET ON MARGIN I WILL BE GETTING PAID 20% AND MY MONEY IS GONNA BE THE US STOCK MARKET APPRECIATING\" SO THEY WERE TRIPPLE DIPPING. THIS MASSIVE INFLUX OF MONEY FROM THE UK AND REST OF THE WORLD IS WHAT LIFTED THE US STOCK MARKET IN 1927 TO 1929 TO THE SKY BEFORE IT POPPED IN 1929.", "created": 1780965710719, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhbn5r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How is the global trade system is supposed to work in theory? China and other americas trade nations have consistently run substantial surpluses on their trade account vs their GDP (2% to 10% of GDP so very very substantial), and trade surpluses in a system that restore equilibrium are typically met over time with a currency appreciation in the export nations currency (bcs low currency is gonna increase demand for its exports making it export more and this increase demand for exports is gonna increase demand for its currency making it appreciate). The exporter currency appreciation is a good thing its kinda like a reward for their efforts to export more than they import, and so the appreciation of the currency effectively makes their citizens richer relative than the rest of the world and richer citizens tend to travel and to import more and more products richer citizens underwrite stronger domestic consumption which gonna bring in more imports bcs of domestic demand for foreign goods. This domestic demand for foreign goods(imports) is gonna boost world exports from other nations which is gonna flourish world trade and its gonna appreciate other exporting nations currency bcs of the increase demand for their exports from this newbie rich nation, so this newbie rich country not did it appreciate its local currency but also appreciate it other exports currency as well bringing the whole system to balance out. Once the deficit countries receive that currency boost (which comes through them exporting more goods) and by them exporting more goods increasing their global market share then you no longer have that anomaly of perpetual surpluses and the system just balance out. That's how the system is meant to balance out and work in theory. The reason why the system isnt working nowadays as designed in theory is bcs china and other exports are diverting the funds (their trade surplus proceeds) which would have appreciated their currency made their citizens richer and instead the money has been used to buy US Treasuries bonds which serve am informal QE that lower interest rates in the US and the Euro Dollar system and enrich americans bcs lower rates and gonna pump stock market and real estate prices which boost demand in the united states and the rest of the world (chinese exports are gonna benefit the most of this new increase demand bcs they have the largest global market share), resulting in even more chines

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhi0tv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Repo Rates are typically quite low in normal times because the Repo deals are collateralized and seen as safe and the repo market is not usually volatile. But this has changed dramatically in September 2019 when the overnight repo rate shot up from around 2% to around 10% in the space of a week. Since this market is SO CRITICAL to the financial world any disruptions can cause ripples throughout the whole system, in basic terms if a market rate spikes from around 2% to around 10% it means that the market participants doesnt wanna lend in this case it seems to have been due to a liquidity crunch, the supply of cash available to lend out have reduced at the same time that demand for cash increased as more securities flooded into the market as a collateral looking for cash to borrow, with an increase in demand and a decrease in supply the rate shot up. The Fed explains that these issues happens mainly due to two events occuring at the same time : firstly corporate tax payments drains the repo market of liquidity and at the same time the repo market was being used to finance an unusually large settlement of treasury auctions. However the BIS have stated that these issues may have been among the problems but they dont justify the huge repo rate spike that occurred. BIS focused on other alarming reasons: Most Repo Market activity moves between four large banks: JP Morgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo, a chart from BIS shows how the repo market is depending more and more on these four institutions basically if these banks even slightly reduce their lending the market would suffer massively. Jamie Damon CEO of JP Morgan has said the bank had the cash available and would have been happy to lend it out and profit from the higher rates but it was unable to since the financial crisis of 2008 banks have to satisfy regulations that require them to hold a certain amount of reserves known as the liquidity coverage ratio. So JP Morgan may have reserves available but are unable to lend them out as they need to hold on to them to satisfy the regulations particularly at the end of the quarter like in September or in December since thats when reporting take place and they will want their own balance sheet to look safer in addition to this banks may have been reluctant to lend as their reserves has been reduced so significantly since the FED started unwinding its QE so banks have been holding to their reserves for th

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhbatw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Carry trade: People around the world are borrowing in US Dollar and then doing whatever they doing in their local economies: taking out a business loans or trying to grow up businesses or JUST SPECULATING. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhflo6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In carry trade the cost of carry is that you are carrying that debt load, so if you are carrying that debt load NOT ONLY YOU HAVE TO PAY OFF THE DEBT AT THE END OF THE TERM BUT YOU ALSO HAVE TO PAY THE INTEREST RATE COST TO SERVICE THAT DEBT AS WELL. - `18:08:22` --- note 6686/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zh8z1k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "What's the difference between Trend and Momentum? A trend means it's trending in a Direction it's going up or down or sideways. - `18:08:22` --- note 6730/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhs0xr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "TYPICALLY BUBBLES HAVE AN ASYMMETRIC SHAPE: THE BOOM IS LONG AND DRAWN OUT SLOW TO START, IT ACCELERATES GRADUALLY UNTIL IT FLATTENS OUT DURING THE TWILIGHT PERIOD. THE BUST IS SHORT AND STEEP BCS IT'S REINFORCED BY THE FORCED LIQUIDATION OF UNSOUND POSITIONS. DISILLUSIONMENT TURNS INTO PANIC REACHING ITS CLIMAX IN A FINANCIAL CRISIS.", "created": 1780965710468, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6731/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhsd3n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The optimal long opportunity is when the MACD is shifting from Negative momentum to positive momentum ( when color turns from dark red to light red). The best short opportunies usually take place when the MACD is going from positive momentum to negative mometum (at the top when color turns from bright green to light green). These 2 are the crosses Kevin svenson really looks for he doesnt really care about macd cross up and cross down from green to red or vice versa that doesnt help him very much bcs by that point the momentum has already shifted and is already in play. The most important thing about MACD is judging momentum.", "created": 1780965710467, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6732/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zh8pjz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "MACD indicator helps judge Momentum. MACD is BEST seen on Monthly chart. Kevin Svenson dont care about macd cross up and cross down from green to red or vice versa bcs by that point the momentum has already shifted and is already in play. People are fully focused on macd cross up and cross down but kevin svenson almost ignore them. What he looks for is the momentum shifts on the macd histogram which take place at the peaks and troughs (bottom) of the macd trends.", "created": 1780965710466, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6733/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zhwasg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Hot money is the one that cause currencies to pump or dump when central banks either hikes or cut rates. Hot money are in for a short gain they in for a quick buck and they invest in govs bonds and they usually follow the money meaning they usually invest in the countries with the highest rates. And that's the same exact mechanism of how a currency appreciate vs another when it's central bank raise interest rates higher than the others. Hot money sells the currency of the lower interest rate and buy the currency of the country with the higher interest rates. The buying and selling of the currencies doesn't only shift the supply of demand for the underlying currencies but it also change the foreign exchange reserves in both countries boosting foreign exchange reserves in the country with the higher rate boosting confidence in that country currency causing it to pump and diminish exchange reserves in the country with the lower rates which diminish confidence in that currency causing it to dump ( that's bcs most hot money is in us dollar, maybe a Lil bit of euro and yen but a very very small proportion). If hot money makes let's say 30% in the currency fluctuations alone they would immediately exit that country's market (they wouldn't wait for the profit from the gov bonds they would immediately sell that foreign gov bonds get the profit and exit the country). Hot money knows that this is a very risky game that's why they opt in makes a quick profit and opt out.", "created": 1780965710465, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6734/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5x00zheqsu", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "REAL ESTATE PRICE BOOMS ARE CAUSED BY EASY CREDIT AND LOOSE FINANCIAL CONDITIONS: THE SIMPLEST BUBBLE CASE IS A REAL ESTATE BOOM THE TREND THAT PRECIPITATES IT IS THAT CREDIT BECOMES CHEAPER AND MORE EASILY AVAILABLE, THE MISCONCEPTION IS THAT THE VALUE OF THE COLLATERAL IS INDEPENDENT OF THE AVAILABILITY OF CREDIT AS A MATTER OF FACT THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE AVAILABILITY OF CREDIT AND THE VALUE OF THE COLLATERAL IS REFLEXIVE WHEN CREDIT BECOMES CHEAPER AND MORE EASILY AVAILABLE ACTIVITY PICK UPS AND REAL ESTATE VALUES RISE, THERE ARE FEWER DEFAULTS, CREDIT PERFORMANCE IMPROVES AND LENDING STANDARDS ARE RELAXED. SO AT THE HEIGHT OF THE BOOM THE AMOUNT OF CREDIT INVOLVED IS AT ITS MAXIMUM AND A REVERSAL PERCIPITATES FORCED LIQUIDATION DEPRESSING REAL ESTATE PRICES. YET THIS MISCONCEPTION CONTINUES TO OCCUR IN VARIOUS GUISES. NOT ALL BUBBLES INVOLVE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT SOME ARE BASED ON EQUITY LEVERAGING.", "created": 1780965710464, "pinned": false, "source": "3rd book.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w2ld7qb77", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Any indicator on its own probably doesnt mean too much but when a number of indicators: 5 or 6  point to the same conclusion : its time to pay attention.\r\n\r\nCrypto and Risk Assets are directly tied to Liqudity. When there is plenty of liquidity they Pump , when liquidity JUST starts to drain (just the start of the drain) crypto and Risk Assets DUMP.\r\n\r\nFED controls liquidity through Treasuries Held Outright , REPO, SWAPS , Reverse Repo and Treasury General Account and interest Rates. \r\n\r\nFED uses REPO, SWAPS , interest rate cuts, increase Bank Reserves to pump liquidity into the system and raise interest rates, Reverse Repo and Treasury General Account, shrink Bank Reserves to drain liquidity from the system.\r\n\r\nSwaps and QE increase liquidity and dollar supply therefore cause DXY to Dump, QT shrink liquidity and Dollar supplu causing DXY to Pump.\r\n\r\nSwaps: Loans extended by the Fed to friendly countries to help with Dollar shortage in the EuroDollar Market (Dollar shortage causing Dollar to be too strong) (usually Swap lines are extended in 30 days tenor but during crises are extended in 7 days or even overnight tenor). Swaps are form of a loan that has to be paid back with interest. How does the Swap line mechanism work? The Friendly countries have an account at the FED so the US will deposit Dollars in those foreign countries account at the FED, at the same time those countries will deposit their own currency in an account for the FED at their Central Bank. And then the USA and the friendly country have to SWAP Back 30 days, 7 days or overnight with interest paid to the USA. So when the USA is printing money to give the Rest of the world, the Rest of the world is printing even more Money to give to the USA.\r\ninitially when the USA extend swap lines and countries draw down those swap lines its negative for the dollar short term however its positive for the Dollar long term since those swap loans have to be paid back with interest. Whenever the USA extends the swap lines is just reinforce the Dollar as the Reserve currency bcs its just extending more US Dollar Debt that the rest of the world have to pay back with interest.\r\nThats why regardles of what happen in the short term \"Dollar dumping during QE era, High swap lines volume or whatnot\" The Dollar will ALWAYS rise long term vs other currencies, its just a matter of time before Dollar gets too strong again because all the m

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w1e03yt9m", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "CREDIT SPREAD A KEY GAUGE OF CORPORATE DEFAULT RISK: Since The Fed has hiked interest rates to more than 5% last year, the financial world has been keeping an eye on how interest rates affect companies' abilities to pay back their loans today. We can dive into this topic by looking at 1 indicator: credit spread, which is a crucial gauge for corporates Default risk that can offer clues to investor confidence and stock market trends. But first what exactly is credit spread? Simply put it refers to the difference in the yield between 2 debt securities. What does credit spread tell us about corporate Default risk? When the economy hits a rough patch and businesses start to look shaky, heightened corporate default risk cause investors to pull their money out of high-risk assets. Consequently, the prices of higher bond slide, pushing their yields higher and thus widening the credit spread. This had been the case of past economic downturns, such as the Dotcom bubble in 2002, the financial crisis in 2008 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. As the credit spread rose, indicating more corporate defaults, the S&P 500 fell in tandem. But when the default fear ease higher bond prices recover, yields decline and the credit spread narrows. On the stock market front investors regain confidence, pushing stock prices back towards levels that reflect their assessment on how well companies are doing. In a nutshell, widening credit for us signals, growing concerns about companies not being able to pay back their loans while narrowing spread means Investors are not too worried. Fast forward to the present You can see the credit spread in the US is not on the rise but remains relatively low at around 9 to 10% Suggesting low default risk a minimal chance of a credit crunch in the near term.", "created": 1780964094251, "pinned": false, "source": "HIGH YIELDS FINANCIAL NOTES.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w1e03r08g", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHERE TO SPOT THE LEVERAGE IN THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM? The leverage is ALWAYS in the weaker parts of the corporate sector. That is those firms that are essentially high yields, especially the worst part of the high yield. (which are C Level and lower) and among fallen angels which are a Trillion dollars (fallen angels are bonds that have gone from investment grade to below investment grade) That is THE LEVERAGE IN THE SYSTEM and that leverage is financed a lot by the SHADOW BANKING SYSTEM NOT THE TRADITIONAL BANKS So you cant see it in the balance sheets of the banks. As long as the economy is growing even if the balance sheets of corps are poor but you have revenues and you have some earnings growth, you can manage your debt just fine, you are not going to have a default. But now in addittion to balance sheet problem, you also have an PNL problem that if there was going to be a recession, of course the revenues and the profits of these firms that are already weak are gonna hit and thats where the credit spreads can widen. BUT WHEN THEY WIDEN THEY OFTEN WIDEN EXCESSIVELY NOT ONLY FOR HIGH YIELD BUT ALSO FOR HIGH GRADE. AND IN A RECESSSION, EVEN THE HIGH GRADE ARE GOING TO BE TO SOME EXTENT AT GREATER RISK. SO REALLY, CREDIT MARKETS ARE KEY BCS WE HAVE A HUGE AMOUNT OF LEVERAGE IN THE CORP SECTOR WITH BALANCE SHEETS THAT WERE EXCESSIVE LEVERAGED BUT AS LONG AS PNL IS DOING WELL YOU DONT HAVE TO WORRY ABOUT IT. BUT WHEN THERE IS A SHOCK TO PNL AND YOU HAVE BAD BALANCE SHEETS THEN YOU HAVE A CREDIT CRISIS AND THE RECESSION BECOMES VERY SEVERE. IT COULD BE AS SEVERE AS 2008.", "created": 1780964094246, "pinned": false, "source": "HIGH YIELDS FINANCIAL NOTES.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w165n89r1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why does taiwan dollar / usd pumping always flash the start of a bull run in risk assets? A strengthening Taiwan Dollar (TWD) against the U.S. Dollar (USD) \u2014 or \"TWD/USD pumping\" \u2014 often signals the start of a bull run in global risk assets for a few key macroeconomic and liquidity-related reasons: 1. Global Tech Cycle & Semiconductor Demand Taiwan is the epicenter of global semiconductor manufacturing (TSMC, UMC). When TWD strengthens, it's often because of surging foreign demand for Taiwanese exports, especially chips a leading indicator for global tech and manufacturing upcycles. Tech bull markets usually correlate with early-stage equity rallies, especially in NASDAQ, crypto, and emerging markets. 2. Capital Inflows & Global Liquidity A rising TWD often reflects hot money inflows into Asia, signaling risk-on sentiment. Investors rotate out of USD (a safe-haven currency) into emerging markets, indicating confidence in growth assets. This trend typically begins when the USD index (DXY) stalls or weakens, releasing global dollar pressure \u2014 a green light for risk assets. 3. USD Liquidity Release TWD/USD strength is a proxy for easing USD funding conditions in Asia. It often tracks or even leads: Falling cross-currency basis swaps Rising Asia FX reserves Loosening financial conditions. 4. Correlation With Crypto and Equities Historically, TWD/USD rallies precede or coincide with: Crypto breakouts (BTC, ETH, meme coins) Tech equity rebounds Commodities uptrends This is because it reflects reflation trades and manufacturing optimism, both supportive of beta assets. Summary: TWD/USD pumping = signal of global liquidity returning, USD pressure easing, Asia tech cycle starting, and risk assets (especially tech, crypto, EM) entering a bullish phase. what are the metrics to track hot money globally? ChatGPT said: To track hot money flows globally (short-term capital that moves quickly in and out of countries seeking yield or safety), you need to monitor a mix of currency, interest rate, bond, and liquidity indicators that reflect risk appetite, capital flight, or sudden inflows. Here are the most important hot money tracking metrics : \u8125 \uae62 \uae63 1. Cross-Border Capital Flow Metrics Metric What It Shows Tools Capital account / Financial account flows Net inflow/outflow of hot money IMF BOP, BIS, national central banks Portfolio investment flows Equities and bond buying by foreigners IM
- `18:08:22` --- note 6884/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w165nkfxd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FINANCIAL CRISIS EARLY DETECTION CHECKLIST Daily Market Health Check - DXY (Dollar Index): Stable or declining = healthy | Sharp rise (>2% in a week) = warning - Repo Rates (SOFR): Near Fed Funds rate = healthy | Repo spike (>50bps over Fed Funds) = warning - High Yield Spreads (HYG/Spreads): Stable/tightening = healthy | Sharp widening (>100bps) = warning - Bank Stocks (BKX Index): Stable or outperforming = healthy | Underperforming S&P 500 by >5% = warning - 2y/10y Yield Curve: Positive or flattening = healthy | Deep inversion (< -50bps) = warning - Oil and Copper Prices: Stable or rising = healthy | Sharp drops (>10% in a week) = warning - EM Currencies (CEW Index): Stable or appreciating = healthy | Rapid decline (>5% in a week) = warning - VIX (Volatility Index): Below 20-30 = healthy | Spike above 30 = warning Weekly Deep Dive Checklist - Review cross-currency basis swaps (EUR/USD, USD/JPY) - Check corporate bond market flows (HYG volume, issuance health) - Scan big bank CDS prices (JPM, GS, DB) - Watch EM bond spreads (EMB ETF, sovereign spreads) - Assess Treasury market liquidity (bid/ask spreads widening?) Red Alert Signals - Repo market spike + Dollar surge - Credit spreads blowing out across sectors - Bank stocks plunging relative to broader market - Treasury yields collapsing while stocks fall - Oil and copper collapsing together - EM contagion (currency crashes, capital controls) - VIX spiking above 40-50 Useful Links - Dollar Index (DXY): TradingView DXY - Repo Rates (SOFR): FRED SOFR - High Yield Spreads: FRED HY Spreads - Bank Stocks (BKX): TradingView BKX - Yield Curves: FRED 2s/10s - VIX Index: TradingView VIX Final Rule Credit breaks first. Dollar spikes second. Equities panic third. Stay vigilant. Catch it early. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5w165nfh14", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "IN A CREDIT CRISIS HEDGES SUDDENLY DISAPPEAR: even positions that are supposed to protect you from losses (hedges) can fail or become ine \u01af ective during a severe financial crisis. Here\u2019s why: 1. Counterparty Risk Spikes \uf0b7 Hedges like credit default swaps (CDS) or interest rate swaps rely on the other party being able to pay . \uf0b7 In a crisis, counterparties go bankrupt or become illiquid , so your hedge might be worthless even if it's \u201cin the money.\u201d 2. Correlation Goes to One \uf0b7 Assets that are normally uncorrelated start moving together. \uf0b7 A hedge that was designed to move opposite your main position now crashes too. \uf0b7 Example: In 2008, even safe- haven assets like gold and Treasuries sold o \u01af briefly due to forced liquidations. 3. Liquidity Evaporates \uf0b7 Instruments used to hedge (like CDS, options, futures) may become illiquid. \uf0b7 You can\u2019t sell or adjust your hedge at a fair price. \uf0b7 Bid-ask spreads blow out, so you eat losses even when \u201ctechnically\u201d hedged. 4. Margin Calls Kill Hedgers \uf0b7 Even if your hedge gains value, you may face margin calls on your core position and be forced to liquidate your hedge early , locking in losses. 5. Model Breakdown \uf0b7 Many hedging strategies rely on models assuming normal market behavior . \uf0b7 In a credit crisis, those models break down , leading to improper risk exposure . \uf0b7 Example: VaR-based hedging strategies underestimate tail risk. Bottom Line: In a credit crisis, the financial system is so stressed that your safety net either breaks, gets pulled out, or becomes useless \u2014this is why hedges \"disappear.\" EXAMPLE 1: Let\u2019s break down how hedges disappeared during the Lehman Brothers collapse (2008) \u2014 a textbook example of counterparty and systemic risk destroying risk protection. \uaee0 \uaee1 Context: Lehman was a major counterparty in global derivatives \u2014 swaps, CDS, repo, you name it. When they filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 , it shattered confidence in the financial system.    How Hedges Failed: 1. Credit Default Swaps (CDS) Failed \uf0b7 Hedge funds and banks used CDS to protect against defaults. \uf0b7 But Lehman was a seller of CDS . So when it collapsed, those hedges became worthless or highly uncertain. \uf0b7 Even if you were \u201cright\u201d and held CDS protection, if your counterparty was Lehman , you were out of luck. 2. - `18:08:22` --- note 6935/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxo2xjq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In summary, the 3-month JGB yield can be a useful indicator for assessing global liquidity conditions, but it should be considered alongside other financial and economic indicators for a more comprehensive view. Changes in this yield can signal shifts in investor sentiment, interest rate expectations, and global economic conditions, all of which play a role in determining liquidity in financial markets.", "created": 1780964022650, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6936/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxo99j3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "4-Currency Flows: Changes in the yield on Japanese government bonds can impact currency flows. If the yield on JGBs becomes more attractive relative to yields in other currencies, it may lead to an influx of foreign capital into Japan, causing its currency, the yen, to appreciate. Conversely, a declining yield may lead to a weaker yen as investors seek higher yields elsewhere. 5-Global Economic Conditions: Global liquidity conditions are closely tied to the state of the global economy. A strong global economy typically corresponds to ample liquidity, while a weak global economy can lead to tighter liquidity conditions. Changes in the 3-month JGB yield can be an indicator of how global economic conditions are impacting liquidity.", "created": 1780964022649, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6937/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxo93me", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "3-Global Liquidity Conditions: When global liquidity is ample, investors have more funds available for investment, and this can put downward pressure on yields, including the 3-month JGB yield. Conversely, when global liquidity tightens, investors may pull back from riskier assets, leading to higher yields on safe assets like JGBs.", "created": 1780964022648, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6938/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxo8y1q", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2-Interest Rate Expectations: Changes in the 3-month JGB yield can also reflect expectations about future interest rates. If the yield rises, it may suggest expectations of tighter monetary policy by the Bank of Japan or a more favorable economic outlook. Conversely, a falling yield might indicate expectations of looser monetary policy or economic concerns.", "created": 1780964022647, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 6939/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxomqmw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "1-Safe Haven Indicator: Japanese government bonds, especially shorter-term ones, are considered safe-haven assets. When global financial markets become uncertain or turbulent, investors tend to flock to safe assets like Japanese government bonds. As a result, the yield on these bonds tends to decline during periods of heightened global risk aversion.", "created": 1780964022646, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 6985/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzsxo6p13", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why does the Fed printing really doesnt matter? First bcs when the Fed prints it prints for the US and the rest of the world. Then the banks send the securities to the fed and the fed pays for it with money that comes out of thin air but here is the part that matters: what do the banks actually do with that money? They give it back to the FED in the form of excess reserves, bank deposit at the Fed. So that money never went anywhere, it was created , it is on the balance sheet, but it all went to the assets side which were securities and it never went into the economy.", "created": 1780964022599, "pinned": false, "source": "final financials book 2.docx"}

- `18:08:22` --- note 7642/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzq6m9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "ECB Data Portal \u2013 Indices of Consumer Prices (ICP) datasetdata.ecb.europa.eu \u2013 (Example of dataset page showing SDMX and CSV download links, confirming API availability for inflation data)", "created": 1780964020886, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7643/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzlz6i", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "ECB Data Portal \u2013 SDMX RESTful API Documentationdata.ecb.europa.eudata.ecb.europa.eu \u2013 (Details on constructing queries, using wildcards/OR for multiple series, and available query parameters like updatedAfter)", "created": 1780964020885, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7644/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpz1jey", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Data consistency: When mixing sources, we\u2019ll ensure the units and definitions are consistent. (E.g., if ECB\u2019s data for unemployment is a percentage, but an alternate source provides a rate in a different form, we convert it appropriately). We will also note in documentation if any indicator is coming from an alternate source.", "created": 1780964020880, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7645/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzv015", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This way, the scheduler/real-time fetch will attempt the API first, and if it gets an error or empty result, it can try the alternate. We should also log when fallbacks are used, in case the primary source is down or has changed.", "created": 1780964020879, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7646/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpznb3h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "def fetch_us_inflation(): try: return fetch_sdmx('ICP', key_for_us_cpi) except Exception: return fetch_alternate_us_cpi() # maybe scrape BLS or use IMF", "created": 1780964020878, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7647/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzs2tr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Implementation of fallbacks: In code, we can abstract the data sources by indicator. For each indicator, define a primary fetch method (usually ECB API) and a fallback method. For example:", "created": 1780964020877, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7648/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzgeud", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "CSV bulk downloads: The ECB portal itself provides bulk download links (as CSV or SDMX-ML) for entire datasetsdata.ecb.europa.eu. In a pinch, if the API retrieval of specific series isn\u2019t working, one could download the whole dataset and filter it. For example, download the ICP dataset CSV and extract US inflation. However, this is heavy and not ideal for real-time use (the files can be large). It could be part of a one-time initialization or a fallback if the API is down. We will prefer the API for regular operation.", "created": 1780964020875, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7649/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzh6ea", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "For certain niche indicators like PMI, which might be proprietary (Markit PMIs) or not in ECB data, we might use national sources. For instance, China\u2019s official PMI is published by the National Bureau of Statistics on their website. If they offer a CSV or JSON feed, we can use that. If not, we could resort to scraping the HTML page announcing the PMI. Web scraping would involve fetching the page and using a library like BeautifulSoup to extract the number. We must ensure this doesn\u2019t violate terms of service \u2013 if the data is public (press release), and no API is provided, gentle scraping might be acceptable. Similarly, many national statistics bureaus (or central banks) provide CSV downloads for key data (e.g. a monthly time series CSV).", "created": 1780964020873, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7650/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzeuuf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Alternate APIs and data sources: If an indicator is not in the ECB Data Portal, it might be available from other open sources:", "created": 1780964020871, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7651/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpz9pyz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "While the ECB SDMX API is extensive, not every global indicator may be directly available. We must plan for fallback data retrieval methods for any indicators or regions not covered by the ECB\u2019s datasets:", "created": 1780964020870, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7652/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzp797", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Handling Missing Indicators and Data Fallbacks", "created": 1780964020869, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzcgiv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Using the API for global indicators: To fetch an indicator, we need to know its dataset and series key. Many global macro series are available through ECB\u2019s data portal (often sourced from Eurostat, IMF, or national data). For example, Euro Area inflation is in the ICP dataset (HICP index), and Euro Area GDP growth is in the MNA (Main National Accounts) datasetdata.ecb.europa.eudata.ecb.europa.eu. The portal lists thousands of time series per countrydata.ecb.europa.eu, and dataflows can be discovered by querying the API\u2019s dataflow resourcedata.ecb.europa.eu. In practice, we can identify series keys either by using the ECB\u2019s web interface and noting the \u201cSeries key\u201d (each data page shows it), or by querying metadata.", "created": 1780964020808, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7691/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpz9ejx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "parameters can refine the query. Common parameters include date ranges (startPeriod/endPeriod), limiting number of observations, or filtering by last update date. Particularly useful is updatedAfter={date} which lets us retrieve data updated after a certain timestampdata.ecb.europa.eu \u2013 perfect for polling new releases. The API can return data in XML (SDMX-ML) by default, but it also supports JSON and CSV formats via content negotiation or query parameters (e.g. ?format=sdmx-json or ?format=csvdata)data.ecb.europa.eu. The ECB Data Portal even provides direct CSV bulk download links for each dataset (as shown for the ICP dataset)data.ecb.europa.eu.", "created": 1780964020807, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 7692/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vzrpzl3fv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "key is the series key identifying the specific indicator (combination of dimensions like country, indicator code, etc.)data.ecb.europa.eu. For instance, a series key for a daily EUR/USD exchange rate might be D.USD.EUR.SP00.A (Daily frequency, USD measured against EUR, reference rate type, average value)data.ecb.europa.eudata.ecb.europa.eu. The series key is constructed by joining dimension values with dots in the order defined by the dataset\u2019s Data Structure Definition (DSD). We can also use wildcards or OR operators in the key. For example, leaving a dimension blank will wildcard it, and using + allows querying multiple values. An example given in ECB\u2019s documentation: D.USD+JPY.EUR.SP00.A would fetch exchange rates for USD and JPY against the EURdata.ecb.europa.eu (two series in one call).", "created": 1780964020806, "pinned": false, "source": "finacial platform chatgpt project.docx"}
