- `18:08:22` --- note 9015/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr9a1k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Warren Buffett: \"A business that earns 12% (Net Margin is what tell you what percentage a business earns) when the government bond is 3% is one hell of a business \u2014 and that's why they sell for very fancy prices.\"", "created": 1780963296571, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9016/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrvtzt", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Our investments continue to be few in number and simple in concept: the truly big investment idea can usually be explained in a short paragraph.\" \u2014 Warren Buffett", "created": 1780963296570, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9017/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr91kx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Volatility transfers wealth from those who can't handle it to those who can.", "created": 1780963296569, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9018/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr46my", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The higher the valuation multiples, the greater the sell-off. The extent of the decline in top U.S. stocks over the bear market largely depends on how expensive they are.", "created": 1780963296568, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9019/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrnmy2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "NO SINGLE FORCE DRIVES GLOBAL LIQUIDITY MORE THAN A WEAKENING US DOLLAR. WATCH THE DOLLAR - EVERYTHING ELSE FOLLOWS!", "created": 1780963296567, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9020/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr8zff", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cCASH COMBINED WITH COURAGE IN A CRISIS IS PRICELESS.\u201d \u2014 WARREN BUFFETT", "created": 1780963296565, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9021/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr3olq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "FED RATE CUT CYCLES ALWAYS SEEM TO COME WITH A MAJOR MARKET SHAKEOUT.", "created": 1780963296564, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9022/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadra9u4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The stock market has created more wealth for more people than any other institution in human history. And all you have to do is participate and wait.", "created": 1780963296562, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9023/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrmmg3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Volatility is the price of admission\u2014the prize inside is superior long-term returns.\" \u2014 Morgan Housel", "created": 1780963296561, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9024/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrnp2j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"If you can find a company that can get away with raising prices year after year without losing customers you've got a terrific investment.\" \u2014 Peter Lynch", "created": 1780963296560, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9025/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadry7hy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Warren Buffett: \"There is nothing about the price action of a stock that tells you whether you should keep owning it. What tells you whether you should keep owning it is what you expect the company to do in the future.\"", "created": 1780963296559, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9026/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrli16", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cBuy when everyone else is selling and hold until everyone else is buying.\u201d \u2014 J. Paul Getty", "created": 1780963296558, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9027/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr9tmd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cThe real key to making money in stocks is not to get scared out of them.\u201d \u2013 Peter Lynch", "created": 1780963296557, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9028/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadra4xq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT hurts risk assets more\u2014it\u2019s the Fed pulling the rug out, not just raising the bar. Rate hikes are a slow choke; QT\u2019s a swift kick. Look at 2022: hikes started the slide, but QT (peaking at $95 billion/month) turned it into a rout. For max damage, pair them up\u2014risk assets don\u2019t stand a chance. Watch the Fed\u2019s balance sheet shrinkage pace and the MOVE Index (bond volatility); those scream QT pain louder than rate dots.", "created": 1780963296556, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9029/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrj818", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk Asset Type: Crypto and tech hate QT most\u2014liquidity droughts kill speculative bubbles. Blue-chip stocks weather hikes better but still crack under heavy QT.", "created": 1780963296555, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9030/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr2t9k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT\u2019s Killer in Extremes: Big QT ($100 billion/month) or sudden shifts (2013 tantrum) crush faster than hikes. It\u2019s less predictable\u2014markets freak when the Fed\u2019s balance sheet shrinks unexpectedly.", "created": 1780963296554, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9031/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrxc7k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Rate Hikes Dominate Early: If rates jump from low levels (0% to 2%), the shock can outweigh QT\u2019s slow burn\u2014think 2022\u2019s early phase. Hikes reset expectations; QT piles on later.", "created": 1780963296553, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9032/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrnx3u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT Usually Wins: It\u2019s the bigger wrecking ball. QT hits liquidity head-on, and risk assets\u2014stocks, crypto, growth plays\u2014live or die by cash flows. The 2018 QT experiment showed even small doses can spark chaos; 2022\u2019s combo with hikes was a bloodbath, but QT\u2019s dollar drain amplified the pain. Historical data (Fed balance sheet shrinks) ties QT to sharper risk asset drops than rate hikes alone.", "created": 1780963296551, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9033/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadromdz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why It\u2019s Worse: QT\u2019s a direct liquidity killer\u2014hikes tighten credit, but QT rips money out of circulation. It\u2019s like draining the pool while everyone\u2019s swimming; risk assets drown faster.", "created": 1780963296549, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9034/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr2yx4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Damage Level: QT\u2019s brutal when it\u2019s aggressive. In 2018, modest QT ($50 billion/month) sparked a 20% S&P 500 drop in Q4 and rattled crypto. In 2022, paired with hikes, it helped push risk assets into a bear market\u2014Nasdaq fell 33%, Bitcoin 65%. The 2013 \u201cTaper Tantrum\u201d (just talk of QT) tanked emerging markets 10-20% in weeks.", "created": 1780963296548, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9035/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrpfx8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Dollar Surge + Global Crunch: QT turbocharges the DXY\u2014fewer dollars = scarcity. This crushes commodity prices and slams countries with dollar debt, amplifying a global risk-off spiral that buries risk assets.", "created": 1780963296547, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9036/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrnwkk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Yield Spike: QT drives up bond yields (fewer buyers = lower prices). Investors ditch riskier plays for Treasuries offering 4%+ returns, triggering outflows from equities and emerging markets. It\u2019s a stampede to safety.", "created": 1780963296546, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9037/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrb6n4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Liquidity Vacuum: QT yanks dollars out of the system\u2014$50 billion a month in 2022, for example. Risk assets thrive on excess cash; when it vanishes, stocks, crypto, and junk bonds crater fast as banks and funds hoard what\u2019s left.", "created": 1780963296545, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9038/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr7oeq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT is when the Fed shrinks its balance sheet, sucking cash out by selling bonds or letting them mature. It\u2019s a sharper blow to risk assets:", "created": 1780963296544, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9039/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr28am", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Quantitative Tightening (QT): The Gut Punch", "created": 1780963296543, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9040/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrix9n", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why It\u2019s Limited: If hikes are telegraphed (like 2022\u2019s cycle), markets brace for it. And if rates start low, early hikes don\u2019t sting as much\u20140% to 1% isn\u2019t a death blow.", "created": 1780963296542, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9041/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr2cwr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Damage Level: Rate hikes hurt consistently but gradually. In 2022, the Fed\u2019s hikes from 0% to 4.5% tanked the S&P 500 by 20% and Bitcoin by 60%+. It\u2019s painful, but the pain builds over months as markets adjust.", "created": 1780963296541, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9042/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadroh8j", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk-Off Shift: Higher rates signal the Fed\u2019s slamming the brakes, spooking investors. They ditch speculative bets (Nasdaq, meme coins) for safer stuff like bonds, dragging risk asset prices down.", "created": 1780963296540, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9043/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrqm0e", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stronger Dollar: Hikes boost the DXY (dollar index) as investors chase higher U.S. yields. A pricier dollar slams dollar-priced assets\u2014Bitcoin drops, emerging market stocks stumble\u2014since they\u2019re costlier for global buyers.", "created": 1780963296539, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9044/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrw09z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Higher Borrowing Costs: Rate hikes make loans pricier for companies and investors. Growth stocks (like tech) and crypto projects, which often rely on cheap debt, get squeezed as funding dries up.", "created": 1780963296538, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9045/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr7e28", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Raising interest rates increases borrowing costs and tightens financial conditions. It\u2019s a steady punch to risk assets:", "created": 1780963296537, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9046/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrs5g8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed Hiking Rates: The Slow Bleed", "created": 1780963296536, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9047/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr2xo0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When it comes to hurting risk assets\u2014like stocks, crypto, tech companies, or emerging markets\u2014both Fed rate hikes and quantitative tightening (QT) can deliver a beating, but QT tends to hit harder, especially in extreme doses. Here\u2019s why, broken down clearly:", "created": 1780963296535, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9048/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrpos1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHICH HURT RISK ASSETS THE MOST FED HIKING RATES OR QT?", "created": 1780963296534, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9049/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrryip", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "For raw power, QE\u2019s more important\u2014it\u2019s the Fed going all-in, drowning risk assets in liquidity. Rate cuts are critical too, but they\u2019re more like a supporting act\u2014great for nudging things along, less so for explosive rallies. If the Fed\u2019s picking one to save risk assets in a pinch, QE\u2019s the go-to; just check the 2020 playbook. But together? That\u2019s when risk assets really go ballistic. Keep an eye on the Fed\u2019s balance sheet (QE) and rate forecasts\u2014those tell you where the party\u2019s at.", "created": 1780963296533, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9050/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrcq4p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk Asset Type: Crypto and growth stocks love QE\u2019s tidal wave\u2014look at Bitcoin\u2019s $5,000-to-$69,000 run in 2020-2021. Safer risk assets (like blue-chip stocks) lean more on rate cuts for steady gains.", "created": 1780963296532, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9051/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrfkxm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Normal Times: Rate cuts take the lead. In 2019, with no recession, three small cuts were enough to juice stocks 20-30% without needing QE\u2019s heavy artillery.", "created": 1780963296531, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9052/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr34bn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Crisis Mode: QE\u2019s king. In 2008 or 2020, when markets were bleeding, QE stopped the collapse and lit a fire under risk assets. Rate cuts alone wouldn\u2019t have moved the needle enough.", "created": 1780963296530, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9053/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrjb4o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE Usually Trumps: It\u2019s the bigger bazooka. QE directly floods the system with money, forcing it into risk assets fast and hard. Rate cuts encourage borrowing, but QE hands out cash like candy\u2014no one has to ask for it. Data backs this: QE phases (2009-2014, 2020) saw risk assets (Nasdaq, Bitcoin) outpace gains from rate-cut-only periods (like 2019).", "created": 1780963296528, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9054/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrnnje", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Which Wins for Risk Assets?", "created": 1780963296527, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9055/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrufdy", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Limit: QE\u2019s overkill if the economy\u2019s already humming\u2014too much cash can spark inflation fears, spooking risk assets later.", "created": 1780963296526, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9056/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrttk4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Strength: QE shines in crises or when markets are starved for cash. Post-2008, QE1 ($1.7 trillion) sent the S&P 500 up 84% from its low and sparked Bitcoin\u2019s early rise. In 2020, $3 trillion in QE fueled a 67% S&P rebound and a 5x crypto boom.", "created": 1780963296525, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9057/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrewk0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global Splash: The extra dollars from QE spill worldwide, weakening the DXY and igniting a global risk-on frenzy. Emerging markets, commodities, and crypto all catch fire as liquidity surges.", "created": 1780963296524, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9058/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrkmzp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Forced Risk-Taking: QE crushes bond yields (e.g., Treasuries drop to 1% or less). Investors\u2014pension funds, hedge funds\u2014can\u2019t settle for tiny returns, so they pile into riskier stuff like Nasdaq stocks or Bitcoin, driving prices sky-high.", "created": 1780963296523, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9059/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr2w6r", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Massive Cash Dump: QE doesn\u2019t just lower rates\u2014it pumps billions (or trillions) directly into banks and markets. That cash doesn\u2019t sit still\u2014it flows into stocks, crypto, junk bonds, anything with a pulse\u2014supercharging risk assets.", "created": 1780963296522, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9060/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrqe6v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE is when the Fed buys bonds with freshly \u201cprinted\u201d money, flooding the system with cash. For risk assets, it\u2019s like hitting the nitro button:", "created": 1780963296521, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9061/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr9pdx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed Injecting Liquidity via QE: The Rocket Fuel", "created": 1780963296520, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9062/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadri9ii", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Limit: If rates are already low (like near 0%), further cuts lose oomph\u2014there\u2019s only so much juice left to squeeze.", "created": 1780963296519, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9063/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrjyki", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Strength: Rate cuts matter most when the economy\u2019s slowing but not in freefall. They\u2019re a reliable tailwind\u2014think 2019, when the Fed cut rates from 2.5% to 1.75%, and the S&P 500 jumped 28% as risk assets rallied.", "created": 1780963296518, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9064/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrluhh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk-On Signal: Cuts tell markets the Fed\u2019s got their back, boosting confidence. Investors shift from bonds to stocks or crypto, but it\u2019s not an instant flood\u2014more like a rising tide.", "created": 1780963296517, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9065/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrslmc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Weaker Dollar: Rate cuts often soften the DXY, making dollar-priced assets (like Bitcoin or equities) cheaper for global buyers. This spurs demand and pumps prices.", "created": 1780963296516, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9066/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr5mgx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Cheaper Money: Lower rates cut borrowing costs for companies and investors. Tech stocks, startups, and crypto projects\u2014stuff that thrives on debt or speculation\u2014get a lift as cash becomes affordable.", "created": 1780963296515, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9067/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr61wh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Lowering interest rates makes borrowing cheaper and signals the Fed\u2019s supporting growth. It\u2019s a green light for risk assets, but its impact is more gradual:", "created": 1780963296514, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9068/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrchq5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed Cutting Rates: The Steady Fuel", "created": 1780963296513, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9069/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr7c1y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "For risk assets\u2014like stocks, crypto, tech companies, or emerging markets\u2014both Fed rate cuts and quantitative easing (QE) are huge drivers, but their importance depends on context. Generally, QE packs a bigger punch for risk assets, especially in extreme scenarios, while rate cuts are more of a steady booster. Here\u2019s why, broken down simply:", "created": 1780963296512, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9070/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadr76e2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "which is more important for risk assets? fed cuting rates or fed injecting liquidity through QE?", "created": 1780963296511, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9071/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrlxfl", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It\u2019s not just the Fed\u2014China\u2019s policies or ECB rates play a role too. And if cuts come during a U.S. crisis, liquidity might not jump if fear trumps cheap money. Still, watch the Fed\u2019s rate decisions and the DXY\u2014they\u2019re the heartbeat of global cash flow.", "created": 1780963296510, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9072/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrfvna", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The dollar\u2019s king\u2014used in 60% of global reserves and 40% of payments. Fed rate hikes act like a vacuum, sucking liquidity out of the world; cuts are like a pump, flooding it back in. Risk assets (stocks, crypto) and emerging markets feel the swings most because they depend on cheap, plentiful money. Plus, the Fed\u2019s moves signal confidence (cuts) or caution (hikes), swaying global sentiment.", "created": 1780963296509, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9073/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrn1k5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Real Example: In 2020, the Fed slashed rates to near 0% amid the pandemic. The DXY fell from 100 to 89, global liquidity surged\u2014stocks roared back (S&P 500 up 67% from its low), Bitcoin rocketed from $5,000 to $29,000, and emerging markets saw record inflows.", "created": 1780963296507, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9074/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrkjnx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk-On Boom: Cheap money fuels speculation. Investors pour cash into equities, crypto, and growth assets, amplifying liquidity as markets heat up. It\u2019s like the Fed\u2019s handing out free drinks\u2014everyone\u2019s ready to party.", "created": 1780963296506, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9075/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrp1ug", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Capital Flows Outward: Low U.S. rates push investors to hunt for yield elsewhere\u2014think foreign stocks, emerging market bonds, or real estate. This outflow of dollars from the U.S. juices liquidity in riskier corners of the world, sparking growth and spending.", "created": 1780963296505, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9076/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadrpwr5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Weaker Dollar, Easier Access: Rate cuts often weaken the DXY\u2014cheaper dollars mean commodities and dollar-based debt cost less for non-U.S. players. Emerging markets with dollar loans breathe easier, freeing up cash for spending or investment, which lifts global liquidity.", "created": 1780963296504, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9077/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4ggc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "More Dollars Flowing: Lower rates spur U.S. banks and firms to borrow and lend more. This floods the system with dollars, which spill into global markets through trade, investment, or loans\u2014boosting liquidity everywhere.", "created": 1780963296502, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9078/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqd0j9", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the Fed lowers rates, it makes borrowing cheaper, pumping liquidity into the global system. Here\u2019s how:", "created": 1780963296501, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9079/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq04fb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed Cutting Interest Rates: Opening the Floodgates", "created": 1780963296500, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9080/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqnsdw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Real Example: In 2022, the Fed raised rates from near 0% to 4.5% to fight inflation. The DXY jumped from 95 to 114, emerging market currencies tanked (e.g., India\u2019s rupee hit record lows), and global liquidity tightened\u2014Bitcoin crashed from $47,000 to $16,000, and stocks took a 20%+ hit.", "created": 1780963296499, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9081/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq3b4u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk-Off Mode: Expensive borrowing cools speculative bets. Investors dump stocks, crypto, and junk bonds for cash or Treasuries, reducing the money sloshing into riskier global assets. It\u2019s like the party\u2019s over\u2014everyone\u2019s hoarding instead of spending.", "created": 1780963296498, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9082/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq3bvo", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Capital Flows Back to the U.S.: Higher U.S. rates pull money out of riskier markets\u2014like emerging economies or global stocks\u2014as investors chase better returns in \u201csafe\u201d U.S. bonds. This outflow dries up liquidity in places like Brazil or India, where dollars were fueling growth.", "created": 1780963296497, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9083/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadql2ou", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stronger Dollar, Higher Costs: Rate hikes typically boost the DXY (dollar index) because investors flock to higher-yielding U.S. assets like Treasuries. A stronger dollar makes dollar-priced goods (oil, commodities) and dollar-denominated debt pricier for the rest of the world. Countries and companies with dollar debts need more local currency to pay up, squeezing their cash reserves and cutting liquidity.", "created": 1780963296496, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9084/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq6iim", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fewer Dollars Flowing: Higher rates mean U.S. banks and businesses lend less\u2014why borrow at 5% when it was 2%? Less lending shrinks the pool of dollars circulating, both domestically and globally, since U.S. credit often funds international trade and investment.", "created": 1780963296495, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9085/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqxkj7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the Fed hikes rates, it increases the cost of borrowing money in the U.S. This drains global liquidity in a few key ways:", "created": 1780963296494, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9086/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqi74t", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fed Raising Interest Rates: Tightening the Spigot", "created": 1780963296493, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9087/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqd8ii", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Federal Reserve raising or cutting interest rates directly influences global liquidity\u2014the amount of money flowing through the world economy. Since the U.S. dollar is the dominant global currency, these moves ripple far beyond the U.S. Here\u2019s how it works, broken down simply:", "created": 1780963296492, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9088/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq3841", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES THE FED RAISING OR CUTTING INTEREST RATES AFFECT THE GLOBAL LIQUIDITY?", "created": 1780963296491, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9089/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq5pcs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed\u2019s not the only player\u2014China\u2019s stimulus, ECB policy, or Japan\u2019s yen moves matter too. But because the dollar\u2019s king, QE or QT sets the tone. QE = party time for global liquidity; QT = the hangover. Watch the Fed\u2019s balance sheet size (it\u2019s public data) and the DXY for clues on where liquidity\u2019s headed next.", "created": 1780963296490, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9090/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqvdrw", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The U.S. dollar isn\u2019t just America\u2019s currency\u2014it\u2019s the world\u2019s. About 60% of global reserves and 40% of international payments are in dollars. When the Fed does QE, it\u2019s like opening a firehose of cash that spills everywhere. When it does QT, it\u2019s like shutting off the tap, leaving everyone scrambling. Risk assets (stocks, crypto) and emerging markets feel it most because they thrive on excess liquidity and cheap money.", "created": 1780963296489, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9091/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgnst", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why It\u2019s a Big Deal Globally", "created": 1780963296488, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9092/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq7bh2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Real Example: In 2018, the Fed\u2019s QT (shrinking its balance sheet by $50 billion/month) coincided with a DXY jump from 89 to 97. Emerging markets tanked (Turkey\u2019s lira crashed 30%), U.S. stocks wobbled, and global growth slowed as liquidity evaporated.", "created": 1780963296487, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9093/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqzjsr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk-Off Squeeze: Higher U.S. rates from QT cool the carry trade\u2014borrowing dollars becomes expensive, so those flows dry up. Investors ditch stocks, crypto, and junk bonds for safety, draining liquidity from riskier corners of the globe.", "created": 1780963296486, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9094/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq3xmr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stronger Dollar, Pressure Mounts: QT often strengthens the DXY\u2014fewer dollars = more scarcity. A pricier dollar makes commodities and dollar-denominated debt costlier for non-U.S. players, choking trade and investment flows. Countries with big dollar debts (like Argentina or Turkey) get squeezed hard.", "created": 1780963296485, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9095/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqh39u", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Higher U.S. Yields, Capital Pullback: QT lifts U.S. bond yields (fewer buyers = lower prices). Investors yank money from riskier foreign markets to park in \u201csafe\u201d U.S. Treasuries offering better returns. Emerging markets and risk assets see outflows, shrinking global liquidity.", "created": 1780963296484, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9096/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqy360", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Fewer Dollars, Less Liquidity: As the Fed takes dollars back (or stops replacing them), banks have less cash to lend or invest. Since dollars are the lifeblood of global trade and finance, this tightens liquidity worldwide\u2014less money to go around.", "created": 1780963296483, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9097/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqalz1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QT is the opposite\u2014 the Fed shrinks its balance sheet by selling bonds or letting them mature without reinvesting the proceeds. This sucks money out of the system. Here\u2019s the global fallout:", "created": 1780963296482, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9098/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqjqlm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Quantitative Tightening (QT): Draining the System", "created": 1780963296481, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9099/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq5x7z", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Real Example: Post-2008, the Fed\u2019s QE rounds (2008-2014) pumped over $4 trillion into the system. Global liquidity soared\u2014emerging market stocks rallied, commodity prices spiked (oil hit $100+), and even Bitcoin got its early legs as cheap money flowed everywhere.", "created": 1780963296480, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9100/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqp0p2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Carry Trade Fuel: Low U.S. rates from QE make borrowing dollars cheap. Investors borrow in dollars, convert to higher-yielding currencies (like Brazilian real or Turkish lira), and invest there. This spreads liquidity but also risks blowups if the dollar reverses.", "created": 1780963296479, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9101/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq2zku", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Weaker Dollar, Hotter Markets: QE often weakens the DXY (dollar index) because more dollars = less scarcity. A cheaper dollar makes commodities (oil, metals) and assets (stocks, crypto) more affordable globally, sparking risk-on buying and juicing liquidity further.", "created": 1780963296478, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9102/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqdnku", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Lower U.S. Yields, Global Hunt for Returns: QE pushes down U.S. interest rates (bond yields drop when prices rise). Investors\u2014pension funds, hedge funds, sovereign wealth funds\u2014chase higher returns elsewhere, pouring cash into foreign stocks, bonds, or emerging markets. This amplifies liquidity beyond U.S. borders.", "created": 1780963296477, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9103/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqwx4x", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "More Dollars, More Liquidity: The Fed\u2019s purchases inject billions\u2014or trillions\u2014of dollars into U.S. banks. Those banks then lend, invest, or park that cash elsewhere, boosting the supply of dollars worldwide. Since the dollar\u2019s the global reserve currency, this floods international markets with liquidity.", "created": 1780963296476, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9104/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq5hob", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "QE is when the Fed \u201cprints money\u201d (digitally) to buy assets like U.S. Treasuries or mortgage-backed securities from banks. This pumps cash into the financial system. Here\u2019s how it ripples globally:", "created": 1780963296475, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9105/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqmik1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Quantitative Easing (QE): Flooding the System", "created": 1780963296474, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9106/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq8ka7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Federal Reserve\u2019s actions\u2014quantitative easing (QE) or quantitative tightening (QT)\u2014have a massive impact on global liquidity, which is basically the amount of money sloshing around in the world economy. Here\u2019s how each works and why it matters, explained simply:", "created": 1780963296473, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9107/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqno5o", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES THE FED QE OR QT AFFECTS GLOBAL LIQUIDITY?", "created": 1780963296472, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9108/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq62jz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It\u2019s not a one-way street. If the DXY dumps because the U.S. economy\u2019s tanking (not just Fed policy), equities might still stumble. But generally, a weaker dollar greases the wheels for stocks and sends risk assets into overdrive\u2014it\u2019s the market\u2019s green light to party.", "created": 1780963296471, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9109/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadquc3b", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In late 2020, the DXY slid from 100 to 89 as the Fed kept rates near zero and signaled easy money. The S&P 500 jumped 16% in Q4 alone, Bitcoin soared from $10,000 to $29,000, and risk assets like Tesla stock went parabolic. A weak dollar was like rocket fuel for anything with a pulse.", "created": 1780963296470, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9110/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq41u7", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk assets\u2014tech stocks, Bitcoin, meme coins\u2014thrive when money\u2019s loose and optimism\u2019s high. A falling DXY often ties to lower U.S. interest rates or a Fed \u201cpivot\u201d to stimulus, creating a playground for speculative bets. Cheap borrowing and a weaker dollar supercharge growth stocks and volatile assets that love a hot economy.", "created": 1780963296468, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9111/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqabfr", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why Risk Assets Shine Brightest", "created": 1780963296467, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9112/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq1utv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Big U.S. multinationals\u2014like Microsoft or Pepsi\u2014earn heaps overseas. A weaker dollar means those foreign profits (in euros, yen, etc.) convert to more USD, juicing their earnings. Stronger profits = higher stock prices, which lifts indexes like the Nasdaq or Dow and fuels the rally.", "created": 1780963296466, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9113/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqztef", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A dumping DXY often signals a \u201crisk-on\u201d mood. Investors ditch safe havens like the dollar or Treasuries and pile into riskier assets\u2014stocks, crypto, small-caps\u2014hunting for higher returns. This is especially true if the dollar\u2019s weakening because the Fed\u2019s cutting rates or pumping money, making cash cheap and plentiful again.", "created": 1780963296464, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9114/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq7dpf", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A weaker dollar makes dollar-priced commodities\u2014like oil, gold, or copper\u2014cheaper for non-U.S. buyers. Demand rises, prices climb, and commodity-linked stocks (energy, mining, materials) rally. Since equities often ride broader economic vibes, this lifts the whole market, especially growth-oriented sectors.", "created": 1780963296462, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9115/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4rve", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Lots of global debt (especially in emerging markets) is in dollars. When the DXY falls, those countries or companies need less of their local currency (now relatively stronger) to pay off dollar-denominated loans. This eases financial pressure, lowers default risks, and boosts confidence in riskier investments like stocks or high-yield bonds.", "created": 1780963296460, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9116/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqos7l", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A weaker dollar makes U.S. assets\u2014like stocks or real estate\u2014less expensive for investors holding stronger foreign currencies. Picture a Japanese investor with yen: if the dollar drops, their yen buys more dollars, so grabbing shares of Nvidia or Tesla becomes a bargain. This spurs buying, pushing equity prices up.", "created": 1780963296458, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9117/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqo92v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) \"dumps\"\u2014meaning the dollar weakens against major currencies like the euro, yen, or pound\u2014it tends to lift equities (stocks) and other assets, especially riskier ones like tech stocks, crypto, or emerging market investments. Here\u2019s why this happens, laid out simply:", "created": 1780963296456, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9118/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq716y", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHY DOES DXY DUMPING PUMPS EQUITIES AND ALL ASSETS ESPECIALLY RISK ASSETS?", "created": 1780963296455, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9119/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqcy8p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "It\u2019s not always a perfect correlation. If the dollar pumps because the U.S. economy looks unstoppable (not just Fed tightening), equities might hold up better. But usually, a rising DXY is a headwind for stocks and a sledgehammer for riskier plays\u2014it\u2019s like the market\u2019s mood ring turning cold and cautious.", "created": 1780963296454, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9120/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqimp0", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In 2022, the DXY shot up from 95 to 114 as the Fed jacked rates to fight inflation. Equities (S&P 500) dropped over 20%, and Bitcoin crashed from $47,000 to below $20,000. Risk assets got smoked because the strong dollar signaled a world where money wasn\u2019t free anymore.", "created": 1780963296453, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9121/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgpg1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Risk assets\u2014think tech stocks, Bitcoin, or speculative meme coins\u2014rely on optimism, cheap borrowing, and excess cash sloshing around. A pumping DXY often means the opposite: tighter financial conditions, higher interest rates, and a gloomier outlook. Investors pull back from gambling on high-growth or volatile stuff and hunker down in cash or bonds.", "created": 1780963296451, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9122/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqa7wp", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Why Risk Assets Get Crushed Most", "created": 1780963296450, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9123/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqjao4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Big U.S. firms like Nike or Coca-Cola make tons of money overseas. A stronger dollar shrinks the value of those foreign earnings when converted back to USD. Weaker profits = lower stock prices. This effect ripples through indexes like the S&P 500, amplifying the equity dump.", "created": 1780963296449, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9124/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgbee", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the DXY climbs, it\u2019s often tied to a \u201cflight to safety.\u201d Investors ditch riskier assets (stocks, crypto, small-cap companies) for the dollar or U.S. Treasuries, seen as safe havens. This is especially true if the Fed\u2019s hiking rates to strengthen the dollar\u2014it signals tighter money, which cools economic growth and hammers risk assets that thrive on cheap cash.", "created": 1780963296447, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9125/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq3bp5", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A stronger dollar makes commodities priced in dollars (oil, gold, copper) more expensive for non-U.S. buyers. Demand drops, prices fall, and companies tied to commodities\u2014like energy firms or miners\u2014see their stock values tank. Since equities often track broader economic health, this drags the whole market down, especially cyclical or growth stocks.", "created": 1780963296445, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9126/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq9qps", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A lot of global debt, especially in emerging markets, is denominated in dollars. When the DXY pumps, those countries or companies need more of their local currency (which is now weaker) to pay back that dollar-based debt. This squeezes their finances, raising default risks and spooking investors. Risk assets\u2014like stocks or junk bonds\u2014get hit hardest because they\u2019re seen as less safe when economic stress rises.", "created": 1780963296443, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9127/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqpifz", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "A stronger dollar makes U.S. assets (like stocks) more expensive for foreign investors who hold weaker currencies. Imagine a European investor with euros: if the dollar rises, their euros buy fewer dollars, so snapping up shares of Apple or Tesla costs more. This can lead to less buying\u2014or even selling\u2014of U.S. equities, pushing prices down.", "created": 1780963296441, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9128/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq7whk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) \"pumps\"\u2014meaning the dollar strengthens against a basket of major currencies like the euro, yen, and pound\u2014it tends to put downward pressure on equities (stocks) and other assets, especially riskier ones like tech stocks, crypto, or emerging market investments. Here\u2019s why this happens in simpler terms:", "created": 1780963296439, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9129/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq06rq", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHY DOES DXY PUMPING DUMPS EQUITIES AND ALL ASSETS ESPECIALLY RISK ASSETS?", "created": 1780963296438, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9130/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqitmc", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cWe Can't learn without pain.\u201d \u2015 Aristotle", "created": 1780963296437, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9131/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqhnnd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cFormal education will make you a living. Self-education will make you a fortune.\u201d \u2014 Jim Rohn", "created": 1780963296436, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9132/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqebdv", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u201cDon\u2019t pass up something that\u2019s attractive today because you think you will find something better tomorrow.\u201d \u2014 Warren Buffett", "created": 1780963296435, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9133/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqz0h3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Warren Buffett: \"The stock exchange is a big supermarket of companies \u2014 and you're going to be buying stocks. What do you want to have happen? You want those stocks to go down. Way down.\"", "created": 1780963296434, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9134/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqr55p", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\"Cash is to a business as oxygen is to an individual: never thought about when it is present, the only thing in mind when it is absent.\" \u2014 Warren Buffett", "created": 1780963296433, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9135/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqyw10", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stanley Druckenmiller: 'I'm not sure if I'v ever made money shorting.' He ran Duquesne Capital for 30 years, averaging 30% annual returns with zero down years. Long term: 30% CARG. Short positions: 0% (He doesn't know) Don't short the market, and never bet against America.", "created": 1780963296432, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9136/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqp8rs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Stocks bottom 5 months before GDP inflects.", "created": 1780963296431, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9137/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqv8bm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Bear markets don't destroy wealth. Panic selling in bear markets does.", "created": 1780963296430, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9138/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4611", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The average S&P 500 bear market drops -36%. The average bull market gains +114%.", "created": 1780963296429, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9139/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq5sxs", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In short: A weaker yuan could juice Bitcoin by driving Chinese money into it as a hedge, with meme coins possibly tagging along for the ride. But it\u2019s not a straight line\u2014more like a chaotic dance between policy, markets, and human psychology. Keep an eye on that MOVE Index too; if bond volatility spikes alongside this, it might amplify the Fed\u2019s reaction, adding fuel to the crypto.", "created": 1780963296428, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9140/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqlum4", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "And for meme coins, their fate\u2019s more tied to social media buzz than macro shifts.", "created": 1780963296427, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9141/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqnczn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Global Risk Sentiment: A weaker yuan can signal economic trouble in China, the world\u2019s second-largest economy. This rattles global markets, and Bitcoin sometimes benefits as a \u201cdigital gold\u201d hedge against uncertainty\u2014though it can also dip initially if investors dump risky assets like stocks and crypto together. Posts on X and past patterns (e.g., 2013, 2015, 2019) suggest Bitcoin often climbs when the yuan hits key thresholds like 7.2 against the USD.", "created": 1780963296426, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9142/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgzbh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Underground Demand: Even with the ban, Chinese investors find workarounds\u2014over-the-counter (OTC) trading, foreign exchanges like Binance, or stablecoins like Tether (USDT). A weaker yuan often boosts this gray-market activity. For example, data from Chainalysis showed China\u2019s crypto transaction volume hit $86.4 billion between mid-2022 and mid-2023, suggesting the ban isn\u2019t fully stopping the flow. If the yuan keeps sliding, this demand could push Bitcoin prices up.", "created": 1780963296425, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9143/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqwc6v", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Capital Flight Pressure: A weaker yuan reduces its purchasing power, which can spook Chinese investors\u2014especially the wealthy or savvy ones. China has strict capital controls, limiting how much money people can move out of the country (about $50,000 per year). When the yuan drops, some turn to Bitcoin as a way to \"park\" their wealth outside the government\u2019s reach. Bitcoin\u2019s decentralized nature makes it hard for authorities to track, despite China\u2019s crypto trading ban since 2021. Historically, yuan devaluations\u2014like in 2015-2016\u2014coincided with Bitcoin price surges (from $200 to $20,000 over time), as people sought alternatives to a weakening currency.", "created": 1780963296424, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9144/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgixm", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When China weakens the yuan (its currency), it\u2019s usually a deliberate move by the People\u2019s Bank of China to make Chinese exports cheaper and more competitive on the global stage, especially in response to things like U.S. tariffs or economic slowdowns. This has a few ripple effects that can impact Bitcoin. Let\u2019s break it down:", "created": 1780963296423, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9145/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq8j1k", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "how does china weakening the yuan affect bitcoin and meme crypto?", "created": 1780963296422, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9146/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqswnb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "When a pegged currency to the dollar starts weakening (dumping) that\u2019s very concerning bcs the whole reason why it has been pegged in the first place is to keep it strong not weak. (currency weakening signals major problems in the country).", "created": 1780963296421, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9147/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqiqlx", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "DXY PUMPING SIGNALS FOREIGN CAPITAL IS MOVING INTO THE US FROM THE REST OF THE WORLD. DXY DUMPING SIGNALS FOREIGN CAPITAL IS MOVING OUT OF THE US INTO THE REST OF THE WORLD.", "created": 1780963296420, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9148/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4hqn", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "SIGNS FOREIGNERS ARE SELLING US TREASURIES AND MOVING AWAY FROM THE DOLLAR: Dollar Index (DXY) PUMPING 2.2% in couple of days which is a big move for this short a time frame. If China or other foreigners were selling Treasuries to drive yields up to punish the US and to move away from the dollar, they would have to convert those dollars to a foreign currency which means the DXY would have been dumping and not pumping. Otherwise, selling Treasuries and leaving the money in dollars in a US bank is pointless. If they sold enough Treasuries to swing yields as wildly as they did today, the subsequent selling of dollars to exit the US would have driven down the dollar. Instead, it rallied more than usual. This suggests that foreign money was moving into the US, not away from it.", "created": 1780963296419, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9149/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq81ry", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THEN WE MAY HAVE FEW WEEKS OR MONTHS. BASICALLY, THE FED WILL BE FORCED TO DO QE WHEN SHIT HITS THE FAN AND THEY HAVE TO INTERVENE TO BAILOUT THE MARKET.", "created": 1780963296418, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9150/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqgnbb", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHEN IS THE FED FORCED TO DO QE? IT\u2019S ALL ABOUT WHAT HAPPENS IN THE FINANCIAL MARKETS AND IN PARTICULAR IN THE CREDIT MARKETS. IF THAT STARTS TO CRACK AND WE START TO SEE CONTAGION SPREAD THROUGH THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM THEN THE FED IS GOING TO HAVE TO ACT QUICKLY. IF IT DOESN\u2019T AND MARKETS KIND OF MUDDLE THROUGH AND THE EQUITY MARKETS ARE DOWN BUT THE CREDIT MARKET, FIXED INCOME MARKET, CURRENCY MARKETS HOLD TOGETHER. THE ACTUAL FINANCIAL PLUMBING REMAINS KIND OF LIQUID.", "created": 1780963296417, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9151/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4ev6", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In short: High MOVE Index \u2192 more volatility \u2192 forced bond sales \u2192 potential market mess \u2192 Fed swoops in to save the day. That\u2019s the theory!", "created": 1780963296416, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9152/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq73yg", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "So, if the MOVE Index keeps climbing and triggers enough forced selling, it could create chaos in these markets. The Fed, which sees itself as the guardian of financial stability, might decide it has no choice but to step in\u2014cutting rates, buying bonds, or flooding the system with cash (going Brrr) to calm things down and protect those critical markets.", "created": 1780963296415, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9153/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqs8ey", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "This selling can snowball. A flood of bonds hitting the market pushes bond prices down, which drives yields (interest rates) up. Higher yields can spook the broader financial system, especially since Treasuries and corporate bonds are huge markets the Fed cares deeply about. They\u2019re like the backbone of U.S. finance\u2014Treasuries are the \"safe\" asset everyone relies on, and corporate bonds keep businesses funded.", "created": 1780963296414, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9154/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqlsct", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Here\u2019s how it works: When the MOVE Index goes up, it means bond prices are jumping around a lot. This volatility makes life tough for investors or traders who borrow money to buy bonds (like Treasuries or corporate bonds). Why? Because when volatility spikes, the people lending them money (think banks or brokers) get nervous and demand more collateral\u2014aka higher \"margin requirements.\" If these traders don\u2019t have the extra cash or assets to meet those demands, they\u2019re forced to sell their bonds to cover their positions.", "created": 1780963296413, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9155/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqners", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The Fed might step in and start pumping money into the economy again\u2014aka \"going Brrr,\" like a money printer. One signal to watch for this is something called the MOVE Index, which tracks volatility (or wild price swings) in the bond market, specifically U.S. Treasury bonds.", "created": 1780963296412, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9156/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqxnui", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "HOW DOES MOVE INDEX PREDICT QE AND LIQUIDITY?", "created": 1780963296411, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9157/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq9iog", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "In more stable economic times, default rates have been notably lower. For instance, in 2010, the U.S. high-yield bond default rate was 1.3%, a significant decline from the 13.7% observed in 2009. \u200b These variations underscore the sensitivity of junk bond default rates to broader economic conditions and market dynamics.", "created": 1780963296410, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9158/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq2tkd", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2008 Financial Crisis: Default rates increased significantly, with estimates suggesting they approached double-digit levels, reflecting the severe economic stress of the period.\u200b", "created": 1780963296409, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9159/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqlhb3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "2000\u20132002 Economic Downturn: The average default rate surged to 9.2% during this period, influenced by challenges in the telecom industry and a general economic slowdown. \u200b", "created": 1780963296408, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9160/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadquamk", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Early 1990s Recession: The default rate peaked at approximately 11% in 1991 during the mild recession of 1990\u20131991. \u200b", "created": 1780963296407, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9161/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqf7a2", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "\u200bHistorically, the default rates for U.S. junk bonds, also known as high-yield bonds, have varied significantly over time, influenced by economic cycles and market conditions. On average, these default rates have hovered around 5% over the long term. \u200b", "created": 1780963296405, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9162/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqebw3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "Historically what\u2019s the percentage of us junk bonds issuers defaults?", "created": 1780963296404, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9163/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadqdh3d", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WITH BONDS OR CREDIT OR FIXED INCOME WHAT YOU SEE IS WHAT YOU GET. YOU CAN READ WHAT THE PROMISED RETURN IS AND THAT\u2019S EXACTLY WHAT YOU GONNA GET UNLESS THE ISSUER DEFAULTS. AND BY THE WAY THEY PROMISE YOU INTEREST, THEY PROMISE YOU TO PAY YOU YOUR MONEY BACK AT THE END, AND IF THEY DON\u2019T KEEP THAT PROMISE THEY LOSE THE COMPANY. SO, THEY HAVE A LOT OF INCENTIVES TO PAY YOU BACK YOUR MONEY. OVER THE LAST 47 YEARS, 99% OF NON-INVESTMENT CREDIT (JUNK BOND) ISSUERS HAVE PAID AS PROMISED.", "created": 1780963296403, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9164/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadq4l6h", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "CREDIT IS A NEW FANGOLD WORD FOR FIXED INCOME WHICH WAS A NEW-FANGLED WORD FOR BONDS.", "created": 1780963296402, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9165/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadprkhh", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE AVERAGE P/E RATIO OF US STOCKS IS 16. WHAT YOU PAY FOR STOCK MATTERS: US STOCKS HAS RETURNED ABOUT 10% A YEAR FOR THE LAST 100 YEARS BUT NOT WHEN P/E RATIO WAS 19. WHEN THE P/E RATIO AVERAGE 16, THE US STOCKS RETURN AVERAGE 10. BUT WHEN P/E RATIO IS 19 HISTORICALLY THE RETURN HAS BEEN AROUND 1 TO 6% A YEAR BUT CERTAINLY NOT 10% A YEAR. SO, WHAT YOU PAY FOR STOCKS MATTER. AND WHEN THE PRICE OF THE S&P500 IS ELEVATED COMPARED TO HISTORIC LEVELS, YOU SHOULDN\u2019T EXPECT HISTORIC RETURNS.", "created": 1780963296400, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9166/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadpd6ar", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHEN STOCKS DUMP PEOPLE SALE THEIR STOCKS AND RUN FROM THE MARKET BCS THEY THINK IT CONNOTES RISK BUT ACTUALLY IT\u2019S JUST STOCKS GOING ON SALE.", "created": 1780963296399, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9167/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadpon11", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "The riskiest time to invest is when the market looks safest. The safest time to invest is when the market looks riskiest.", "created": 1780963296398, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9168/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vkadp90ab", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE FINANCIAL PLUMBING IS COMPOSED OF : THE CREDIT MARKET (REPO MARKET, BOFA SEMI WORST SPREAD) , FIXED INCOME MARKET (MOVE, BTP BUND) , CURRENCY MARKETS (DXY).", "created": 1780963296397, "pinned": false, "source": "financial notes 10.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9169/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebltb3", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE US ECONOMY IS RELIES SO MUCH ON CONSUMPTION IF THAT STARTS TO SLOW DUE TO UNEMPLOYMENT OF FINANCIAL TURMOIL IN THE STOCK MARKET THAT\u2019S WHEN THE RUBBER HITS THE ROAD.", "created": 1780963183699, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9170/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhveb0y94", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHEN THERE IS SO MUCH UNCERTAINTY OUT THERE PEOPLE AND CORPORATIONS ARE JUST NOT GONNA SPEND MONEY.", "created": 1780963183698, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9171/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebuval", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE FINANCIAL MARKET TURBULANCE AND THE BEGINNING OF SOME ECONOMIC SOFTNESS THAT CEOS SEE CAUSE THEM TO ADOPT AN APPROACH OF CAUTION. AND IN PRACTICE THAT MEANS CAUTION ON HIRING, CAUTION ON CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, CAUTION ON OTHER FORMS OF EXPANSION, AND THIS CAUTIONARY MINDSET WHICH IN ITSELF ISNT GOOD BCS IT BECOMES SELF-FULFILLING IN TERMS OF ECONOMIC WEAKNESS.", "created": 1780963183697, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9172/12122  ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebvea8", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "DOLLAR WEAKENING, EQUITIES WEAKENING AND BONDS WEAKENING ALL AT THE SAME TIME IS VERY UNUSUAL FOR THE UNITED STATES ( THIS BASICALLY MEANS EVERYTHING IS SELLNG OFF). ITS VERY SUSPICIOUS TO SEE THE DOLLAR WEAKENING AND THE BONDS WEAKENING AT THE SAME TIME IS A SIGN OF CAPITAL OUTFLOW OUT OF THE COUNTRY AND IT SIGNIFIES DIMINISHING CONFIDENCE IN THE GROWTH OUTLOOK FOR THIS COUNTRY AND FOR THAT MATTER THE ATTRACTIVENESS OF DOLLAR BASED ASSETS. THAT USUALLY HAPPENS OFTEN IN EMERGING MARKETS BUT NOT IN UNITED STATES.", "created": 1780963183696, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9173/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebgqe1", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "US10Y YIELD SWIGING 0.3 TO 0.5 IN A DAY, CREDIT SPREADS WIDENING, MONEY FLOWING OUT OF LEVERAGED LOAN FUNDS, IPOs GETTING DELAYED, DEALS GETTING PUT OFF ARE SIGNS OF MARKET STRESS AND POSSIBLE BLACK SWAN EVENT.", "created": 1780963183695, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9174/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebsxco", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "WHEN BASIS TRADE COME UNDER A TREMENDOUS AMOUNT OF PRESSURE BCS OF CHANGES IN YIELDS (YIELDS PUMPING HARD) YOU GET AN INCREASED SELLING PRESSURE IN THE FUTURES WHICH FORCE LIQUDATION OF THESE BASIS TRADE WHICH CAUSE HUGE MARGIN CALLS WHICH BASICALLY WOULD JUST EVAPORATE LIQUIDITY, FRACTURE FINANCIAL PLUMBING AND SEND ALL MARKETS INTO CHAOS REAL QUICK. SO BASICALLY YIELDS PUMPING DUE TO TREASURY SELL OFF WOULD CAUSE THE BASIS TRADE UNWIND WHICH WOULD CAUSE A COMPLETE CHAOS IN ALL MARKETS.", "created": 1780963183694, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9175/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebdjul", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "THE SHARP RISE IN YIELDS HAVE MUCH MORE FAR REACHING IMPACTS ON LIQUIDITY OF THE MARKETS, ON STABILITY OF THE MARKETS AND AGAIN WHEN YOU TALK WHAT THE LIFE BLOOD OF THE MARKET ITS NOT STOCKS , ITS ACTUALLY BONDS. EVERYTHING REVOLVES AROUND CREDIT SO A VERY SHARP RISE IN YIELDS ALL OF A SUDDEN DISRUPTS CREDIT AND CREDIT MARKETS, IT DISRUPTS BORROWING MARKETS ACROSS THE BOARD, THERE IS MANY MANY IMPACTS TO THE YIELDS SPIKING SHARPLY WITH LITTLE NOTICE. IT\u2019S A FAR MORE REACHING IMPACT ON FINANCIAL MARKETS. SO IF SMTHG GOES WRONG THAT WOULD CAUSE THE YIELDS SPIKING YOU CAN HAVE A VERY RAPID UNWIND OF THESE VERY HIGH LEVERED BASIS TRADE. SO WHEN WE TALK RISK IN THE MARKET THESE BASIS TRADE PRESENT A HUGE RISK FOR MARKET BCS OF THE AMOUNT OF LIQUIDITY AND LEVERAGE AND THE ASSET THEY ARE INVOLVED IN (TREASURIES WHICH ARE BASICALLY THE BACKBONE OF ALL MARKETS) . SO THESE UNWINDING OF THESE HIGHLY LEVERED TO THE TITS BASIS TRADE IS A HIGH RISK AND A THREAT FOR THE ENTIRE FINANCIAN PLUMBING SYSTEM AND THAT\u2019S A HUGE CONCERN FOR THE MARKETS", "created": 1780963183693, "pinned": false, "source": "basis trade financial notes.docx"}
- `18:08:22` --- note 9176/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "nmq5vhvebir24", "cat": "philosophy", "text": "How do hedge funds execute the basis trade? When hedge fund execute the basis trade they basically short large volume of treasury futures. SO THE MORE THE TREASURY YIELDS SPIKE (DUE TO TREASURY SELL OFF) THE MORE HEDGE FUNDS HAVE TO SHORT. Well if they get caught on the wrong side of the trade THIS BECOMES PROBLEMATIC VERY QUICKLY AND THERE IS A LOT OF LIQUIDITY TIED TO THIS (BASIS TRADE ARE 20 TIMES LEVERAGE). - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-a56315720e79a9ea", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] The spread between SOFR and the Fed\u2019s Overnight Reverse Repo rate has been exhibiting volatility not seen since the repo spike of September 2019, with quarter-end spikes hitting 25 basis points in recent months. This might seem like financial jargon to most, but for those who understand the intricacies of monetary plumbing, it\u2019s the canary in the coal mine: signaling stress fractures in the very foundation of our financial system that could foreshadow another liquidity crisis. The Secured Overnight Financing Rate, (or SOFR) which is a volume-weighted median of tri-party, GCF, and bilateral repo transactions, has begun decoupling from its supposed floor: the RRP rate set by the Federal Reserve. The spread, which (in theory) should remain near zero in a well-functioning market with ample reserves, has been widening persistently throughout 2024 and into 2025. According to Federal Reserve data, the SOFR-RRP spread reached peaks of 24 to 28 basis points during recent quarter-ends, compared to near-zero readings throughout the QE era of 2020-2023.", "created": 1759938449565, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-a586e2c7a96e61e2", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:BAMLH0A3HYC] Credit spreads are always positive: for corporations to attract investors to buy their bonds they must offer a premium. That premium is called \u2019\u2019Credit Spread\u2019: it refers to the fact that corporate bond yields are higher than government bond yields or interest rate swaps. Hence, investors willing to take the risk of a corporate default will be compensated with this premium - the credit spread. \r\nTight credit spreads signal Animal spirits are running loose.\r\n Tight credit spreads mean Investors convinced nothing bad can happen, hence they are receiving a low upfront premium for their risk.", "created": 1756227735498, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-280162bbd3478e75", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:SPX] AFTER A WATERFALL SELLOFF, MARKETS ALWAYS SNAP BACK FAST! A waterfall isn\u2019t a slow grind lower decline, it\u2019s a sharp high velocity plunge like 1987s Black Monday, March 2020. The psychology is brutal: Investors assume deep wounds require slow recoveries, but liquidity flows don\u2019t follow emotions. Institutions know that panic-driven sell-offs create a symmetric rebound. \r\nInstitutions know that panic-driven selloffs create a symmetric rebound. \r\nYOU ALWAYS WANT TO INVEST IN COMPANIES THAT DOMINATE GLOBAL EARNINGS, INNOVATION AND LIQUIDITY. Germany Dax for ex trades at lower valuations but lacks the tech leadership fueling US indices.\r\nHistorically back-to-back 20% yearly gains followed by another 10% or 15% gain confirms THAT WE ARE IN A BULL MARKET, NOT A DEAD CAT BOUNCE OR A BEAR MARKET RALLY. BCS DEAD CAT BOUNCES DON\u2019T LAST 36 MONTHS. A 36 MONTH RALLY IS NO DEAD CAT BOUNCE. The implication, we\u2019re likely in the early stages of a new cycle, not the end. So the back-to-back 20% yearly gains signals that are in an early start of a bull market rather than late stage of a bull market or the beginning of a bear market. Markets do have cyclical surges inside bear markets which we call dead cat bounces, but history shows those rarely extend beyond a year.\r\nDEAD CAT BOUNCES DON\u2019T LAST 36 MONTHS. YES AT THE STOCK LEVELS, WE MIGHT GET RETEST BCS SELLERS MAY PUSH FOR EXITS BUT NO RETESTS AT THE SP500 INDEX LEVEL BCS LIQUIDITY AND FED INTERVENTIONS USUALLY FORCE MARKETS HIGHER . IF YOU DON\u2019T NAIL BOTTOMS YOU BUYING LOWER BUT WE ALWAYS GET A V SHAPE RECOVERY. UNLIKE DOUBLE BOTTOMS WHERE YOU WOULD GET ANOTHER CHANCE TO BUY AT OR CLOSE TO THE BOTTOM. Since 2008 financial crisis, major indices rarely visit their lows. Perfect Examples of that: 1987,2009,2020 and 2025. Most of the Rebounds happen after we hit the 10% or 20% correction. Missing the Bottom doesn\u2019t mean you are out. It just means you will be buying at a higher levels. That\u2019s painful for pride but survivable for portfolios. \r\nMarkets are always symmetrical unless there is a recession. so the faster you decline, the faster the bounce. The ratio is 1.4 to 1.7 so if it took 8 weeks to lose 20%, markets will recov

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-62d124d12bf15199", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:6J2!] the Japanese yen futures which is known for its characteristic as a safe haven currency and as a global funding currency in the Eurodollar system and tends to increase during times of increased uncertainty. Japenese Yen future spiking signals stress in the Eurodollar markets since its the main funding currency there. every times japenese yen futures spiked a global financial crisis and Eurodollar systematic problems emerged Especially if its accompanied by us dollar rising as well.:\r\nApril 2007 This is an important one: it is widely considered the very beginning of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC).\r\n\r\nIn April 2007, New Century Financial (a big subprime lender) went bankrupt. This was one of the first cracks in the system.\r\n\r\nEurodollar market strains started appearing mid-2007 (notably in August when interbank spreads like LIBOR\u2013OIS blew out). April was the early warning phase, not the full-blown liquidity crunch yet.\r\n\r\nOctober 2015\r\n\r\nNo official crisis was declared, but there were noticeable stresses:\r\n\r\nChina had just devalued the yuan in August 2015, triggering global market turmoil and capital outflows.\r\n\r\nCommodity prices collapsed (oil, copper, etc.), stressing EM countries.\r\n\r\nU.S. corporate credit spreads widened, and global dollar funding costs spiked.\r\n\r\nThis period is sometimes referred to as \u201cEurodollar #3\u201d in Jeffrey Snider\u2019s framework \u2014 a wave of dollar shortage/liquidity strain that hurt global trade and EM economies.\r\n\r\nNot labeled a global financial crisis, but it was a significant dollar liquidity shortage episode.\r\n\r\nSummary\r\n\r\nApril 2003 \u2192 No crisis, liquidity was actually abundant due to Fed easing.\r\n\r\nApril 2007 \u2192 Yes, early stage of the Global Financial Crisis (subprime cracks, leading to Eurodollar stress).\r\n\r\nOctober 2015 \u2192 Not a global financial crisis, but a real dollar shortage/liquidity squeeze episode tied to China devaluation and collapsing commodities. \r\n\r\nThe only times The Yen futures spiked and there was no crisis was in april 2003 and the fed was easing then so i guess that countered and overpowered the yen strengthening.", "created": 1756048430000, "pinned": false}
