- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-0261e86e8462d59d", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:WRBWFRBL] Why is Bank Reserves with the FED is a great barometer for liquidity? Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires banks to keep a certain amount of reserves or cash on hold at the FED at all times which aims to improve the banking sector's ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress, bank argued that keeping bank reserves with fed on hold makes it harder for them to lend out cash on a dime when money gets tight. So when liquidity is low especially close to the dates when reporting take place and when liquidity is tight , financial institutions will want their own balance sheet to look safer so banks be holding the little bit of their reserves for themselves however when FED is doing QE taking in treasuries and giving out cash to the market which means Fed is injecting cash into the system for everyone to borrow even if the Repo players stop lending again financial instituions dont really have to worry about cash bcs there is plenty of it in the system , QE aims to boost reserves allowing banks to stay liquid without violating the liquidity coverage ratio rule and in doing so its keep the wheels of financial system spinning. A higher  bank reserves would allow bank to lend more and a lower bank reserves would force banks to lend less.", "created": 1697654543127, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-5f2002643a2723dc", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:THREEFYTP10] The term premium on a 1-year zero-coupon bond is a measure of the compensation that investors require for bearing the risk that interest rates may change over the life of the bond. It is calculated by subtracting the expected 1-year forward rate from the yield on the 1-year zero-coupon bond.\r\n\r\nA positive term premium on a 1-year zero-coupon bond warns us that investors expect interest rates to rise over the next year. This could be due to a number of factors, such as expectations of higher inflation, stronger economic growth, or more aggressive monetary policy from the Federal Reserve.\r\n\r\nA negative term premium on a 1-year zero-coupon bond, on the other hand, warns us that investors expect interest rates to fall over the next year. This could be due to a number of factors, such as expectations of lower inflation, weaker economic growth, or more dovish monetary policy from the Federal Reserve.\r\n\r\nHere are some of the things that a positive term premium on a 1-year zero-coupon bond may warn us about:\r\n\r\nHigher inflation: If investors expect inflation to rise in the future, they will demand a higher yield on bonds in order to compensate for the loss of purchasing power of their investment. This can lead to a higher term premium.\r\nStronger economic growth: If investors expect stronger economic growth in the future, they will demand a higher yield on bonds in order to compensate for the increased risk of the company defaulting on its debt. This can also lead to a higher term premium.\r\nMore aggressive monetary policy from the Fed: If investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in the future, they will demand a higher yield on bonds in order to lock in today's lower rates. This can also lead to a higher term premium.\r\nIt is important to note that the term premium is a complex concept and there is no single agreed-upon way to measure it. The St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank publishes a series on the term premium for 1-year, 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year zero-coupon bonds, which is calculated using a model developed by Darrell Duffie and Kenneth Singleton.\r\n\r\nInvestors can use the term premium to inform their investment decisions. For example, if an investor believes that the term premium is too low, they may want to consider investing in shorter-term bonds in order to reduce their exposure to interest rate risk. On the other hand, if an investor believ

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-d10ef63f60ffedd9", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:USRR] Repo Rates are typically quite low in normal times because the Repo deals are collateralized and seen as safe and the repo market is not usually volatile. But this has changed dramatically in September 2019 when the overnight repo rate shot up from around 2% to around 10% in the space of a week. Since this market is SO CRITICAL to the financial world any disruptions can cause ripples throughout the whole system, in basic terms if a market rate spikes from around 2% to around 10% it means that the market participants doesnt wanna lend in this case it seems to have been due to a liquidity crunch, the supply of cash available to lend out have reduced at the same time that demand for cash increased as more securities flooded into the market as a collateral looking for cash to borrow, with an increase in demand and a decrease in supply the rate shot up. The Fed explains that these issues happens mainly due to two events occuring at the same time : firstly corporate tax payments drains the repo market of liquidity and at the same time the repo market was being used to finance an unusually large settlement of treasury auctions. However the BIS have stated that these issues may have been among the problems but they dont justify the huge repo rate spike that occurred. BIS focused on other alarming reasons: Most Repo Market activity moves between four large banks: JP Morgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo, a chart from BIS shows how the repo market is depending more and more on these four institutions basically if these banks even slightly reduce their lending the market would suffer massively. Jamie Damon CEO of JP Morgan has said the bank had the cash available and would have been happy to lend it out and profit from the higher rates but it was unable to since the financial crisis of 2008 banks have to satisfy regulations that require them to hold a certain amount of reserves known as the liquidity coverage ratio. So JP Morgan may have reserves available but are unable to lend them out as they need to hold on to them to satisfy the regulations particularly at the end of the quarter like in September or in December since thats when reporting take place and they will want their own balance sheet to look safer in addition to this banks may have been reluctant to lend as their reserves has been reduced so significantly since the FED started unwinding its QE so banks have been holding to their res

Since this market is SO CRITICAL to the financial world any disruptions can cause ripples throughout the whole system, in basic terms if a market rate spikes from around 2% to around 10% it means that the market participants doesnt wanna lend in this case it seems to have been due to a liquidity crunch, the supply of cash available to lend out have reduced at the same time that demand for cash increased as more securities flooded into the market as a collateral looking for cash to borrow, with an increase in demand and a decrease in supply the rate shot up. The Fed explains that these issues happens mainly due to two events occuring at the same time : firstly corporate tax payments drains the repo market of liquidity and at the same time the repo market was being used to finance an unusually large settlement of treasury auctions. However the BIS have stated that these issues may have been among the problems but they dont justify the huge repo rate spike that occurred. BIS focused on other alarming reasons: Most Repo Market activity moves between four large banks: JP Morgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo, a chart from BIS shows how the repo market is depending more and more on these four institutions basically if these banks even slightly reduce their lending the market would suffer massively. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-3a48c3cd1313ddb4", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:RRPONTSYD] The reverse repo facility is one of two tools that FED uses in the Repo market. In the Repo market FED will intervene either to keep rates low where they want them or to keep rates high where they want them. If Fed wants to keep rates lower than where they normally would be they use the standard Repo facility to put a lid on interest rates to prevent them from going higher but if Fed wants to keep rates higher than they would be normally they will use the reverse repo facility to put a floor underneath the interest rates to prevent them from going lower (starting March 2021 Fed started to use their Reverse Repo facility to keep a floor underneath interest rates) . \r\n\r\nThe Reverse Repo facility is the tool the Fed uses to put a floor underneath interest rates. They do this by simply paying an interest rate on any cash that comes in to the Reverse Repo facility (Fed pay Reverse Repo a 0.5% interest rate higher than bottom end of the target range of the Federal funds rate). Its a powerful tool since parking money with the FED would guarantee a Risk Free return in the entire market. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-31d3c18fa5dbd740", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:WRESBAL] There are a number of ways to track global liquidity. One common approach is to look at the following indicators:\r\n1-Central bank balance sheets: Central banks play a major role in the global financial system, and their balance sheets can provide insights into the overall level of liquidity. For example, if central banks are expanding their balance sheets through asset purchases, this can be a sign that they are trying to increase liquidity in the system.\r\n2-Money supply: The money supply refers to the total amount of money in circulation in an economy. A growing money supply can be a sign of increasing liquidity.\r\n3-Credit markets: Credit markets are another important source of liquidity. If credit markets are expanding, this can be a sign that liquidity is increasing.\r\n4-Asset prices: Asset prices, such as stock and bond prices, can also be used to track liquidity. Rising asset prices can be a sign of increasing liquidity, while falling asset prices can be a sign of decreasing liquidity.\r\nIn addition to these quantitative indicators, it is also important to consider qualitative factors when tracking global liquidity. For example, it is important to monitor the sentiment of investors and market participants. If investors are becoming more bearish and risk-averse, this can lead to a decrease in liquidity.\r\nHere are some specific data sources that can be used to track global liquidity:\r\nBank for International Settlements (BIS): The BIS publishes a number of indicators on global liquidity, including the global liquidity indicators (GLIs). The GLIs track a variety of factors, including cross-border loans, international debt securities, and foreign exchange reserves.\r\nFederal Reserve Bank of New York: The Fed publishes a number of data series on global liquidity, including the weekly money supply report and the quarterly flow of funds report.\r\nBloomberg and Reuters: These financial data providers publish a variety of data series on global liquidity, including asset prices, credit spreads, and market sentiment indices.\r\nBy tracking these indicators and data series, investors and policymakers can gain a better understanding of the overall level of global liquidity. This information can be used to make informed decisions about investment and financial policy.", "created": 1697374447188, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-7c0a8e0a5f97b148", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:SO32!] The SONIA rate, or Sterling Overnight Index Average rate, is the effective overnight interest rate paid by banks for unsecured transactions in the British sterling market. It is published each London business day by the Bank of England and measures the cost of overnight, unsecured borrowing.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is calculated based on a weighted average of the interest rates paid on unsecured sterling overnight transactions between banks and other financial institutions. The weights are based on the volume of each transaction.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is used in a variety of ways by financial businesses and institutions. For example, it is used to calculate the interest paid on swap transactions and sterling floating rate notes. It is also used as a reference rate for some consumer loans and mortgages.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is considered to be a more reliable and accurate benchmark than LIBOR, the London Interbank Offered Rate, which is being phased out due to concerns about its manipulation.", "created": 1697294431565, "pinned": false}

It is also used as a reference rate for some consumer loans and mortgages.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is considered to be a more reliable and accurate benchmark than LIBOR, the London Interbank Offered Rate, which is being phased out due to concerns about its manipulation.", "created": 1697294391172, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10499/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-4f0cf322258589df", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:ICEEUR:GBW2!] The SONIA rate, or Sterling Overnight Index Average rate, is the effective overnight interest rate paid by banks for unsecured transactions in the British sterling market. It is published each London business day by the Bank of England and measures the cost of overnight, unsecured borrowing.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is calculated based on a weighted average of the interest rates paid on unsecured sterling overnight transactions between banks and other financial institutions. The weights are based on the volume of each transaction.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is used in a variety of ways by financial businesses and institutions. For example, it is used to calculate the interest paid on swap transactions and sterling floating rate notes. It is also used as a reference rate for some consumer loans and mortgages.\r\n\r\nThe SONIA rate is considered to be a more reliable and accurate benchmark than LIBOR, the London Interbank Offered Rate, which is being phased out due to concerns about its manipulation.", "created": 1697294391172, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-3242f4d58d6ea619", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:FEDFUNDS] Everything in the world is priced off the 10 year US treasury bcs its the global Risk free rate. So as the risk free rate rises (as the 10 year us treasury yield rises) it has a dramatic impact on a number of different asset classes, if you do a discounted cash flow analysis as 10 year yield rises now you are dividing by a bigger number, and when you divide by a bigger number you get a smaller evaluation so that has an impact on market prices and this why the FED hike rates thats why the FED wants higher rates bcs its the way the bring down asset prices and slow the economy and as a result bring down inflation. So as interest rates go up you discount your cash flow at a bigger number so you get a lower valuation.", "created": 1696775912919, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-2d412be0d8436cc9", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] Chilean interest rates can also affect the value of the Chilean peso. When Chilean interest rates are high, the peso tends to appreciate in value. This can make it more expensive for foreign buyers to purchase Chilean copper. Conversely, when Chilean interest rates are low, the peso tends to depreciate in value. This can make it cheaper for foreign buyers to purchase Chilean copper. Overall, Chilean interest rates play an important role in financing global copper purchases by affecting both the supply of copper and the value of the Chilean peso.", "created": 1696696889020, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10523/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-6fb7b1eef53cd143", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:SWPT] Bank reserves are a great barometer of liquidity in the system. In a Reverse Repo transactions: The counterparty pays the Fed X million in reserve balances (The cash transferred by participants to the Fed coming out of the bank reserve balance with the FED effectively reduces the amount of reserves in the banking system, impacting the level of liquidity in the financial markets 'draining liquidity') So we have X million in Cash transfered from the banks reserves to the FED reserves which will knee cap its lending operation by 10 times that amount bcs of the fractional reserve lending requirement  which will drain liquidity out of the system. In a Repo transaction: A bank sells $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities to the Fed in exchange for x million in cash. So the FED credit the Bank reserve balance with  x Million in cash. So now the bank have X million more on its reserve balance which will increase its lending capacity by 10 times bcs of the fractional reserve requirement lending which will increase liquidity in the system. SWAPS : FED and a foreign central bank exchanging currencies. This allows a foreign central bank to obtain U.S. dollars from the Fed in exchange for an equivalent amount of its own currency, based on the market exchange rate at the time of the transaction. And that foreign central banks will chaneel those US dollars to its local banks. So SWaps increase US dollar holdings the Eurodollar banks therefore increasing liquidity in the Eurodollar system. When Fed sells securities in an RRP, it injects reserves into the banking system. When the New York Fed repurchases the securities, it drains reserves from the banking system. So by the FED controlling banks reserves either by REPO or Reverse REPO it can control liquidity in the system.", "created": 1696640178674, "pinned": false}

In a Repo transaction: A bank sells $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities to the Fed in exchange for x million in cash. So the FED credit the Bank reserve balance with  x Million in cash. So now the bank have X million more on its reserve balance which will increase its lending capacity by 10 times bcs of the fractional reserve requirement lending which will increase liquidity in the system. SWAPS : FED and a foreign central bank exchanging currencies. This allows a foreign central bank to obtain U.S. dollars from the Fed in exchange for an equivalent amount of its own currency, based on the market exchange rate at the time of the transaction. And that foreign central banks will chaneel those US dollars to its local banks. So SWaps increase US dollar holdings the Eurodollar banks therefore increasing liquidity in the Eurodollar system. When Fed sells securities in an RRP, it injects reserves into the banking system. When the New York Fed repurchases the securities, it drains reserves from the banking system. So by the FED controlling banks reserves either by REPO or Reverse REPO it can control liquidity in the system.", "created": 1696640082976, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-c3a89f9284325773", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:RPONTTLD] A repurchase agreement (repo) transaction with the Fed works as follows: A counterparty, such as a bank or other financial institution in need of short-term funds approaches the Federal Reserve and sells a security to the Fed in exchange for cash. The counterparty agrees to repurchase the security from the Fed at a specified price and time in the future, typically overnight or for a few days. The Fed holds the security as collateral for the loan. Repo transactions are a common way for banks and other financial institutions to borrow cash from the Fed on a short-term basis. They are also used by the Fed to manage the supply of money in the banking system and to implement monetary policy. Here is an example of a repo transaction with the Fed: 1-A bank sells $1 million in U.S. Treasury securities to the Fed in exchange for $1 million in cash. 2-The bank agrees to repurchase the securities from the Fed at the same price the next day. 3-The Fed holds the securities as collateral for the loan. 4-The bank can use the cash from the repo transaction to lend to its customers or to invest in other assets. The Fed can use the repo transaction to inject money into the banking system and to lower short-term interest rates.\r\nThe Fed also conducts reverse repo transactions, in which it sells securities to counterparties with an agreement to repurchase them at a later date. Reverse repo transactions are used to drain money from the banking system and to raise short-term interest rates.\r\n*Interest**: The interest rate in a repo transaction is called the repo rate. It represents the cost of borrowing for the financial institution. The difference between the sale price of the collateral and its repurchase price at maturity is effectively the interest paid by the institution to the Fed.\r\nRepo transactions with the Fed are typically conducted through the New York Fed's Open Market Trading Desk. The Desk is responsible for implementing the monetary policy decisions of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).\r\nRepo transactions with the Fed are a safe and efficient way for banks and other financial institutions to borrow cash and for the Fed to manage the money supply.", "created": 1696636547356, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-221f6f08f2d7242c", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:FEDFUNDS] How do Fed raising rates dries liquidity out of and wrecks the Eurodollar system? The swap rate is calculated as the difference between the interest rates on one currency and another. For example, if the USD interest rate is 3% and the EUR interest rate is 2%, then the USD/EUR swap rate will be 1%. So when Fed hike interest rates to 5% if Eur interest rate is still 2%,\r\nNow the new USD/EUR swap rate will be 3% (it tripeled it went up 300%), and the same thing would work the other way around FED cutting rate would inject liquidity into fx swaps and eurodollar system.", "created": 1696087117473, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-77fde0b56e2b5a23", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] Why the Eurodollar system just keep growing? When dollar pulls back many countries ,banks and corps in the Eurodollar system borrow evem more US Dollar debt, they dont take the dollar pull back as an opportunity to pay down their existing dollar debt but in the contrary they took on even more new US dollar debt. And the reason why ROW entities took even more dollar debt bcs there is so much global demand for dollars (the global system is structurally short on dollars) AND even more importantly if they borrow in dollars they would get a lower rate for ex: if they borrow in dollars they would borrow at 5% but if they borrow in turkish lira they would borrow at 30% (Fed funds rate in US is 5%, turkey interest rate is 30%) and even more importantly they can borrow at even a cheaper rate through the FX swaps mechanisms (borrowing through FX swaps mechanism would be 1% and they can just pay a fee to roll it over).", "created": 1696086237837, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10561/12122  ---

And the reason why ROW entities took even more dollar debt bcs there is so much global demand for dollars (the global system is structurally short on dollars) AND even more importantly if they borrow in dollars they would get a lower rate for ex: if they borrow in dollars they would borrow at 5% but if they borrow in turkish lira they would borrow at 30% (Fed funds rate in US is 5%, turkey interest rate is 30%) and even more importantly they can borrow at even a cheaper rate through the FX swaps mechanisms (borrowing through FX swaps mechanism would be 1% and they can just pay a fee to roll it over).", "created": 1696086211884, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-78498fc30dbe648d", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:JPLG] FX swaps and Carry trade are the two mechanisms that keeps global liquidity for financing and investment flowing in the Eurodollar system, they act as the Oil pump that keep greasing the Eurodollar system without them liquidity would dry up real quick in the Eurodollar system and the Eurodollar system could come to a complete stop. Interest rate rising too much too fast (interest rate volatility) and funding currency pumping (currency of entity originating the loan) are the two reasons why carry trade and Fx swaps blow up causing a massive position unwinding and derivatives liquidation cascade in the system. Carry trade can be monitored through interest rate differential (in japan carry trade for ex: JP02Y-Us02Y) and watching currency pairs (jpy/usd), FX swaps cant be monitoried bcs they are kept off the balance sheet.", "created": 1695945953441, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-66113d5ed1f6f083", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:JPLG] Even though different FX Swaps and global derivatives carry the same Risk as a US Dollar carry trade bcs when DXY pump or interest rate go up that blows up that FX swaps position exactly as in the carry trade and that cause liquidity to evaporate and dry out from the entire eurodollar system. This is how an FX swap transaction is done: A US Bank borrow dollars from money market fund lets say at 1% and lend it to a japenese bank at 2% (the japenese bank would give YEN collateral to the US bank to hold for the length for the loan not bcs the US bank needs it but just as a form of security, the US bank would take that yen and pledge it as a collateral for derivatives or at least invest it in japenese gov bond to earn a yield while its holding that yen for the term of the loan ) Since japenese banks like to borrow in long term , what the US dealer banks would do is borrow in short term and lend in long term so they just borrow in short term and rollover into long term (lets say US dealer bank lend $10,000 to a japanese bank for 3 years term: US banks would from money markets or other source for 1 years and then at the end of that 1 year they would either roll that loan over or pay off that loan and borrow another loan and the end of of year 2 again they would either roll over that loan or pay off that loan and borrow another loan thats how they make up the 3 year loan basically by obtaining 3 one year loans and just rolling them over). But by doing so they are carrying a longetivity and currency Risk. Bcs if they borrow the first year at 1% and lent at 2% for 3 years, when its time to rollver the loan or get a new loan at the beginning of year 2 if interest rate went up to 4% now the US dealer bank have a HUGE PROBLEM BCS THEY LENT AT 2% so now they are 2% under water for that loan so basically the interest rate going up blew up that FX SWAp. Also currency risks pose a threat to FX swaps bcs if they borrow dollar and lend dollars and were given yen to hold as a collateral, as dollar go up and yen dumps now the amount of yen the hold for collateral is worth A LOT less than the value of the dollar they lent out, so if that trade was to blow up the amount they would be recouping is gonna be worth a lot less than what they lent out leaving them with Big losses , even if everything goes as planned and the trade doesnt blow up since the amount of yen the hold as collateral would be worth a lot less th

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-9a1d196589f72da0", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] The global financial system and the global economy were built on a weak Dollar and a low US interest rate , a strong dollar and high US interest rate wrecks it.China Real estate problem: Most of China real estate companies debt is denominated in dollar. AS china revenue drops significantly in yuan. And as yuan dump and dollar pumps.  They are just triple Fucked: a dropping revenue in yuan in bad and when yuan is depreciating that means those little revenues generated are worth less in dollar terms, and in times when dollar is pumping that means it would take a lot more yuan to service that dollar denominated debt, and lets remember the fact that their revenue dumped in yuan dumped. So now they only have a small amount of yuan to service a ballooning dollar debt. So they are Triple Fucked. To put it in perspective we can use the example: lets say you own a business and you have a mortgage for that commercial property and a car payment for a car used in business and all of that was financied with a variable interest rate and every month the interest rate goes up by 10% while you business revenue is decreasing by 10%. How long is that business gonna survive? Not long. you are getting fucked and your troubles are getting bigger by 20% every month. This is a great illustration of DXY pumping while local currency dumping in times of a global slow down does to businesses which will cause biz to go bust and cant pay their debt. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-cfe58424a54a7d04", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:TWEXPYY] Manufacturing tends to lead, Weakness show up in Manufacturing first then spread out to other sectors. If there is fewer New orders then of course the manufacturing sector is going to slow down. New orders contracting is the first sign of future trouble in Manufacturing. And then the other important one is backlogs. When New orders slow down Manufacturers ask employees to go work on backlogs and the problem is if Manufacturing work through the backlogs and there isnt no new orders then Manufacturing sector start laying people off bcs they dont have no work for them which increase unemployment which going to cause a slow down in spending (when people lose their jobs they spend less) and thats going to outflow to the services sector it doesnt go the other way around it just doesnt happen that way.", "created": 1695655193595, "pinned": false}

If there is fewer New orders then of course the manufacturing sector is going to slow down. New orders contracting is the first sign of future trouble in Manufacturing. And then the other important one is backlogs. When New orders slow down Manufacturers ask employees to go work on backlogs and the problem is if Manufacturing work through the backlogs and there isnt no new orders then Manufacturing sector start laying people off bcs they dont have no work for them which increase unemployment which going to cause a slow down in spending (when people lose their jobs they spend less) and thats going to outflow to the services sector it doesnt go the other way around it just doesnt happen that way.", "created": 1695654676268, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-741683dda1183870", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:RBUSBIS] The Global system (global economy, global trade and global finance) was built on a weak Dollar. For the global economy to continue running and for the system to continue functioning you need a weak dollar. A strong Dollar just wrecks it. The worst case for the Dollar for it to fall is when we witness global growth, Europe is growing, China is growing, EM are growing, ROw is growing. Bcs if the world gets into a deflationary spiral then the US treasury would spike and treasury yield would collapse bcs the whole world is scrambling for collateral and want to put their hands on treasuries at any price thats bullish for the dollar and pump the dollar , Also in times of high inflation , us treasury prices would fall , the fed would need to raise rates more to fight inflation which would be bullish and pump the dollar and make the other countries less attractive bcs global investors would be getting paid to keep the dollar that they need for trade, financing and eurodollar loans anyway. All global central banks coordination and intervention has been done in an effort to weaken the dollar, they have never got together and said we need to strengthen the dollar, its always the dollar has gotten really strong we need to add liquidity to get the dollar lower. All the QE programs were designed to weaken the US Dollar, helicopter money is designed to increase US Dollar liquidity, the plaza accord was done to decrease the value of the dollar, the Shanghai Accord was designed to decrease the value of the dollar, All the emergency programs set up during covid they were designed to weaken the dollar and despite all of those programs, despite everything they have thrown at it the DXY is still at 105 and has risen dramatically versus a number of other global currencies. \r\n\r\nYou just can't get your Global macro view right if you get your dollar view wrong. The dollar is the single most important variable when constructing a portfolio. If you get your dollar view wrong that would be just devastating for your portfolio.", "created": 1695306173790, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10665/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

All global central banks coordination and intervention has been done in an effort to weaken the dollar, they have never got together and said we need to strengthen the dollar, its always the dollar has gotten really strong we need to add liquidity to get the dollar lower. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-8373f3bad52f05f4", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:JSGW] The united states can either pump and drain global liquidity either directly through QE and QT but it can also either pump or drain global liquidity indirectly. First thats by Fed hiking or cutting rates : fed hiking rates drain global liquidity BIG time bcs it pumps the Dollar causing capital flight into the Dollar ( global investors needs dollars anyway for trade and loan payments so why not get paid while holding it especially when everything is shit everywhere else and all the other currencies are dumping). Also, The vast majority of European banks and ROW banks rely on bank loans to fund themselves so when FED hikes rate that force other central bank to hike rates or else they would face a capital flight bcs of rate differential so now European and ROW companies are double squeezed : one bcs their central banks raise rates which means the loans they would be obtain from the bank to fund themselves have to be at the high rate and also the fed hiking rates means all their Eurodollar loans now have a higher rate as well and the dollar pumped which means they would need a lot more of their local currency to convert to dollar to pay off their Eurodollar loans. So they are Fucked , its literally triple trouble. Also when FED hikes rates the treauries foreign govs hold now worth less, they worth maybe 25% to 30% less than when them foreign gov bought them. And since the entire global financial system is pyramided in top of treasuries, and not taking into account leverage, and not taking into account that DXY would squeeze their revenue and increase their input which would squeeze them and just deplete their foreign exchange reserves (savings), just the fact that their treasuries are now worth 25% to 30% less means the credit they can obtain in the global market would decrease by 25% to 30% AT LEAST (since they would have to pledge treasuries as collateral to get credit and financing) And all this in an environment of scarce US treasuries to start with, US treasury auction have been oversubscribed by two and half times which means the demand for Us treasuries is two times and half more than the supply and since everything is pyramided in top of US treasuries in times of low liquidity its really really hard to put ur hand on treasuries bcs and all the sudden poof they just disappear. So when they have to pledge US treasuries as a collateral to finance new positions or to pledge more Us treasurie

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-dda1b73707ab4393", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:BTPBUND] There is a relation between a countrys bond market and its currency and the last thing any country wants to see is that the rate that they have to pay on their sovereign bonds to be spiking bcs often that's a sign of distress or people wanting to get paid more to hold a potentially defaulty bond but it is different when the US does it than when ROW does it thats bcs the USA is the global Reserve currency and as the system is designed now if you operate on the global stage you have to have dollars to do it. in 2023 the USA purposefully raising interest rates, they are purposefully tightening policy they want interest rates to go up and stay higher for longer (FED chairman jerome powell has been saying this all year in 2023) so the idea that the yield on us treasuries is going up a lot is a signal that the ROW is rejecting the dollar and rejecting and boycotting us treasuries is just not true. Historically there is two and half times the amount of demand as there is supply for every US treasury auction. While in other countries when yield spike thats an indication that you dont want to hold that currency bcs there is counterpary risk (bond might default) but on the contrary in the USA and bcs there is so much demand for the US dollar and people have to use it for global trade and to borrow and pay off loans in the eurodollar system wether they want to or not . The fact that now they get paid more to hold the US Dollar is like and added bonus and thats part of the reason why the dollar has remained strong in 2023.", "created": 1695223462962, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-e7ed9c59e9bc2803", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:MOVE] Every Us treasury auctions has been oversubscribed meaning there is more demand than the supply the treasury is auctioning off. Historically there is two and half times the amount of demand as there is supply for every US treasury auction.\r\n\r\nWhen countries around the world get their dollars surpluses from their trading with the united states they either turn around and save those in t-bills or medium term us bonds or long term us bonds, that is the method by which their hold their dollar surpluses and so if they get paid more to hold dollar which they already need than they hold Euro or yen or yuan which they dont really need. They are gonna go with the dollar that they need and that pays them more (bcs of higher bond yields) and so capital flows into the dollar and it keeps it relatively strong vs other currencies.", "created": 1695223428744, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-398e982b8a84b94e", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:BND] The Eurozone ALWAYS feels interest rate hikes A LOT more than USA. Hiking too interest rates too much too fast just kills Europe due to :\r\n1- Europe Companies heavy reliance on bank loans for funding ( 80% of european companies rely on bank loans for funding vs 19% in united states). So while 80% of european companies come from bank loans, only 18% of European Companies raise funds through the bond markets ( 8% rated A and Above, 8% rated BBB and above, 2% High Yield Bonds) and 2% of the funding comes from institutional leveraged loans. Meanwhile only 19% of american companies get their funding through bank loans while 70% of American companies raise funds in the bond market (28% rated A and Above, 28% rated BBB and above , 11% High yield Bonds) and 10% of of funding comes from institutional leveraged loans.\r\n2- Europe Heavier Refinancing cliff hitting Quicker and harder due to Europe large number of variable rate mortgages, corporate bonds and loans.", "created": 1695157052363, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-ed407a63bc45a79b", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:CLTOT] Terms of trade is an economic concept that refers to the relative value or exchange rate between a country's exports and imports. It measures the ratio of the average price a country receives for its exports to the average price it pays for its imports. In other words, it assesses how many units of a country's exports are needed to purchase a given quantity of its imports.\r\n\r\nThe formula for calculating the terms of trade is:\r\nTerms of Trade = (Export Price Index) / (Import Price Index)", "created": 1695152543062, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10743/12122  ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-8338b17adfe863ea", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:CLBOT] Chile plays an important role in the Eurodollar Market through its Global Copper Financing Mechanisms. Chile plays a significant role in financing global copper purchases due to its status as the world's leading copper producer. The country's economy is heavily dependent on copper exports, and it has a well-established mining industry. Chili Global Copper Financing Mechanisms: To facilitate copper exports, Chile may employ various financing mechanisms. These could include trade agreements, contracts, and financing arrangements with international buyers and trading partners. Financing arrangements may involve credit terms, prepayments, or hedging strategies to manage price volatility.", "created": 1695151723747, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-6b2566d4ef7b59b3", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:ELD] How can the FED directly influence DXY and push global investor into embracing the dollar which will pump DXY? when the fed hikes rates which will attract immense portion of global investors into the dollar for the simple fact that they use dollars anyway for trades so they might as well get paid in treasury yields while holding it (bcs they can always sell they treasuries to get us dollars), also when FED hikes interest rate too much too fast this volatility Dumps the bond market (treasuries are what all other collateral is pyramed in top of) which will makes global investors run into safety which is running into DXY ( Global Risk off) which will Dump all assets and pump DXY (global investors sell all other assets to buy DXY).\r\n\r\nAnd A global Bond market sell off will cause a global Risk off, volatility in the very highly levered bond market will cause Chaos and Dump in the bond market which will push investors to develerage and Risk off whihc will dump Bond aggregates and PUMP DXY.", "created": 1694899196118, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-c1b209891274f5ab", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:GB30Y] The British Gilt crisis, the biggest DUMP in the british bond market in 240 years: Once elected British PM proposed to cut taxes and reduce regulations to try to spur economic growth and to make ends meet UK would just borrow more money. But the issue the UK had 10% inflation and inflation was expected to hit 13 to 15% or even higher, in this high inflation environment UK prime minister decided that she is going to supercharge the economy with a ton of stimulus well hell inflation then is gonna go to 20%. The fear in the british market was that what she is proposing is actually going to work and its going to create tons of stimulus and a ton of inflation. So the uk bond market and the British pound imploded on themselves bcs if they going to stimulate a 10% inflationary environment investors dont want anything to do with their currency or with their bond market so they gov yield went up and their currency fell. \r\nLets remember the bond market is owned by a bunch of levered players so when the bond market price is tanking, the gov yields are soaring 3,4, it even got to 5% on the 30 year.\r\nBond investors were just getting killed bcs they were owning bonds on leverage. Things got sooo bad in the market that there was a real fear, At 2 pm london they got a tap on the shoulder from BlackRock that said we are not gonna price our liability duration instruments any more bcs we just cant (they are leveraging vehicles as well) and they just realized whats gonna happen at 4 oclock is a bunch of firms are gonna come out and say that they are under regulatory capital and like a lot of other financial firms we borrow every day in the overnight market in order to fund ourselves and when black rock announce that they are not gonna price their liability duration instruments any more, those financial firms are just not gonna get funding.\r\nAnd what did we learn in 2008 you can be solvent and viable and 10 minutes later you are JUST DONE. so what did the bank of England do? they just announced QT a week prior, they reversed it and bought a whole bunch of bonds to Ram up the price way up so that when these firms mark their price they are not below capital requirements.", "created": 1694879534785, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-d62447ad56e19069", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:AGG] How do Gov Bond investors leverage work? And why would anyone do it? The bond market is a highly levered market, If you are a sophisticated financial institutions you can trade treasuries and gov bonds on a 100% leverage.So they buy $100 Million worth of bonds and they have no money (they just pick up the phone and call a dealer and they will get those bonds without putting no collateral) once receiving the bonds institutions pledge those $100 Million of bonds in the Repo market and they get an overnight loan to pay off those gov bonds and they just keep rolling that loan every day. So the bond market has tremendous leverage in it and it has always had that and thats why the bond market has always been unstable over the years. \r\nif you buy $100M of bonds and finance the whole $100M and the price falls 10 points to $90M you are $10M underwater so you need to come up with $10M RIGHT NOW to pledge as a collateral so you keep your position from getting liquidated. So how do you come up with with? you have other bonds that you own outright that arent being financed so you pledge those bonds as more collateral in order to keep your position from getting liquidated.", "created": 1694879291524, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-76b165051123cb93", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:AMEX:AGG] How do Gov Bond investors leverage work? And why would anyone do it? - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-d5af5854f0f75d8c", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:FEDFUNDS] The problem with the bond market is that it can crowd up. when the fed wants to sell that extra slack of treasuries every month. well whos gonna buy it at the time when the bond market is crowded? well somebody will. but how? well the fed will just lower the price by keep raising the interest rate until they suck the money out of somebody else to get that extra slack funded  (by finding a buyer for that extra slack). - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-270852d2c89e307d", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:US10Y] The bond market is 100 times bigger than the stock market. Something else people dont realize about the bond market: How much money do you need to manage a billion dollars in the bond market? None its all leverage, you can leverage the bond market to infinity, you can call Goldman sachs and say hi Im jim bianco i would like to buy a billion dollars worth of bonds. they would say: oh you jim Done. Do bond investors need more than a dollar? No not necessarily its all leverage. In the Equity market you need at least half a billion dollar to buy a billion dollar worth of stocks. so there is a lot of leverage in the bond market. \r\n25% of the entire bond market is held by the fed , before the financial crisis 2008 the Fed held between 8% to 10% and was in the high 10s pre covid, and after the Fed did that enoumous purchases in covid in march and april of 2020 going into 2021 they shot their holding into the mid 20s. At the global stage, bank of japan owns half of their bond market, Global center banks hold on average somewhere in the low 30% range of their bond markets. Its the fact that central banks hold so much of their bond markets that makes the market very attentive to what they say. Central banks are the new bond kings   \r\n\r\nWhen bond yields just explode (PUMP) means that somebody was on a 120% leverage, was caught at the wrong side of the trade, just got liquidated and the dealer had to close his position.\r\nAnd thats the reason people dont understand why the bond market is sooo volatile. its bcs of very high leverage in the bond market and the fact that it doesnt cost any money to leverage the bond market unlike stocks where you have to put at least 50% to leverage it. \r\n\r\nThe metric that bond investors use is Total Return that is the coupon that you get plus the price change. 2022 was the worst year in the recorded history, it was a disaster for the bond market largely bcs not only did the prices go down but also you had no coupon cushion to start the year 2023 is different bcs bonds have a 5% coupon so if prices go down 5% and you are getting a 5% coupon you just end up with a 0 return but no loss. but in 2022 and bcs the coupon was 0% if prices went down 5% then investors ended up with a 5% loss.", "created": 1694799835885, "pinned": false}

Central banks are the new bond kings   \r\n\r\nWhen bond yields just explode (PUMP) means that somebody was on a 120% leverage, was caught at the wrong side of the trade, just got liquidated and the dealer had to close his position.\r\nAnd thats the reason people dont understand why the bond market is sooo volatile. its bcs of very high leverage in the bond market and the fact that it doesnt cost any money to leverage the bond market unlike stocks where you have to put at least 50% to leverage it. \r\n\r\nThe metric that bond investors use is Total Return that is the coupon that you get plus the price change. 2022 was the worst year in the recorded history, it was a disaster for the bond market largely bcs not only did the prices go down but also you had no coupon cushion to start the year 2023 is different bcs bonds have a 5% coupon so if prices go down 5% and you are getting a 5% coupon you just end up with a 0 return but no loss. but in 2022 and bcs the coupon was 0% if prices went down 5% then investors ended up with a 5% loss.", "created": 1694798025402, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-1082ef67e4b72b2d", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:DXY] When the US dramatically increase rates and dramatically tightens monetary policy that push the dollar HIGHER and the rest of the world currencies LOWER which puts ROW countries in crisis.\r\nThe dollar pumping against ROW countries brings disinflationary pressure to the US (bcs it makes imports cheaper) and inflationary pressure to ROW ( makes their imports more expensive).\r\nThe US can print dollar with the snap of a finger but the ROW cant, so the US doesnt and will never have the dollar supply problem but the ROW does. Thats an ENORMOUS advantage for the US that gives it an immense influence over the global trade , the global economy and the global financial system. Bcs of the dollar printing ability and by controlling dollar supply to the ROW either by printing or central banks policy and by monetary policy and the issuance of treasuries, the US can determine what happens to the global trade, global economy, and the global financial system. Only the US can print dollars and only the Us can issue treasuries and since the US treasuries are the main collateral used in the EuroDollar and the global financial system and since the global trades are conducted in US Dollars thats why only the US can replenish the EURODOLLAR system when it comes to a complete stop. ROW slow growth or a declined growth and contraction which contracts lending and increase defaults destroying money supply is what brings the EURODOLLAR system to a complete stop.", "created": 1694714569379, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-a4f9712afbd4df53", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:SPX] people say higher interest rates are bad for stocks, as soon as interest rates start going up you should sell stocks but the reality is the S&P500 went up during everyone of those hiking cycles. Now it didnt go up a lot and a lot of times it ALWAYS went up kinda of AT THE END bcs people were anticipating a FED pivot and rate cuts were coming soon. But at every single rate hike stocks only went PUMPED after a DUMP, so once the fed start hiking stocks DUMP and then they would recover toward the end of the hiking cycle as the market anticipate a fed pivot.\r\nAnd While bonds were getting crushed during fed hikes stocks actually either stayed flat or went higher in all the previous fed rate hikes. For ex: between 1977 to 1981 fed hiked rates from 5.5% to 20% so fed fund rate had a growth rate of 290%  , the logn term bonds dumped 35% while stocks went up 30%. between 2015 and 2018 fed hiked rates from 0.25% to 2.5% a rate growth of 900% long term bond dumped 15% while S&P went up 30%. Between 2022 and 2023 fed hiked from 0.25% to 5.50% a fed fund growth rate of 2000% long term bonds dumped by 35% while stocks intially dumped 25% they recovered and end up only down 5% by the end of 2023.", "created": 1694714472773, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-07b82b9c7b16ede1", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:FEDFUNDS] By hiking rates the fed are depressing the price of us treasuries which are a HUGE source of collateral off of which new loans are made and for leverage. so a lower treasury prices means a lower credit and lower leverage in the system. so when FED raise rates to Dump the price of treasuries, they are devaluing the amount of collateral in the system and therefore they are restricting the amount of new loans that can be pyramided in top of that collateral winding down leverage in the system and contracting credit in the system which will choke the economy and financial market which will result in slow growth which will entame inflation which was the FED goal from the getgo of hiking rates.", "created": 1694708690264, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22` --- note 10826/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-be0d023ed3f7b197", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:SPX] Technical indicators: are nothing more than expressions of filters so a technical indicator is nothing more than a filter that tries to get rid of noise, some of them are lagging and some of them try to be forward looking by looking at turning points in the market. The question you have to ask yourself is not whats the magic behind this filter but how persistent is the behavior in the market that will allow you to apply the filter so what you tend to find is that certain types of indicators are very good when the market is quiet when we dont expect a lot of news announcements to come bcs the one thing that shocks the market is news that then creates policy shifts and anticipation about the future as as long as your are okay with applying these things during periods where you dont expect big shocks then yes technical indicators should work just fine.\r\na lot of technical indicators are nothing more than adding a whole bunch of numbers together and dividing them by something. A moving Average is nothing more than expression of of Momentum so MA 20 is add the last 20 price numbers together and divide by 20. RSI: look at the positive returns then look at the negative returns to the average then divide one by the other.\r\nIs it necessary to use technical indicators when you trading? Absolutely Not, they are just a filter to filter out noise when applying macro trends. Technical indicators along chart patterns they are more to serve as tool to timing the market in the short term (over a day period or even a week), to time entries and exits but Macro is the king that rules.\r\nWhats the difference between an indicator and a strategy? An indicator is a component of a trading strategy so its an input that will cause a particular bias in the market but that bias is usually used in a binary way: buy or sell but its more important than that its about how much do you buy how much do you sell and ultimately when do you get out and how do you protect of i you look at a portfolio view you have indicators per asset that then have to be combined for instance it could be that in one indicator your have less confidence and then you look at another indicator and then you weigh them appropriately. So an indicator is about allowing you to create a bias about the future while a strategy about combining these strategies into a trading view.", "created": 1694524492408, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10827/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-5a5331256ac45d20", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:JPINTR] Here are some of the currencies commonly used in carry trade strategies: 1-Japanese Yen (JPY): The Japanese yen has historically been a popular currency for carry trades due to Japan's long-standing low-interest rate policy. Traders often borrow yen at low rates and invest in higher-yielding currencies.\r\n2-Swiss Franc (CHF): The Swiss franc has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Switzerland's traditionally low-interest rates. 3- Taiwan New Dollar (TWD):  The Taiwan New Dollar has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Taiwan traditionally low-interest rates\r\n4-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar is frequently used as a funding currency in carry trades, especially when interest rates in the United States are low, as it provides access to a wide range of higher-yielding currencies. 4-Australian Dollar (AUD): The Australian dollar is a popular target currency for carry trades because of Australia's relatively high-interest rates compared to other developed economies. 5-New Zealand Dollar (NZD): Similar to the Australian dollar, the New Zealand dollar is often used in carry trades due to New Zealand's comparatively high-interest rates. 6-Euro (EUR): The euro can be involved in carry trades, especially when there is a significant interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, making it an attractive target for investors. 7-British Pound (GBP): The British pound can also be part of carry trade strategies, with traders borrowing in currencies like the Japanese yen or Swiss franc and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in GBP.", "created": 1694391916495, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10866/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-dea4698b9747cfdb", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] What is the carry trade? Some countries have higher interest rates than others and so its natural to want to invest in those higher interest rate countries. For ex: in the 90s a favorite carry trade was buying dollars and selling yen so it meant borrowing in yen where the interest rate was close to 0 and then investing in dollars where you were getting 5%. Well that just sounds great. Well its great as long as the currency is moving to ur advantage or holding still. Bcs there are two components to the carry trade: the interest rate differential but there is also the move in the currency so you want the currency to move in your favor as well so for instance lets look at the dollar/yen: if you buy dollar yen you are earning 5% a year then you are hoping that dollar will appreciate against the yen as well so you will be double dipping and you get a double whammy and thats really what the carry trade does. The carry trade says or postulates that the higher interest rate currency will actually attract investors which will make the currency move in your favor and you are going to double whammy on the market move as well as the interest rate which is much higher than the currency that you are selling effectively borrowing against. The carry trade works however the carry trade is a macro expression that the world is benign, when the world goes pear-shaped carry trades get unwound heavily and a nice example is 1998 as well as 2007. in 1998 people had to unwind dollar yen bcs they were incurring losses and getting liquidated on a lot of other positions primarily driven by the Russian default. In October 1998 Dollar yen more or less within a day managed to move from 120 to 104 or lower so there are 17 big figures in a day where sometimes price just gapped. This is like a 17% move on the currency in one day which is virtually unheard of and there was blood on the street on this and people lost Billions of dollars on this. So when you have these massive global shocks carry trades get affected and so in 2007 you had a very similar situation, there was already the flare up into the great financial crisis, the credit crunch that we saw and what happened in August of 2007 was again that the yen crosses bcs again yen was at the time a favorite funding currency meaning a currency with low interest rate that allows me to borrow in yen and invest in higher yielding currencies those yen crosses got heavily un
- `18:08:22` --- note 10871/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---
- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-79346a3ef83a9068", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] whats The easiest way to trade currencies? Currencies are traded by looking at the 3 Month time frame. you just look at the currency index today versus 3 months ago if its positive you buy, if its negative you sell it. This is called Momentum and we know that Momentum has been very very successful in a lot of markets thats why you have trend following hedge funds like winton and Aspect and a whole bunch of others having Billions of Dollars in this type of strategies. So what happens if you apply this very simple momentum startegy to currency indices?\r\nTrading currency indices over the last 40 years on this very simple 3 months momentum more or less generated you the same return as the S&P 500 returns. In terms of portfolio Construction we need to think about how does this currency index trading compare to other assets. in 2008 during the great financial crisis whereas the S&P went bust , the funding currency japenese yen and Dxy trade went up. So you will be making money on currencies while you are loosing money on the S&P 500 which gives you a great hedge and offers stability to your portfolio. \r\n3 Months Momentum is a very easy to trade its not rocket science and has been working perfectly for 40 years, its the idea to find uncorrelated signals to put them together to construct your portfolio to give you stability. People Always say I dont wanna swing too much but the truth is you dont want to risk too much so that you can actually really leverage thats how you end up making 80% to 100% a year.", "created": 1694377261084, "pinned": false}
- `18:08:22` --- note 10872/12122 >>> MACRO/RISK-RELEVANT <<< ---

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-2527f06e1640be66", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] As long as the funding country (Japan or switzerland) pin down yields and keep manipulating to stay low at certain determined range (which will keep devaluing the currency) and as long as the funding currency is stable or depreciating. And As long as the country where the carry trade is invested hikes rates or keep them stable (just not suddenly cutting them creating volatility) and the currency of the country where the carry trade is invested is stable or appreciating then the carry trade is profitable and will be leverade and used to invest in Risk assets around the globe providing them with liquidity causing Global Risk assets to PUMP. A wind down and Dumping of the carry trade will drain liquidity injected into Global Risk Assets causing them to DUMP.", "created": 1694189277641, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-4430d2235e0d96cc", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] The biggest enemy of a levered carry trader is YIELD VOLATILITY, carry traders dont want yields on either side to SWING AROUND, they just want them to STAY STILL and that way they can just maintain their yield spread especially if they are using leverage. the narrow of the yield carry trade: either by the yield of the borrowing currency go up or by the yield on the invested currency going down would cause a levered carry trader to get liquidated thats why YIELD volatility cause carry trader to get liquidated which unwind their positions which DUMP RISK assets around the globe.", "created": 1694183228956, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-904b3a9a8f7572b2", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] A carry trade is basically when you sell or borrow with or fund with a low yielding currency like the yen and you buy a relatively higher yielding currency like the Aussie Dollar. By doing so you are capturing the yield differentials between AUD rates and JPY rates and bcs yen rates are always like on the floor perpetually for many decades, yen has been used as the go to cheap funding currency. So the thing is Carry traders of course they want a juicy yield spread and so a global QE environment provides no such yield differentials indeed but what carry traders REALLY want or rather what THE ENEMY of a levered carry trader is : Yield Volatility bcs if you are long Aussie yen carry trade and capturing that yield spread on leverage, things are great as long as that yield spread either stays static from when you open the trade or if it widens BUT if the Aussie to JGB yield spread were to COMPRESS either bcs JGB yields go up or Aussie yields pull down causing that yield differential to narrows then carry traders accounts gets debited by the broker and if they are on a lot of leverage their positions gets liquidated. Thats why the biggest enemy of a levered carry trader is YIELD VOLATILITY, carry traders dont want yields on either side to SWING AROUND, they just want them to STAY STILL and that way they can just maintain their yield spread especially if they are using leverage.\r\nHere are some of the currencies commonly used in carry trade strategies: 1-Japanese Yen (JPY): The Japanese yen has historically been a popular currency for carry trades due to Japan's long-standing low-interest rate policy. - `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-3b27219d27fe4b56", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] Aussie yen AUDJPY is a currency pair that sometimes exhibits sort of risk assets price action largely due to its use as a carry trade. A carry trade is basically when you sell or borrow with or fund with a low yielding currency like the yen and you buy a relatively higher yielding currency like the Aussie Dollar. By doing so you are capturing the yield differentials between AUD rates and JPY rates and bcs yen rates are always like on the floor perpetually for many decades, yen has been used as the go to cheap funding currency.  AUDJPY used to be the go to carry trade currency pair, it still is to a certain extent but it really was bcs of the fact that japan yields were on the floor and Aussie rates yielded several points higher. So what happens every trading day that investors have a positive carry trade (positive yield spread) they get their trading account credited, so what traders would do is to go long the AUD/JPY carry trade and use leverage and by using leverage it juices up your carry returns and then you use those proceeds to go long Risk assets or anything really. in mid 2000s japan retail massively crowded into the Aussie yen carry trade and much of that found its way into help fuel the subprime CDO Bubble in the US leading up to 2008 and then pre Lehman brothers collapse in like july 2008 the leverage long AUDJPY carry trade saw a face ripping vicious unwind in which AUDJPY basically got cut in half within 3 months. Aussie Dollar got destroyed , yen surged. since then AUDJPY carry trade still be used on and off as a carry trade of choice to fund risk positions such as beling long spx and so therefore AUDJPY and SPX would sometime correlate and correlate very tightly", "created": 1694112196931, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-a2a8c80299b2e2af", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:CH03Y] Carry trade is a trading strategy where investors borrow funds in a currency with a low-interest rate and invest them in a currency with a higher interest rate. The goal is to profit from the interest rate differential between the two currencies. Here are some of the currencies commonly used in carry trade strategies: 1-Japanese Yen (JPY): The Japanese yen has historically been a popular currency for carry trades due to Japan's long-standing low-interest rate policy. Traders often borrow yen at low rates and invest in higher-yielding currencies.\r\n2-Swiss Franc (CHF): The Swiss franc has also been a favored funding currency for carry trades because of Switzerland's traditionally low-interest rates.\r\n3-US Dollar (USD): The US dollar is frequently used as a funding currency in carry trades, especially when interest rates in the United States are low, as it provides access to a wide range of higher-yielding currencies. 4-Australian Dollar (AUD): The Australian dollar is a popular target currency for carry trades because of Australia's relatively high-interest rates compared to other developed economies. 5-New Zealand Dollar (NZD): Similar to the Australian dollar, the New Zealand dollar is often used in carry trades due to New Zealand's comparatively high-interest rates. 6-Euro (EUR): The euro can be involved in carry trades, especially when there is a significant interest rate differential between the eurozone and other currencies, making it an attractive target for investors. 7-British Pound (GBP): The British pound can also be part of carry trade strategies, with traders borrowing in currencies like the Japanese yen or Swiss franc and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in GBP.\r\nIt's essential to note that carry trades involve substantial risk, as exchange rates can fluctuate and erode potential profits. Additionally, market conditions and interest rate differentials can change over time, impacting the attractiveness of specific currencies for carry trade strategies. Traders should carefully assess the current economic and interest rate environment before implementing such strategies.\r\n\r\n\r\nwhat are carry trade funding currencies? Carry trade funding currencies are the currencies that traders typically borrow or sell short as part of a carry trade strategy. These currencies are chosen because they have low-interest rates, making them suitable for borrowing funds at a l

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-5a14ce6e4fdc624e", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:RBUSBIS] The Real Broad Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is a measure used in economics and finance to assess the value of a country's currency in comparison to a basket of other currencies, adjusted for inflation. It is called \"real\" because it takes into account changes in the price levels or inflation rates in different countries. The \"broad\" aspect means that it considers a wide range of trade partners and currencies rather than just a few major trading partners.\r\n\r\nHere's how the calculation generally works:\r\n\r\nNominal Exchange Rate: Start with the nominal exchange rate, which is the current market exchange rate between a country's currency and a basket of foreign currencies.\r\n\r\nInflation Adjustment: Adjust the nominal exchange rate for differences in inflation rates between the home country and its trading partners. This is usually done by dividing the nominal exchange rate by a measure of relative price levels or consumer price indices in the home country and its trading partners.\r\n\r\nTrade Weights: Apply trade weights to the currencies of the trading partners. The weights are typically based on the volume of trade between the home country and its trading partners. This means that currencies of countries with which the home country has a higher volume of trade will have a larger impact on the REER.\r\n\r\nIndex Calculation: Combine all these factors to create an index that reflects the real, inflation-adjusted value of the home country's currency against a basket of foreign currencies.\r\n\r\nThe REER is useful for assessing a country's competitiveness in international trade. If the REER appreciates, it may indicate that a country's goods and services have become more expensive relative to its trading partners, potentially leading to a decrease in exports and an increase in imports. Conversely, if the REER depreciates, it may indicate improved competitiveness in international markets.\r\n\r\nCentral banks, policymakers, and economists often monitor the REER to understand the dynamics of a country's exchange rate and its potential impact on the economy. It helps them make informed decisions about monetary policy, trade policies, and other economic measures.\r\n\r\nIt's important to note that there are variations in the methodology for calculating the REER, and different organizations may use slightly different approaches and data sources. Additionally, the choice of trading

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-2ba362f8209ff5c4", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:UNTAGGED] Google trends shows bitcoin and ethereum and matic and memecoins and uniswap volume on defillama TOP, make sure to choose 2004 to present in time frame.\r\n\r\nTiming is EVERYTHING when it comes to memecoins. Timing is what would dictate if a memecoin would pump 20x (meme season) or 2x (bear market). Google trends and uniswap volume on defillama show meme coins TOP. Its VERY IMPORTANT to sell the entire bag at the TOP bcs after that all u get is a HUGE Drawdown and MEGA DUMPS. \r\nSigns of MEME coins TOP: 1- 24 hour volume succeed the coin marketcap. 3-lower highs in the higher time frame chart 4-Number of holders decrease 5-Growth of holders slow down 6-Large whales start selling 7-funding rate for the coin shifts from negative to positive.\r\n\r\nMost meme coins ONLY survive for one hype cycle other than dogecoin so its not worth it to HODL hoping for another bull market to arrive.", "created": 1693934327652, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-2237d530f2283188", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:DXY] The dollar and currencies around the world is a relative game. You must pay attention not only to Fed actions but also to Other central banks actions and economies around the world especially Europe, Japan and china. From 2014 to 2019 the dollar just went sideways to higher while US interest rate were very close to 0, the FED only did one rate hike in 2015 and one in 2017 and then in 2018 and 2019 they hiked like 3 or 4 times and leading into COVID they were cutting rates and the DXY was still at 102. So the Dollar can go up even when the FED isnt hiking interest rates, the dollar can go up on a risk off environment, the dollar can go up because of what other countries around the world are doing regardless what the FED is doing, the dollar can go up if the world gets into a global financial crisis or a global credit crunch where everbody needs dollars bcs its the currency that underlies the entire global system.  in 2022 the dollar went higher mainly due to rate hikes happening and the perception that rate hikes were going to continue. Once rate hikes stopped rising aggressively and the anticipation for further rate hikes started to fall then the dollar fell slightely, then people started to say now the dollar is really done its going to keep going down and they have totally forgotten that last decade the dollar did very WHERE there were very few to NO rate hikes. So just because the dollar went up in 2022 because of the rate hikes, people assume thats the only thing that cause it to go up but they forget that the dollar can go up for a lot of other different reasons. There are many reasons that can push the dollar higher. The reason the dollar went higher in some of 2023 is the FED remained hawkish backed with some hawkish data that say they are probably gonna hike again in September but ALSO the fact that these other countries are having to slow down their expectations for future rate hikes.  Part of the reason that the dollar did well in july and august 2023 is that the EURO dumped and part of the reason why the EURO pull back is that there's this chatter out of Europe that they are not going to be able to continue to raise interest rates and even if they do they are not going to be able to stay higher for longer as previously anticipated so even if the FED doesnt hike again and even if they start to cut if rates have to be cut quicker in Europe bcs their Economy is contracting even faster

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-095bfffee0070f73", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:KRX] Large Mega cap Companies (Magnificent 7 stocks: Facebook + Apple + Tesla + Nividia + Microsoft + Amazon + Google) dont need banks, they are almost like central banks in and of themselves, they can borrow in capital markets, they have no problem getting financial services, they are entities on their own. These companies can go to the corporate bond market and borrow at rates very close to what the US gov gets. But when you get to the mere mortal companies the other 2993 of the Russell 3000 they need banks, they need financial services, they need money transfer facilities, they need loans, they need a lot of services from banks. This squeeze that we are seeing in banks might be holding back a lot of those other companies which why collectively they only pushed the index 3% Not much more profit than what you would have been in money market funds bcs money market funds are up 2.6% for the year. Unlike the mega companies who can borrow directly from the corp bond market, When the Bottom 1000 or Bottom 1500 companies of the Russell 3000 needs money they have to borrow from the banks and in times when banks are raising their rates bcs of the bank walk those companies have to pay a higher cost for credit which squeezes their profits.\r\nBank create money out of thin air when it hands out a loan, when borrowers go and get a loan like a mortgage the bank open them a deposit account and deposit that mortgage or that loan money into that deposit account bascially creating money out of thin air. Banks are in the business of creating money but they cant do it into infinity bcs Banks have loan to deposit ratio, capital ratios, and lots of regulations and FDIC , Federal Reserve and Office controller of currency metrics to adhere to in order to limit the amount of money that they can create. So when deposits flee banks at the rate they are doing now in 2023 bank walk it severly impacts their ability to generate or create new money and that severely impacts their ability to hand out loans and thats why only the magnificent 7 stocks are doing great in 2023 while the other 2993 companies are struggling, its not only not banks not handing them loans and credit why they are struggling but their conduit for financial services. As bank not in  the greatest profitability position, pain in 2993 companies will keep mounting. So bottom line as long as the bank walk continues the bank stocks will continue to struggle, an

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-e6745cdc31a952a3", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:USCA] People criticize the USA for having a whopping current account deficit and they keep saying well of course this is about the lack of competitiveness of US industry thats just complete BULLSHIT. What it shows you is the SUPER competitiveness of USA finance thats what is really telling you bcs the balance of payments by definition must balance and if you have got a big surplus on your financial side you by definition gonna have a deficit on your manufacturing or trade side and thats exactly whats happening on the USA balance of payments book. What the USA does is that it acts as the banker of the world and thats what the dollar system or the international financial system is, so if the Rest of the world wants to borrow dollars they borrow dollars and the US supplies them US bank supply and if they want to invest their surpluses in US financial markets they can and that works seamlessly as it has done for decades.", "created": 1693449760539, "pinned": false}

- `18:08:22`   {"id": "tv-2c4add103062d71f", "cat": "thesis", "text": "[TV:THREEFYTP1] Term Premium especially on 1 year 0 coupon Bond going negative signals systematic collateral Risk problems, it has prewarned and DUMPED significantly before Every financial crisis. Term premium goes negative when there is a shortage in the coupon supply (shortage of treasury bond and notes supply) either bcs of the debt ceiling or bcs of QT or other Fed reserves actions.\r\nHuge buying pressure of treasuries due to collateral shortage depress the term premium significantly causing it to go negative in extreme dire collateral shortage cases. \r\nThe negative term premium suggests there is a huge EXCESS demand for treasuries (suggests there is EXTRA demand out of the ordinary).", "created": 1693414168490, "pinned": false}
